3.q: Grace, 52, has chronic osteoarthritis pain. She asks how she can manage flare-ups at home alongside her prescribed paracetamol. Which advice is most appropriate to support self-management?
o: Take her husband's leftover codeine tablets for bad days
Double her paracetamol dose on days when the pain is worse
Rest in bed until the pain fully settles after each flare-up
Pace activities and use local heat alongside regular analgesia
3.w: Self-management of long-term pain combines pacing, gentle activity and non-drug measures such as heat with analgesia taken as prescribed (P4.5, P4.8). Medicine doses must not exceed the prescription or licensed maximum.

n.0: Taking medicines prescribed for someone else is unsafe and unlawful for prescription-only medicines.
n.1: Doubling paracetamol risks exceeding the maximum daily dose and liver toxicity.
n.2: Prolonged bed rest worsens stiffness and deconditioning in osteoarthritis.

3.q: A doctor needs to tell Mrs Ibrahim, 70, who speaks Somali and limited English, that her husband has died in intensive care. Her adult niece is with her. What is the most appropriate way to communicate?
o: Wait until her son arrives to translate later that day
Use a professional Somali interpreter for the conversation
Give the news in simple English and check she understands
Ask the niece to interpret, as she is family and will support her
3.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; reliance on family is strongly discouraged. Code 7.2 meet language needs; Annexe A 2.9.

n.0: Delaying the news without reason causes distress; an interpreter can be arranged now.
n.2: Simple English risks misunderstanding when news is this serious.
n.3: Relying on family is discouraged; the niece is also grieving and may filter the news.

3.q: At handover a colleague describes Mrs Evans, 91, who is medically fit for discharge but waiting for a care package, as 'just another bed-blocker'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Challenge the language and refocus on her needs
Laugh it off to keep handover moving quickly
Report the colleague to the NMC after the shift
Raise it at the colleague's appraisal in a few months
3.w: Code 1.1 and 1.3: treat people with respect and avoid assumptions; Code 3.4: challenge poor practice and discriminatory attitudes. Age is a protected characteristic (Equality Act 2010 s4).

n.1: Letting it pass condones an ageist label; Code 3.4 requires discriminatory attitudes to be challenged.
n.2: A first remark is best challenged directly and locally; NMC referral is for serious fitness to practise concerns.
n.3: Waiting months misses the chance to challenge it now and protect Mrs Evans's dignity.

3.q: Leo, 4, weighs 15 kg and is not bleeding. His Hb is 62 g/L. The team aims for a post-transfusion Hb of 90 g/L and uses the BSH formula with a factor of 4: volume (mL) = (desired Hb - actual Hb) x weight x 4 / 10. What volume of red cells should be prescribed?
o: 420 mL
168 mL
112 mL
300 mL
3.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline): (90 - 62) = 28 g/L; 28 x 15 x 4 = 1680; 1680 / 10 = 168 mL (about 11 mL/kg), below the 20 mL/kg top-up check.

n.0: 420 mL uses a factor of 10 instead of 4; it is 28 mL/kg and an over-transfusion.
n.2: 112 mL uses an Hb rise of about 19 g/L instead of 28 g/L.
n.3: 300 mL is a flat 20 mL/kg, the upper check limit, not the calculated volume.

3.q: At the 08:00 round, Pearl, 81, refuses her prescribed ramipril, saying it makes her dizzy. She has capacity and understands the reason for the tablet. How should the nurse record and act on this?
o: Record 'refused' with her reason and inform the prescriber
Leave the box blank and mention it at the handover
Record 'given', as the tablet was offered at the correct time
Leave the tablet on her locker and record it once she takes it
3.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 17: records are kept of medicines administered, withheld or declined, completed at the time or as soon as possible; the reason is recorded and the prescriber or team informed where appropriate. Dizziness may need a medication review.

n.1: A blank box is unauditable and may lead someone else to give a second dose.
n.2: Recording a refused dose as given is a false record.
n.3: She has declined it; leaving tablets unattended is unsafe and the refusal still needs recording.

3.q: A student nurse is about to auscultate the chest of Mrs Hall, 68, who has a productive cough. Which technique should the supervising nurse advise?
o: Listen at one point on each side for a few seconds
Listen over her clothing to protect her dignity
Listen at the front of the chest, which is enough for a review
Sit her upright and compare each side at matching points
3.w: Chest auscultation (Annexe B 2.8) is done with the person upright where possible, the stethoscope on bare skin, comparing left with right at matching points front and back so that differences in air entry and added sounds can be detected.

n.0: A single point per side cannot detect localised changes such as basal crackles.
n.1: Clothing muffles and distorts breath sounds; dignity is maintained in other ways.
n.2: The bases are best heard from the back, so front-only listening misses findings.

3.q: At a major incident, Daniel reaches a young woman lying on the ground with a lower leg wound that is spurting blood. She is conscious. Using the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool, what should he do?
o: Categorise her as P2 because she is conscious and breathing
Ask her to walk to the casualty clearing area for assessment
Apply pressure or a tourniquet and categorise her as P1
Assess her breathing rate first and then decide her triage category
3.w: Catastrophic bleeding is the first step in MITT (NHS England 2023): control it with pressure, a tourniquet or haemostatic packing and categorise the casualty as P1 (P6.12).

n.0: Being conscious does not lower the priority of catastrophic bleeding, which makes the casualty P1.
n.1: Walking her would worsen the bleeding and delay life-saving control.
n.3: Catastrophic bleeding is assessed and controlled before breathing in MITT; delaying control risks death from haemorrhage.

3.q: Five minutes after IM adrenaline 300 micrograms for anaphylaxis, Leo, 8, remains wheezy with a respiratory rate of 36 and a heart rate of 150. He is on high-flow oxygen, the paediatric team is on the way and IV access is being attempted. What should the nurse do next?
o: Give IV chlorphenamine and reassess in 15 minutes
Wait a further 10 minutes for the first dose to work
Give a second IM dose of adrenaline 300 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone before any further adrenaline
3.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist, and give an IV fluid bolus if circulation problems continue.

n.0: Antihistamines are third-line and must not be used to treat ABC problems in the emergency phase.
n.1: RCUK sets the repeat at 5 minutes; waiting longer allows airway and circulatory compromise to progress.
n.3: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for the routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

3.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
3.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

3.q: Jean, 48, is nil by mouth for 24 hours before planned surgery and has no cardiac, renal or nutritional problems. The junior doctor asks you to check the volume she is prescribing for routine maintenance. Under NICE CG174, what is the daily routine maintenance water requirement for an adult?
o: 60-70 mL/kg/day
40-50 mL/kg/day
10-15 mL/kg/day
25-30 mL/kg/day
3.w: NICE CG174: routine maintenance is 25-30 mL/kg/day of water, about 1 mmol/kg/day each of potassium, sodium and chloride, and 50-100 g/day of glucose.

n.0: 60-70 mL/kg/day risks fluid overload.
n.1: 40-50 mL/kg/day exceeds adult maintenance needs.
n.2: 10-15 mL/kg/day would cause dehydration in most adults.

3.q: After removing Mrs Fox's urinary catheter, the nurse wants to provide appropriate information. Which information is most important to give at this stage?
o: How the catheter was inserted on admission
The cost to the NHS of treating catheter-related infections
When to expect to pass urine and what to report if not
Which brand of catheter was used during her stay
3.w: Proficiency P4.3: provide accurate information after interventions. Annexe A 2.8: provide information and respond to questions about treatment and care.

n.0: Past insertion details do not help her manage the next few hours.
n.1: Cost information does not support her recovery or safety.
n.3: Product details are not needed for her to recognise problems.

3.q: Oscar, 8, is autistic and is distressed in the outpatient waiting area, covering his ears and rocking. His appointment is in 40 minutes. What reasonable adjustment should the nurse offer?
o: A quiet room to wait in until the clinician is ready
Move him to the front of the queue ahead of urgent cases
Rebook the appointment for another day
Ask his parents to calm him so he does not upset others
3.w: Reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010 s20) for autistic children include reducing sensory overload and waiting, such as a quiet waiting space or a call when the clinician is ready, so the child can attend the appointment.

n.1: Clinical priority is still based on need; pushing ahead of urgent cases is not a reasonable adjustment.
n.2: Rebooking delays his care when a simple adjustment would allow the appointment.
n.3: Leaving his family to manage his distress places the burden on them and ignores the duty to adjust.

3.q: Tasha is a registered nursing associate working in Manchester. She is moving to Edinburgh and asks whether she can practise there in her registered nursing associate role. What is the most accurate answer?
o: No, until she completes a Scottish conversion course for the role
No, because nursing associates are regulated for practice in England
Yes, once she transfers to the Scottish part of the NMC register
Yes, because NMC registration applies in all four UK nations
3.w: Nurses and midwives are regulated by the NMC across the UK, but nursing associates are regulated in England only (FACTS S-CODE). This is an example of devolved differences in health workforce policy (P7.2).

n.0: No Scottish conversion course creates a regulated nursing associate role in Scotland.
n.2: There is no Scottish part of the register for nursing associates.
n.3: This is true for nurses and midwives, but the nursing associate role is regulated in England only.

3.q: Following a fall caused by a missed risk assessment, Mrs Doyle, 80, develops anxiety and disturbed sleep. The hospital is deciding whether this is prolonged psychological harm under the statutory duty of candour. Which threshold applies?
o: Psychological harm lasting at least 14 days in total over the admission
Psychological harm lasting at least 3 months after discharge
Psychological harm lasting, or likely to last, 28 continuous days or more
Psychological harm needing a referral to mental health services
3.w: Reg 20(7): prolonged psychological harm means psychological harm which a service user has experienced, or is likely to experience, for a continuous period of at least 28 days.

n.0: The regulation uses 28 continuous days, not 14 days.
n.1: The threshold is 28 continuous days, not three months.
n.3: Referral is not the legal test; the test is duration of at least 28 continuous days.

3.q: Agnieszka, 52, uses an insulin pen at home and has brought it into hospital. Her lunchtime dose is due, but the ward has run out of pen needles. A colleague suggests drawing the dose out of the pen cartridge with an insulin syringe. What should the nurse do?
o: Obtain pen needles from pharmacy or another ward and give it
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using an insulin syringe
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using a 1 mL syringe
Omit the dose until pen needles are delivered tomorrow
3.w: An NHS England patient safety alert (2016) warned of severe harm and death from withdrawing insulin from pen devices, as cartridges are not designed for this and dosing errors result. Insulin is a high-risk medicine (P4.14); the correct device should be obtained promptly so the dose is not omitted.

n.1: Withdrawing insulin from a pen cartridge is unsafe whichever syringe is used.
n.2: A standard 1 mL syringe adds a further risk of unit-to-mL confusion and overdose.
n.3: Omitting insulin for a day risks hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis when needles can be sourced.

3.q: Nurse Rose delegates afternoon observations on Mrs Lee, 81, to a healthcare assistant. Which instruction is clearest?
o: "Do her observations at 14:00; tell me at once if systolic is under 100."
"Keep an eye on Mrs Lee this afternoon and let me know of any concerns."
"Do Mrs Lee's obs whenever you have a moment this afternoon."
"Do Mrs Lee's observations and write them on the chart."
3.w: Code 11.1: delegate only within competence and make sure instructions are fully understood. Annexe A 1.11: clear instructions when delegating.

n.1: This is vague and gives no time or reporting threshold.
n.2: No time is set and no reporting instructions are given.
n.3: There is no time or instruction on what to report.

3.q: Vincent, 48, attends the practice nurse for a wound dressing. While checking his record, the nurse sees he smokes 20 cigarettes a day. They have about a minute before the next patient. Which approach reflects very brief advice on smoking?
o: Ask about smoking and advise him to cut down gradually by himself
Ask, advise that medicines plus specialist support work best, and offer referral
Explain the diseases caused by smoking in detail over the next 20 minutes
Wait until he says he is ready to quit before raising the topic of smoking
3.w: NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking; NICE NG209 (2021, updated 2025): very brief advice is Ask (record smoking status), Advise (the best way to stop is with a combination of medication and specialist support) and Act (offer referral to local stop smoking support); it takes about 30 seconds.

n.0: VBA advises that the most effective way to stop is medication combined with specialist behavioural support, not quitting unaided.
n.2: Very brief advice takes about 30 seconds; a long lecture is not the VBA model and is not feasible here.
n.3: VBA is offered to everyone who smokes at every opportunity, whatever their stated readiness.

3.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
3.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

3.q: On a children's ward, a nurse notices that the family of Marius, 6, who are Roma, are repeatedly asked to leave at night while other parents are allowed to stay at the bedside. No clinical reason is recorded. The nurse raises a concern. Which article of the Human Rights Act 1998 is engaged together with Article 8?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair hearing in court
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security of person
3.w: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights. Treating one family differently because of ethnicity, in relation to family life (Article 8), engages Articles 14 and 8 together. The nurse should also challenge discrimination under the Code and the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings in legal proceedings.
n.1: Article 9 concerns belief and religion; the issue is unequal treatment based on ethnicity.
n.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, which is not described.

3.q: Mrs Harper, 58, is choosing between two treatment options for her knee. She asks the nurse what she would do. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to decide by tomorrow morning
Tell her which of the two options the nurse would personally choose
Advise her to follow whatever the consultant recommends
Explore what matters to her and each option's risks and benefits
3.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11: patients must be made aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions; P4.2 shared decision making.

n.0: Written information alone, with a deadline, does not support shared decision making.
n.1: Personal preference replaces her own values and undermines shared decision making.
n.2: This removes her from the decision instead of supporting an informed choice.

3.q: Mr Hughes, 70, tells Ama, a Black staff nurse, that he does not want 'someone like her' looking after him. Ama is upset. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse in charge?
o: Reassign Ama quietly to avoid any further conflict
Challenge the remark, support Ama and report the incident
Ask Ama to carry on and to disregard the remark
Tell Mr Hughes he must leave the ward for his behaviour
3.w: Code 3.4: challenge discriminatory attitudes and behaviour; Code 20.2: treat people fairly without discrimination, bullying or harassment. Proficiency P1.4: understand and challenge discriminatory behaviour; report through local policy.

n.0: Reassigning without challenge colludes with the discrimination; Code 3.4 and 20.2 require it to be challenged.
n.2: This leaves the racist behaviour unchallenged and fails to support the colleague.
n.3: Withdrawing care is disproportionate; the behaviour should be challenged while care continues safely.

3.q: Ian, 35, has type 1 diabetes and is shaky and sweaty at a community clinic. He is alert and able to swallow. His capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. After giving 15-20 g of glucose tablets, his symptoms are no better at 15 minutes. What should you do?
o: Give a further 15-20 g of oral glucose
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give him a meal containing complex carbohydrate
Recheck his blood glucose again in 30 minutes
3.w: RCUK first aid 2025: treat hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L) in a person who can swallow with 15-20 g glucose; repeat if symptoms persist after 15 minutes; give a snack once recovered.

n.1: He is alert and swallowing, so oral treatment is repeated before an emergency call.
n.2: A snack follows recovery; complex carbohydrate alone is too slow while still hypoglycaemic.
n.3: Waiting another 30 minutes leaves hypoglycaemia untreated.

3.q: Baby Ruby, born at term to a mother with type 1 diabetes, is 4 hours old. She has been jittery and her pre-feed blood glucose on the ward blood gas analyser is 0.8 mmol/L. What is the priority?
o: Repeat the measurement on a handheld meter to confirm it
Urgent medical review for IV access and glucose treatment
Give 40% glucose gel and recheck glucose in 4 hours
Give a breastfeed and recheck glucose before the next feed
3.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice points 19-21: blood glucose below 1.0 mmol/L at any time is severe hypoglycaemia; arrange urgent medical review including IV access and glucose. Gel may be used only as an interim measure while IV access is obtained.

n.0: Ward blood gas analysers are accurate; many handheld meters are inaccurate below 2.0 mmol/L, so repeating delays treatment.
n.2: Gel is an interim measure while IV access is obtained, and a 4-hour recheck is far too late.
n.3: Feeding alone is not enough for glucose below 1.0 mmol/L at any time; BAPM requires urgent medical review and IV glucose.

3.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
3.q: Ruby, aged 4, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She is quiet. Heart rate is 165 beats/min, capillary refill time 4 seconds, and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. A student says the normal blood pressure is reassuring. What is the best response?
o: Disagree, because low blood pressure is a late sign in children
Agree, because a normal blood pressure shows her circulation is coping
Disagree, because her breathing rate is a better guide than her pulse
Agree, but ask for the blood pressure to be rechecked in an hour
3.w: Children compensate for circulatory failure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so blood pressure stays normal until late; hypotension signals decompensation and risk of arrest (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill already indicate compensated shock needing urgent escalation.

n.1: Blood pressure is maintained in compensated shock, so a normal reading does not rule it out.
n.2: Breathing rate matters, but here her heart rate and capillary refill show compensated shock; no single sign outranks the others.
n.3: Waiting an hour delays treatment of compensated shock.

3.q: George Hall, 80, has a NEWS2 score of 1. His nurse, Precious, feels uneasy: he is quieter than usual and has not eaten, though nothing specific is abnormal. She is unsure whether to act on this feeling. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase his observations and discuss her concern with the medical team
Ask the healthcare assistant to repeat the observations at the next round
Record her impression and continue observations at the planned frequency
Wait until his score reaches 5 so that escalation is clearly justified
3.w: NEWS2 supports, and does not replace, clinical judgement (RCP 2017; NICE NG253). For scores of 1-4 the registered nurse decides on monitoring frequency and escalation. Acting on clinical concern under uncertainty, by increasing monitoring and escalating, is safe practice (P6.11 accept and manage uncertainty; Code 13.3 ask for help).

n.1: Repeating routine observations later does not address her clinical concern now.
n.2: Recording a concern without acting on it leaves a possible deterioration unaddressed.
n.3: Waiting for a threshold ignores the nurse's assessment and may delay recognition of deterioration.

3.q: Mrs Dawson, 84, has a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and is on a ward in England. She tells the nurse she wants to go home today rather than wait for physiotherapy. A junior doctor says, 'She has dementia, so she can't make that decision.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: She can go home, because a person with dementia keeps all their rights
A best interests meeting should be arranged before any assessment
Her capacity for this decision must be assessed, not assumed from diagnosis
Her daughter should be asked to decide, as she is her next of kin
3.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition. Capacity must be assessed for this decision at this time.

n.0: Whether she can safely go home depends on whether she has capacity for this decision; that has not yet been assessed.
n.1: Best interests decisions (s4) follow a finding that the person lacks capacity; the assessment comes first.
n.3: Next of kin has no legal power to make decisions for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.

3.q: Ben, 4, has just been diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive condition. Genetic testing shows his mother is a carrier and his father is unaffected. His parents ask about the risk for a future son. What is the chance that a future son will be affected?
o: 1 in 2
1 in 4
Nil, as his father is unaffected
1 in 8
3.w: X-linked recessive inheritance: a carrier mother passes her affected X to half of her children. Each son has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected; each daughter a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier.

n.1: 1 in 4 is the chance across ALL children (sons and daughters) of an affected son, not the chance for a son.
n.2: Sons inherit their X chromosome from the mother, so the father's status does not protect a son.
n.3: 1 in 8 does not apply to any child of a carrier mother.

3.q: Amara, a breastfed baby, weighed 3.4 kg at birth. On day 5 she weighs 3.02 kg. She is alert and feeding every 2 to 3 hours, and her mother is anxious. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure her mother that losing up to 15% of birth weight is normal in the first week
Weigh Amara twice daily to track the trend closely
Advise formula top-ups after every breastfeed until birth weight is regained
Assess Amara clinically and take a detailed feeding history, including observing a feed
3.w: Amara has lost 0.38 kg, about 11% of her birth weight (0.38 / 3.4 x 100). NICE NG75 rec 1.1.2: if an infant loses more than 10% of birth weight, perform a clinical assessment for dehydration or illness, take a detailed feeding history and consider direct observation of feeding by someone with appropriate expertise.

n.0: More than 10% loss is the NICE threshold for assessment; 15% is not a normal figure.
n.1: NG75 rec 1.1.5 advises weighing no more often than daily; twice-daily weights add anxiety without useful information.
n.2: Routine formula top-ups can end breastfeeding (NG75 rec 1.1.6); assessment and feeding support come first.

3.q: A student nurse on an adolescent ward plans to carry out a Gillick competence assessment before asking Hannah, 16, to consent to a lumbar puncture. Hannah has no known cognitive impairment. Which response by the registered nurse is best?
o: Gillick is correct, but her parent must also countersign the form
At 16 the MCA presumption of capacity applies, not Gillick
Gillick is correct, as it applies to every patient under 18
At 16 she needs a formal MCA assessment before every procedure
3.w: Gillick competence is the test for under-16s. From 16 the MCA 2005 presumption of capacity applies and FLRA 1969 s8 makes her consent effective; capacity is assessed only if there is reason to doubt it.

n.0: Parental countersignature is not required for a 16-year-old's effective consent.
n.2: Gillick applies to children under 16, not to all under-18s.
n.3: The presumption of capacity means a formal assessment is needed only where there is doubt.

3.q: Bridget, 58, is due to have her first red cell transfusion before surgery. She asks the nurse what she should know about it. According to NICE NG24, which information should the nurse include?
o: That she will be able to give blood herself once she has recovered
That she will no longer be eligible to donate blood after a transfusion
That she cannot refuse once the transfusion has been prescribed
That a transfusion has no risks if the bedside checks are completed
3.w: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2: give verbal and written information on the reason for transfusion, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, that the person is no longer eligible to donate blood, and encourage questions; document the discussion (1.14.3).

n.0: NG24 states people who have had a transfusion are no longer eligible to donate blood.
n.2: A person with capacity may refuse a transfusion; consent remains her decision.
n.3: Transfusion carries risks that must be explained even with correct checks.

3.q: Pauline, 67, has a fine-bore nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. Her morning medicines are due through the tube. The tube was placed and confirmed yesterday. What check should the nurse make before giving them?
o: Inject air and listen over the stomach for a 'whoosh'
Test an aspirate and confirm a pH of 5.5 or below
Check the tube is not coiled by looking in her mouth
Test an aspirate with blue litmus paper for a colour change
3.w: NICE CG32 monitoring and NHS patient safety alerts on nasogastric tubes: confirm gastric placement before each use by testing an aspirate with CE-marked pH paper, accepting pH 5.5 or below; if no aspirate or pH above 5.5, do not use the tube and escalate (X-ray may be needed). A misplaced tube used for feeding is a Never Event.

n.0: The 'whoosh' test is unreliable and must not be used to confirm placement.
n.2: A mouth check may find coiling, but it does not confirm the tip is in the stomach.
n.3: Litmus paper is not sensitive enough to confirm gastric placement.

3.q: Mrs Oyelaran, 79, is being discharged to a care home. Her son repeatedly tells staff in front of her that she 'has to go' and answers questions for her. When asked, Mrs Oyelaran looks at her son and says, 'I suppose so.' What should the nurse do first?
o: Refer her for an assessment of her mental capacity
Ask her son to sign the agreement on his mother's behalf
Record that she has agreed to the move to the care home
Speak with Mrs Oyelaran alone to explore her own wishes
3.w: Valid consent must be given voluntarily, free from pressure by others. The nurse should first speak with Mrs Oyelaran privately to establish her own view. Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)), so concern about influence is not a reason to question capacity.

n.0: There is nothing to suggest an impairment of mind or brain; pressure from a relative raises a question of voluntariness, not capacity.
n.1: A son has no authority to consent for an adult unless he holds a relevant LPA or deputyship; nothing suggests this.
n.2: Her hesitant answer under pressure may not be voluntary; recording it as agreement could be invalid.

3.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
3.q: Leah, aged 2, has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and is now drowsy, responding only to voice. Airway and breathing are satisfactory, and fluids are being started for poor perfusion. What should the nurse check next under D?
o: Her temperature
Her weight
Her blood glucose
Her serum sodium
3.w: Under D (disability), assess conscious level (AVPU), pupils and posture, and check blood glucose: young children have limited glycogen stores and become hypoglycaemic quickly when unwell (RCUK 2025; T2 physiological differences). Hypoglycaemia is a treatable cause of reduced consciousness.

n.0: Temperature belongs to E (exposure), after D.
n.1: Weight is needed for dosing but does not assess her reduced consciousness.
n.3: Sodium matters with fluid therapy, but a bedside glucose is the immediate D check for drowsiness.

3.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
3.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

3.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
3.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

3.q: Sofia, 9, has a two-month history of night cough and wheeze. Her GP suspects asthma and refers her to the practice nurse for objective testing under NICE NG245. Which test should be done first?
o: Peak flow variability recorded over 2 weeks
Bronchial challenge testing with methacholine
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO)
Skin prick testing to house dust mite
3.w: NICE NG245 Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN, November 2024): in children aged 5-11, measure FeNO first (35 ppb or more supports asthma); if not confirmed, do spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, then peak flow variability.

n.0: Peak flow variability is a later step in the NG245 diagnostic sequence for 5-11 year olds.
n.1: Bronchial challenge is a specialist test used when earlier tests are inconclusive.
n.3: Skin prick testing identifies sensitisation but does not diagnose asthma.

3.q: Two weeks after discharge from an acute mental health unit, a former patient messages Sam, his named nurse, asking to meet for coffee to say thank you. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Meet in a public place as the patient has been discharged
Accept if the patient's care coordinator agrees to it
Decline the invitation and keep contact professional
Meet once with a colleague present to say goodbye
3.w: Code 20.5-20.6: do not take advantage of vulnerability; stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past.

n.0: Code 20.6 boundaries extend to people who have been in your care in the past.
n.1: Another professional's agreement does not change the boundary set by Code 20.6.
n.3: A social meeting, even accompanied, blurs the professional relationship with a former patient.

3.q: Theo, 18 months, has croup. He now has stridor at rest, moderate sternal recession and is agitated. His mother asks the nurse to look in his throat to see what is causing the noise. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Take a throat swab now to check for a bacterial infection
Avoid examining his throat; keep him calm on his mother's lap
Use a tongue depressor quickly while his mother holds him still
Lie him flat on the trolley to examine his throat more easily
3.w: NICE CKS Croup (last revised May 2022) and NHS croup advice: keep the child calm and upright; do not examine the throat, which can precipitate complete obstruction (and epiglottitis must be considered). Stridor at rest with recession is moderate croup needing admission.

n.0: Throat swabbing distresses the child and risks obstruction; croup is viral and needs no swab.
n.2: A tongue depressor can trigger laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction in a child with stridor.
n.3: Lying flat and distress worsen airway obstruction; the child should stay upright and calm.

3.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
3.q: Daniel, aged 7, has acute asthma. An hour ago he had marked recession and a respiratory rate of 40. Now his recession is less obvious, his respiratory rate is 18, he is drowsy and SpO2 is 87% in oxygen. What is the most likely explanation?
o: His asthma is improving, as his work of breathing has reduced
He has a normal rate for his age, so treatment can be reduced
He is falling asleep, which shows his anxiety has settled
He is tiring and decompensating, so an emergency call is needed
3.w: Decreasing work of breathing with bradypnoea, falling consciousness and SpO2 below 90% are signs of decompensated respiratory failure (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Exhaustion can look like improvement; this child is at risk of arrest and needs an emergency response.

n.0: Less recession here reflects exhaustion, not improvement, given his drowsiness and falling saturations.
n.1: A rate of 18 after 40, with drowsiness and SpO2 of 87%, is bradypnoea from exhaustion, not a normal finding.
n.2: Drowsiness with hypoxaemia is a sign of hypercapnia and exhaustion, not relaxation.

3.q: Aaron, aged 5, has been in hospital for a week. His father has stayed every night and tells the nurse he feels he has to do all Aaron's care or the nurses will think he is a bad parent. What is the best response?
o: Reassure him he can choose how much care he gives and nurses will share it
Advise him to go home each night so that he is less tired in the day
Tell him that resident parents are expected to give all the basic care
Suggest he cuts down his visits so Aaron learns to settle with the staff
3.w: In family-centred care, parents' participation is negotiated and voluntary; they should not feel pressured to take on care. Acknowledging his feelings and agreeing what he wants to do, with nurses sharing care and offering breaks, supports both parent and child (P3.4, P4.2).

n.1: Telling him to go home removes his choice and may increase Aaron's distress.
n.2: There is no expectation that resident parents do all care; this adds pressure and is incorrect.
n.3: Reducing parental presence is not the aim and can increase a young child's separation distress.

3.q: Clive, 80, had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) that was still active when he died on a cardiology ward. The registered nurse has verified his expected death. Which action relating to the device is the nurse's responsibility?
o: Instigate deactivation and tell the mortuary or funeral director about the device
Record the device in the notes, as no further action is needed after death
Ask his family to inform the funeral director that a device is present
Remove the device before Clive is transferred to the mortuary
3.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the RN must instigate the process for deactivation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator where applicable, and must notify the funeral director or mortuary of any infections, radioactive implants, implantable devices and whether an ICD is still active.

n.1: An active ICD remains a hazard to people handling the body, so deactivation must be arranged.
n.2: Notifying the mortuary or funeral director is the verifying nurse's responsibility, not the family's.
n.3: Ward nurses do not remove implanted devices; the RN instigates deactivation and passes on the information.

3.q: A GP practice nurse in England identifies that a parent's alcohol use may be affecting her 6-year-old patient's care. The nurse wonders whether the s16LA information sharing duty applies to primary care. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to health staff on a child protection plan
It applies to local authorities and the police, not health
It applies to NHS trusts, but not to GP practices
It applies to providers including GPs and dentists
3.w: The statutory guidance states the duty applies to section 11 organisations (including ICBs, NHS trusts and the police), designated education and childcare agencies, and providers delivering services for them, which includes GPs, dentists and other primary care providers.

n.0: The duty is not limited to children with a child protection plan.
n.1: Health bodies such as ICBs and NHS trusts are relevant persons under the duty.
n.2: GPs and other primary care providers are expressly included.

3.q: Which entry in a patient's nursing notes best meets the Code's requirements for record keeping?
o: Pt fell again, prob drunk as usual. Dr aware, all fine, will watch. JL
Afternoon: patient found on floor but appears OK. Will monitor. Nurse
14:30 Patient on floor, probably slipped on wet floor, unhurt and settled
14:30 Found on floor by bed. Alert, uninjured. Dr Khan informed. J Lee, RN
3.w: Code 10.4: attribute entries to yourself, clearly written, dated and timed, without unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation; Code 10.2 record steps taken.

n.0: This includes speculation and judgemental language and lacks a time (Code 10.4).
n.1: No exact time, vague content and not attributed to a named person.
n.2: The cause is speculation, it is not attributed and no escalation is recorded.

3.q: Kwame, 64, has motor neurone disease and is now thought to be in his last days. The team are deciding who should talk with him about his prognosis. He knows the ward sister well and trusts her, and she has experience of these conversations. According to NICE NG31, what should guide the choice of professional?
o: Their seniority and grade within the treating medical team
Which professional the family would prefer to lead the conversation
Which professional first made the diagnosis of his condition
Their competence and confidence, and their rapport with the person
3.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.2.2: identify the most appropriate available multiprofessional team member to explain the dying person's prognosis, based on the professional's competence and confidence and their rapport with the person.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.2.2 does not base the choice on grade; a senior doctor without rapport may not be the most appropriate person.
n.1: Family views matter, but NG31 rec 1.2.2 bases the choice on the professional's competence, confidence and rapport with the person.
n.2: The diagnosing clinician is not the NG31 criterion; competence, confidence and rapport are.

3.q: Ruth, 64, has chronic kidney disease and symptomatic anaemia with a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. She is not bleeding and does not have acute coronary syndrome. The doctor plans a red cell transfusion. In line with NICE NG24, what is the recommended approach?
o: Transfuse 1 unit, then reassess and check haemoglobin
Transfuse until haemoglobin reaches at least 110 g/L
Transfuse 2 units, then check haemoglobin the next day
Transfuse 3 units to avoid repeated cannulation
3.w: NICE NG24 (updated 2026): use a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a target of 70-90 g/L after transfusion, and consider single-unit transfusions for adults without active bleeding, clinically reassessing and checking haemoglobin after each unit before giving more.

n.1: 110 g/L is well above the NG24 post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L.
n.2: Two units without reassessment risks overtransfusion and circulatory overload.
n.3: Multiple units without reassessment conflicts with single-unit transfusion and raises overload risk.

3.q: After Arthur, 89, dies at home, his son asks the district nurse what to do with Arthur's remaining tablets, including morphine sulfate modified-release tablets and blister packs from the pharmacy. What advice is most appropriate?
o: Put them in a sealed bag in the household waste collection
Return all the medicines to a community pharmacy for disposal
Hand them in at the GP surgery reception to be destroyed
Flush the tablets down the toilet so they cannot be misused
3.w: Safe disposal of medicines (AnnexB.11.11; NICE NG46 on disposal of CDs that belonged to a person who has died): unwanted medicines, including controlled drugs, are returned to a community pharmacy, which disposes of them under the relevant regulations.

n.0: Household waste allows diversion and environmental contamination.
n.2: Surgery reception staff are not the route for patient-returned medicines; pharmacies accept them.
n.3: Flushing medicines contaminates water supplies and is not an approved disposal route.

3.q: Asif, 55, weighs 70 kg and is nil by mouth after surgery. He needs routine IV maintenance fluids. Using NICE CG174, what is the appropriate total daily water range?
3.w: NICE CG174: 25-30 mL/kg/day. 70 kg x 25 = 1,750 mL; 70 kg x 30 = 2,100 mL. CG174 also notes that intake rarely needs to exceed 3 L/day.

n.0: 700-1,050 mL uses 10-15 mL/kg/day, below CG174 maintenance.
n.2: 3,500-4,200 mL is well above maintenance and risks overload.
n.3: 2,800-3,500 mL uses 40-50 mL/kg/day, above maintenance.

3.q: Ruth, a staff nurse, is writing a referral to a dietitian for Mrs Smith, 63, who has lost weight after bowel surgery. The electronic record includes her full medical history, including a termination of pregnancy 30 years ago. What should Ruth include in the referral?
o: The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything except the termination of pregnancy
Her full medical history so the dietitian has the whole picture
A summary written after asking her family
3.w: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data. UK GDPR data minimisation also requires data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. Only information relevant to nutrition should be shared.

n.1: Removing one sensitive item still shares other irrelevant data; relevance, not sensitivity, decides what is sent.
n.2: Sending the full history exceeds what the dietitian needs and breaches the minimum necessary principle.
n.3: Families are not a source for a clinical referral, and involving them without consent breaches confidentiality.

3.q: A new wound treatment costs £30,000 more per patient than standard care and produces 1.5 more QALYs per patient. Using NICE's standard threshold in force since April 2026, what is the incremental cost per QALY and how does it compare?
o: £30,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, below the threshold range
£45,000 per QALY, above the threshold range
3.w: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = extra cost / extra QALYs = £30,000 / 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY. This is below the standard range of £25,000-£35,000 per QALY, so the treatment would usually be considered cost-effective (P7.3). Two steps: calculate, then compare with the current threshold.

n.0: This ignores the QALY gain and uses the extra cost alone.
n.1: The calculation is right, but £20,000 is below the current £25,000-£35,000 range, not within it.
n.3: This multiplies cost by QALYs instead of dividing.

3.q: Ivy, 82, has fallen on the ward and is lying on the floor. She is alert, says her hip hurts and her right leg looks shortened and externally rotated. What should the nurse do?
o: Help her to stand with two staff and walk her back to bed
Leave her on the floor until her family arrive
Use a standing hoist to lift her straight back into the chair
Keep her still, get her reviewed and use flat-lift equipment
3.w: After a fall, check for injury before moving. A shortened, externally rotated leg suggests a hip fracture: keep her still, call for medical review, give analgesia as prescribed and use flat-lifting equipment such as a scoop stretcher, in line with local post-fall protocols and Annexe B 7.3.

n.0: Standing a person with a suspected fracture risks further injury and pain.
n.1: Waiting for family delays medical review and pain relief.
n.2: A standing hoist needs weight bearing, which is unsafe with a suspected fracture.

3.q: Frank Ellis, 74, uses a walking frame and fell once at home last month. He has capacity and wants to walk to the day room for lunch. His daughter asks the nurse to keep him in his chair so he cannot fall again. Which response best reflects positive risk management?
o: Let Mr Ellis walk to the day room after he signs a disclaimer accepting the risk of falling
Arrange for him to use a wheelchair to reach the day room until physiotherapy can review him
Agree with the daughter and keep him seated at lunchtimes until he is discharged home
Agree a plan with Mr Ellis for supervised walking with his frame and record the discussion
3.w: Positive risk management weighs benefits and harms with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so they can do what matters to them, rather than removing all activity (P6.10 risk management versus risk aversion). Mr Ellis has capacity, so his decision is respected (MCA 2005 s1), and the plan and discussion are documented (Code 10).

n.0: A disclaimer does not manage the risk or remove the nurse's duty of care; it replaces planning with paperwork.
n.1: Using a wheelchair when he can walk with his frame reduces independence and mobility without a clinical reason.
n.2: Keeping him seated is risk aversion: it removes activity he values, causes deconditioning and overrides the choice of a person with capacity.

3.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
3.q: Grace, aged 3, on a children's ward, has suspected sepsis with a non-blanching rash and mottled skin. The senior clinician has reviewed her and taken blood cultures. By when should she receive a broad-spectrum antimicrobial?
o: Once the blood culture result is available
Within 3 hours of meeting a high risk criterion
Within 1 hour of meeting a high risk criterion
Within 6 hours, after the lactate result is known
3.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.7.2: for people under 16 with suspected sepsis and 1 or more high risk criteria, give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial without delay, within 1 hour of identifying that they meet any high risk criterion. A non-blanching rash and mottled skin are high risk criteria.

n.0: Culture results take days; waiting would dangerously delay treatment.
n.1: The 3-hour window applies to the antibiotic decision for moderate to high risk, not high risk.
n.3: Lactate guides fluids and escalation; it does not delay antibiotics in high risk sepsis.

3.q: Daniel, 52, is on a surgical ward breathing room air. His observations are: RR 18, SpO2 97%, BP 124/78, pulse 86, alert, temperature 37.4°C. His NEWS2 is 0. What is the minimum frequency of his observations under NEWS2?
o: Hourly
12-hourly
Every 30 minutes
4-6 hourly
3.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017) chart 4: an aggregate score of 0 requires a minimum of 12-hourly monitoring.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for a single parameter scoring 3 or a total of 5 or more.
n.2: Every 30 minutes is not a NEWS2 chart 4 frequency; it is the NG253 recalculation interval for high sepsis risk.
n.3: 4-6 hourly is the minimum for a total score of 1-4.

3.q: Isla, 14, sees the school nurse about severe acne and asks for advice about a GP appointment. The nurse judges her competent to make this decision. Isla asks that her parents are not told, as she is embarrassed. There are no safeguarding concerns. How should the nurse respond?
o: Respect her wishes, as she is owed the same duty of confidence as an adult
Tell her that the matter will be shared with her parents by her GP
Agree to tell her parents unless she arranges the appointment herself
Inform her parents, because she is under 16 and they hold parental responsibility
3.w: Young people are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults. With no risk of serious harm, a competent 14-year-old's wish for privacy should be respected, while encouraging her to involve her parents if she wishes (Code 5).

n.1: The GP owes Isla the same duty of confidence; there is no automatic sharing with parents.
n.2: Making disclosure conditional on her behaviour is coercive and has no basis when there is no risk of harm.
n.3: Parental responsibility does not entitle parents to a competent child's confidential information.

3.q: Kenneth, 68, lives in England and asks the practice nurse what the NHS bowel cancer screening programme will offer him. He has no bowel symptoms. Which answer is accurate?
o: A home test kit every 2 years
A home test kit every year
A colonoscopy every 5 years
A one-off camera test at age 70
3.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): everyone aged 50 to 74 is offered a bowel cancer screening home test kit every 2 years; people aged 75 or over can ask for a kit every 2 years.

n.1: The bowel screening kit is sent every 2 years, not annually.
n.2: Colonoscopy is a diagnostic test offered after a positive screening result, not the routine screen.
n.3: The current programme offers a home test kit every 2 years from 50 to 74.

3.q: A CDOP reviews the deaths of three infants in its area that involved co-sleeping after parental alcohol use. The panel recommends a local safer sleep campaign. What is the main purpose of the CDOP review, as described in Working Together 2026?
o: Independent scrutiny to find modifiable factors and prevent deaths
Determination of the medical cause of death in place of the coroner
Investigation of the deaths to decide whether criminal charges should follow
Disciplinary review of practitioners involved in each child's care
3.w: The CDOP review is the final, independent scrutiny of a child's death by professionals with no responsibility for the child during life. It aims to identify modifiable factors that could be altered to prevent future deaths and to share learning, including with the National Child Mortality Database.

n.1: The coroner retains responsibility for inquests into the cause of death.
n.2: Criminal investigation is the responsibility of the police and CPS.
n.3: CDOP reviews are for learning, not for disciplining individuals.

3.q: Roger, 61, is on an oncology ward having chemotherapy. He says he feels nauseated before each meal and has been leaving most of his food. He has a prescription for a regular antiemetic. Which nursing action is most appropriate first?
o: Encourage large meals to settle his stomach
Withhold all food until the nausea fully resolves
Give the prescribed antiemetic before meals and review it
Offer strong-smelling hot food to stimulate appetite
3.w: Annexe B 5.5: identify and manage nausea and vomiting. Give prescribed antiemetics at a time that covers meals, assess the response, and use measures such as small frequent meals and reducing food odours.

n.0: Large meals worsen nausea; small frequent meals are better tolerated.
n.1: Withholding all food risks malnutrition.
n.3: Strong food smells often worsen nausea.

3.q: According to NICE NG89, which person should not be offered anti-embolism stockings for VTE prophylaxis?
o: A person with peripheral arterial disease
A person having elective hip replacement
A person with a BMI of 32 kg/m²
A person with a previous DVT
3.w: NICE NG89 rec 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease, peripheral arterial bypass grafting, peripheral neuropathy, fragile skin, dermatitis, gangrene, recent skin graft, severe oedema, material allergy or major limb deformity.

n.1: Hip replacement patients may be offered stockings when indicated.
n.2: Obesity is a VTE risk factor and is not a contraindication to stockings.
n.3: Previous DVT raises VTE risk and is not a contraindication to stockings.

3.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
3.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

3.q: Siobhan, 58, two days after a laparotomy, has a NEWS2 of 9: RR 25, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 102/64, alert, temperature 38.4°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Request a ward doctor review within 4 hours and repeat the observations hourly
Recheck the observations in 30 minutes before escalating
Inform the medical team immediately and request a critical care assessment
Increase observations to 4-hourly and inform the nurse in charge
3.w: A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring, the registered nurse immediately informs the medical team (at least specialist registrar level) and requests emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies (RCP NEWS2 2017 chart 4). Her score: RR 3, SpO2 2, pulse 2, BP 1, temperature 1 = 9.

n.0: A 4-hour review is far too slow for a high-risk score.
n.1: Delaying escalation to recheck wastes time; the score already meets the emergency threshold.
n.3: 4-hourly observations apply to a total of 1-4.

3.q: Kathleen, 90, lives at home with a long-term urinary catheter. Her daughter asks the community nurse to start weekly bladder washouts to stop Kathleen getting urine infections. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange weekly 0.9% sodium chloride washouts to reduce infection risk
Explain washouts do not prevent infection and support daily meatal washing
Request antibiotic prophylaxis to be given at every catheter change
Arrange to change the catheter every week to limit bacterial colonisation
3.w: NICE CG139: bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection; the meatus is washed daily with soap and water. Catheters are changed when clinically necessary or per manufacturer, and antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter change is not offered routinely.

n.0: CG139 says washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection.
n.2: CG139 says do not routinely offer antibiotic prophylaxis when changing long-term catheters.
n.3: Catheters are changed according to clinical need or the manufacturer's advice, not weekly.

3.q: Mr Tran, 52, speaks little English and is due to have a chest drain inserted later today. His consultant has asked the nurse to make sure he understands the procedure and its risks before he agrees. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Rely on his nodding to show that he understands
Use pictures and gestures to explain the main steps of the procedure
Arrange a professional interpreter for the consent discussion
Give him an English information leaflet to read first
3.w: Consent must be informed: the person needs to understand the procedure, material risks and alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 7.2 requires reasonable steps to meet people's language and communication needs, so a professional interpreter should be used for the discussion.

n.0: Nodding may reflect politeness rather than understanding, so it is not evidence of informed consent.
n.1: Pictures and gestures may support communication but cannot convey material risks and alternatives reliably for a chest drain.
n.3: A leaflet in a language he cannot read well does not inform him and does not meet Code 7.2.

3.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
3.q: During the E (exposure) part of an ABCDE assessment of Kai, a 5-month-old with suspected sepsis, what should the nurse do?
o: Leave him uncovered so that the rash can be monitored
Bathe him in tepid water to cool him
Delay exposure until his temperature has been measured
Examine him in stages and keep him covered and warm
3.w: Infants have a large surface area to weight ratio and lose heat quickly, so the whole body (including skin for rashes and injuries) should be examined while preventing heat loss, uncovering in stages and covering again (T2 physiological differences; RCUK ABCDE).

n.0: Leaving an infant uncovered risks hypothermia, which worsens outcomes in sepsis.
n.1: Tepid sponging is not recommended (NICE NG143) and risks cooling a sick infant.
n.2: Exposure is needed to find rashes or injuries; measuring temperature does not replace examining the skin.

3.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
3.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

3.q: Alfie, 4 months, is brought to the GP practice for his routine immunisations. The practice nurse notices a 1 cm bruise on his cheek. His mother says his 3-year-old sister probably hit him with a toy. Alfie is otherwise well and cannot yet roll over. What should the nurse do?
o: Follow the local bruising protocol for urgent paediatric assessment and referral
Give the immunisations and ask the health visitor to check the bruise at home
Record the bruise and the explanation, then review it at the next immunisations
Reassure the mother, as the explanation offered is consistent with the bruise
3.w: Bruising in a child who is not independently mobile is rare accidentally and is a recognised indicator of physical abuse (NICE CG89: suspect maltreatment). Local safeguarding partnership protocols require urgent paediatric assessment and a children's social care referral, whatever explanation is given.

n.1: Delegating a later home check delays the assessment the protocol requires.
n.2: Waiting weeks for a review leaves a possibly abused infant unprotected.
n.3: A plausible explanation does not remove the need for assessment in a non-mobile infant.

3.q: During the morning medication round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the drug trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. Several injections are still due. What should Lewis do with the full container?
o: Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Leave it open and start a second container beside it on the trolley
Press the contents down to make room for the remaining needles
Use it until it is completely full, then seal it before lunch
3.w: NIPCM ch 1.9: sharps containers must be disposed of when the manufacturer's fill line is reached, labelled with point of origin and dates of assembly and disposal, and use the temporary closure when not in use.

n.1: A full container left open is a sharps hazard; it should be locked and removed.
n.2: Pushing down sharps risks a needlestick injury and overfills the container.
n.3: Filling past the fill line risks protruding sharps and injury.

3.q: Leo, 4, is admitted to the children's ward for IV antibiotics. His father says Leo weighed 'about two and a half stone' at the GP a few months ago. What should the nurse do before medicines are prescribed?
o: Weigh Leo now and record his weight in kilograms
Convert two and a half stone to kilograms and record it
Estimate his weight using an age-based formula
Use the weight in his GP record from a few months ago
3.w: Children's doses are weight-based, so the child should be weighed on admission and the weight recorded in kilograms. Estimated, converted or old weights are a recognised source of dosing error.

n.1: Converting an old, approximate weight in stones adds conversion error to an out-of-date figure.
n.2: Age-based estimates are for emergencies when weighing is not possible; Leo can be weighed.
n.3: A weight from months ago may be inaccurate in a growing or unwell child.

3.q: Harvey, aged 4 months, is being monitored at home for faltering growth. His mother asks the community children's nurse how often he should be weighed. He is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Usually no more often than weekly at his age
Usually no more often than daily until he gains weight
Usually no more often than fortnightly at his age
Usually no more often than monthly at his age
3.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.27: when there is concern about faltering growth, weigh usually no more often than daily if under 1 month, weekly between 1 and 6 months, fortnightly between 6 and 12 months and monthly from 1 year. Weighing too often adds parental anxiety (rec 1.2.28).

n.1: Daily weighing is the limit for babies under 1 month; at 4 months it adds anxiety without benefit.
n.2: Fortnightly is the guide for 6 to 12 months, not 4 months.
n.3: Monthly is the guide from 1 year of age.

3.q: A practice nurse in England plans to share concerns about Leo, 5, with children's social care under the s16LA duty. She intends to share whether or not his father agrees. How should she approach the conversation with the father?
o: Leave him uninformed, as the duty does not require openness
Ask for his consent, then withhold if he refuses it
Ask for his consent, then share anyway if he refuses it
Explain openly what will be shared and why, not asking consent
3.w: The statutory guidance says that where the lawful basis is public task or legal obligation, practitioners should avoid seeking consent if they intend to share anyway, and should not imply that the family's agreement decides the matter. Where safe, they should be open and transparent about what is shared and why.

n.0: Practitioners should be transparent with families where it is safe to do so.
n.1: Lack of consent is not a reason to withhold information under the duty.
n.2: Seeking consent that will then be overridden is misleading and is discouraged by the guidance.

3.q: Deborah, 46, received IM adrenaline 500 micrograms for anaphylaxis 5 minutes ago. She remains wheezy with BP 84/52 mmHg. What should happen next?
o: Wait a further 15 minutes before repeating adrenaline
Give chlorphenamine IV and wait for it to take effect
Sit her upright with her legs lowered to ease breathing
Give a second IM adrenaline dose and an IV crystalloid bolus
3.w: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and give an IV crystalloid bolus (adults 500-1,000 mL) for circulatory problems, with high-flow oxygen and monitoring.

n.0: RCUK advises a repeat dose after 5 minutes, not 15.
n.1: Antihistamines are not used to treat ABC problems in anaphylaxis.
n.2: With hypotension she should lie flat with or without legs raised; sitting with legs down worsens circulation.

3.q: Ella, 15, was diagnosed with mild depression 2 weeks ago and was offered watchful waiting. At review her low mood is unchanged. She has no suicidal ideas and no other mental health problems. What does NICE NG134 recommend now?
o: A further 6 weeks of watchful waiting before any treatment
A choice of psychological therapy, such as digital or group CBT
Referral for inpatient admission to a CAMHS unit
Fluoxetine started by the GP with review in 4 weeks
3.w: NICE NG134 Depression in children and young people: for 12 to 18 year olds with mild depression continuing after 2 weeks of watchful waiting, without significant comorbidity or active suicidal ideas, offer a choice of psychological therapies (digital CBT, group CBT, group IPT or group NDST) for about 2 to 3 months.

n.0: Watchful waiting is for about 2 weeks; prolonging it delays effective treatment.
n.2: Inpatient care is for severe depression with high risk, not mild depression.
n.3: NG134 says antidepressant medication should not be used for the initial treatment of mild depression in children and young people.

3.q: A community children's nurse is uneasy after Aisha, 13, repeats extremist slogans she has seen online, but the nurse is not sure whether this is a real concern or bravado. According to the Prevent duty guidance, which approach should the nurse use?
o: Discuss the concern with Aisha's parents to decide together
Wait for a second incident before taking action
Notice, check and share the concern through the Prevent lead
Refer straight to the Channel panel for assessment
3.w: Prevent duty guidance (2023, paras 42-43) says the notice, check, share procedure should be applied: notice the concern, check it with the organisation's Prevent or designated safeguarding lead, and share it if a referral is needed.

n.0: Parents may be involved later, but the guidance route is to check with the Prevent or safeguarding lead.
n.1: Waiting for a further incident risks missing the chance to support Aisha early.
n.3: Channel receives referrals that have been through the Prevent process; practitioners do not refer straight to the panel.

3.q: Daniel, 13, is to have planned spinal surgery next month. Which approach to preparation best suits his stage of development?
o: Give detailed information, invite his questions and involve him in decisions
Speak mainly with his parents and let them decide how much to tell him
Prepare him on the morning of surgery to avoid weeks of worry
Use doll play to act out the operation with him and his younger sister
3.w: Adolescents can think abstractly and want detailed, honest information, privacy and a say in decisions about their care. Preparation well ahead, with time for questions (and a pre-admission visit if available), supports autonomy and reduces anxiety (P4.3; T2 play therapy and preparation).

n.1: Excluding a 13-year-old from information about his own surgery ignores his developing autonomy.
n.2: A last-minute explanation suits toddlers, not an adolescent facing major planned surgery.
n.3: Doll play suits younger children and may feel patronising to an adolescent.

3.q: Mrs Nolan, 74, has cellulitis of the leg and is otherwise well. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97%, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 84, alert, temperature 39.3°C. Using NEWS2 Chart 1, what is her temperature score and her aggregate score?
o: Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 2
Temperature scores 3, giving a NEWS2 total of 3
Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 4
Temperature scores 1, giving a NEWS2 total of 1
3.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017) Chart 1: temperature 39.1°C or above scores 2; 38.1-39.0 scores 1. All other parameters score 0 (RR 12-20, SpO2 96% or above, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert, on air), so the aggregate is 2.

n.1: No temperature band scores 3 for fever; 3 is for 35.0°C or below.
n.2: The other parameters all score 0, so the total equals the temperature score of 2.
n.3: A score of 1 applies to 38.1-39.0°C; 39.3°C is in the 39.1 or above band.

3.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
3.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

3.q: Freya, 17, is admitted after a road traffic collision with a head injury. She is confused, cannot retain information about her injuries and needs a CT scan and a central line. Her parents cannot be reached. On what legal basis should the team act?
o: The Mental Capacity Act 2005, in her best interests
Section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969 (her consent)
The Gillick test, as she is under 18 years old
The Mental Health Act 1983, as she is confused
3.w: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from age 16. If a 16 or 17-year-old lacks capacity for a decision, treatment can be given in their best interests under ss4-5 of the MCA, involving family where possible.

n.1: FLRA s8 gives effect to a 16 or 17-year-old's own consent; Freya cannot currently consent.
n.2: Gillick competence applies to children under 16.
n.3: The MHA 1983 authorises treatment for mental disorder, not treatment of a physical head injury.

3.q: Agency nurse Paul's electronic record login has expired. A permanent colleague offers him her smartcard so he can document his care until IT resets his access. What should Paul do?
o: Use her card and add his own name at the start of each entry
Use her card and ask her to check his entries afterwards
Wait until his access returns and write all entries then
Decline and use the approved paper back-up until access returns
3.w: Code 10.4: attribute entries to yourself; Code 10.5: keep records secure. Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely; P1.15 digital skills for safe practice.

n.0: Entries would still be attributed to her login, breaching Code 10.4 and information security.
n.1: Her checking does not correct the false attribution of entries to her.
n.2: Delaying documentation risks missing information; Code 10.1 requires timely records.

3.q: Becca, a care home nurse, receives Mr Ian Moss, 79, back from hospital. The discharge letter says his furosemide was stopped, but the boxes sent with him and the care home's medicines record still include it. The GP practice is open. What should Becca do?
o: Contact the hospital or GP to reconcile the medicines and report the gap
Stop the furosemide, as the discharge letter is the most recent document
Continue the furosemide until the next routine GP visit
Ask Mr Moss which tablets he has been taking and follow his answer
3.w: Transitions between settings are a common point of medicines error. Discrepancies are resolved by medicines reconciliation with the prescriber and the information gap is reported for learning (P7.6 complexities of care across integrated settings; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; Code 18).

n.1: Acting on one document without clarifying a conflict risks error if the letter itself is wrong.
n.2: Continuing a possibly stopped diuretic for days risks harm while the discrepancy is unresolved.
n.3: Mr Moss's account is useful information but does not replace clarification with the prescriber.

3.q: Ade has finished helping Margaret, who has influenza, to wash. He is wearing gloves, an apron, goggles and a fluid-resistant surgical mask. In which order should he remove this PPE?
o: Mask, eye protection, apron, then gloves
Eye protection, gloves, mask, then apron
Apron, gloves, mask, then eye protection
Gloves, apron, eye protection, then mask
3.w: NIPCM appendix 6: remove gloves, then apron or gown, then eye protection, then the FRSM or respirator, followed immediately by hand hygiene. The most contaminated items (gloves and the front of the apron) come off first.

n.0: Removing the mask first means touching the face with contaminated gloves still on.
n.1: Handling goggles before glove removal transfers contamination from the gloves to the face area.
n.2: Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off before the apron, not after it.

3.q: On a surgical ward, Femi asks the ward manager about the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 because a new bariatric care pathway is being written. Which step do the regulations require the employer to take first?
o: Set a maximum weight that any member of staff may lift on the ward
Reduce the risk of injury to the lowest level by providing equipment
Avoid hazardous manual handling so far as is reasonably practicable
Assess the risk of injury from every manual handling task on the ward
3.w: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 set out a hierarchy for employers: avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable; assess the risk of injury from any hazardous operations that cannot be avoided; and reduce that risk to as low as reasonably practicable (HSE, Manual handling at work).

n.0: The HSE states that the law does not set specific weight limits; weight is one factor in the risk assessment.
n.1: Reducing risk is the third step, after avoidance and assessment.
n.3: Assessment is the second step and applies to hazardous handling that cannot be avoided, not to every task.

3.q: Amir, 9 months, is 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion. He has become irritable and flushed. His temperature has risen from 36.9°C to 38.5°C and his heart rate from 130 to 175. What should the nurse do first?
o: Stop the transfusion, assess ABCDE and call the doctor urgently
Continue, as infants often become irritable during transfusions
Slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 30 minutes
Give paracetamol and continue the transfusion
3.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) key practice point: monitoring is essential because infants cannot report symptoms. A temperature rise of this size with tachycardia early in a transfusion may signal a serious reaction; stop the transfusion, keep the line open, assess ABCDE and get urgent medical review (SHOT/BSH reaction guidance).

n.1: Irritability with fever and tachycardia must be treated as a possible reaction in an infant who cannot describe symptoms.
n.2: Slowing the rate does not stop exposure to a possibly incompatible component.
n.3: Paracetamol may mask fever and does not address a possible serious reaction.

3.q: A practice nurse is preparing a short presentation for a safeguarding update and reads the 2015 Welsh study of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) among adults. Roughly what proportion of the adults surveyed reported four or more ACEs?
o: About 47%
About 30%
About 5%
About 14%
3.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): 47% of Welsh adults reported at least one ACE and 14% reported four or more.

n.0: Forty-seven per cent reported at least one ACE, not four or more.
n.1: Thirty per cent is not a figure from the study for 4+ ACEs.
