4.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): compared with people with no ACEs, those with 4+ ACEs were 4 times more likely to be a high-risk drinker, 6 times more likely to smoke, 11 times more likely to have smoked cannabis and 20 times more likely to have been incarcerated.

n.1: Twenty times relates to having been incarcerated, not high-risk drinking.
n.2: The study reported a fourfold, not twofold, increase in high-risk drinking.
n.3: Eleven times relates to having smoked cannabis, not high-risk drinking.

4.q: Baby Ruby, born at term to a mother with type 1 diabetes, is 4 hours old. She has been jittery and her pre-feed blood glucose on the ward blood gas analyser is 0.8 mmol/L. What is the priority?
o: Repeat the measurement on a handheld meter to confirm it
Urgent medical review for IV access and glucose treatment
Give 40% glucose gel and recheck glucose in 4 hours
Give a breastfeed and recheck glucose before the next feed
4.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice points 19-21: blood glucose below 1.0 mmol/L at any time is severe hypoglycaemia; arrange urgent medical review including IV access and glucose. Gel may be used only as an interim measure while IV access is obtained.

n.0: Ward blood gas analysers are accurate; many handheld meters are inaccurate below 2.0 mmol/L, so repeating delays treatment.
n.2: Gel is an interim measure while IV access is obtained, and a 4-hour recheck is far too late.
n.3: Feeding alone is not enough for glucose below 1.0 mmol/L at any time; BAPM requires urgent medical review and IV glucose.

4.q: On a children's ward in England, the nurse is caring for Lily, 15, who needs a decision about a minor procedure. A student nurse asks whether the Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs this decision. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to children of any age if parents agree
Its powers generally apply to people aged 16 and over
Its powers apply to people aged 18 and over
It applies to anyone over 12 who is in hospital
4.w: MCA 2005 s2(5): the powers under the Act do not generally apply to a person under 16 (subject to s18(3), which concerns property). Decisions for Lily follow the law on children's consent and parental responsibility.

n.0: Parental agreement does not bring a child under 16 within the MCA.
n.2: The MCA starts at 16, not 18; it covers 16 and 17 year olds.
n.3: There is no age-12 threshold in the MCA; s2(5) sets 16.

4.q: A nurse on placement with the local public health team reads a report stating that 120 people in a town of 100,000 were newly diagnosed with tuberculosis between January and December 2025. Which epidemiological measure does this figure describe?
o: Prevalence
Mortality rate
Case fatality rate
Incidence
4.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: incidence is the number of new cases of a disease arising in a population over a given period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a point or over a period. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2 (epidemiology).

n.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or period, not only the new cases arising in the year.
n.1: A mortality rate counts deaths in a population, not new diagnoses.
n.2: Case fatality is the proportion of people with a disease who die from it.

4.q: Kai, 16, weighs 92 kg. A medicine is prescribed at 10 mg/kg per dose, giving 920 mg. The usual adult dose is 500 mg. What should the nurse do?
o: Query it, as the dose is above the usual adult dose
Give 920 mg, as Kai is still under 18 years old
Give 500 mg and inform the prescriber after the dose
Give 920 mg, as his dose is calculated from his weight
4.w: BNF for Children principle: a weight-calculated dose should not normally exceed the adult dose. A large adolescent's weight-based dose of 920 mg is almost double the adult dose, so the prescriber must review it before administration.

n.1: Being under 18 does not justify exceeding the adult dose in a 92 kg adolescent.
n.2: The nurse cannot give a dose other than that prescribed; the prescription must be amended first.
n.3: Weight-based calculation is capped at the adult dose in larger children; 920 mg exceeds it.

4.q: Ernest, 81, has Parkinson's disease with a tremor and struggles to get food to his mouth. He is eating less than half his meals. Which intervention should be tried first to help him eat?
o: Provide adapted cutlery, a plate guard and help
Give his meals later, when the ward is quieter
Refer him for insertion of a nasogastric feeding tube
Prescribe oral nutritional supplements three times a day
4.w: Annexe B 5.3: assist with eating and drinking and use feeding and drinking aids. Adapted cutlery, plate guards and non-slip mats, plus assistance (for example via a red tray system or protected mealtimes), address the cause of his poor intake.

n.1: Delaying meals does not address his difficulty and may mean food is cold.
n.2: Enteral feeding is not indicated when oral intake can be improved with help.
n.3: Supplements may follow, but his barrier is a physical one that aids can address first.

4.q: Ethan, 11, has anaphylaxis after eating sesame. Despite two correctly given IM adrenaline doses 5 minutes apart and a fluid bolus, he remains hypotensive and wheezy. The paediatric registrar is present. What does RCUK guidance advise now?
o: Get critical care help early for IV adrenaline infusion
Give a third IM dose and observe for 30 minutes
Give IV hydrocortisone as the main next treatment
Give oral cetirizine and continue close observations
4.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): refractory anaphylaxis is no improvement in respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms despite 2 appropriate IM doses; IV adrenaline infusion is the basis of treatment, with expert (critical care) help sought early.

n.1: IM doses may continue every 5 minutes while help arrives, but observing for 30 minutes delays the infusion that refractory anaphylaxis needs.
n.2: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment and do not act fast enough here.
n.3: Non-sedating oral antihistamines are for persisting skin symptoms after stabilisation, not for hypotension and wheeze.

4.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing patients' names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has most directly been breached?
o: Accuracy (keeping data up to date)
Storage limitation (retention periods)
Purpose limitation (use for stated purposes)
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
4.w: UK GDPR Article 5 requires personal data to be processed securely, protecting against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5 also requires records to be kept securely.

n.0: Nothing suggests the content is inaccurate; the problem is security.
n.1: Storage limitation concerns keeping data no longer than necessary, not leaving it unsecured.
n.2: Purpose limitation concerns using data for the purpose it was collected; handover is a legitimate purpose.

4.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
4.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

4.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
4.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

4.q: Chloe, 14, is admitted to a general paediatric ward overnight after taking an overdose of paracetamol. She is medically stable on treatment. According to NICE NG225, which arrangement should be in place while she is on the ward?
o: Joint daily review by paediatric and children's mental health teams
A mental health review once she is medically fit for discharge
A weekly multidisciplinary meeting led by her GP and school nurse
Transfer to an adult mental health ward for assessment
4.w: NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022) rec 1.7.24: children and young people admitted to a paediatric ward after self-harm should have 24-hour access to CAMHS/CYPMHS or age-appropriate liaison psychiatry, a joint daily review by paediatric and mental health teams, daily family access and regular MDT meetings.

n.1: Mental health input starts during the admission, with joint daily review, not at discharge.
n.2: NG225 specifies regular MDT meetings between the paediatric team and mental health services, not weekly GP-led meetings.
n.3: An adult ward is not age-appropriate; NG225 keeps her on the paediatric ward with CYPMHS input.

4.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
4.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

4.q: Ama, 68, has dark brown skin and is cared for in bed after a stroke. Over her heel you find an area that feels warmer and firmer than the surrounding skin, with a slightly purplish tone. It does not blanch with diascopy. What should you do?
o: Apply a dressing and recheck the area at the weekly skin review
Massage the area to stimulate blood flow and recheck it at the next shift
Record it as normal skin pigmentation and continue the current care plan
Start prevention and recheck her skin at least every 2 hours
4.w: NICE CG179: in darker skin tones non-blanching erythema may appear as colour change or discolouration, and warmth and firmness are additional signs. If non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention (including heel offloading) and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until it resolves.

n.0: Weekly review is far too infrequent; CG179 sets at least 2-hourly checks until resolved.
n.1: Massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179.
n.2: Dismissing changes as pigmentation misses early pressure damage in darker skin.

4.q: Amina, 15, attends a sexual health clinic in England with painful periods. During the consultation she tells the nurse that she was 'cut' when she was 7 during a family visit abroad. What must the nurse do under the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
o: Seek Amina's consent before reporting, as she is 15 and competent
Report the case to the police personally, usually by calling 101
Inform the clinic's safeguarding lead, who will make the police report
Refer Amina to children's social care, who will decide whether to inform the police
4.w: Section 5B of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 requires regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales to report to the police when a girl under 18 discloses that FGM has been carried out on her. Home Office procedural information recommends reporting by calling 101; the duty is personal and does not require consent.

n.0: The duty applies regardless of consent, and complying with it does not breach confidentiality.
n.2: The duty is personal to the professional who hears the disclosure and cannot be transferred to a safeguarding lead.
n.3: A social care referral is good practice alongside, but the legal duty is a report to the police.

4.q: A surgical registrar asks Priya, a registered nurse, to obtain Mrs Kaur's signature on a consent form for a laparoscopic procedure tomorrow. Priya has never seen this operation and does not know its specific risks or alternatives. What should Priya do?
o: Read the consent form aloud and witness Mrs Kaur's signature
Decline and ask the registrar to take consent from Mrs Kaur
Ask Mrs Kaur whether she has any questions before she signs
Obtain the signature and ask the registrar to explain risks later
4.w: Valid consent needs the person to be informed of material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 13 requires nurses to work within the limits of their competence, asking a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it (13.3). Priya cannot give that information, so the clinician who can should seek consent.

n.0: Reading the form does not allow Priya to answer questions about risks and alternatives she does not know.
n.2: Priya could not answer Mrs Kaur's questions about this operation's risks, so her consent would not be properly informed.
n.3: A signature obtained before the risks are explained does not show informed consent; the form is evidence, not consent itself.

4.q: A nurse is deciding whether to share information about Yasmin, 13, who is living in a refuge with her mother after fleeing domestic abuse. Under the s16LA statutory guidance, in which circumstance may the nurse decide not to share particular information?
o: When Yasmin's father, who has parental responsibility, objects
When the family has not given consent to the sharing
When sharing would be more detrimental to Yasmin than not sharing
When the nurse feels uncomfortable about the possible consequences
4.w: The duty does not apply in extremely limited circumstances where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing, for example where disclosing a refuge address would place the child at immediate risk (statutory guidance, Limitation: detriment to the child). Other relevant information should still be shared and the decision recorded.

n.0: Parental objection is not a reason to withhold under the duty.
n.1: Lack of consent is expressly not a reason to withhold.
n.3: Practitioner discomfort is not a reason to withhold; the guidance says seek prompt advice instead.

4.q: On a ward round you notice that the urinary drainage bag of Bernard, 79, is lying on the floor beside his chair, and later it is hooked over the bed rail above his waist while he is repositioned. What is the correct positioning of the drainage bag?
o: Level with the bladder to reduce traction on the catheter
Above the bladder when moving, then below it when seated
Below the level of the bladder and not touching the floor
On the floor beside the bed to keep the tubing straight
4.w: NICE CG139 (catheter care): the drainage bag is positioned below the level of the bladder to maintain flow and prevent reflux, and kept off the floor to avoid contamination, using a stand where needed.

n.0: At bladder level, drainage slows and urine can pool or reflux.
n.1: Raising the bag above the bladder allows contaminated urine to flow back towards the bladder.
n.3: A bag on the floor becomes contaminated and increases the risk of catheter-associated infection.

4.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
4.q: Leah, aged 2, has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and is now drowsy, responding only to voice. Airway and breathing are satisfactory, and fluids are being started for poor perfusion. What should the nurse check next under D?
o: Her temperature
Her weight
Her blood glucose
Her serum sodium
4.w: Under D (disability), assess conscious level (AVPU), pupils and posture, and check blood glucose: young children have limited glycogen stores and become hypoglycaemic quickly when unwell (RCUK 2025; T2 physiological differences). Hypoglycaemia is a treatable cause of reduced consciousness.

n.0: Temperature belongs to E (exposure), after D.
n.1: Weight is needed for dosing but does not assess her reduced consciousness.
n.3: Sodium matters with fluid therapy, but a bedside glucose is the immediate D check for drowsiness.

4.q: Mr Blake, 85, has dementia and was admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Staff describe him as 'a lovely quiet man' who sleeps most of the day, eats little and is slow to respond. His family say he is usually chatty. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Hypoactive delirium needing assessment
Expected tiredness from his pneumonia
Progression of his dementia over two days
Low mood related to being in hospital
4.w: NICE CG103 notes hypoactive delirium is easily missed. Recent changes in cognition, physical function (reduced movement, appetite, sleep) and social behaviour (withdrawal), reported by family, are indicators of delirium needing assessment with the 4AT (rec 1.3.1, 1.6.1).

n.1: Attributing a marked change from his baseline to tiredness risks missing delirium.
n.2: Dementia progresses gradually; a change over two days points to delirium.
n.3: Low mood may cause withdrawal, but slowed responses and drowsiness developing over days point to delirium first.

4.q: Freya, aged 6, asks the nurse whether her blood test will hurt. Which reply is most appropriate?
o: "Big girls like you don't cry, so you will be fine."
"You might feel a quick sharp pinch; squeeze my hand."
"It won't hurt if you are brave and keep nice and still."
"Don't worry about that; let's talk about something nice."
4.w: Honest, age-appropriate language about what will be felt, with a coping strategy such as squeezing a hand, maintains trust and helps the child cope. False reassurance or shaming undermines trust and future cooperation (AnnexA.3.7; P4.3).

n.0: Shaming her for possible tears increases distress and is not therapeutic.
n.2: Promising no pain is untrue and links pain with not being brave.
n.3: Avoiding the question leaves her worried and does not help her cope.

4.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
4.q: Tia, aged 3, is critically unwell with pneumonia and receiving oxygen through a face mask. Her saturations are 100%. What saturation target should the nurse aim for?
4.w: RCUK 2025 paediatric guidance: target SpO2 of 94 to 98% in critical illness and after return of spontaneous circulation, avoiding both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia. Oxygen should be titrated down to keep within this range.

n.0: Aiming for 100% risks hyperoxaemia; oxygen should be titrated to 94 to 98%.
n.1: 92 to 96% is not the RCUK paediatric target and allows lower saturations than advised.
n.2: 88 to 92% is a target for adults at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, not for a critically ill child.

4.q: Hilda, 74, has had a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding after a stroke. You aspirate gastric contents and test them on CE-marked pH paper. Which reading confirms gastric placement so that feeding can start?
o: pH 8.5 or above
pH 6.0 or below
pH 7.0 or above
pH 5.5 or below
4.w: NICE CG32: gastric tube position is confirmed by pH 5.5 or below on pH paper. Position must be confirmed after placement and before each use by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary (rec 1.7.17).

n.0: pH 8.5 is alkaline and suggests a non-gastric position.
n.1: pH 6.0 is above the 5.5 threshold and does not confirm gastric placement.
n.2: pH 7 or above may indicate the tube is in the lung or intestine.

4.q: At a ward meeting, a healthcare assistant says that safeguarding children is the job of social services and that hospital staff only treat injuries. The children's nurse wants to correct this using the relevant statute. Which statement is accurate?
o: NHS trusts must refer every child who attends with any injury to children's social care under s17
NHS trusts must carry out child protection investigations themselves under section 47 of the Children Act 1989
NHS trusts lead local safeguarding arrangements in place of the police under the Children Act 2004
NHS trusts must arrange their functions to safeguard and promote children's welfare (Children Act 2004 s11)
4.w: Section 11 of the Children Act 2004 requires named bodies, including NHS trusts and ICBs, to make arrangements to ensure their functions are discharged having regard to the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children.

n.0: Section 17 concerns services for children in need; there is no duty to refer every injured child, only those where there are concerns.
n.1: Section 47 enquiries are the local authority's duty; health staff contribute information but do not lead them.
n.2: The three statutory safeguarding partners are the local authority, the ICB and the chief officer of police; trusts are not partners and do not replace the police.

4.q: Lucy is formula feeding her 2-week-old son and shows the nurse how she makes up feeds: she fills the bottle with cooled boiled water from a jug left out overnight, then adds the powder. What should the nurse advise?
o: Add the powder first, then fill with cold tap water
Use bottled mineral water at room temperature for each feed
Use cooled boiled water from the jug if it was boiled within 24 hours
Use freshly boiled water left no more than 30 minutes, at 70°C or above
4.w: NHS formula preparation guidance: make up each feed with freshly boiled water left to cool for no more than 30 minutes so it is at least 70°C, which kills bacteria such as Cronobacter in the powder. Water first, then powder.

n.0: Cold tap water does not make the powder safe, and adding powder first gives an inaccurate concentration.
n.1: Bottled mineral water can contain high sodium and is not hot enough to make the powder safe.
n.2: Water that has stood overnight is below 70°C and will not kill bacteria in the powder.

4.q: Ruby, 2, wakes at night with a barking cough and noisy breathing when she is upset. At rest in the emergency department she has no stridor, no recession and is alert and playing. Which treatment does NICE CKS recommend?
o: Steam inhalation at home before bedtime
A five-day course of oral amoxicillin
A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg
Nebulised adrenaline before discharge home
4.w: NICE CKS Croup (last revised May 2022): prescribe a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg to be taken immediately for mild croup, and advise that symptoms usually resolve within 48 hours.

n.0: Steam is not recommended for croup; it is ineffective and risks scalds.
n.1: Croup is viral, so antibiotics are not indicated.
n.3: Nebulised adrenaline is for moderate to severe croup needing admission; Ruby has mild croup.

4.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first approach?
o: Tell him firmly to sit down and stop shouting
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen to him
Call security to restrain him before he leaves
Stand in the doorway to block his exit from the ward
4.w: Annexe A 3.5: de-escalation strategies and techniques. Code 13.4 personal safety; calm voice, open posture and listening come before restrictive interventions.

n.0: Commands can escalate agitation; de-escalation uses calm listening.
n.2: Restraint is a last resort; de-escalation should be tried first.
n.3: Blocking his exit increases risk and may escalate the situation.

4.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
4.q: Kai, aged 2, is 4 hours after hernia repair. He is grimacing, kicking, arching, crying steadily and hard to console. His FLACC score is 8. Analgesia is prescribed. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck the FLACC score in 4 hours before taking action
Give the prescribed analgesia and reassess once it has had time to work
Use distraction and comfort measures and avoid medicines at his age
Ask his parents to settle him and record the score as behaviour
4.w: Two steps: interpret, then act. A FLACC score of 7 to 10 indicates severe pain. The nurse should give the prescribed analgesia promptly, use comfort and distraction alongside, and reassess pain after the medicine has had time to work to judge whether it is effective (AnnexB.3.5; P4.8).

n.0: Waiting 4 hours leaves severe pain untreated.
n.2: Distraction helps, but severe post-operative pain needs analgesia; age 2 is no reason to withhold prescribed medicines.
n.3: Labelling the score as behaviour ignores severe pain that needs treatment.

4.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
4.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

4.q: Noah, 5 months, has unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot and is awaiting surgery. While crying during a blood test he becomes deeply blue, breathes fast and then becomes limp. What should the nurse do first?
o: Sit him upright and encourage him to keep crying
Lie him flat and raise his legs on a pillow
Calm him and hold him with his knees drawn up to his chest
Give a rapid bolus of IV fluid before calling for help
4.w: A hypercyanotic (tet) spell: crying increases right-to-left shunting. First aid is to calm the infant and place him in the knee-chest position, which raises systemic vascular resistance and pulmonary blood flow; then give oxygen and call for urgent medical help.

n.0: Continued crying worsens the shunt and cyanosis.
n.1: Lying flat with legs raised does not increase systemic resistance in the way the knee-chest position does.
n.3: Fluids may be prescribed by the medical team, but positioning and calling for help come first.

4.q: Ayesha, 5, weighs 18 kg and needs a red cell transfusion. The junior doctor writes the prescription as '1 unit red cells'. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the unit and record the volume given afterwards
Ask for it to be rewritten as a volume in millilitres
Give half the unit and return the rest to the laboratory
Give the whole unit, as one unit is the smallest available
4.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) section 6.1.2: to prevent over-transfusion, paediatric blood components are prescribed in millilitres rather than units (unless a local risk-assessed protocol allows units for larger, older children), with the volume calculated from weight.

n.0: Recording afterwards does not prevent over-transfusion; the volume must be prescribed first.
n.2: The nurse cannot decide the volume; the prescriber must calculate and prescribe it in mL.
n.3: A whole adult unit (about 270 mL) may be about 15 mL/kg or more for an 18 kg child without any calculation; the prescription must state a volume.

4.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
4.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

4.q: Kwame, 64, has motor neurone disease and is now thought to be in his last days. The team are deciding who should talk with him about his prognosis. He knows the ward sister well and trusts her, and she has experience of these conversations. According to NICE NG31, what should guide the choice of professional?
o: Their seniority and grade within the treating medical team
Which professional the family would prefer to lead the conversation
Which professional first made the diagnosis of his condition
Their competence and confidence, and their rapport with the person
4.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.2.2: identify the most appropriate available multiprofessional team member to explain the dying person's prognosis, based on the professional's competence and confidence and their rapport with the person.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.2.2 does not base the choice on grade; a senior doctor without rapport may not be the most appropriate person.
n.1: Family views matter, but NG31 rec 1.2.2 bases the choice on the professional's competence, confidence and rapport with the person.
n.2: The diagnosing clinician is not the NG31 criterion; competence, confidence and rapport are.

4.q: Ruth, 85, has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible but no bone, tendon or muscle is exposed. Using the international NPIAP-EPUAP classification, which category is this?
o: Category 2
Suspected deep tissue injury
Category 3
Category 4
4.w: NPIAP-EPUAP classification (used per NICE CG179): category 3 is full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible but bone, tendon or muscle not exposed. Category 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle; category 2 is partial-thickness loss.

n.0: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss of dermis, such as a shallow open wound or blister.
n.1: Suspected deep tissue injury is an area of purple or maroon intact skin or a blood-filled blister.
n.3: Category 4 involves exposed bone, tendon or muscle.

4.q: Lily, 6, has a life-limiting neurodegenerative condition. A newly qualified nurse sees 'Advance Care Plan' in her notes and assumes this means Lily is not for resuscitation. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: An Advance Care Plan is the same document as a DNACPR order
An Advance Care Plan is a legal order made by the family court
An Advance Care Plan applies once Lily is in the last days of life
An Advance Care Plan covers wishes and care; it is not a DNACPR order
4.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.14: all children with life-limiting conditions should have an Advance Care Plan in their record (wishes, place of care, management of life-threatening events) and it should not be confused with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order. Resuscitate unless a DNACPR order is in place.

n.0: NG61 says the Advance Care Plan should not be confused with a DNACPR order.
n.1: An Advance Care Plan is agreed with the child and family and the team, not made by a court.
n.2: Advance Care Planning starts early and is reviewed regularly, not only in the last days.

4.q: Kerry, 35, smokes 20 cigarettes a day. She says, "I know I should stop, but it's the only thing that calms me." Which response reflects motivational interviewing?
o: "Here is a leaflet listing all the risks of smoking."
"You must stop smoking now for the sake of your long-term health."
"What are the good and less good things about smoking for you?"
"Let's agree a date this week when you will stop."
4.w: Annexe A 3.1: motivational interview techniques. MI explores ambivalence through open questions and reflection rather than persuasion.

n.0: Giving information without exploring her views is not MI.
n.1: Direct persuasion tends to increase resistance; MI explores ambivalence.
n.3: Setting a date before exploring her ambivalence skips the MI process.

4.q: Under NICE guidance on violence and aggression (NG10), when may manual restraint be used in a health setting?
o: As the first response whenever a person raises their voice
As a last resort when de-escalation fails and harm is likely
As a routine measure to give medicines a person has refused
As a punishment for breaking ward rules on two occasions
4.w: NICE NG10 and Annexe B 2.17: restrictive interventions are used as a last resort, after de-escalation and other strategies fail, when there is a real risk of harm, and must be proportionate and for the shortest time possible.

n.0: Raised voices call for de-escalation, not restraint.
n.2: Restraint is not a routine method of giving refused medicines; covert or compulsory treatment has its own legal safeguards.
n.3: Restraint is never punitive; this would breach human rights and the Code.

4.q: Fatima, 45, is admitted for an elective procedure. She asks that only female staff provide her intimate personal care because of her religious beliefs. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree to her request if her religion is recorded on the notes
Arrange female staff for her personal care where possible
Explain that personal care will be given by whoever is on duty that shift
Ask her to bring a female relative to give her personal care
4.w: Proficiency P1.14: provide non-discriminatory, person-centred, sensitive care reflecting people's values, beliefs and culture. Code 1.3 and 2.4; religion or belief is a protected characteristic (Equality Act s4).

n.0: Respecting a preference does not depend on paperwork; it should be accommodated where possible now.
n.2: This disregards her beliefs; P1.14 requires care that reflects people's values, beliefs and culture.
n.3: This shifts care onto family and may not be safe or what she wants.

4.q: Mrs Patel, 58, is two days after bowel surgery. Her NEWS2 is 4. On assessment the nurse notices her knees are mottled and her lips look slightly blue. How should these findings change the nurse's view of her risk?
o: Her NEWS2 of 4 shows low risk, so routine monitoring is enough
They are expected after surgery and do not change her risk
They should be rechecked once her NEWS2 rises to 5 or more
She may be at higher risk than her NEWS2 score suggests
4.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider a higher risk of severe illness or death from sepsis than NEWS2 suggests if the person has a mottled or ashen appearance or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue. These are signs of physical ill health (Annexe B 1.2.1) needing urgent escalation.

n.0: NG253 says these signs indicate higher risk than the score alone suggests.
n.1: Mottling and cyanosis are not normal post-operative findings.
n.2: Waiting for the score to rise delays escalation of signs that already indicate higher risk.

4.q: Fred, 72, has crusting around both eyelids after a viral illness. You are asked to clean his eyes. Which technique is correct?
o: Use one swab for each eye, wiping back and forth across the lid
Use one swab for both eyes, wiping from outer to inner corner
Use a fresh swab for each eye, wiping from inner to outer corner
Use a dry cotton bud inside the lower lid to remove crusts
4.w: Eye care principles: use sterile saline and a separate swab for each eye, wiping once from the inner canthus outward, so that debris and infection are not carried into the tear duct or the other eye (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wiping back and forth reintroduces debris to the eye.
n.1: Sharing a swab and wiping inward risks cross-infection and moving debris into the tear duct.
n.3: Inserting a cotton bud inside the lid risks corneal injury.

5.q: A health visitor is planning the new birth review for baby Theo, born 5 days ago. Which approach best meets the Healthy Child Programme expectations?
o: A telephone call from the named health visitor within 6 weeks
A clinic appointment with any available team member at 4 weeks
A group session at the children's centre at 6 to 8 weeks
A home visit by the named health visitor within the first 2 weeks
5.w: The new birth review takes place in the first 2 weeks (usually 10 to 14 days). The antenatal, new birth and 6 to 8 week reviews should be delivered face to face in the home by a health visitor, and named health visitors should deliver the statutory reviews (Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme, Part 2, 2026; NHS, baby reviews).

n.0: A telephone call does not meet the face-to-face home expectation, and 6 weeks is too late for this review.
n.1: A clinic appointment at 4 weeks is outside the timing and setting for the new birth review.
n.2: A group session at 6 to 8 weeks is not the individual new birth review.

5.q: A student nurse is about to auscultate the chest of Mrs Hall, 68, who has a productive cough. Which technique should the supervising nurse advise?
o: Listen at one point on each side for a few seconds
Listen over her clothing to protect her dignity
Listen at the front of the chest, which is enough for a review
Sit her upright and compare each side at matching points
5.w: Chest auscultation (Annexe B 2.8) is done with the person upright where possible, the stethoscope on bare skin, comparing left with right at matching points front and back so that differences in air entry and added sounds can be detected.

n.0: A single point per side cannot detect localised changes such as basal crackles.
n.1: Clothing muffles and distorts breath sounds; dignity is maintained in other ways.
n.2: The bases are best heard from the back, so front-only listening misses findings.

5.q: Lauren is leading a test of a new structured handover sheet on one night shift. The test has finished and she is now comparing the number of omitted items with what the team predicted. Which stage of the PDSA cycle is this?
o: Plan
Act
Do
Study
5.w: In Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA), Plan sets the objective and predictions, Do carries out the test and collects data, Study analyses the results and compares them with predictions, and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (NHS England PDSA guidance; P6.4).

n.0: Plan is where the objective, prediction and data collection are agreed before the test.
n.1: Act follows Study and decides what to do next with the change.
n.2: Do is the stage of carrying out the test and recording data and observations.

5.q: Zainab, 14, is being exploited by a gang who meet her outside school and at a shopping centre. Her parents have reported her missing each time and are desperate to protect her. How does Working Together 2026 describe this type of harm and the parents' role?
o: Peer-on-peer bullying, managed by the school
Extra-familial harm, with parents as partners in protecting her
Intra-familial harm, with parents as the focus of enquiries
Neglect, as her parents are unable to keep her safe
5.w: Working Together 2026 describes extra-familial harm as harm occurring outside the home, for example in peer groups, schools, shopping centres and online. Parents are often not the source of risk and should be worked with as partners in protecting the child.

n.0: Gang exploitation is exploitation, not bullying.
n.2: The risk comes from outside the family; parents are not the source of harm.
n.3: Her parents are actively trying to protect her, so neglect does not fit.

5.q: Mr Price, 69, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and depression. He is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on air and he is struggling to finish sentences; his capillary glucose is 11.2 mmol/L. Which need should the nurse prioritise first?
o: His dietary intake and weight
His raised blood glucose
His low mood and anxiety
His breathing and oxygenation
5.w: When prioritising care for a person with comorbidities (P3.13), immediate threats to life come first. Severe hypoxaemia and breathlessness are an airway and breathing priority needing escalation and oxygen to a prescribed target; the other needs are addressed once he is stable.

n.0: Nutrition is important for recovery but is not the immediate priority.
n.1: A glucose of 11.2 mmol/L needs monitoring but is not an immediate threat compared with hypoxaemia.
n.2: His mood matters but is not the most urgent need while he is hypoxic.

5.q: Fatima, 57, is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has no history of lung disease and her SpO2 is 90% on air. What target oxygen saturation range should be prescribed?
5.w: BTS oxygen guideline and NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.10.1: the target for most acutely ill adults is 94-98%.

n.0: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some people with COPD.
n.2: 92-96% is not the standard BTS adult target range.
n.3: Aiming for 98-100% risks hyperoxaemia; BTS notes higher saturations are associated with harm.

5.q: Sam, 15, is assessed as competent and is receiving treatment for an eating disorder. His father asks the nurse for a copy of Sam's clinical notes. Sam has said he does not want his parents to read them, although he is happy for his care plan to be discussed with them. What should the nurse do?
o: Release the notes once the father submits a written request
Refuse to discuss any aspect of Sam's care with his father
Ask for Sam's views, as a competent young person decides on access
Release the notes, as his father holds parental responsibility
5.w: A competent young person's confidential information is generally disclosed only with their agreement. Sam's views on access to his records should be sought and respected, while sharing what he agrees to (his care plan) to support family involvement, a key part of eating disorder care.

n.0: A written request does not change whose consent is needed.
n.1: Sam agrees to his care plan being discussed; refusing all contact would undermine family-based treatment.
n.3: Parental responsibility does not override a competent young person's confidentiality.

5.q: Amira, 12, is in hospital after an appendicectomy. She shows the nurse messages from someone she met in an online game who says he is 14, asks her to keep their chats secret, move to a private app and send photos in her pyjamas. What should the nurse do?
o: Advise Amira to block the contact and reassure her parents
Tell Amira to stop using online games while in hospital
Recognise possible grooming and follow safeguarding procedures
Ask the contact directly through the app to confirm his age
5.w: Requests for secrecy, moving to a private platform and requests for images are signs of online grooming, which Working Together 2026 includes within child sexual abuse. The nurse should follow safeguarding procedures, preserve the messages and involve police (for example via a CEOP report) as advised.

n.0: Blocking the contact loses evidence and does not address possible abuse of Amira or others.
n.1: Restricting game use does not protect her or address the grooming.
n.3: Contacting the suspect could alert him and is not a nurse's role.

5.q: Theo, 18 months, has croup. He now has stridor at rest, moderate sternal recession and is agitated. His mother asks the nurse to look in his throat to see what is causing the noise. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Take a throat swab now to check for a bacterial infection
Avoid examining his throat; keep him calm on his mother's lap
Use a tongue depressor quickly while his mother holds him still
Lie him flat on the trolley to examine his throat more easily
5.w: NICE CKS Croup (last revised May 2022) and NHS croup advice: keep the child calm and upright; do not examine the throat, which can precipitate complete obstruction (and epiglottitis must be considered). Stridor at rest with recession is moderate croup needing admission.

n.0: Throat swabbing distresses the child and risks obstruction; croup is viral and needs no swab.
n.2: A tongue depressor can trigger laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction in a child with stridor.
n.3: Lying flat and distress worsen airway obstruction; the child should stay upright and calm.

5.q: In October 2026 a community children's nurse in England is worried that Noah, 7, is often hungry and tired at clinic. She plans to share this with his school's designated safeguarding lead so they can offer support. Noah's mother refuses consent. What is the correct position?
o: The nurse must wait until concerns reach the threshold for a referral
The nurse should share the information, as consent is not required under s16LA
The nurse needs the mother's consent before sharing, as there is no s47 enquiry
The nurse can share once a court has authorised disclosure to the school
5.w: From 30 September 2026, s16LA of the Children Act 2004 requires relevant persons to share information that may help another relevant person safeguard or promote a child's welfare. Consent is not required and lack of consent is not a reason to withhold (statutory guidance, September 2026). The nurse should usually tell the mother what is being shared and why, unless that would put Noah at risk.

n.0: No statutory threshold has to be met before the duty applies; it covers early help and unmet needs.
n.2: Consent is not required under the duty, and sharing is not limited to s47 enquiries.
n.3: No court authorisation is needed; the duty itself requires sharing.

5.q: Derek, 59, has a history of alcohol misuse. He has eaten almost nothing for 7 days and his BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Nutrition support is planned. Using NICE CG32 criteria, what is his refeeding risk and the appropriate starting approach?
o: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Low risk: start at full requirements of 25-35 kcal/kg/day
Moderate risk: start at 50% of requirements without thiamin
No risk: offer normal ward meals without any monitoring
5.w: NICE CG32: high refeeding risk includes two or more of BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little or no intake for over 5 days, or alcohol misuse. Derek has three. Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly, and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days, with electrolyte monitoring.

n.1: Full requirements in a high-risk person can precipitate refeeding syndrome.
n.2: He meets the high-risk criteria, and thiamin is needed.
n.3: Unmonitored feeding ignores his high refeeding risk.

5.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
5.q: Ella, aged 10, has abdominal pain after surgery. She says her pain is '7 out of 10', but her mother thinks she is exaggerating because she is chatting with friends. What should the nurse do?
o: Wait until Ella looks distressed before giving analgesia
Score Ella's pain on the FLACC scale instead
Use the mother's estimate, because she knows Ella best
Accept Ella's self-report and act on it, then reassess
5.w: Self-report is the preferred measure of pain when a child can give it; children may use distraction or socialising to cope, so behaviour can underestimate pain. The nurse should believe and act on Ella's score, give prescribed analgesia and reassess (P4.8; AnnexB.3.5).

n.0: Waiting for visible distress leaves pain untreated and ignores her report.
n.1: FLACC is for children who cannot self-report and is validated up to 7 years.
n.2: Parents' views help, but a capable child's own report takes priority.

5.q: Ella, aged 6, is reviewed for poor growth. Her BMI is calculated and plotted on the BMI centile chart; it lies below the 0.4th centile. Her parents are both of average height. What does this finding suggest, and what is needed?
o: A small build that needs no intervention given average parental height
Probable undernutrition that needs assessment and intervention
A primary growth disorder that needs growth hormone treatment
Normal variation that should be rechecked in 12 months
5.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.4: in a child over 2 years, a BMI below the 2nd centile may reflect undernutrition or a small build, but a BMI below the 0.4th centile suggests probable undernutrition that needs assessment and intervention.

n.0: A small build can explain a BMI below the 2nd centile, but below the 0.4th centile NICE says undernutrition is probable.
n.2: A low BMI points to undernutrition; growth disorders are suggested by low height compared with mid-parental height, and treatment would follow specialist diagnosis.
n.3: A BMI below the 0.4th centile needs action now, not a recheck in a year.

5.q: At the bedside check, the nurse notices that the compatibility label on a unit of red cells for Catherine, 60, reads 'Catherine Smyth', while her wristband reads 'Catherine Smith'. Her date of birth and hospital number match. What should the nurse do?
o: Proceed, as the date of birth and hospital number both match
Do not start, and contact the transfusion laboratory to resolve it
Ask a second nurse to countersign the discrepancy and proceed
Correct the spelling on the wristband and then proceed
5.w: BSH (2017): all identifiers on the wristband and the component label must match exactly at the bedside; any discrepancy means the component is not given until resolved with the transfusion laboratory. Wrong component transfused is a leading SHOT-reported error.

n.0: Partial matches are not acceptable; every identifier must match.
n.2: A second signature does not resolve a mismatch in identifiers.
n.3: Changing the wristband to fit the unit conceals the discrepancy and is unsafe.

5.q: A surgical registrar asks Priya, a registered nurse, to obtain Mrs Kaur's signature on a consent form for a laparoscopic procedure tomorrow. Priya has never seen this operation and does not know its specific risks or alternatives. What should Priya do?
o: Read the consent form aloud and witness Mrs Kaur's signature
Decline and ask the registrar to take consent from Mrs Kaur
Ask Mrs Kaur whether she has any questions before she signs
Obtain the signature and ask the registrar to explain risks later
5.w: Valid consent needs the person to be informed of material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 13 requires nurses to work within the limits of their competence, asking a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it (13.3). Priya cannot give that information, so the clinician who can should seek consent.

n.0: Reading the form does not allow Priya to answer questions about risks and alternatives she does not know.
n.2: Priya could not answer Mrs Kaur's questions about this operation's risks, so her consent would not be properly informed.
n.3: A signature obtained before the risks are explained does not show informed consent; the form is evidence, not consent itself.

5.q: On a children's ward, a nurse notices that the family of Marius, 6, who are Roma, are repeatedly asked to leave at night while other parents are allowed to stay at the bedside. No clinical reason is recorded. The nurse raises a concern. Which article of the Human Rights Act 1998 is engaged together with Article 8?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair hearing in court
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security of person
5.w: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights. Treating one family differently because of ethnicity, in relation to family life (Article 8), engages Articles 14 and 8 together. The nurse should also challenge discrimination under the Code and the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings in legal proceedings.
n.1: Article 9 concerns belief and religion; the issue is unequal treatment based on ethnicity.
n.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, which is not described.

5.q: Ruby, 7 months, has anaemia and needs her first red cell transfusion. A newly qualified nurse asks which type of component the laboratory will issue for a child of her age. What does BSH recommend?
o: Red cells with neonatal or infant specification
A standard adult unit with half removed on the ward
Platelets with neonatal or infant specification
A standard adult unit, as she is older than 4 months
5.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline): recipients under 1 year should be transfused with components of neonatal or infant specification (1C), such as paediatric 'paedipacks' or infant large-volume red cells.

n.1: Components are not split on the ward; the laboratory supplies suitable paediatric packs.
n.2: Platelets do not treat anaemia; red cells are needed.
n.3: The neonatal or infant specification applies to all recipients under 1 year, not just under 4 months.

5.q: Ellie qualified six weeks ago. At the start of a night shift she is told she will be the only registered nurse for 28 patients on an unfamiliar ward, and has never taken charge. What should she do first?
o: Accept the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Raise her concerns at once with the person in charge and record it
Leave the ward and return to her own ward for safety
Accept the shift and phone her own ward manager at home
5.w: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 and NMC Raising concerns guidance support escalation and keeping a record.

n.0: Delaying until the morning leaves patients at risk; Code 16.2 requires her to raise concerns immediately.
n.2: Leaving abandons patients; she must raise the concern so safe cover is arranged.
n.3: Her absent manager cannot change tonight's staffing; the site lead or person in charge must be told now.

5.q: After the unexpected death of a young patient, several members of the ward team seem shaken. The ward manager wants to support the team's resilience. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Offer the team extra shifts to keep them occupied
Ask each nurse to write a statement about what went wrong
Encourage the team to move on and focus on the next shift
Hold a supportive debrief and signpost wellbeing services
5.w: Proficiency P6.11: accept and manage uncertainty and develop resilience in self and others. Code 8.7 support colleagues; Code 25.2 support staff you are responsible for.

n.0: More shifts may increase fatigue and do not address distress.
n.1: Statements may be needed for review, but they do not address the team's wellbeing.
n.2: This dismisses the emotional impact and misses the chance to support resilience.

5.q: On a home visit, community nurse Faye watches Mrs Dobson give her husband his insulin. She injects into the same small area of his abdomen each time and Faye notices lumpy skin there. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to review the insulin dose at the next appointment
Show her how to rotate sites, observe her practice and document it
Take over all of Mr Dobson's insulin injections from now on
Leave an injection technique leaflet for Mrs Dobson to read
5.w: Nurses monitor and evaluate the quality of care delivered by lay carers (P5.7). Teaching site rotation, observing Mrs Dobson's technique and recording the plan supports safe care and independence; lumpy injection sites can alter insulin absorption.

n.0: Dose review may be needed later, but the technique problem must be addressed directly now.
n.2: Taking over removes the couple's independence when the issue can be corrected by teaching.
n.3: A leaflet without demonstration and observation does not confirm the technique has changed.

5.q: A registered nurse on a surgical ward calls in sick. The bed manager suggests replacing her with an extra healthcare assistant because the total number of staff on shift would stay the same. Six patients on the ward have intravenous antibiotics due. What is the best response from the nurse in charge?
o: Accept the healthcare assistant, as total staff numbers meet the ward's planned establishment
Ask the healthcare assistant to give the IV antibiotics under her direct supervision
Accept the healthcare assistant and give all six patients' IV antibiotics herself
Explain that registered nurse tasks cannot be covered and escalate the skill mix gap
5.w: Safety depends on skill mix as well as numbers (P6.2; NICE SG1 Box 1 takes skill mix into account). Registered nurse tasks such as IV medicines and assessment cannot be delegated to a healthcare assistant (Code 11.1), so the gap must be escalated.

n.0: Matching headcount ignores the registered nurse time that patients' needs require.
n.1: IV antibiotic administration is outside a healthcare assistant's role; supervision does not make delegation appropriate.
n.2: Taking on extra IV work on top of her own role risks delayed doses elsewhere and hides the shortfall.

5.q: Leah sees that a colleague has posted a joke on a public social media page about 'the difficult patient in bed 4', with enough detail for others on the ward to identify the patient. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Message the colleague privately and take no further action
Report the post to the social media platform as offensive
Raise it with her manager through the trust's concern channels
Reply publicly to the post telling the colleague to delete it
5.w: NMC social media guidance: concerns about colleagues' inappropriate use of social media should be raised through the proper channels in line with Raising concerns guidance. Code 5.1, 16.1, 20.10.

n.0: A private word may be reasonable first, but identifiable patient information online is a confidentiality breach that needs escalating.
n.1: Platform reporting may remove the post but does not address the professional concern locally.
n.3: Engaging publicly spreads the content further; NMC guidance points to raising concerns through proper channels.

5.q: Dorothy, 86, has advanced dementia. For three days she has spat out her anticonvulsant and pushed staff away at medicine rounds. Her son suggests hiding it in her tea. What is the nurse's most appropriate first step?
o: Assess her capacity to make this specific decision about the medicine
Arrange for the medicine to be given by injection instead
Hide the medicine in her tea, as she has a diagnosis of dementia
Stop the anticonvulsant, as she is repeatedly refusing it
5.w: The MCA 2005 (ss1-3) requires a capacity assessment that is decision-specific and time-specific; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. Only if she lacks capacity can a best interests decision about covert administration follow (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21).

n.1: Changing the route needs a prescriber and does not address capacity or consent.
n.2: A diagnosis does not prove lack of capacity (MCA s2(3)); covert use also needs a best interests process.
n.3: Stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures; the refusal needs assessment, not unilateral cessation.

5.q: Kyle, a staff nurse, notices that Bev, a healthcare assistant, has become quiet and withdrawn since a relative criticised her in front of colleagues. Bev's care remains of a good standard. What is the most appropriate way for Kyle to support and motivate her?
o: Give Bev lighter tasks for the next few shifts so that she can recover
Speak with Bev privately, acknowledge her good care and ask how she is
Report Bev's change in mood to the ward manager for a formal welfare review
Tell Bev that complaints are part of the job and she should not take it personally
5.w: Leaders guide, support and motivate others (P5.6) and the Code asks registrants to work cooperatively and support the staff they are responsible for (Code 8, 25.2). Specific recognition and a private, supportive conversation help restore confidence and show that her work is valued.

n.0: Changing her work without discussion may suggest a lack of confidence in her.
n.2: Escalating to a formal process before talking with her is disproportionate.
n.3: Dismissing her feelings is unsupportive and unlikely to restore motivation.

5.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
5.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

5.q: A nurse on an intensive care unit in England is caring for four patients for whom organ donation after death may be possible. None has recorded a decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. Which patient is excluded from deemed consent?
o: Leah, 30, who had not discussed donation with her family
Amy, 17, a student who has lived in England all her life
Victor, 75, who completed treatment for bowel cancer last year
Paul, 60, who moved to England from Wales three years ago
5.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England: the opt-out law does not apply to people under 18, people who lack capacity to understand the arrangements for a significant period before death, visitors and people not living in England voluntarily, or people who lived in England for less than 12 months before their death.

n.0: Not having discussed donation does not exclude an adult; her family are approached about any known views.
n.2: Medical history affects suitability, not whether deemed consent applies; age 75 is not an exclusion.
n.3: He has lived in England for more than 12 months and is an adult, so he is not in an excluded group.

5.q: Marion, 85, lives in a care home and has had diarrhoea for 3 days. Staff say she has been drinking very little and seems more tired than usual. You are assessing her hydration status on admission. Which combination of findings most suggests dehydration?
o: Ankle oedema, crackles in the lungs and weight gain
Dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and tachycardia
Moist mouth, pale dilute urine and normal skin turgor
Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and polyuria
5.w: Dehydration commonly presents with dry mucous membranes, thirst, reduced and concentrated urine, tachycardia and postural hypotension (Annexe B 5.4). CG174 indicators of fluid need include HR over 90 and systolic under 100.

n.0: Oedema, crackles and weight gain suggest fluid overload.
n.2: A moist mouth and pale dilute urine suggest adequate hydration.
n.3: Raised BP and bounding pulse do not indicate dehydration.

5.q: Nadia, 34, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her carer says she eats best with familiar foods, small portions and verbal prompting. Ward staff often place her tray and leave. Her intake is now poor. What is the best action?
o: Use the carer's advice in her plan and support her at meals
Ask the carer to come in at every mealtime to feed her
Refer her for a swallowing assessment before her next meal
Start oral supplements and continue placing her tray
5.w: Annexe B 5.3 and the Equality Act 2010 s20: make reasonable adjustments and give assistance with eating. Personalising meals and providing prompting and support is the nursing team's responsibility and addresses the cause of her poor intake.

n.1: Carers may help, but meeting her nutritional needs remains the ward's responsibility.
n.2: There is no indication of a swallowing problem; the issue is support with eating.
n.3: Supplements do not address the lack of support at mealtimes.

5.q: Ken, 63, has interrupted sutures in a healing abdominal wound. The plan says to remove them today. When you remove the first two alternate sutures, the wound edges begin to gape. What should you do?
o: Remove all remaining sutures and apply adhesive strips
Remove the rest and redress the wound in 24 hours
Stop, leave the other sutures and inform the surgeons
Remove the rest and apply a tight pressure bandage
5.w: Removing alternate sutures first allows the wound to be checked for adequate healing. If the edges separate, stop, leave the remaining sutures in place, support the wound and inform the team for review (Annexe B 4.6).

n.0: Removing all sutures from a gaping wound risks dehiscence.
n.1: Removing the remaining sutures risks wound dehiscence.
n.3: A pressure bandage does not replace adequate wound closure.

5.q: Amira, 13, is going home after an overdose of her mother's sertraline tablets. She has a safety plan agreed with the CAMHS team. Her mother asks what she can do at home to help keep Amira safe. What should the nurse advise?
o: Lock away or remove medicines and other means Amira could use
Check Amira's bedroom every 15 minutes through the night
Keep Amira off school until her CAMHS follow-up
Avoid talking with Amira about her self-harm to prevent ideas
5.w: NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022): the safety plan should establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them with the person and family; families are given information on reducing access to means and on getting help in a crisis.

n.1: Fifteen-minute night checks are not practical home advice and do not remove access to means.
n.2: Keeping her off school is not part of NG225 safety planning and can increase isolation.
n.3: Talking openly about self-harm does not plant ideas; avoiding it can increase isolation.

5.q: Mrs Hart, 83, has dementia and lacks capacity. For three nights she has called out repeatedly, disturbing other patients. A colleague suggests asking for regular night-time lorazepam 'so everyone gets some sleep'. She has not been reviewed for pain or constipation. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Move her to a side room and close the door at night
Assess for pain, constipation and delirium before considering medication
Request regular lorazepam, as other patients on the bay also need sleep
Give PRN lorazepam tonight and review tomorrow whether it helped her
5.w: Using sedation to control behaviour for others' convenience is chemical restraint and must be in her best interests and the least restrictive option (MCA s1(5)-(6)). NICE NG97 rec 1.7.1: before any treatment for distress in dementia, assess for and address causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care, so she should be assessed first.

n.0: Isolating her behind a closed door is restrictive and does not address the cause of her distress.
n.2: Medication for the benefit of others is not in her best interests and is a restrictive practice.
n.3: Giving sedation before assessing for treatable causes skips the least restrictive approach.

5.q: Maeve, 79, has dementia and lacks capacity. When she had capacity she made a written, signed and witnessed advance decision refusing antipsychotic medication. The team confirms it is valid and applicable. She is now refusing a newly prescribed antipsychotic. Her family ask for it to be given covertly. What applies?
o: Respect the advance decision and do not give the antipsychotic
Give it covertly, as a best interests meeting overrides the advance decision
Give it covertly until a court decides on the advance decision
Give it covertly if her family and the GP both agree
5.w: Under the MCA 2005 ss24-26, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same effect as a capacitous refusal and binds professionals. Best interests decisions cannot override it, so the antipsychotic cannot be given, covertly or otherwise.

n.1: A best interests decision cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision.
n.2: Treatment may be given to prevent serious deterioration while a court decides on validity, but here validity is confirmed.
n.3: Family and GP agreement does not override a binding advance refusal.

5.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
5.q: Ruby, aged 6, has suspected sepsis with high risk criteria. Her venous lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. She has had antibiotics. What else does NICE NG254 recommend?
o: Consider a fluid bolus and recheck her lactate in 4 hours
Give oral fluids and repeat her observations every hour
Start maintenance fluids and review on the next ward round
Give a fluid bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care
5.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.7.5: for children under 12 with suspected sepsis, any high risk criteria and lactate over 4 mmol/L, give an IV fluid bolus without delay (within 1 hour) and refer to a critical care specialist or team to review management, including central access and inotropes.

n.0: 'Consider a bolus' applies when lactate is below 2 mmol/L; above 4, a bolus is given and critical care involved.
n.1: Oral fluids are not adequate resuscitation for a child with high risk sepsis and a raised lactate.
n.2: Maintenance fluids do not treat shock, and waiting for a ward round delays critical care.

5.q: A nurse is deciding whether to share information about Yasmin, 13, who is living in a refuge with her mother after fleeing domestic abuse. Under the s16LA statutory guidance, in which circumstance may the nurse decide not to share particular information?
o: When Yasmin's father, who has parental responsibility, objects
When the family has not given consent to the sharing
When sharing would be more detrimental to Yasmin than not sharing
When the nurse feels uncomfortable about the possible consequences
5.w: The duty does not apply in extremely limited circumstances where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing, for example where disclosing a refuge address would place the child at immediate risk (statutory guidance, Limitation: detriment to the child). Other relevant information should still be shared and the decision recorded.

n.0: Parental objection is not a reason to withhold under the duty.
n.1: Lack of consent is expressly not a reason to withhold.
n.3: Practitioner discomfort is not a reason to withhold; the guidance says seek prompt advice instead.

5.q: Valerie, 58, is choking in a hospital café. She cannot cough, speak or breathe but remains conscious. Help has been called. What should you do first?
o: Perform a blind finger sweep
Give up to 5 back blows
Start chest compressions
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
5.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): for severe obstruction in a conscious person, give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until relieved.

n.0: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in and are not part of the algorithm.
n.2: Chest compressions start once she becomes unconscious.
n.3: Abdominal thrusts come after 5 back blows.

5.q: Grace, 7, is dying at a children's hospice. She takes small sips of water but can no longer drink much. Her parents ask whether she needs a drip. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start IV fluids now, as dying children need full hydration to be comfortable
Support sips and mouth care; discuss if a drip is in her best interests
Stop offering drinks, as sipping fluids may cause her more discomfort
Pass a nasogastric tube so she can have full maintenance fluids
5.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions recs 1.3.48-1.3.51: encourage and support the child to drink if she wants to and is able, continue lip and mouth care, and discuss with the family whether enteral or IV fluids are in her best interests, as they may be a burden and may change the place of care.

n.0: NG61 says IV fluids may be a burden for a dying child; starting them is a best interests decision, not routine.
n.2: NG61 says encourage and support drinking if she wants to and is able.
n.3: A nasogastric tube is a best interests decision discussed with the family, not routine.

5.q: Martin, 66, is eating lunch in a ward day room when he clutches his throat. He is coughing forcefully, red in the face and can speak a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between his shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Lie him on the floor and start chest compressions
5.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): with an effective cough (mild obstruction), encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration to an ineffective cough or until the obstruction is relieved.

n.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough in a conscious person.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts follow back blows when the cough is ineffective.
n.3: CPR is started if the person becomes unconscious.

5.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
5.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

5.q: Margaret, 64, is breathless and anxious. Her SpO2 is 82% on air and she is drowsy with RR 30. She has no history of lung disease. Help has been called. What oxygen should be given first?
o: 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask with humidification
4 L/min via a simple face mask and reassess
15 L/min via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask
2 L/min via nasal cannulae and titrate up
5.w: BTS guideline: in critical illness or severe hypoxaemia start high-concentration oxygen via a reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then titrate down to a target of 94-98% once stable (NG253 rec 1.10.1).

n.0: 28% Venturi is a controlled low-concentration device for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.1: A simple face mask at 4 L/min risks CO2 rebreathing and is inadequate here.
n.3: 2 L/min nasal cannulae delivers far too little oxygen for severe hypoxaemia.

5.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
5.q: Sophie, aged 18 months, has gastroenteritis. Which finding is a red flag sign that she is at increased risk of progressing to shock (NICE CG84)?
o: She has had three loose stools today
Her eyes appear sunken
She is thirsty and drinking eagerly
Her temperature is 37.9°C
5.w: NICE CG84 Table 1: red flag symptoms and signs of clinical dehydration include appearing unwell or deteriorating, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnoea and reduced skin turgor. Children with red flags need ORS only (no other oral fluids) and closer monitoring.

n.0: Loose stools are expected in gastroenteritis; their number alone is not a red flag sign.
n.2: Thirst is a feature of dehydration but not one of the red flag signs.
n.3: A mild fever is common in gastroenteritis and is not a dehydration red flag.

5.q: Noah, 3, has Kawasaki disease after 6 days of fever, red palms and a strawberry tongue. He is prescribed IV immunoglobulin and oral aspirin. His mother says she was told children should not have aspirin. What should the nurse explain?
o: Aspirin is safe for him because he is over 2 years old
Kawasaki disease is a recognised reason to prescribe aspirin
The aspirin is a prescribing error and she should refuse it
Aspirin is used to bring down his fever more quickly
5.w: Aspirin is not given to under 16s unless prescribed, with Kawasaki disease a recognised exception: it is prescribed with IV immunoglobulin to reduce inflammation and the risk of coronary artery complications (NHS Kawasaki disease guidance).

n.0: The under-16 restriction is not about being over 2; it applies to all children unless prescribed for a specific reason.
n.2: Aspirin is deliberately prescribed in Kawasaki disease; it is not an error.
n.3: Aspirin in Kawasaki disease reduces inflammation and clot risk in the coronary arteries; it is not used as an antipyretic.

5.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
5.q: Alfie, aged 2, weighs 12 kg and has gastroenteritis. He is still breastfed and his mother asks what he can drink. He has no red flag signs. Which advice follows NICE CG84?
o: Continue breastfeeding and avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks
Give plain water in place of milk until vomiting has stopped for 24 hours
Stop breastfeeding and give diluted fruit juice until the diarrhoea settles
Give flat cola and stop all milk feeds for 48 hours
5.w: NICE CG84: in children with gastroenteritis without red flags, continue breastfeeding and other milk feeds, encourage fluid intake, discourage fruit juices and carbonated drinks, and offer oral rehydration solution (ORS) as supplemental fluid to those at increased risk of dehydration.

n.1: Water lacks electrolytes, and CG84 advises continuing breastfeeding and milk feeds rather than replacing them.
n.2: Breastfeeding should continue, and fruit juice can worsen diarrhoea.
n.3: Fizzy drinks are discouraged and milk feeds should continue.

5.q: Mr Lin, 72, needs a urinary catheter. Before starting, what information is most important for the nurse to give him?
o: The infection statistics for catheters in the trust
The size of catheter and type of lubricant being used
How long the nurse has been carrying out catheterisation
Why it is needed, what it involves and what he will feel
