7.q: Cathy, 66, has a new itchy, raised red rash on her trunk two days after starting a new antibiotic. She is alert, her observations are normal and her lips and tongue are not swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Advise her to stop the antibiotic once she is at home
Wait until the rash has spread before reporting it
Give the next dose and apply an emollient to the rash
Withhold the next dose and inform the prescriber promptly
7.w: A new rash after starting a medicine may be an adverse drug reaction. Without anaphylaxis features, withhold the next dose pending review and inform the prescriber promptly; document it and consider a Yellow Card report (Annexe B 4.4; P4.15).

n.0: Advice to stop treatment needs prescriber review and does not address her current care.
n.1: Delay risks progression of a drug reaction.
n.2: Giving another dose of a possible cause risks a more serious reaction.

7.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
7.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

7.q: Mrs Agnes Doyle, 84, lives alone and is recovering from pneumonia on a medical ward in England. She will need help with personal care at home. Which organisation is responsible for assessing her need for care and support at home?
o: Her GP practice
The integrated care board
The local authority
The acute hospital trust
7.w: Under the Care Act 2014, local authorities assess adults who appear to need care and support and are responsible for social care (and public health) in their area. The ward nurse refers so assessment can be planned before discharge (P7.1 interagency working; FACTS S-CA, S-ICS).

n.0: The GP provides health care but does not carry out Care Act assessments.
n.1: The ICB plans and funds NHS health services, not adult social care assessments.
n.3: Hospital staff contribute to discharge planning, but the statutory needs assessment is the local authority's duty.

7.q: A new wound treatment costs £30,000 more per patient than standard care and produces 1.5 more QALYs per patient. Using NICE's standard threshold in force since April 2026, what is the incremental cost per QALY and how does it compare?
o: £30,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, below the threshold range
£45,000 per QALY, above the threshold range
7.w: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = extra cost / extra QALYs = £30,000 / 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY. This is below the standard range of £25,000-£35,000 per QALY, so the treatment would usually be considered cost-effective (P7.3). Two steps: calculate, then compare with the current threshold.

n.0: This ignores the QALY gain and uses the extra cost alone.
n.1: The calculation is right, but £20,000 is below the current £25,000-£35,000 range, not within it.
n.3: This multiplies cost by QALYs instead of dividing.

7.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
7.q: Jamal, aged 4, has had an appendicectomy. He can talk about how he feels and points to pictures. Which pain tool is most suitable?
o: The Wong-Baker FACES scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale
A score based on his heart rate
A 0 to 10 numerical rating scale
7.w: Self-report is preferred when a child can give it. The Wong-Baker FACES scale is a self-report tool for people aged 3 and over, using faces from no hurt to hurts worst (Wong-Baker FACES Foundation; AnnexB.3.1).

n.1: The Glasgow Coma Scale assesses conscious level, not pain.
n.2: Heart rate changes with many factors and is not a validated pain score on its own.
n.3: Numerical scales are generally used from about 7 to 8 years, when children understand number ranges.

7.q: Jake, 10, has type 1 diabetes. In the school nurse's office he is shaky and sweaty and his capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. He is alert and able to swallow. What should the nurse give first?
o: A slice of wholemeal toast and a glass of milk
A chocolate bar and a biscuit
15 g of fast-acting glucose, such as juice
IM glucagon 1 mg into the thigh
7.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.89: treat mild to moderate hypoglycaemia immediately with oral fast-acting glucose (10-20 g; liquid may be easier), recheck within 15 minutes, then give complex carbohydrate.

n.0: Toast and milk are complex carbohydrate, given after glucose has been restored, not first.
n.1: Fat in chocolate slows glucose absorption; fast-acting glucose works within 5-15 minutes.
n.3: Glucagon is for severe hypoglycaemia when oral treatment is unsafe; Jake can swallow.

7.q: Sunita, 59, is admitted to a surgical ward for elective knee surgery. She is mobile, has no history of pressure damage and her skin is intact. The ward has several types of support surface available. According to NICE CG179, which mattress should she be given?
o: High-specification foam mattress
Sheepskin mattress topper
Water-filled mattress overlay
Standard hospital foam mattress
7.w: NICE CG179: use a high-specification foam mattress for all adults admitted to secondary care, and consider a dynamic support surface if one is not sufficient for those at high risk.

n.1: Sheepskins are not the recommended pressure-redistributing surface for adults.
n.2: Water-filled overlays are not the CG179 standard support surface.
n.3: A standard foam mattress does not meet the CG179 recommendation.

7.q: Nadia, a staff nurse, reports that she gave an evening dose of a medicine to the wrong patient after two patients with similar names were moved into adjacent beds. The patient is unharmed. Which response from the ward manager best reflects a just culture?
o: Remove Nadia from medicine rounds until she has completed a formal assessment
Ask Nadia to apologise to the team for the extra work the incident has created
Record a formal warning on Nadia's file because she did not check identity
Thank Nadia for reporting, support her and review the system factors involved
7.w: A just culture treats honest error as an opportunity to learn, supports the person involved and looks at system contributors (here, similar names placed side by side). This encourages reporting, which PSIRF and Code 14 and 16 depend on (P5.2; P6.6). Reckless conduct is handled differently.

n.0: Removing her from duties for an honest error with clear system causes discourages reporting; support and reflection are more proportionate.
n.1: Asking her to apologise to colleagues shames her and adds nothing to learning.
n.2: Formal sanctions for unintentional error undermine reporting and ignore the system factors.

7.q: Before the ambulance service arrives, off-duty nurse Imran stops at a multi-vehicle collision on a dual carriageway. Traffic is still moving past and one car is leaking fuel. Several people appear injured. What should Imran do first?
o: Start assessing the nearest injured person in the car that is leaking fuel
Check that the scene is safe, then call 999 and describe the incident clearly
Move all the injured people away from the vehicles to the hard shoulder
Leave the scene, as he is off duty and is not covered by trust indemnity
7.w: Code 15.1-15.3: offer help in an emergency within the limits of your knowledge and competence, taking account of your own safety. Scene safety comes first, then early alert to emergency services with clear information (the M/ETHANE structure) so the right response is sent (P6.12).

n.0: Approaching a leaking vehicle beside moving traffic before assessing danger risks creating another casualty.
n.2: Moving injured people without assessment can worsen injuries and exposes Imran to traffic.
n.3: The Code expects registrants to offer help in emergencies outside work, within competence and safety.

7.q: Nadia is about to irrigate a large infected leg wound for Doreen, 81. Splashing of wound fluid towards her face is likely. There are no full-face visors on the ward. Which facial protection should Nadia wear?
o: A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with separate eye protection
A Type II surgical mask and her own prescription glasses
A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask without eye protection
An FFP3 respirator without separate eye protection
7.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: where splashing of blood or body fluids onto the face is anticipated and a full-face visor is not available, wear a Type IIR FRSM with eye protection. Regular corrective spectacles are not considered eye protection.

n.1: A Type II mask is not fluid resistant, and corrective spectacles do not count as eye protection.
n.2: The mask protects the nose and mouth, but the eyes remain exposed to the expected splashes.
n.3: An FFP3 respirator protects against airborne particles; it does not protect the eyes from splashes.

7.q: Jack, aged 4, is admitted with two adults who introduce themselves as his mums. The admission form has fields for 'mother' and 'father'. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask which of them is the biological mother before continuing
Record the second adult as a family friend until legal papers are seen
Ask them how they would like to be named and record both as parents
Record one adult as mother and leave the father field blank
7.w: Family-centred care respects the diversity of family structures and avoids assumptions. The nurse should ask how the family describes itself and record both parents, using their preferred terms, while confirming parental responsibility through the usual process if consent issues arise (P3.4; T2 family cultures).

n.0: Asking about biology is intrusive and not needed to care for Jack.
n.1: Labelling a parent as a friend is disrespectful and inaccurate.
n.3: Leaving one parent off the record is inaccurate and excludes her from her child's care.

7.q: Ms Clarke, 38, agrees to have a wound swab taken after the nurse explains why it is needed and what it involves. The swab is taken without problems. According to Code 4.2, what should the nurse also make sure of?
o: That the consent is confirmed again by the doctor
That Ms Clarke signs a consent form for the swab
That the consent obtained is documented in her record
That a second nurse witnesses Ms Clarke's agreement
7.w: Code 4.2: make sure that you get properly informed consent and document it before carrying out any action. Verbal consent is valid for a wound swab; the record should show it was obtained.

n.0: The nurse taking the swab obtains the consent; the doctor does not need to confirm it.
n.1: Written consent is not required for a routine swab; verbal consent is valid if documented.
n.3: There is no requirement for a witness to verbal consent for a routine procedure.

7.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
7.q: Amira, aged 9, has been reviewed twice for abdominal pain after an operation. Her father remains very worried that she is getting worse and feels his concerns have not been acted on. What should the nurse tell him?
o: He can call the Martha's Rule number for a rapid review by another team
He should wait for the consultant ward round the following morning
He can ask for a second opinion at her next outpatient appointment
He should make a formal complaint to the Patient Advice and Liaison Service
7.w: Martha's Rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review from a different team if they remain worried that the patient is deteriorating and feel their concerns are not being addressed. Each hospital has its own number; it is not a second opinion (NHS England, Martha's Rule). The nurse should also escalate herself.

n.1: Waiting until the morning ignores a family's concern about deterioration.
n.2: Martha's Rule is distinct from a second opinion and is for possible deterioration now, not at a later appointment.
n.3: PALS handles complaints and concerns about services, not urgent clinical deterioration.

7.q: Ava, 9, is autistic and does not use speech. She uses a picture symbol book. Before a blood test, the nurse wants to prepare her. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Do the test quickly without explanation to avoid anxiety
Use her symbol book to show each step, at her own pace
Give her a written leaflet about blood tests to read
Explain the procedure verbally to her parents only
7.w: Communication should be adapted to the child's preferred format (NG213 rec 1.1.17; Annexe A communication skills), using augmentative and alternative communication such as symbols, with preparation and time to process each step.

n.0: Proceeding without explanation increases fear and distress for an autistic child.
n.2: A written leaflet does not match Ava's preferred communication format.
n.3: Talking only to parents excludes Ava from information about her own care.

7.q: A children's ward has three children with norovirus gastroenteritis. A parent of one child asks whether using the alcohol hand gel by the bed is enough after changing nappies. What should the nurse advise?
o: Use the alcohol hand gel after each nappy change
Wash hands with soap and warm running water, then dry well
Wear gloves for nappy changes so hand washing is not needed
Use antibacterial hand wipes after every nappy change instead
7.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s rec 1.8.2.1: washing hands with soap (liquid if possible) in warm running water and careful drying are the most important factors in preventing spread. Alcohol gel is less effective against norovirus.

n.0: Alcohol gel does not reliably inactivate norovirus and does not remove soiling.
n.2: Gloves reduce contamination, but hands still need washing after removing them.
n.3: Wipes do not replace washing with soap and running water.

7.q: Mr Ito, 38, has a head injury. On assessment his eyes open to pressure on the fingertip, he is talking but disorientated about time and place, and he localises to a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
7.w: GCS: eye opening to pressure = 2; confused speech = 4; localising = 5. Total 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 out of 15 (range 3-15). Any fall in GCS after head injury needs urgent escalation.

n.0: Orientated speech scores 5 and obeying commands 6; he is confused and localises.
n.1: Eye opening to speech scores 3; he opens his eyes only to pressure, which scores 2.
n.2: Inappropriate words score 3; he is talking in sentences but confused, which scores 4.

7.q: Your close colleague, going through a divorce, asks you not to mention that she has given several time-critical medicines over an hour late this week. She promises it will stop. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree to keep it confidential if she promises to improve
Offer support but explain you must tell the nurse in charge
Give her time-critical medicines for her so the delays stop
Report her to the NMC without speaking to anyone locally
7.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but this must never compromise patient safety. Code 16.1: raise and escalate safety concerns; 19.1 reduce harm.

n.0: Code 8.7 says support must not compromise patient safety; late time-critical medicines need escalating.
n.2: Covering for her hides the problem and leaves the risk unmanaged.
n.3: Local escalation and support should come first; referral is not the immediate proportionate step.

7.q: Sarah and Tom have a son, Jack, 3, who has cystic fibrosis. Neither parent has the condition. They are planning another baby and ask the nurse what the chance is that their next child will have cystic fibrosis. What is the correct answer?
o: 1 in 2 for each pregnancy
1 in 4 across all future pregnancies
1 in 4 for each pregnancy
2 in 3 for each pregnancy
7.w: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive. Two unaffected carrier parents have a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of an affected child in EACH pregnancy, a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and 1 in 4 of a non-carrier. Chance does not change with previous outcomes.

n.0: 1 in 2 is the chance in each pregnancy for an autosomal dominant condition with one affected parent, or of a carrier child here.
n.1: The risk applies independently to each pregnancy; it is not shared out across them.
n.3: 2 in 3 is the chance that an UNAFFECTED sibling is a carrier, not the chance of an affected child.

7.q: Ruth, 64, has chronic kidney disease and symptomatic anaemia with a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. She is not bleeding and does not have acute coronary syndrome. The doctor plans a red cell transfusion. In line with NICE NG24, what is the recommended approach?
o: Transfuse 1 unit, then reassess and check haemoglobin
Transfuse until haemoglobin reaches at least 110 g/L
Transfuse 2 units, then check haemoglobin the next day
Transfuse 3 units to avoid repeated cannulation
7.w: NICE NG24 (updated 2026): use a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a target of 70-90 g/L after transfusion, and consider single-unit transfusions for adults without active bleeding, clinically reassessing and checking haemoglobin after each unit before giving more.

n.1: 110 g/L is well above the NG24 post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L.
n.2: Two units without reassessment risks overtransfusion and circulatory overload.
n.3: Multiple units without reassessment conflicts with single-unit transfusion and raises overload risk.

7.q: Mr Dunn, 66, is going home on a new medicine. He says he 'doesn't get on with reading' and has left his leaflet unopened. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explain in plain words with pictures, then use teach-back
Explain it once in full medical terms to be accurate
Ask the pharmacist to post a copy of the leaflet to him
Give him a second copy of the leaflet in larger print
7.w: Proficiency P2.10: provide information in accessible ways; Annexe A 2.2 clear language and appropriate materials; Annexe A 2.6 repetition and positive reinforcement; Code 7.4 check understanding.

n.1: Medical terms reduce understanding; Code 7.1 requires terms people can understand.
n.2: Posting the same written information will not help him understand it.
n.3: Larger print does not address difficulty with reading.

7.q: Leah, 7 weeks, has a temperature of 38.3°C and is feeding less. The practice nurse obtains a clean catch urine sample, which is cloudy and smells offensive. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start oral amoxicillin and review in 24 hours
Refer her immediately to a paediatric specialist
Send the sample for culture and review in 48 hours
Dipstick the urine and start oral trimethoprim
7.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) and NICE NG143: babies under 3 months with suspected UTI are referred immediately to paediatric specialist care; a temperature of 38°C or more under 3 months is red (high risk), and parenteral antibiotics are given.

n.0: Oral antibiotics in the community are not appropriate for a febrile baby under 3 months.
n.2: Waiting 48 hours for culture is unsafe for a febrile baby under 3 months.
n.3: Oral treatment in primary care is for children over 3 months; Leah needs specialist care.

7.q: A nurse on placement with the local public health team reads a report stating that 120 people in a town of 100,000 were newly diagnosed with tuberculosis between January and December 2025. Which epidemiological measure does this figure describe?
o: Prevalence
Mortality rate
Case fatality rate
Incidence
7.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: incidence is the number of new cases of a disease arising in a population over a given period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a point or over a period. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2 (epidemiology).

n.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or period, not only the new cases arising in the year.
n.1: A mortality rate counts deaths in a population, not new diagnoses.
n.2: Case fatality is the proportion of people with a disease who die from it.

7.q: Mr Hussain, 69, has died on a medical ward after an expected death. The death is not being referred to the coroner. His family tell the nurse that their faith requires family members to wash his body and that they would like to do this themselves. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that hospital policy requires staff to wash all deceased patients
Leave the washing to the family and support them with the rest of his care
Ask the mortuary staff to wash him before he is released to the family
Wash him before the family arrive so that they are spared any distress
7.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): wash the deceased unless requested not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons, or the death is being referred to the coroner; key contacts may wish to assist and should be supported. NMC Code 1.3 and 1.5: recognise diversity and individual choice, and respect and uphold people's human rights.

n.0: Care after death guidance says wash the deceased unless asked not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons.
n.2: Washing by mortuary staff would also override the family's wish to carry out the washing themselves.
n.3: This disregards the family's stated religious wishes, which the guidance says must be respected.

7.q: Mrs Gill, 87, has delirium and lacks capacity to understand her risk of falling. At night she repeatedly tries to climb out of bed and is unsteady. A healthcare assistant suggests putting the bed rails up. Which action best follows the least restrictive principle?
o: Request a sedative to help her stay in bed at night
Raise both bed rails while she is asleep at night
Tuck the sheets in tightly so she cannot get out
Use a low bed with a crash mat and closer observation
7.w: MCA 2005 s1(6): before acting, consider whether the purpose can be achieved as effectively in a way less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom of action. A low bed, crash mat and closer observation reduce injury risk without confining her; rails may increase harm if she climbs over them.

n.0: Sedation to keep her in bed is chemical restraint and may worsen delirium and falls risk.
n.1: Bed rails restrict her movement and may increase the height and severity of a fall if she climbs over them.
n.2: Tucking sheets to prevent her leaving bed is a form of restraint and risks entrapment.

7.q: Poppy, aged 10 months, had a birth weight on the 50th centile. Her weight is now just below the 9th centile, a fall across 2 centile spaces on the UK-WHO chart. She is well, active and developing normally. Which interpretation is correct?
o: This needs urgent admission for investigation of an underlying cause
This meets the threshold if her length has also dropped by 2 centile spaces
This meets the threshold for concern and needs clinical and feeding assessment
This needs no action because her current weight is above the 2nd centile
7.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.1: a fall across 2 or more weight centile spaces when birthweight was between the 9th and 91st centiles is a threshold for concern about faltering growth. Rec 1.2.6 then advises a clinical, developmental and social assessment with a detailed feeding history.

n.0: NG75 rec 1.2.32 advises against admission unless the child is acutely unwell or there is a specific indication such as starting tube feeding.
n.1: The NG75 weight threshold stands on its own; a parallel fall in length is not required.
n.3: Below the 2nd centile is one threshold, but a fall across 2 centile spaces from a middle birthweight is a separate trigger.

7.q: Sophie is about to insert a peripheral intravenous cannula into the forearm of Malik, 45. She has selected the vein and performed hand hygiene. According to NICE CG139, how should she prepare the skin at the insertion site?
o: Clean with a 70% alcohol wipe, then palpate the vein again
Clean with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride and pat the skin dry with gauze
Apply povidone-iodine and wipe it off before inserting
Clean with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
7.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate the skin at the insertion site with chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol before inserting a peripheral vascular access device or PICC. The solution must dry to work, and the cleaned site is not re-palpated.

n.0: Re-palpating the vein after cleaning contaminates the Key-Site, and alcohol alone is not the CG139 product.
n.1: Saline cleans but does not decontaminate the skin.
n.2: CG139 specifies chlorhexidine in alcohol; wiping antiseptic off before it has acted also defeats it.

7.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for alcohol intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She refuses to let staff contact anyone. Under the Children Act 2004 s16LA duty in force since 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
o: Seek Kerry's consent again and share the information if she agrees
Share once a safeguarding threshold has been reached
Record the concern and share if it happens again
Share the relevant information with children's social care now
7.w: Children Act 2004 s16LA (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, in force 30 September 2026) requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, without a threshold and without needing consent, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child. A young child alone at home needs immediate action.

n.0: Consent is not required under s16LA, and waiting for it delays protection of a child at immediate risk.
n.1: s16LA sets no threshold; the information is relevant to his safety and must be shared.
n.2: A 3-year-old alone at home is at immediate risk; waiting for a repeat leaves him unprotected.

7.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
7.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

7.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which abbreviation practice best supports safe record keeping when documenting medicines and care in the notes. Which approach should she follow?
o: Write terms in full unless the trust approves the abbreviation
Use abbreviations for drug names to save time in busy shifts
Use the abbreviations she learned during her training abroad
Use any abbreviation that colleagues on the ward understand
7.w: Code 10.4: records must be clearly written and not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. Annexe A 1.8 accurate, clear, legible records.

n.1: Abbreviating drug names risks medication errors and breaches Code 10.4.
n.2: Abbreviations vary between countries and may not be understood here.
n.3: Local shorthand may be misread by others; Code 10.4 says no unnecessary abbreviations.

7.q: Alfie, 4 months, is brought to the GP practice for his routine immunisations. The practice nurse notices a 1 cm bruise on his cheek. His mother says his 3-year-old sister probably hit him with a toy. Alfie is otherwise well and cannot yet roll over. What should the nurse do?
o: Follow the local bruising protocol for urgent paediatric assessment and referral
Give the immunisations and ask the health visitor to check the bruise at home
Record the bruise and the explanation, then review it at the next immunisations
Reassure the mother, as the explanation offered is consistent with the bruise
7.w: Bruising in a child who is not independently mobile is rare accidentally and is a recognised indicator of physical abuse (NICE CG89: suspect maltreatment). Local safeguarding partnership protocols require urgent paediatric assessment and a children's social care referral, whatever explanation is given.

n.1: Delegating a later home check delays the assessment the protocol requires.
n.2: Waiting weeks for a review leaves a possibly abused infant unprotected.
n.3: A plausible explanation does not remove the need for assessment in a non-mobile infant.

7.q: Noah, 7, needs a general anaesthetic for dental extractions in England. His father, who was never married to Noah's mother, attends alone. Noah was born in 2019 and his father is named on the birth certificate. Can the father give consent for Noah's treatment?
o: No, he needs a parental responsibility agreement signed by the mother
Yes, every biological father holds parental responsibility from birth
No, an unmarried father needs a court order to hold parental responsibility
Yes, being registered on the birth certificate gave him parental responsibility
7.w: Under s4(1)(a) of the Children Act 1989 an unmarried father acquires parental responsibility by being registered as the father on the birth register; this applies to births registered in England and Wales from 1 December 2003. One person with PR can usually give valid consent.

n.0: A PR agreement is an alternative route, not needed when the father is already registered.
n.1: Biological fatherhood alone does not confer PR; an unmarried father needs registration, an agreement or an order.
n.2: A court order is one route to PR, but registration on the birth certificate is sufficient for births registered from 1 December 2003.

7.q: Amira, 12, is in hospital after an appendicectomy. She shows the nurse messages from someone she met in an online game who says he is 14, asks her to keep their chats secret, move to a private app and send photos in her pyjamas. What should the nurse do?
o: Advise Amira to block the contact and reassure her parents
Tell Amira to stop using online games while in hospital
Recognise possible grooming and follow safeguarding procedures
Ask the contact directly through the app to confirm his age
7.w: Requests for secrecy, moving to a private platform and requests for images are signs of online grooming, which Working Together 2026 includes within child sexual abuse. The nurse should follow safeguarding procedures, preserve the messages and involve police (for example via a CEOP report) as advised.

n.0: Blocking the contact loses evidence and does not address possible abuse of Amira or others.
n.1: Restricting game use does not protect her or address the grooming.
n.3: Contacting the suspect could alert him and is not a nurse's role.

7.q: On a children's ward, a nurse notices that the family of Marius, 6, who are Roma, are repeatedly asked to leave at night while other parents are allowed to stay at the bedside. No clinical reason is recorded. The nurse raises a concern. Which article of the Human Rights Act 1998 is engaged together with Article 8?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair hearing in court
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security of person
7.w: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights. Treating one family differently because of ethnicity, in relation to family life (Article 8), engages Articles 14 and 8 together. The nurse should also challenge discrimination under the Code and the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings in legal proceedings.
n.1: Article 9 concerns belief and religion; the issue is unequal treatment based on ethnicity.
n.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, which is not described.

7.q: Martin, 66, is eating lunch in a ward day room when he clutches his throat. He is coughing forcefully, red in the face and can speak a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between his shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Lie him on the floor and start chest compressions
7.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): with an effective cough (mild obstruction), encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration to an ineffective cough or until the obstruction is relieved.

n.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough in a conscious person.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts follow back blows when the cough is ineffective.
n.3: CPR is started if the person becomes unconscious.

7.q: Derek, 59, has a history of alcohol misuse. He has eaten almost nothing for 7 days and his BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Nutrition support is planned. Using NICE CG32 criteria, what is his refeeding risk and the appropriate starting approach?
o: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Low risk: start at full requirements of 25-35 kcal/kg/day
Moderate risk: start at 50% of requirements without thiamin
No risk: offer normal ward meals without any monitoring
7.w: NICE CG32: high refeeding risk includes two or more of BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little or no intake for over 5 days, or alcohol misuse. Derek has three. Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly, and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days, with electrolyte monitoring.

n.1: Full requirements in a high-risk person can precipitate refeeding syndrome.
n.2: He meets the high-risk criteria, and thiamin is needed.
n.3: Unmonitored feeding ignores his high refeeding risk.

7.q: Sophie is 22 weeks pregnant. A scan has shown that her baby has a life-limiting condition and she plans to continue the pregnancy. When does NICE NG61 advise that discussions about an Advance Care Plan should begin?
o: After the baby reaches 28 days old and leaves neonatal care
During the pregnancy, with the right professionals involved
Once the baby has been born and assessed by a neonatologist
When the baby is first admitted to hospital after birth
7.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions: begin discussing an Advance Care Plan with parents during the pregnancy if there is an antenatal diagnosis of a life-limiting condition, considering who should take part (for example obstetric, neonatal and palliative care teams).

n.0: Waiting four weeks after birth misses planning for birth and the neonatal period.
n.2: Waiting until birth leaves no plan in place for decisions at delivery.
n.3: A first admission may be an emergency, which is too late for planning.

7.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first approach?
o: Tell him firmly to sit down and stop shouting
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen to him
Call security to restrain him before he leaves
Stand in the doorway to block his exit from the ward
7.w: Annexe A 3.5: de-escalation strategies and techniques. Code 13.4 personal safety; calm voice, open posture and listening come before restrictive interventions.

n.0: Commands can escalate agitation; de-escalation uses calm listening.
n.2: Restraint is a last resort; de-escalation should be tried first.
n.3: Blocking his exit increases risk and may escalate the situation.

7.q: Harry, 6, is brought to the emergency department by a neighbour. He is drowsy with a non-blanching rash, a heart rate of 160 bpm and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. His parents are on a flight and cannot be contacted. The doctor prescribes immediate IV antibiotics. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the neighbour to sign the consent form as the responsible adult present
Withhold antibiotics until a parent can be reached, documenting the delay
Give treatment without delay in Harry's best interests while contact attempts continue
Ask the hospital legal team to obtain a court order before starting antibiotics
7.w: Harry shows signs of possible meningococcal sepsis, a life-threatening emergency. When no one with parental responsibility is available and treatment cannot wait, clinicians may give necessary treatment in the child's best interests under the doctrine of necessity, while continuing to contact the parents and documenting the reasons.

n.0: A neighbour has no parental responsibility and cannot give valid consent.
n.1: Delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcal sepsis risks death; necessity justifies immediate treatment.
n.3: Courts are used for disputes or non-urgent refusals; seeking an order here would dangerously delay emergency treatment.

7.q: Pat, 75, has a venous leg ulcer with no red flags. Mild compression was started at her first visit, and strong compression bandaging is now being considered. Before strong compression is applied, what assessment must be completed?
o: A wound swab for culture and sensitivity
A Doppler ankle brachial pressure index
A full blood count to check for anaemia
A capillary blood glucose measurement
7.w: NWCSP Leg Ulcer Recommendations (2023): with no red flags, mild compression (up to 20 mmHg) can start straight away, but a full assessment including a Doppler ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI), within 14 days, is needed before strong compression (40 mmHg or more), because strong compression on a limb with arterial insufficiency can cause ischaemia (Annexe B 4.6 pressure bandaging).

n.0: A wound swab is not needed to decide on compression and is taken only with signs of infection.
n.2: FBC does not assess arterial supply to the limb.
n.3: Glucose is relevant to healing but does not determine whether compression is safe.

7.q: During a home visit to 6-week-old Theo, the community children's nurse notes the nursery thermometer reads 24°C. Theo is in a cot with a duvet and a hat on. What advice should the nurse give?
o: Keep the room at 16-20°C and take off his hat and duvet
Keep the room at 24°C but replace the duvet with a quilt
Keep the room at 24°C, as young babies need extra warmth
Keep the hat on at night and turn the room down to 22°C
7.w: Lullaby Trust safer sleep advice: the recommended room temperature is 16-20°C; babies should not wear hats indoors for sleep and should sleep in a clear cot without duvets or pillows. Overheating increases SIDS risk.

n.1: 24°C is above the recommended range, and quilts are as risky as duvets.
n.2: Overheating increases SIDS risk; 16-20°C is advised.
n.3: 22°C is still above the recommended range, and hats for sleep cause overheating.

7.q: Before entering the room of Margaret, 71, who has influenza and needs help to wash, Ade gathers an apron, a fluid-resistant surgical mask, goggles and non-sterile gloves. In which order should Ade put this equipment on?
o: Mask, eye protection, gloves, then apron
Apron, mask, eye protection, then gloves
Apron, gloves, eye protection, then mask
Gloves, apron, mask, then eye protection
7.w: NIPCM appendix 6 sets the order for putting on PPE as apron or gown, FRSM or respirator, eye protection, then gloves. Gloves go on last so that they are not contaminated while the other items are adjusted.

n.0: The apron goes on first; putting it on last means pulling it over gloves and face protection.
n.2: The mask is fitted before eye protection and gloves; adjusting a mask with gloved hands risks contamination.
n.3: Putting gloves on first means they touch the apron ties, mask and goggles while fitting them.

7.q: Leo, 8, has background oral morphine for end of life pain. He also has 2 anticipatory doses before daily dressing changes and needed 2 breakthrough doses yesterday. The team is reviewing his daily background dose. Which doses should be left out of that calculation?
o: Both the anticipatory and breakthrough doses
The anticipatory doses before dressing changes
The regular background doses
The breakthrough doses given yesterday
7.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.3.31: consider anticipatory doses for predictable pain (dressings, moving and handling), and do not include anticipatory doses when calculating the required daily background dose. Breakthrough use informs titration of background analgesia (1.3.30).

n.0: Breakthrough doses should be considered; only anticipatory doses are excluded.
n.2: The regular background doses are the basis of the calculation.
n.3: Breakthrough doses show uncontrolled pain and inform titration of the background dose.

7.q: Kai, 10, had surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot as a baby and is at increased risk of infective endocarditis. His mother asks how to reduce the risk at his routine dental check-ups. What should the nurse advise, in line with NICE CG64?
o: Take amoxicillin before every routine check-up
Use chlorhexidine mouthwash before each dental visit
Delay check-ups until he moves to adult services
Keep up good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups
7.w: NICE CG64 recs 1.1.2-1.1.4: give people at increased risk clear information on maintaining good oral health, symptoms of endocarditis and the risks of piercing or tattooing. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routine, and chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered.

n.0: A routine check-up is not an invasive procedure, and antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended.
n.1: CG64 rec 1.1.4 says chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered as prophylaxis for dental procedures.
n.2: Poor dental health increases endocarditis risk; regular check-ups are encouraged.

7.q: Before a short handover, Graham, a staff nurse, needs to ask a healthcare assistant to monitor Mr Okafor, 70, who had a hypotensive episode earlier. Which instruction is clearest?
o: 'Please check Mr Okafor's BP and pulse at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is under 100.'
'Please keep an eye on Mr Okafor this afternoon and let me know how he gets on.'
'Please do the usual observations on everyone in bay 2, including Mr Okafor, this afternoon.'
'Please do Mr Okafor's observations when you have time and tell me if anything looks off.'
7.w: AnnexA.1.11 requires clear verbal, digital or written information and instructions when delegating or handing over. An instruction stating what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when removes ambiguity (Code 11.2; AnnexA.4.1.2).

n.1: 'Keep an eye on' does not specify what to measure, when, or what to report.
n.2: A general bay instruction does not flag Mr Okafor's specific risk or what to report.
n.3: There is no time set or threshold for reporting; 'anything off' depends on the assistant's interpretation.

7.q: Harry, 8, has a cough and cold. His mother asks a practice nurse whether she can give him a codeine-containing cough medicine left over from his older brother. What should the nurse advise?
o: Do not give it, as codeine is not used for cough under 12
Give it at night to help him sleep through the cough
Give half the amount given to his older brother
Give it, as codeine is effective for cough in children
7.w: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2015): codeine-containing medicines must not be used for cough and cold in children under 12, because of the risk of opioid toxicity and limited evidence of benefit.

n.1: Night-time use still exposes him to the opioid toxicity risk under 12.
n.2: A reduced amount does not make codeine appropriate under 12.
n.3: The MHRA found limited evidence that codeine is effective for cough in children.

7.q: At the end of a shift, the nurse is evaluating Mrs Dunn's care plan for pain after a hip fracture. Which entry best documents her progress?
o: Pain management ongoing; patient seems a lot more comfortable this afternoon.
Patient complained of pain all morning but is settled now.
14:30 Pain 7/10 moving at 12:00; 3/10 at 13:00 after oxycodone. Plan continued.
Analgesia given as prescribed. Continue current plan as per care plan.
7.w: Code 10.1-10.4: complete records accurately at the time, attributing, dating and timing entries without speculation. P3.15 requires documenting progress against goals; a timed, measured pain score before and after the intervention shows whether the plan is working.

n.0: 'Seems more comfortable' gives no measurement and is open to interpretation.
n.1: 'Complained' is judgemental, and the entry gives no times, scores or interventions.
n.3: This records an action but not its effect, so progress cannot be evaluated.

7.q: Ben, a theatre nurse, has developed persistent back pain that is making patient transfers difficult. He has not told anyone. Which action best reflects his professional responsibility for his own health?
o: Wait until his annual appraisal to mention the problem
Seek occupational health advice and discuss adjustments
Take regular painkillers and keep doing transfers as before
Avoid transfers by swapping tasks with colleagues informally
7.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role. Proficiency P1.6: take responsibility for a healthy lifestyle to maintain fitness for practice; Code 19.4 personal precautions.

n.0: Waiting delays support; Code 20.9 requires maintaining the health needed for the role now.
n.2: Masking symptoms risks harm to himself and patients and does not address fitness for his role.
n.3: Informal swaps hide the problem and may leave the team short of safe handlers.

7.q: Ms Hunt, 55, has had the same leg ulcer care plan for three weeks. Measurements show the wound has not reduced in size, and she says the dressing leaks and stops her going out. What should the nurse do?
o: Reassess the wound with her and revise the plan, referring if needed
Ask her to stay at home more until the leaking settles down
Continue the plan, as wounds can take several months to heal
Change to a more absorbent dressing without discussing it with her
7.w: P3.15: work in partnership to monitor, evaluate and reassess care plans, readjusting goals and documenting progress. Lack of progress and a poor experience for the person mean the plan should be reviewed with her, with referral (for example to tissue viability) if needed (P3.16).

n.1: Restricting her life to suit the dressing is not person-centred and does not address the problem.
n.2: Continuing an unchanged plan ignores evidence that it is not working.
n.3: Changing the plan without her involvement is not partnership working.

7.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
7.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

7.q: A ward manager is introducing Making Every Contact Count (MECC) and explains the first level of intervention to her team. Which description matches a MECC Level 1 very brief intervention?
o: Oral discussion and negotiation with follow-up and possible referral for support
High-intensity specialist sessions over several weeks for people at high risk
An individual discussion lasting more than 30 minutes over one or more sessions
Giving information or signposting, taking from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes
7.w: NHS England, Making Every Contact Count consensus statement (2016): MECC uses day-to-day interactions to support positive changes to physical and mental health and wellbeing. Level 1 very brief intervention takes from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes and enables information giving or signposting; Level 2 brief intervention involves discussion, negotiation or encouragement.

n.0: This describes a MECC Level 2 brief intervention.
n.1: High-intensity interventions are delivered by specialist services, not as MECC very brief interventions.
n.2: This describes an extended brief intervention (NICE PH49), which is more intensive than Level 1.

7.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
7.q: Daniel, aged 7, has acute asthma. An hour ago he had marked recession and a respiratory rate of 40. Now his recession is less obvious, his respiratory rate is 18, he is drowsy and SpO2 is 87% in oxygen. What is the most likely explanation?
o: His asthma is improving, as his work of breathing has reduced
He has a normal rate for his age, so treatment can be reduced
He is falling asleep, which shows his anxiety has settled
He is tiring and decompensating, so an emergency call is needed
7.w: Decreasing work of breathing with bradypnoea, falling consciousness and SpO2 below 90% are signs of decompensated respiratory failure (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Exhaustion can look like improvement; this child is at risk of arrest and needs an emergency response.

n.0: Less recession here reflects exhaustion, not improvement, given his drowsiness and falling saturations.
n.1: A rate of 18 after 40, with drowsiness and SpO2 of 87%, is bradypnoea from exhaustion, not a normal finding.
n.2: Drowsiness with hypoxaemia is a sign of hypercapnia and exhaustion, not relaxation.

7.q: Agnes, 55, has received her cervical screening invitation. She tells the nurse she has heard mixed things about screening and is unsure whether to go. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that cervical screening is compulsory for women of her age group
Advise her that screening prevents every case of cervical cancer
Give balanced information on benefits and limits, and support her choice
Book her test now and explain the details at her appointment
7.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): deciding whether to have screening is a personal choice; benefits (early detection, preventing some deaths) are weighed against risks and limitations (false positives and negatives, anxiety, difficult decisions). Code 4.2: make sure informed consent is obtained.

n.0: Screening is a personal choice; NHS screening is offered, not mandated.
n.1: Screening tests are not 100% accurate; this overstates the benefit and is misleading.
n.3: Booking before she has decided bypasses informed choice.

7.q: Isla, 10 months, has been choking on a grape. After two rounds of back blows and chest thrusts she becomes limp and unresponsive. The nurse lays her on a firm surface and opens her airway, but cannot see the grape. What should the nurse do next?
o: Continue cycles of back blows and chest thrusts
Give 5 rescue breaths and start CPR at 15:2
Give 5 abdominal thrusts with Isla lying on her back
Perform a single finger sweep to feel for the grape
7.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: if a choking child becomes unconscious, open the airway, remove the object only if clearly visible, give 5 rescue breaths and continue with CPR (15:2 if trained). Compressions help dislodge the object.

n.0: Back blows and thrusts are for the conscious child; once unconscious the algorithm moves to rescue breaths and CPR.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants, and an unconscious child needs rescue breaths and CPR.
n.3: A finger is used to remove an object only when it is clearly visible; blind sweeping can impact it further.

7.q: Mr Kapoor, 67, has capacity and has told Hayley, his nurse, that he does not want the proposed amputation and would prefer palliative wound care. On the ward round the surgeon starts to describe the operation date without asking his views. What should Hayley do?
o: Say that Mr Kapoor has shared views about the operation and invite him to explain them
Record Mr Kapoor's wishes in his nursing notes once the ward round has finished
Wait until after the ward round and then ask Mr Kapoor whether he has changed his mind
Tell the surgeon that Mr Kapoor has asked her to cancel the operation on his behalf
7.w: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable; Code 2.5 respect the right to refuse treatment). Inviting Mr Kapoor to speak supports his autonomy without speaking over him (MCA 2005 s1 principles).

n.1: Recording his wishes is necessary but does not ensure they are heard in the decision being made now.
n.2: Waiting allows a decision to be made without him; he has already expressed his wishes.
n.3: Hayley should not overstate or speak for him when he can speak for himself.

7.q: Irene, 72, is admitted with rheumatoid arthritis. Her new inpatient chart has methotrexate 10 mg once daily written in the regular section. Her repeat prescription list from home shows methotrexate 10 mg once weekly on Mondays. What should the nurse do?
o: Withhold it and contact the prescriber urgently to clarify
Give 10 mg on Monday, and correct the chart frequency herself
Give 10 mg daily until the pharmacist reviews the chart next week
Give 10 mg today, as it is written on the current drug chart
7.w: Methotrexate for non-cancer conditions is usually taken once weekly; daily dosing causes serious toxicity, and overdose of methotrexate for non-cancer treatment is on the NHS Never Events list (2018, updated 2021). The discrepancy must be clarified with the prescriber before any dose (P4.14).

n.1: Changing a prescription is not within the nurse's role; the prescriber must amend it.
n.2: Daily dosing for a week would cause the very overdose the Never Events list targets.
n.3: Giving a daily dose that conflicts with her weekly regimen risks a fatal overdose.

7.q: Mr Evans, 69, has expressive aphasia after a stroke. He understands speech but struggles to find words. Which approach best supports communication?
o: Finish his sentences for him to reduce his frustration
Use closed questions, picture boards and extra time
Ask his wife to answer all questions on his behalf
Speak more loudly and repeat each sentence twice
7.w: Annexe A 2.5: identify the need for and manage alternative communication techniques. Code 7.3: use a range of verbal and non-verbal methods.

n.0: Finishing sentences may misrepresent what he means and reduces his control.
n.2: He can understand and should be supported to communicate for himself.
n.3: His difficulty is expressing words, not hearing; volume does not help.

7.q: Ava, 3 weeks, born at 39 weeks, is brought to the children's emergency department with a two-day cold. While on the observation trolley she stops breathing for 20 seconds and becomes dusky, then recovers with stimulation. What does this presentation most suggest?
o: Bronchiolitis with apnoea, needing urgent medical review
Normal periodic breathing of a term newborn during sleep
Reflux episode needing smaller, more frequent feeds
Croup, needing a single dose of oral dexamethasone
7.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): young infants (particularly under 6 weeks) may present with apnoea without other clinical signs. Apnoea is a red flag for immediate referral and urgent medical review.

n.1: Periodic breathing involves brief pauses of a few seconds without colour change; a dusky 20-second apnoea is not normal.
n.2: Reflux does not explain apnoea with colour change alongside a viral illness; the risk of bronchiolitis apnoea must be assumed.
n.3: Croup causes barking cough and stridor in older infants and toddlers, not apnoea at 3 weeks.

7.q: Before a transfer, Rosa checks the mobile hoist on her ward. The examination label shows that its last thorough examination under LOLER was eight months ago, and no examination scheme with different intervals is displayed. What should Rosa do?
o: Use the hoist, because lifting equipment is examined every 12 months
Take the hoist out of use, report it and use another hoist that is in date
Carry out a visual pre-use check and continue if the hoist looks sound
Use the hoist for this transfer and report the overdue date at handover
7.w: Under LOLER 1998, lifting equipment and accessories used for lifting people must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months (other lifting equipment every 12 months) unless an examination scheme sets other intervals. A hoist overdue for examination should not be used to lift a person and should be reported (HSE, Thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment).

n.0: The 12-month interval applies to lifting equipment that is not used to lift people; patient hoists fall under the 6-month interval.
n.2: A pre-use check is good practice but does not replace the thorough examination by a competent person that LOLER requires.
n.3: Knowingly using equipment that is overdue for its statutory examination puts the patient at risk; the problem must be dealt with before the transfer.

7.q: Joyce, 85, is dying in hospital and can take only sips of fluid. Her husband asks the nurse, 'If she has a drip, will it keep her alive longer? And if she doesn't, will she die sooner?' Which response is most accurate?
o: Without a drip she will die sooner from dehydration, so the team will advise starting one
It is uncertain whether a drip would lengthen her life, or whether going without would shorten it
Drips are not used at the end of life because they cause fluid overload in older people
A drip would give her several more days of life, so one is usually started at this stage
7.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.5: tell the person and those important to them that clinically assisted hydration may relieve distressing symptoms of dehydration but may cause other problems, and that it is uncertain whether giving it prolongs life or whether not giving it hastens death.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.4.5 states it is uncertain whether withholding clinically assisted hydration hastens death.
n.2: Clinically assisted hydration can be a therapeutic trial (rec 1.4.8); it is not ruled out, though overload is a risk to monitor.
n.3: NG31 rec 1.4.5 states it is uncertain whether clinically assisted hydration prolongs life or the dying process.

7.q: A children's nurse inserting a urinary catheter for Maryam, 9, after surgery notices genital appearances that she believes show FGM. She has not had specialist FGM training and is unsure of the type. What should she do?
o: Report to the police, as the duty applies once signs appear to show FGM
Report once a doctor's diagnosis of FGM is recorded in the notes
Ask a gynaecologist to examine Maryam and confirm the type of FGM first
Record the findings and ask the parents whether FGM has been carried out
7.w: Under the procedural information, the duty applies at the point a professional sees physical signs that appear to show FGM in the course of their work. A full clinical diagnosis is not required, and no further examination should be carried out for the purpose of confirming it.

n.1: A medical diagnosis is not required before the duty applies.
n.2: An examination solely to confirm FGM should not be carried out; the duty applies on what was observed.
n.3: Asking the parents first may put Maryam at risk and does not discharge the duty.

7.q: Agnieszka, 52, uses an insulin pen at home and has brought it into hospital. Her lunchtime dose is due, but the ward has run out of pen needles. A colleague suggests drawing the dose out of the pen cartridge with an insulin syringe. What should the nurse do?
o: Obtain pen needles from pharmacy or another ward and give it
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using an insulin syringe
Draw the dose from the pen cartridge using a 1 mL syringe
Omit the dose until pen needles are delivered tomorrow
7.w: An NHS England patient safety alert (2016) warned of severe harm and death from withdrawing insulin from pen devices, as cartridges are not designed for this and dosing errors result. Insulin is a high-risk medicine (P4.14); the correct device should be obtained promptly so the dose is not omitted.

n.1: Withdrawing insulin from a pen cartridge is unsafe whichever syringe is used.
n.2: A standard 1 mL syringe adds a further risk of unit-to-mL confusion and overdose.
n.3: Omitting insulin for a day risks hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis when needles can be sourced.

7.q: At the bedside check, the nurse notices that the compatibility label on a unit of red cells for Catherine, 60, reads 'Catherine Smyth', while her wristband reads 'Catherine Smith'. Her date of birth and hospital number match. What should the nurse do?
o: Proceed, as the date of birth and hospital number both match
Do not start, and contact the transfusion laboratory to resolve it
Ask a second nurse to countersign the discrepancy and proceed
Correct the spelling on the wristband and then proceed
7.w: BSH (2017): all identifiers on the wristband and the component label must match exactly at the bedside; any discrepancy means the component is not given until resolved with the transfusion laboratory. Wrong component transfused is a leading SHOT-reported error.

n.0: Partial matches are not acceptable; every identifier must match.
n.2: A second signature does not resolve a mismatch in identifiers.
n.3: Changing the wristband to fit the unit conceals the discrepancy and is unsafe.

7.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
7.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

7.q: During a patient safety study day, a nurse asks what makes an incident a Never Event rather than another serious incident. Which statement is correct?
o: It is any incident that causes harm lasting 28 days or more to a patient
It is wholly preventable because national barriers should be in place
It is any incident that a coroner later finds was caused by staff error
It is any incident in which a patient dies as a direct result of their care
7.w: NHS England's Never Events policy and framework (2018, list updated 2021) defines Never Events as patient safety incidents that are wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations providing strong systemic protective barriers are available nationally and should have been implemented by all providers. They are recorded on LFPSE with a learning response under PSIRF.

n.0: Twenty-eight days is the duration used for prolonged pain or psychological harm in the statutory candour definitions, not the Never Event test.
n.2: A coroner's finding does not define the category; it is defined by the national barriers that should have prevented it.
n.3: Death is not the defining feature; a Never Event may cause no harm, and many deaths are not Never Events.

7.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
7.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

7.q: Fatima, 45, is admitted for an elective procedure. She asks that only female staff provide her intimate personal care because of her religious beliefs. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree to her request if her religion is recorded on the notes
Arrange female staff for her personal care where possible
Explain that personal care will be given by whoever is on duty that shift
Ask her to bring a female relative to give her personal care
7.w: Proficiency P1.14: provide non-discriminatory, person-centred, sensitive care reflecting people's values, beliefs and culture. Code 1.3 and 2.4; religion or belief is a protected characteristic (Equality Act s4).

n.0: Respecting a preference does not depend on paperwork; it should be accommodated where possible now.
n.2: This disregards her beliefs; P1.14 requires care that reflects people's values, beliefs and culture.
n.3: This shifts care onto family and may not be safe or what she wants.

7.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
7.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

7.q: Mia, 14, has lost 6 kg in 3 months by restricting food and exercising heavily. Her BMI centile is still within the normal range. Her mother asks the school nurse whether Mia is ill enough to be referred. What is the best response?
o: Monitor her weight monthly at school for 6 months
Refer her now; a normal BMI does not rule out an eating disorder
Refer her once she has missed three menstrual periods
Wait until her BMI centile has fallen below the 2nd centile
7.w: NICE NG69 Eating disorders: do not use single measures such as BMI or duration of illness to determine whether to offer treatment; rapid weight loss with restriction and over-exercise warrants referral to a community eating disorder service.

n.0: Months of monitoring delays assessment of a rapidly progressing eating disorder.
n.2: Amenorrhoea is not required for diagnosis or referral, and waiting delays treatment.
n.3: Waiting for a low BMI ignores NG69 and allows dangerous weight loss to continue.

7.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
7.q: Lily, aged 2, weighs 14 kg and has clinical dehydration without shock. Oral rehydration is prescribed in line with NICE CG84. How much ORS is needed for her fluid deficit, and over what time?
o: 700 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance fluid
700 mL over 24 hours, in place of maintenance fluid
1,400 mL over 4 hours, including maintenance
280 mL over 1 hour, then reassess
7.w: NICE CG84: for oral rehydration therapy give 50 mL/kg for fluid deficit replacement over 4 hours as well as maintenance fluid. 50 mL x 14 kg = 700 mL over 4 hours, given frequently in small amounts, plus maintenance.

n.1: The deficit is replaced over 4 hours, and maintenance must also be given.
n.2: 1,400 mL is 100 mL/kg, the IV deficit used after shock, not the oral deficit.
n.3: 280 mL is 20 mL/kg and not the CG84 regimen.

7.q: After hearing his cancer has spread, Mr Ward, 70, falls silent and starts to cry. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Step out of the room and return once he is calmer
Reassure him that many people live for years with this
Stay with him, allow silence and acknowledge his feelings
Explain the treatment options to him while he takes it in
7.w: Annexe A 2.9 convey compassion during difficult conversations; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; P1.12 support people who are emotionally vulnerable.

n.0: Leaving may feel like abandonment at a vulnerable moment.
n.1: This may be inaccurate and closes down his emotions.
n.3: Giving more information while he is distressed is unlikely to be absorbed.

7.q: Siobhan, 58, two days after a laparotomy, has a NEWS2 of 9: RR 25, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 102/64, alert, temperature 38.4°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Request a ward doctor review within 4 hours and repeat the observations hourly
Recheck the observations in 30 minutes before escalating
Inform the medical team immediately and request a critical care assessment
Increase observations to 4-hourly and inform the nurse in charge
7.w: A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring, the registered nurse immediately informs the medical team (at least specialist registrar level) and requests emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies (RCP NEWS2 2017 chart 4). Her score: RR 3, SpO2 2, pulse 2, BP 1, temperature 1 = 9.

n.0: A 4-hour review is far too slow for a high-risk score.
n.1: Delaying escalation to recheck wastes time; the score already meets the emergency threshold.
n.3: 4-hourly observations apply to a total of 1-4.

7.q: A nurse joining a residential home notices that all residents are got up and dressed by 6 am to suit staff rotas, toileted at fixed times regardless of need, and given meals in the same order every day. Residents' preferences are not recorded. Which type of abuse does this most suggest?
o: Neglect and acts of omission
Organisational abuse
Psychological abuse
Physical abuse
7.w: Organisational abuse (Care Act statutory guidance para 14.17) includes poor care practice within an institution or service, for example rigid routines that serve the organisation rather than the people in its care.

n.0: Fixed toileting may neglect individual needs, but para 14.17 places neglect and poor practice arising from an institution's structure, policies and routines under organisational abuse.
n.2: Psychological abuse involves emotional harm such as threats or humiliation by an individual; the problem described is a system of care.
n.3: No physical harm or force is described.

7.q: On admission, Gemma, 35, lists citalopram as her only regular medicine. When asked about other products, she says she has been taking St John's wort from a health food shop for low mood. What should the nurse do?
o: Record it as a herbal product that needs no further review or action
Remove it from her locker and dispose of it in the sharps bin
Record it and inform the prescriber, as it interacts with citalopram
Advise her to double her citalopram dose instead of using it
7.w: Medicines reconciliation includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5; P4.15). St John's wort taken with an SSRI such as citalopram increases the risk of serotonin syndrome and interacts with many other drugs, so it is documented and the prescriber or pharmacist informed.

n.0: Herbal products can cause significant interactions and must be reviewed.
n.1: Patients' own products are not removed without consent, and sharps bins are not for medicines.
n.3: Changing a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision and could cause toxicity.

7.q: A ward nurse tells the trust's safeguarding lead that a 13-year-old patient disclosed FGM to her during a dressing change. The safeguarding lead says she will phone the police herself so that the nurse can return to her busy shift. What is the correct position?
o: The safeguarding lead can report, as a regulated professional in the same trust
The safeguarding lead must report, as the nurse is not trained in FGM
The nurse must make the report herself, as the duty cannot be transferred
Either can report, as both are regulated professionals in the trust
7.w: The mandatory reporting duty is a personal duty: the professional who receives the disclosure must make the report, and the responsibility cannot be transferred. The nurse should still involve the safeguarding lead for support and wider safeguarding action.

n.0: Working in the same trust does not allow the duty to be passed to another person.
n.1: Training level does not change who holds the duty.
n.3: Being regulated in the same trust does not allow the duty to be shared or passed on; it stays with the nurse who heard the disclosure.

7.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
7.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

7.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
7.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

7.q: A ward's controlled drugs register has been completed and a new book started. The ward clerk asks how long the old register must be kept. Under NICE NG46, what is the minimum retention period?
o: 1 year from the date of the last entry
2 years from the date of the last entry
6 months from the date the book was closed
7 years from the date of the first entry
7.w: NICE NG46: controlled drugs registers must be kept for 2 years from the date of the last entry, in line with the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. (Records of destruction of patients' own CDs are kept for a minimum of 7 years.)

n.0: 1 year is shorter than the legal minimum.
n.2: 6 months is well below the 2-year requirement.
n.3: 7 years applies to records of destruction of patients' own CDs, and the period runs from the last entry.

7.q: At 02:00 police bring Mia, 2, to the emergency department after finding her alone at home while both parents were heavily intoxicated. The officer says Mia has been taken into police protection under the Children Act 1989. For how long can police protection last?
o: Up to 72 hours
Up to 24 hours
Up to 8 days
Up to 28 days
7.w: Under s46 of the Children Act 1989 no child may be kept in police protection for more than 72 hours. If longer protection is needed, the local authority must apply to court, for example for an emergency protection order under s44.

n.1: 24 hours is the basic detention limit for an adult arrested under PACE, not the police protection limit.
n.2: Eight days is the maximum initial duration of an emergency protection order under s45, not police protection.
n.3: 28 days is not a Children Act time limit for emergency protection of a child.

7.q: Arthur, 88, is dying on a medical ward. His breathing has become noisy with a rattling sound. He is unconscious and appears settled. His daughter is upset and asks whether he is 'drowning'. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Explain that a medicine will be given now to stop the noise completely
Start oxygen through a face mask to make his breathing feel more comfortable
Explain that the noise means fluid on his lungs that needs a diuretic injection
Explain the noise is unlikely to be causing him discomfort, and reposition him
7.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.29 and 1.5.30: assess the cause of noisy respiratory secretions and the impact on the person and those important to them; reassure them that although the noise can be distressing it is unlikely to cause discomfort; consider non-drug measures such as repositioning.

n.0: Medicines are considered if secretions distress the dying person (rec 1.5.31), and they may not stop the noise completely.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen; offer it for known or suspected symptomatic hypoxaemia.
n.2: Noisy secretions in the last days are not treated as pulmonary oedema; the guidance is reassurance and non-drug measures first.

7.q: A nurse is giving Hana, aged 12 weeks, her routine injections. Which site should be used for the intramuscular vaccines?
o: The ventrogluteal site of the hip
The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
The anterolateral aspect of the thigh
The dorsogluteal muscle of the buttock
7.w: The UKHSA schedule lists the thigh as the usual site for the 8, 12 and 16 week injections; intramuscular vaccines go into the anterolateral thigh in infants, with the deltoid or thigh used from 1 year.

n.0: The ventrogluteal site is not a recommended site for routine infant vaccines.
n.1: The deltoid is too small in young infants; the upper arm is used from around 1 year.
n.3: The buttock is not recommended for vaccines because of fat depth and sciatic nerve risk.

7.q: Ruth, a staff nurse, is writing a referral to a dietitian for Mrs Smith, 63, who has lost weight after bowel surgery. The electronic record includes her full medical history, including a termination of pregnancy 30 years ago. What should Ruth include in the referral?
o: The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything except the termination of pregnancy
Her full medical history so the dietitian has the whole picture
A summary written after asking her family
7.w: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data. UK GDPR data minimisation also requires data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. Only information relevant to nutrition should be shared.

n.1: Removing one sensitive item still shares other irrelevant data; relevance, not sensitivity, decides what is sent.
n.2: Sending the full history exceeds what the dietitian needs and breaches the minimum necessary principle.
n.3: Families are not a source for a clinical referral, and involving them without consent breaches confidentiality.
