7.q: Joan, 87, is wearing anti-embolism stockings after surgery. She has significantly reduced mobility and spends most of the day in bed. Under NICE NG89, how often should her skin be inspected?
o: When she reports pain or discomfort in her legs
Once a day when the stockings are removed for washing
Once a week when the stockings are changed for new ones
2 or 3 times a day, especially heels and bony prominences
7.w: NICE NG89: remove stockings daily for hygiene and skin inspection; in people with significantly reduced mobility, poor skin integrity or sensory loss, inspect the skin 2 or 3 times a day, particularly over heels and bony prominences. Stop stockings if there is marking, blistering or discolouration.

n.0: Waiting for symptoms misses early damage; NG89 sets routine checks 2 or 3 times a day for people with significantly reduced mobility.
n.1: Daily removal and inspection is the minimum for everyone; she needs more frequent checks because of her significantly reduced mobility.
n.2: Weekly inspection would miss pressure damage.

7.q: A ward pharmacist explains to nursing staff how NICE judges whether a new medicine is cost-effective in its technology appraisals. Since April 2026, what is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold?
o: £100,000 to £300,000 per QALY gained
£20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
7.w: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold in technology appraisals rose from £20,000-£30,000 to £25,000-£35,000 per QALY gained from April 2026 (NICE, Changes to NICE's cost-effectiveness thresholds; P7.4 implications of current health policy).

n.0: This higher range applies to highly specialised technologies for ultra-rare diseases, not the standard threshold.
n.1: This was the threshold before April 2026.
n.2: This is not a NICE threshold range.

7.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
7.q: Freddie, aged 4 months, is found unresponsive in his cot and breathing noisily. The nurse calls for help and opens his airway. How should his head be positioned?
o: Turned to one side, with the neck extended over a pillow
In the neutral position, with the head level and face parallel to the bed
Flexed forward slightly, with the chin resting down towards the chest
Fully extended, with the head tilted back as far as it will go
7.w: Infants have a large occiput and a short neck, and the soft trachea is easily compressed by over-extension. RCUK paediatric life support: open an infant's airway with the head in the neutral position and chin lift; children need a slightly more extended 'sniffing' position (T2 physiological differences; AnnexB.2.7).

n.0: Turning and extending over a pillow does not open the airway and over-extends the neck.
n.2: Flexion pushes the chin to the chest and obstructs the airway, which the large occiput already tends to do.
n.3: Over-extension kinks the soft infant trachea and can obstruct the airway.

7.q: A ward team cannot agree whether to share a patient's HIV status with a care agency that will provide personal care at home. The patient has capacity but has not been asked yet. Who in the organisation is responsible for advising on difficult decisions about confidential information?
o: The ward matron on duty
The Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
The Data Protection Officer at the ICO
The Caldicott Guardian
7.w: The Caldicott Guardian is the senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of patient information and enabling appropriate sharing; the Caldicott principles advise involving them in difficult decisions. The first step remains asking the patient.

n.0: The matron can support the team but is not the designated lead for confidentiality decisions.
n.1: Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support staff to raise concerns; they do not advise on confidentiality decisions.
n.2: The ICO is the external regulator; it does not advise on individual sharing decisions within a trust.

7.q: Nurse Adebayo nearly gives insulin to the wrong patient but notices at the bedside check, so no dose is given. A colleague says there is no need to report it because nothing happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss it at the next team meeting without making a report
Make a note in her own reflective log for revalidation
Tell the patient about the near miss and make no further record
Report the near miss through the local incident reporting system
7.w: The NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (refreshed December 2024) covers openness within organisations, including reporting adverse incidents and near misses. Code 19.1 requires action to reduce the likelihood of mistakes and near misses.

n.0: Discussion helps learning, but candour guidance expects near misses to be reported formally so the system can learn.
n.1: Personal reflection is useful but does not replace organisational reporting of the near miss.
n.2: Telling the patient is not enough; the near miss must still be documented and reported (Code 14.3, 19.1).

7.q: A neonatal nurse cares for a baby with neonatal abstinence syndrome. The mother used heroin throughout pregnancy and missed antenatal care. A pre-birth assessment was not done. Under Working Together 2026, which category of harm can occur during pregnancy through maternal substance misuse?
o: Neglect
Child sexual exploitation
Emotional abuse
Physical abuse
7.w: Working Together 2026 states that neglect may occur during pregnancy, for example as a result of maternal substance abuse. Parts of the guidance apply to unborn children, which is why pre-birth assessments are made.

n.1: CSE involves exploiting a child for sexual activity and is unrelated.
n.2: Emotional abuse is not the category the guidance links to substance misuse in pregnancy.
n.3: Physical abuse involves inflicted harm such as hitting or poisoning a child; the guidance places substance misuse in pregnancy under neglect.

7.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
7.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

7.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
7.q: A nurse is attaching a three-lead cardiac monitor to Isla, aged 5, using the UK colour code. Where should the electrodes be placed?
o: Yellow on the right shoulder, green on the left shoulder, red on the left lower chest
Red on the right shoulder, yellow on the left shoulder, green on the left lower chest
Red on the left shoulder, yellow on the right shoulder, green on the right lower chest
Green on the right shoulder, red on the left shoulder, yellow on the left lower chest
7.w: In the UK (IEC) colour code for three-lead monitoring, red goes on the right shoulder (right arm), yellow on the left shoulder (left arm) and green on the left lower chest or abdomen (left leg). Placing electrodes on bony areas away from muscle helps reduce interference (AnnexB.2.5).

n.0: This places all three colours in the wrong positions.
n.2: This reverses red and yellow and places green on the wrong side.
n.3: Green belongs on the left lower chest, not the right shoulder.

7.q: Hannah, a staff nurse, is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Derek Lowe, 58. At the bedside he tells her he is allergic to penicillin. His allergy band was missing and the chart says 'no known allergies'. No dose was given. What should Hannah do about reporting?
o: Report herself to the NMC, as she nearly gave a contraindicated drug
Record it as a near miss on the trust's patient safety reporting system
Tell the ward manager verbally, as no harm reached the patient
Correct the chart and allergy band, as no report is needed without harm
7.w: Near misses are patient safety events and must be recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred (P6.8; Code 14 and NMC/GMC candour guidance 2024, which covers reporting near misses). Local systems feed the national Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service. The chart and band must also be corrected and the prescriber informed.

n.0: Self-referral to the regulator is not the response to a near miss caught by correct checks; this is a system issue for local reporting.
n.2: Verbal reporting alone loses the learning; near misses are formally recorded on the local system.
n.3: Correcting the records is needed, but near misses are reported because they reveal weaknesses before harm occurs.

7.q: Ellie, aged 8 weeks, is due her first immunisations. The nurse notices that the record of her newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is not available. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the injections and check the SCID result before rotavirus
Give all three vaccines today because SCID is very rare
Delay all three vaccines until the screening result is found
Give the oral rotavirus vaccine and delay the two injections
7.w: Rotavirus vaccine is live, and the UKHSA schedule states it should only be given after checking the SCID screening result (the same applies to BCG). The inactivated injected vaccines can still be given on time. Two steps: identify which vaccine is live, then act.

n.1: The schedule requires the SCID result to be checked before the live rotavirus vaccine, however rare the condition.
n.2: The inactivated injections are safe and should not be delayed.
n.3: Oral administration does not make it safe; rotavirus is the live vaccine that needs the SCID check, and the injections should not be delayed.

7.q: Ahmed, 9, has a life-limiting condition and is seen by neurology, respiratory, gastroenterology and the community team. His parents say they do not know who is in charge of his care. What does NICE NG61 recommend?
o: A named medical specialist who leads on and coordinates his care
His GP coordinates his care, as he is seen by several teams
His parents choose which consultant to contact for each problem
The specialist who saw him most recently leads his care
7.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.2: every child with a life-limiting condition should have a named medical specialist who leads on and coordinates their care; explain that this person may change if the care needed or setting changes.

n.1: The GP is involved, but NG61 names a medical specialist as care lead.
n.2: Leaving parents to coordinate between consultants is what NG61 seeks to avoid.
n.3: Leadership by whoever saw him last gives no consistent coordination.

7.q: Albert, a resident in a care home, died last night. This morning his close friend Ted, another resident, asks the nurse where Albert is, as he did not come to breakfast. Albert's family have been informed. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask the activities coordinator to tell residents at next week's meeting
Avoid telling Ted, to prevent him becoming upset during breakfast
Tell Ted sensitively that Albert has died and offer him time and support
Say that Albert has gone into hospital so that Ted is not distressed
7.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): residents in communal settings such as care homes often build significant relationships with other residents and will need to be informed; the RNVoEAD guidance asks the nurse to recognise the emotional impact on surrounding residents and prompt support. Code 2 and 20.2: act with honesty.

n.0: Delaying news for a week is not compassionate support for a close friend who is asking now.
n.1: Residents in communal settings have often built close relationships and need to be informed and supported.
n.3: Giving false information is dishonest (Code 20.2) and delays Ted's grieving.

7.q: Priya, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant and attends her antenatal appointment in October, during the flu season. She has had no vaccines in this pregnancy. According to the UKHSA schedule, which vaccines should she be offered now?
o: Flu, pertussis and RSV vaccines, all at this appointment
Pertussis vaccine now, with the flu vaccine after the birth
RSV vaccine now, with the pertussis vaccine from 28 weeks
Inactivated flu vaccine and the pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
7.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: in pregnancy, inactivated flu vaccine at any stage during the flu season; pertussis (Tdap) from 16 weeks (ideally before 32 weeks but may be given later); RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) from 28 weeks.

n.0: RSV vaccine is offered from 28 weeks of pregnancy, so it is not due at 20 weeks.
n.1: Inactivated flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy during the flu season.
n.2: This reverses the timings: pertussis is from 16 weeks and RSV from 28 weeks.

7.q: Grace, 68, is admitted to a surgical ward. Three months ago she was an inpatient in a hospital abroad after a car accident. She has no symptoms of infection. What is the most appropriate placement while admission screening is arranged?
o: A single room with contact precautions while screening for CPE
A bay with other patients recently treated abroad, pending results
An open bay, after starting prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
An open bay, with screening repeated if she develops a fever
7.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 lists patients who have been inpatients in any hospital in the UK or abroad as a possible cross-infection risk for multidrug-resistant organisms such as carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE). She should be placed in a single room with contact precautions pending screening, and the decision documented.

n.1: Cohorting is for patients with the same confirmed infection; unscreened patients may carry different organisms.
n.2: Prophylactic antibiotics do not clear carriage and drive resistance, contrary to NICE NG15 stewardship.
n.3: CPE carriage is usually symptomless, so waiting for a fever leaves the bay exposed.

8.q: Monica, 55, had abdominal surgery five days ago. Her wound edges are now red and swollen, the area is hot and tender, and there is cloudy discharge. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Which conclusion best fits these findings?
o: The wound is in the normal maturation phase
The wound is showing signs of a moisture lesion
The wound shows a normal inflammatory response
The wound shows signs of infection
8.w: Increasing redness, swelling, heat, pain, purulent or cloudy exudate and fever at day 5 indicate wound infection, which needs escalation and review. Mild early inflammation in the first few days is normal, but it should be settling, not worsening (Annexe B 4.6).

n.0: Maturation (remodelling) is a late phase lasting months and does not cause fever and pus.
n.1: Moisture lesions are caused by incontinence or sweat on the skin, not surgical wound infection.
n.2: Normal inflammation is mild and settles early; worsening signs with fever suggest infection.

8.q: A student nurse asks which infants count as 'not independently mobile' for the purpose of bruising protocols. Maya, 7 months, can roll from front to back but cannot crawl, cruise or bottom shuffle. How should Maya be classified?
o: Independently mobile, as she can roll over without help
Independently mobile, as she is older than 6 months
Not independently mobile, as she cannot crawl or shuffle
Not independently mobile until she is able to walk unaided
8.w: NICE CG89 (child maltreatment, last updated December 2025) defines a child as independently mobile if they can crawl, bottom shuffle, pull themself up to stand, stand unaided, cruise, walk with a push-along walker or walk, and says age alone should not decide. Rolling is not on the list, so Maya is not independently mobile and a bruise on her would need assessment under the protocol.

n.0: Rolling is not independent mobility for this purpose.
n.1: Mobility is defined by ability, not by age.
n.3: A child who crawls, cruises or bottom shuffles is mobile even before walking.

8.q: Mrs Dawson, 84, has a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and is on a ward in England. She tells the nurse she wants to go home today rather than wait for physiotherapy. A junior doctor says, 'She has dementia, so she can't make that decision.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: She can go home, because a person with dementia keeps all their rights
A best interests meeting should be arranged before any assessment
Her capacity for this decision must be assessed, not assumed from diagnosis
Her daughter should be asked to decide, as she is her next of kin
8.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition. Capacity must be assessed for this decision at this time.

n.0: Whether she can safely go home depends on whether she has capacity for this decision; that has not yet been assessed.
n.1: Best interests decisions (s4) follow a finding that the person lacks capacity; the assessment comes first.
n.3: Next of kin has no legal power to make decisions for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.

8.q: A nurse involved in a child death review asks where the information from all child death reviews in England is analysed nationally to identify trends and inform prevention. Which body is this?
o: The Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch
The National Child Mortality Database
The Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel
The Care Quality Commission
8.w: Working Together 2026 states that child death review partners must arrange for information from all deaths reviewed to be analysed by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD), which identifies trends and similarities to inform local and national prevention.

n.0: HSIB (now HSSIB) investigates selected patient safety incidents, not all child deaths.
n.2: The Panel oversees serious safeguarding case reviews, not all child deaths.
n.3: The CQC regulates providers and does not analyse all child death reviews.

8.q: Jake, 10, has type 1 diabetes. In the school nurse's office he is shaky and sweaty and his capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. He is alert and able to swallow. What should the nurse give first?
o: A slice of wholemeal toast and a glass of milk
A chocolate bar and a biscuit
15 g of fast-acting glucose, such as juice
IM glucagon 1 mg into the thigh
8.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.89: treat mild to moderate hypoglycaemia immediately with oral fast-acting glucose (10-20 g; liquid may be easier), recheck within 15 minutes, then give complex carbohydrate.

n.0: Toast and milk are complex carbohydrate, given after glucose has been restored, not first.
n.1: Fat in chocolate slows glucose absorption; fast-acting glucose works within 5-15 minutes.
n.3: Glucagon is for severe hypoglycaemia when oral treatment is unsafe; Jake can swallow.

8.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
8.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

8.q: Mr Kapoor, 67, has capacity and has told Hayley, his nurse, that he does not want the proposed amputation and would prefer palliative wound care. On the ward round the surgeon starts to describe the operation date without asking his views. What should Hayley do?
o: Say that Mr Kapoor has shared views about the operation and invite him to explain them
Record Mr Kapoor's wishes in his nursing notes once the ward round has finished
Wait until after the ward round and then ask Mr Kapoor whether he has changed his mind
Tell the surgeon that Mr Kapoor has asked her to cancel the operation on his behalf
8.w: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable; Code 2.5 respect the right to refuse treatment). Inviting Mr Kapoor to speak supports his autonomy without speaking over him (MCA 2005 s1 principles).

n.1: Recording his wishes is necessary but does not ensure they are heard in the decision being made now.
n.2: Waiting allows a decision to be made without him; he has already expressed his wishes.
n.3: Hayley should not overstate or speak for him when he can speak for himself.

8.q: Deshawn, 15, attends the emergency department with a cut to his hand. He has two mobile phones, £300 in cash and was found by police in a town 80 miles from home. His mother says he has gone missing four times this month. Which form of harm do these features most strongly suggest?
o: Neglect by his parents at home
Child criminal exploitation
Child sexual exploitation online
Radicalisation towards extremism
8.w: Working Together 2026 defines child criminal exploitation as coercing, controlling, manipulating or deceiving a child into criminal activity, with county lines as an example. Multiple phones, unexplained cash, repeated missing episodes and being found far from home are classic indicators.

n.0: His mother is reporting the missing episodes; the indicators point to harm from outside the family.
n.2: Nothing described suggests sexual activity in exchange for something.
n.3: There is no indication of extremist ideology.

8.q: During equality training, a healthcare assistant asks which personal characteristic is protected under section 4 of the Equality Act 2010. Which of these is a protected characteristic?
o: Pregnancy and maternity
Body weight or size
Socioeconomic background
Caring responsibilities
8.w: Equality Act 2010 s4 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

n.1: Weight is not a protected characteristic, although a related condition may amount to a disability.
n.2: Socioeconomic background is not one of the nine protected characteristics in s4.
n.3: Being a carer is not itself a listed characteristic in s4.

8.q: Agnes, 79, has type 2 diabetes with reduced sensation in her feet. Her toenails are long and thickened, and she asks you to cut them during her bath. What is the most appropriate action?
o: File her nails down after soaking her feet for 20 minutes
Explain the risk and refer her to the podiatry service
Ask a healthcare support worker to cut them carefully
Cut her nails straight across with sterile nail clippers
8.w: People with diabetes and reduced sensation are at high risk of foot ulceration from minor trauma, so thickened nails should be cut by a podiatrist. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during nail care.

n.0: Prolonged soaking softens skin and can cause maceration in a person with diabetes.
n.2: Delegating a task that needs specialist assessment does not reduce the risk.
n.3: Cutting thickened nails in a person with diabetic neuropathy risks injury and ulceration.

8.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which abbreviation practice best supports safe record keeping when documenting medicines and care in the notes. Which approach should she follow?
o: Write terms in full unless the trust approves the abbreviation
Use abbreviations for drug names to save time in busy shifts
Use the abbreviations she learned during her training abroad
Use any abbreviation that colleagues on the ward understand
8.w: Code 10.4: records must be clearly written and not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. Annexe A 1.8 accurate, clear, legible records.

n.1: Abbreviating drug names risks medication errors and breaches Code 10.4.
n.2: Abbreviations vary between countries and may not be understood here.
n.3: Local shorthand may be misread by others; Code 10.4 says no unnecessary abbreviations.

8.q: A ward team wants to reduce the number of missed doses of time-critical medicines. Using the Model for Improvement, which question should they answer first?
o: Who was responsible for the missed doses last month?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
What are we trying to accomplish?
How will we know that a change is an improvement?
8.w: The Model for Improvement (used in NHS England improvement resources) asks three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? (the aim); How will we know that a change is an improvement? (measures); What change can we make that will result in improvement? (change ideas). Changes are then tested with PDSA cycles. Setting the aim comes first (P6.4).

n.0: Improvement methods look at system causes rather than individual blame, and this is not one of the model's questions.
n.1: Change ideas are the third question, chosen once the aim and measures are agreed.
n.3: Measures are the second question; they depend on a clear aim.

8.q: Deborah, 46, received IM adrenaline 500 micrograms for anaphylaxis 5 minutes ago. She remains wheezy with BP 84/52 mmHg. What should happen next?
o: Wait a further 15 minutes before repeating adrenaline
Give chlorphenamine IV and wait for it to take effect
Sit her upright with her legs lowered to ease breathing
Give a second IM adrenaline dose and an IV crystalloid bolus
8.w: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and give an IV crystalloid bolus (adults 500-1,000 mL) for circulatory problems, with high-flow oxygen and monitoring.

n.0: RCUK advises a repeat dose after 5 minutes, not 15.
n.1: Antihistamines are not used to treat ABC problems in anaphylaxis.
n.2: With hypotension she should lie flat with or without legs raised; sitting with legs down worsens circulation.

8.q: Under NICE guidance on violence and aggression (NG10), when may manual restraint be used in a health setting?
o: As the first response whenever a person raises their voice
As a last resort when de-escalation fails and harm is likely
As a routine measure to give medicines a person has refused
As a punishment for breaking ward rules on two occasions
8.w: NICE NG10 and Annexe B 2.17: restrictive interventions are used as a last resort, after de-escalation and other strategies fail, when there is a real risk of harm, and must be proportionate and for the shortest time possible.

n.0: Raised voices call for de-escalation, not restraint.
n.2: Restraint is not a routine method of giving refused medicines; covert or compulsory treatment has its own legal safeguards.
n.3: Restraint is never punitive; this would breach human rights and the Code.

8.q: Hilda, 83, has end-stage pulmonary fibrosis and is in the last days of life. She says she feels breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 95% on air and her chest is unchanged on examination. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
o: Use a fan and positioning, and check whether an opioid is prescribed
Arrange an arterial blood gas sample to guide oxygen therapy
Start oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula to ease her breathing
Give the 'as required' hyoscine butylbromide from her anticipatory box
8.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.16 and 1.5.17: consider non-pharmacological management of breathlessness (for example a fan), do not routinely start oxygen unless symptomatic hypoxaemia is known or suspected, and consider an opioid, a benzodiazepine or both.

n.1: An invasive test unlikely to change care should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.1.4).
n.2: With saturation of 95% she is not hypoxaemic; NG31 rec 1.5.16 says do not routinely start oxygen for breathlessness.
n.3: Hyoscine butylbromide is used for secretions or bowel obstruction, not for breathlessness.

8.q: Ahmed, 28, is distressed and tearful after hearing bad news. Which skill is the cornerstone of mental health first aid in this situation?
o: Offering a sedative medicine
Distracting him with other topics
Listening non-judgementally
Giving clear advice on solutions
8.w: Mental health first aid centres on approaching the person, listening non-judgementally, giving support and information, and encouraging appropriate professional help (Annexe B 2.14).

n.0: Medication is not a first aid response to normal distress.
n.1: Distraction can invalidate his feelings and block disclosure.
n.3: Jumping to advice can feel dismissive before the person feels heard.

8.q: Nurses on a surgical ward want to check whether pain scores are reassessed within 30 minutes of giving analgesia, as their trust policy requires. They plan to review 40 recent patient records against this requirement. What type of activity is this?
o: Service evaluation, because it describes current care with no standard
Research, because it collects data from patient records
A PDSA cycle, because it tests a change to practice on a small scale
Clinical audit, because it measures care against a set standard
8.w: Clinical audit is a quality improvement cycle that measures the effectiveness of care against agreed standards and acts to bring practice in line with them (HQIP definition). Here an existing policy standard is being measured, so it is audit (P6.4, P6.7).

n.0: Service evaluation describes current care without reference to a standard; this project has a defined standard.
n.1: Research generates new knowledge, for example by testing a hypothesis; reviewing records against an existing standard is not research.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; no change is being tested here, only current practice measured.

8.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
8.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

8.q: Nadia, a staff nurse, reports that she gave an evening dose of a medicine to the wrong patient after two patients with similar names were moved into adjacent beds. The patient is unharmed. Which response from the ward manager best reflects a just culture?
o: Remove Nadia from medicine rounds until she has completed a formal assessment
Ask Nadia to apologise to the team for the extra work the incident has created
Record a formal warning on Nadia's file because she did not check identity
Thank Nadia for reporting, support her and review the system factors involved
8.w: A just culture treats honest error as an opportunity to learn, supports the person involved and looks at system contributors (here, similar names placed side by side). This encourages reporting, which PSIRF and Code 14 and 16 depend on (P5.2; P6.6). Reckless conduct is handled differently.

n.0: Removing her from duties for an honest error with clear system causes discourages reporting; support and reflection are more proportionate.
n.1: Asking her to apologise to colleagues shames her and adds nothing to learning.
n.2: Formal sanctions for unintentional error undermine reporting and ignore the system factors.

8.q: Ethan, 14, attends a clinic with his mother. The nurse wants to complete a psychosocial assessment. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask Ethan to fill in a questionnaire and pass it to his mother to check
See Ethan alone for part of the visit and explain confidentiality limits
See Ethan with his mother throughout so she can add any missing detail
Ask his mother to answer the questions because Ethan is still under 16
8.w: Good adolescent practice is to see the young person on their own for part of the consultation and to explain at the start what will stay confidential and when information may need to be shared to keep them or others safe (NICE NG204 rec 1.5.2 offer young people time on their own; Doukrou and Segal 2018, HEEADSSS). This respects developing autonomy (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Passing his answers to his mother breaches the confidence he would expect and discourages honest answers.
n.2: Young people are less likely to disclose risks such as substance use or self-harm in front of a parent.
n.3: Young people under 16 can give their own history, and a parent may not know about many psychosocial risks.

8.q: Mr Tran, 52, speaks little English and is due to have a chest drain inserted later today. His consultant has asked the nurse to make sure he understands the procedure and its risks before he agrees. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Rely on his nodding to show that he understands
Use pictures and gestures to explain the main steps of the procedure
Arrange a professional interpreter for the consent discussion
Give him an English information leaflet to read first
8.w: Consent must be informed: the person needs to understand the procedure, material risks and alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 7.2 requires reasonable steps to meet people's language and communication needs, so a professional interpreter should be used for the discussion.

n.0: Nodding may reflect politeness rather than understanding, so it is not evidence of informed consent.
n.1: Pictures and gestures may support communication but cannot convey material risks and alternatives reliably for a chest drain.
n.3: A leaflet in a language he cannot read well does not inform him and does not meet Code 7.2.

8.q: A doctor needs to tell Mrs Ibrahim, 70, who speaks Somali and limited English, that her husband has died in intensive care. Her adult niece is with her. What is the most appropriate way to communicate?
o: Wait until her son arrives to translate later that day
Use a professional Somali interpreter for the conversation
Give the news in simple English and check she understands
Ask the niece to interpret, as she is family and will support her
8.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; reliance on family is strongly discouraged. Code 7.2 meet language needs; Annexe A 2.9.

n.0: Delaying the news without reason causes distress; an interpreter can be arranged now.
n.2: Simple English risks misunderstanding when news is this serious.
n.3: Relying on family is discouraged; the niece is also grieving and may filter the news.

8.q: Pat, 75, has a venous leg ulcer with no red flags. Mild compression was started at her first visit, and strong compression bandaging is now being considered. Before strong compression is applied, what assessment must be completed?
o: A wound swab for culture and sensitivity
A Doppler ankle brachial pressure index
A full blood count to check for anaemia
A capillary blood glucose measurement
8.w: NWCSP Leg Ulcer Recommendations (2023): with no red flags, mild compression (up to 20 mmHg) can start straight away, but a full assessment including a Doppler ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI), within 14 days, is needed before strong compression (40 mmHg or more), because strong compression on a limb with arterial insufficiency can cause ischaemia (Annexe B 4.6 pressure bandaging).

n.0: A wound swab is not needed to decide on compression and is taken only with signs of infection.
n.2: FBC does not assess arterial supply to the limb.
n.3: Glucose is relevant to healing but does not determine whether compression is safe.

8.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
8.q: Leah, aged 2, has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and is now drowsy, responding only to voice. Airway and breathing are satisfactory, and fluids are being started for poor perfusion. What should the nurse check next under D?
o: Her temperature
Her weight
Her blood glucose
Her serum sodium
8.w: Under D (disability), assess conscious level (AVPU), pupils and posture, and check blood glucose: young children have limited glycogen stores and become hypoglycaemic quickly when unwell (RCUK 2025; T2 physiological differences). Hypoglycaemia is a treatable cause of reduced consciousness.

n.0: Temperature belongs to E (exposure), after D.
n.1: Weight is needed for dosing but does not assess her reduced consciousness.
n.3: Sodium matters with fluid therapy, but a bedside glucose is the immediate D check for drowsiness.

8.q: On a ward round you notice that the urinary drainage bag of Bernard, 79, is lying on the floor beside his chair, and later it is hooked over the bed rail above his waist while he is repositioned. What is the correct positioning of the drainage bag?
o: Level with the bladder to reduce traction on the catheter
Above the bladder when moving, then below it when seated
Below the level of the bladder and not touching the floor
On the floor beside the bed to keep the tubing straight
8.w: NICE CG139 (catheter care): the drainage bag is positioned below the level of the bladder to maintain flow and prevent reflux, and kept off the floor to avoid contamination, using a stand where needed.

n.0: At bladder level, drainage slows and urine can pool or reflux.
n.1: Raising the bag above the bladder allows contaminated urine to flow back towards the bladder.
n.3: A bag on the floor becomes contaminated and increases the risk of catheter-associated infection.

8.q: A nurse is helping to design a local prevention strategy and wants to apply a life course approach. Which statement best reflects that approach?
o: Accept that adult health is fixed by genes, so early action changes little
Begin prevention once a long-term condition has been diagnosed in the person
Act early and at key transitions, as health is shaped across the whole of life
Focus prevention on older adults, as most long-term disease occurs in later life
8.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): a life course approach considers the critical stages, transitions and settings where large differences can be made, taking action early and appropriately across the life course and reducing health inequalities throughout life.

n.0: The approach rests on evidence that early and timely action changes lifelong outcomes.
n.1: Waiting for diagnosis misses the critical earlier stages the approach targets.
n.3: A life course approach acts at every stage, including early years, not just in later life.

8.q: Mr Shah, 69, has motor neurone disease. He shows the nurse a document he wrote and signed refusing mechanical ventilation. It was witnessed but contains no statement that it applies even if his life is at risk. He now lacks capacity and is in respiratory failure. What is the status of the document?
o: It is not valid because it was not drafted by a solicitor
It is not valid as a refusal of this life-sustaining treatment
It is valid because it is written, signed and witnessed
It is valid because his family confirm these were his wishes
8.w: MCA 2005 s25(5)-(6): an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed, witnessed and include a statement by the person that it is to apply even if life is at risk. Without that statement it does not apply to ventilation, although it must still inform the best interests decision.

n.0: There is no requirement for a solicitor to draft an advance decision.
n.2: Writing, signature and witness are necessary but not sufficient; the life-at-risk statement is missing.
n.3: Family confirmation cannot supply a missing statutory formality.

8.q: Ben, 7, starts having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the playroom of the children's ward. He is on the floor next to a toy box. What should the nurse do first?
o: Note the time, move the toy box away and cushion his head
Hold his arms and legs firmly to stop him injuring himself
Lift him on to the nearest bed to examine him
Place a padded tongue depressor between his teeth
8.w: Seizure first aid (NHS febrile seizures guidance, NG217): note the start time, protect the child from injury by moving hard objects and cushioning the head, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, and place in the recovery position when the jerking stops.

n.1: Restraining limbs can cause injury and does not shorten the seizure.
n.2: Lifting a convulsing child risks injury to both; protect him where he is.
n.3: Nothing should be put in the mouth; it can break teeth or obstruct the airway.

8.q: A community nurse in England is asked by a student which organisation in their integrated care system plans NHS services for the local population and manages the local NHS budget. What is the correct answer?
o: The integrated care partnership (ICP)
The upper-tier local authority
The local provider collaborative
The integrated care board (ICB)
8.w: Each of the 36 integrated care systems in England has one integrated care board, an NHS organisation responsible for planning health services for its population and managing the NHS budget (Health and Care Act 2022; ICSs legally established 1 July 2022) (P7.6; FACTS S-ICS).

n.0: The ICP is a joint committee of NHS bodies and upper-tier councils that develops the integrated care strategy; it does not hold the NHS budget.
n.1: Upper-tier local authorities are responsible for social care and public health, not NHS budgets.
n.2: Provider collaboratives bring trusts together to plan and deliver services but do not hold the ICS's NHS budget.

8.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
8.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

8.q: Ahmed, 9, has a life-limiting condition and is seen by neurology, respiratory, gastroenterology and the community team. His parents say they do not know who is in charge of his care. What does NICE NG61 recommend?
o: A named medical specialist who leads on and coordinates his care
His GP coordinates his care, as he is seen by several teams
His parents choose which consultant to contact for each problem
The specialist who saw him most recently leads his care
8.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.2: every child with a life-limiting condition should have a named medical specialist who leads on and coordinates their care; explain that this person may change if the care needed or setting changes.

n.1: The GP is involved, but NG61 names a medical specialist as care lead.
n.2: Leaving parents to coordinate between consultants is what NG61 seeks to avoid.
n.3: Leadership by whoever saw him last gives no consistent coordination.

8.q: Kieran, 16, attends the day surgery unit alone for an elective knee arthroscopy. He has capacity and signs the consent form after a full discussion. His mother phones to say she has not been asked and wants to give consent herself. What is the legal position?
o: His consent needs countersigning by a second clinician
His mother's consent is also needed because he is under 18
His own consent is valid and parental consent is not needed
The surgery must wait until his mother can attend in person
8.w: Section 8(1) of the Family Law Reform Act 1969 makes the consent of a 16 or 17-year-old to surgical, medical or dental treatment as effective as an adult's, and states that consent from a parent or guardian is then not necessary.

n.0: No countersignature is required for a capacitous 16-year-old's consent.
n.1: FLRA 1969 s8 removes the need for parental consent once a 16-year-old has effectively consented.
n.3: Parental attendance is not a legal requirement for a 16-year-old's valid consent.

8.q: Ava, 3 weeks, born at 39 weeks, is brought to the children's emergency department with a two-day cold. While on the observation trolley she stops breathing for 20 seconds and becomes dusky, then recovers with stimulation. What does this presentation most suggest?
o: Bronchiolitis with apnoea, needing urgent medical review
Normal periodic breathing of a term newborn during sleep
Reflux episode needing smaller, more frequent feeds
Croup, needing a single dose of oral dexamethasone
8.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): young infants (particularly under 6 weeks) may present with apnoea without other clinical signs. Apnoea is a red flag for immediate referral and urgent medical review.

n.1: Periodic breathing involves brief pauses of a few seconds without colour change; a dusky 20-second apnoea is not normal.
n.2: Reflux does not explain apnoea with colour change alongside a viral illness; the risk of bronchiolitis apnoea must be assumed.
n.3: Croup causes barking cough and stridor in older infants and toddlers, not apnoea at 3 weeks.

8.q: Frank Ellis, 74, uses a walking frame and fell once at home last month. He has capacity and wants to walk to the day room for lunch. His daughter asks the nurse to keep him in his chair so he cannot fall again. Which response best reflects positive risk management?
o: Let Mr Ellis walk to the day room after he signs a disclaimer accepting the risk of falling
Arrange for him to use a wheelchair to reach the day room until physiotherapy can review him
Agree with the daughter and keep him seated at lunchtimes until he is discharged home
Agree a plan with Mr Ellis for supervised walking with his frame and record the discussion
8.w: Positive risk management weighs benefits and harms with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so they can do what matters to them, rather than removing all activity (P6.10 risk management versus risk aversion). Mr Ellis has capacity, so his decision is respected (MCA 2005 s1), and the plan and discussion are documented (Code 10).

n.0: A disclaimer does not manage the risk or remove the nurse's duty of care; it replaces planning with paperwork.
n.1: Using a wheelchair when he can walk with his frame reduces independence and mobility without a clinical reason.
n.2: Keeping him seated is risk aversion: it removes activity he values, causes deconditioning and overrides the choice of a person with capacity.

8.q: Ayaan, 4, is treated for an acute asthma attack in the emergency department. The doctor asks the nurse to give oral prednisolone early as recommended in the asthma pathway. What dose is appropriate for Ayaan's age?
o: 20 mg
40 mg
10 mg
60 mg
8.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): oral prednisolone given early: 10 mg under 2 years, 20 mg for 2-5 years, 30-40 mg over 5 years, usually for up to 3 days.

n.1: 30-40 mg is for children over 5; Ayaan is 4.
n.2: 10 mg is the dose for children under 2.
n.3: 60 mg exceeds the recommended paediatric dose for any age band.

8.q: After a stroke, Hilary, 77, can manage only pureed food and thickened fluids and cannot swallow tablets. Her prescription includes a modified-release tablet. A healthcare support worker suggests crushing it into her pudding. What should the nurse do first?
o: Crush it finely and mix it with a spoonful of pudding
Ask the pharmacist about a suitable alternative formulation
Omit the tablet and record that she is unable to swallow
Break the tablet in half so that it is easier to swallow
8.w: Altering a medicine's form, such as crushing, can change how it works and makes its use unlicensed; modified-release tablets in particular must not be crushed because the whole dose may be released at once. Pharmacist advice is sought before crushing or opening (RPS guidance on crushing cited in RPS/RCN 2019; AnnexB.11.6).

n.0: Crushing a modified-release tablet can cause dose dumping and toxicity.
n.2: Omitting the dose without seeking an alternative leaves her untreated.
n.3: Splitting a modified-release tablet can also disrupt its release mechanism, and swallowing is unsafe.

8.q: Maddie, 6, has cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency. Her mother says Maddie has greasy, foul-smelling stools and is not gaining weight. Maddie takes her pancreatic enzyme capsules only with breakfast. What advice should the nurse give, with the dietitian?
o: Stop the enzymes for a week to see if her stools change
Give a double dose of enzymes with breakfast only
Give enzymes with every fat-containing meal and snack
Reduce the fat in her diet so that she needs fewer enzymes
8.w: NICE NG78 Cystic fibrosis: diagnosis and management recs 1.7.2 and 1.7.6: offer oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and adjust the dose to minimise malabsorption; enzymes are taken with all fat-containing meals, snacks and milk drinks. Calorie intake is increased, not reduced.

n.0: Stopping enzymes would worsen malabsorption and weight loss.
n.1: Enzymes act on the food eaten at that time; a large breakfast dose does not cover later meals.
n.3: Children with CF need high-energy diets; reducing fat worsens faltering growth.

8.q: Noah, 3, has Kawasaki disease after 6 days of fever, red palms and a strawberry tongue. He is prescribed IV immunoglobulin and oral aspirin. His mother says she was told children should not have aspirin. What should the nurse explain?
o: Aspirin is safe for him because he is over 2 years old
Kawasaki disease is a recognised reason to prescribe aspirin
The aspirin is a prescribing error and she should refuse it
Aspirin is used to bring down his fever more quickly
8.w: Aspirin is not given to under 16s unless prescribed, with Kawasaki disease a recognised exception: it is prescribed with IV immunoglobulin to reduce inflammation and the risk of coronary artery complications (NHS Kawasaki disease guidance).

n.0: The under-16 restriction is not about being over 2; it applies to all children unless prescribed for a specific reason.
n.2: Aspirin is deliberately prescribed in Kawasaki disease; it is not an error.
n.3: Aspirin in Kawasaki disease reduces inflammation and clot risk in the coronary arteries; it is not used as an antipyretic.

8.q: Evie, aged 7, has been diagnosed with leukaemia. Her parents tell the nurse that her brother Sam, 5, has started wetting the bed and asking whether he will get ill too. Which nursing response best reflects family-centred care?
o: Include Sam, with honest age-appropriate information and play support
Advise the parents to keep Sam away from the ward to protect him from worry
Suggest the parents wait until Sam is older before talking about Evie's illness
Refer Sam to his GP for investigation of the new bed wetting
8.w: Family-centred care recognises that a child's illness affects the whole family, including siblings, who may feel anxious, jealous or responsible. Honest, age-appropriate information, involvement in visits and play specialist support help siblings cope (P3.4, P4.2).

n.1: Excluding Sam is likely to increase his anxiety and fantasies about the illness.
n.2: Delaying explanation leaves a worried child without support at a time of change.
n.3: New bed wetting here is a likely response to family stress; a medical referral alone misses his emotional needs.

8.q: Mrs Kerr, 66, fell and hit her head. Her GCS has fallen from 14 to 11 over an hour, and her right pupil is now larger than the left and slow to react to light. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the findings and inform the next ward round
Call for an urgent medical review as an emergency
Recheck her neurological observations in 1 hour
Dim the lights and recheck her pupils in 30 minutes
8.w: A falling GCS with a new unequal, sluggish pupil after head injury suggests rising intracranial pressure, a neurological emergency (Annexe B 2.12). Immediate escalation is needed; she also scores 3 on NEWS2 for an altered level of consciousness.

n.0: A ward round is far too late for an acute neurological deterioration.
n.2: Waiting an hour delays treatment of possible raised intracranial pressure.
n.3: Changing the lighting does not address the deterioration and delays escalation.

8.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
8.q: Ali, 7 months, has bronchiolitis and is on oxygen. His saturations have been 91 to 92%. He becomes quiet and floppy; his heart rate falls from 170 to 55 beats/min and he has poor perfusion despite effective bag-mask ventilation by the team. What should happen next?
o: Start chest compressions
Recheck the heart rate in 5 minutes
Give a fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg
Increase the oxygen and observe
8.w: Two steps: recognise that bradycardia in a hypoxic infant is pre-terminal, then act. RCUK 2025: start chest compressions if the heart rate is below 60 beats/min with poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation.

n.1: Waiting 5 minutes in a pre-arrest state risks cardiac arrest.
n.2: Fluids do not treat hypoxic bradycardia; compressions are needed when HR is below 60 with poor perfusion despite ventilation.
n.3: Oxygen and ventilation are already being given; the criteria for compressions are met.

8.q: Nurse Ella is discharging Mr Kerr, 70, with a leg wound to the district nursing team. Which referral content is most useful?
o: The wound plan, next dressing date, allergies and ward contact
A request for the team to phone the ward for details
A brief note saying that a leg wound needs regular care at home
A copy of the full nursing notes for the whole admission
8.w: Annexe A 1.9: share written reports clearly. Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care; Code 10.2 identify risks so colleagues have the information they need.

n.1: This delays care and relies on verbal handover.
n.2: This lacks the detail needed for safe continuity.
n.3: Bulk notes bury the key information the team needs.

8.q: Ms Reid, 38, has a learning disability, epilepsy and type 1 diabetes. She has missed three diabetes clinic appointments, and her carer says the waiting room makes her very anxious. What is the most appropriate response by the community nurse?
o: Write to her to say that further missed appointments will be noted
Discharge her from clinic, as she has not attended three times
Ask her carer to attend the clinic in her place to collect advice
Arrange reasonable adjustments such as a first or quiet appointment
8.w: P7.5 requires responding to the challenges of person-centred care for people with complex needs, and the Equality Act 2010 s20 imposes a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Adjusting the appointment removes the barrier to her care.

n.0: A warning letter does not address the cause of her non-attendance.
n.1: Discharging her penalises her for a barrier the service can adjust, worsening inequality.
n.2: Her carer cannot receive her care or examinations for her; she needs to be seen.

8.q: A 2-year-old dies following severe physical abuse. The local authority, on behalf of the safeguarding partners, notifies the Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel. Under Working Together 2026, within what time should the rapid review be submitted to the Panel?
o: Within 45 working days of the notification
Within 6 months of the notification
Within 15 working days of the notification
Within 5 working days of the notification
8.w: Working Together 2026 requires serious incident notification within five working days of the safeguarding partners becoming aware, and the rapid review to be submitted to the Panel within 15 working days of the notification.

n.0: 45 working days is the maximum assessment timescale for children's social care.
n.1: Six months relates to completing a local child safeguarding practice review, not the rapid review.
n.3: Five working days is the timescale for the notification itself.

8.q: Leah, 16, has juvenile idiopathic arthritis. At her clinic appointment her mother always answers for her. Leah says she wants to manage her own condition. What should the nurse do to support her transition?
o: Offer Leah time with the team without her parents present
Ask her mother to stay away from future appointments
Continue directing questions to her mother until Leah is 18
Arrange for Leah to start attending the adult clinic now
8.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) recs 1.2.19-1.2.21: ask the young person how they want parents involved and help them develop confidence by giving them the chance to raise concerns separately from parents, while respecting the parents' role.

n.1: Excluding her mother entirely ignores Leah's own preferences and the family's role.
n.2: Waiting until 18 ignores Leah's wishes and her developing independence.
n.3: Transfer timing is planned, not triggered by one consultation; this skips preparation.

8.q: Edna, 80, is admitted to a medical ward from home after a fall. She has limited mobility and a previous sacral pressure ulcer. Under NICE CG179, when should her pressure ulcer risk be assessed and documented?
o: When a skin change is first noticed
Within 72 hours of admission
At the first weekly skin review
On admission to the ward
8.w: NICE CG179 (2014): assess and document pressure ulcer risk for adults on admission to secondary care or care homes, and reassess if clinical status changes.

n.0: Waiting for skin change means prevention starts after damage has begun.
n.1: 72 hours delays prevention in someone at risk, contrary to CG179.
n.2: A weekly review would leave her unassessed during the high-risk early period.

8.q: Oscar, 6, is having a convulsive seizure on the children's ward that has lasted 5 minutes. He has a working IV cannula, the resuscitation trolley is at the bedside and he has no individual emergency plan. Which first-line treatment does NICE NG217 recommend?
o: IV levetiracetam
IV lorazepam
Rectal diazepam
Buccal midazolam
8.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.3: without an individualised plan, give buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, or IV lorazepam if IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available, as they are here.

n.0: Levetiracetam is the second-line treatment after two benzodiazepine doses.
n.2: Rectal diazepam is a community alternative and is slower than IV lorazepam when IV access exists.
n.3: Buccal midazolam is the first-line community option; with IV access and resuscitation facilities NG217 advises IV lorazepam.

8.q: Aiden, aged 2, needs a nasogastric tube passed. A health play specialist is not available. Which distraction is most suited to his age?
o: Blowing and popping bubbles or watching a light-up toy
Counting backwards from 100 in his head
Guided imagery about his favourite holiday
Explaining the anatomy of the nose using a diagram
8.w: Distraction should match developmental stage: toddlers respond to simple, sensory, attention-grabbing activities such as bubbles, light-up or musical toys and songs (AnnexA.3.8 distraction and diversion strategies).

n.1: Counting backwards from 100 is beyond a 2-year-old's ability.
n.2: Guided imagery needs abstract thinking suited to older children and adolescents.
n.3: A diagram is a preparation tool for older school-age children, not a distraction for a toddler.

8.q: A journalist telephones a medical ward asking how a well-known footballer admitted that morning is doing. The admission has already been reported on local news. The nurse who answers is the most senior person on the ward. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Confirm that he is a patient but share no clinical details
Decline to comment and refer the caller to the communications team
Give a brief general update, as the admission is already public
Ask the patient's consultant to call the journalist back later
8.w: Code 21.6: cooperate with the media only when appropriate, always protecting the confidentiality and dignity of people receiving care. Code 5.1 respects privacy; trust communications teams handle media enquiries with the patient's consent.

n.0: Confirming that someone is a patient is itself a disclosure of confidential information (Code 5).
n.2: Media reports do not remove the duty of confidentiality (Code 5.1); no information should be shared without consent and agreed process.
n.3: Passing the request to a clinician bypasses the trust's media process; media contact goes through the communications team.

8.q: A red cell transfusion for Graham, 66, started at 14:00. Baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate were recorded at 13:30 and were normal. According to BSH guidance, when should the next set of observations be taken?
o: At 14:30, 30 minutes after the start
At 15:00, 1 hour after the start
At 14:15, 15 minutes after the start
At the end of the unit, within 60 minutes
8.w: BSH (2017) observations: baseline no more than 60 minutes before starting, then pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, and again no more than 60 minutes after the end. Severe reactions often occur early in the unit.

n.0: The BSH timepoint is 15 minutes, not 30.
n.1: Waiting an hour misses the early period when serious reactions usually start.
n.3: End-of-unit observations are needed, but an observation at 15 minutes comes first.

8.q: A parent asks the children's community nurse what an education, health and care (EHC) plan is. Which explanation is correct?
o: An NHS continuing care plan funded by the integrated care board
A legal plan from the local authority setting out needs and support up to 25
A hospital care plan written by the consultant for a child's admissions
A school behaviour plan agreed between teachers and parents
8.w: SEND Code of Practice: 0 to 25 years (2015) and Children and Families Act 2014: an EHC plan is a legal document issued by the local authority describing a child or young person's special educational needs and the education, health and social care provision to meet them, from birth to 25.

n.0: Continuing care is a separate NHS assessment, although it can inform the EHC plan.
n.2: EHC plans are issued by the local authority, not written by hospital consultants.
n.3: A school behaviour plan has no statutory status and does not cover health and social care.

8.q: Ten minutes apart, Tariq, the nurse in charge, is told that Mr Lee, 63, has new central chest pain and that Mrs Burns, 81, was found sitting on the floor and has been helped back to bed by a healthcare assistant. She says she is fine. What should Tariq do?
o: Assess Mrs Burns first, as any fall needs a post-fall assessment before other care
Ask Mrs Burns' family to sit with her and see Mr Lee once she has been checked
Ask the healthcare assistant to record Mr Lee's ECG while he reviews Mrs Burns
Assess Mr Lee now and ask the assistant to record Mrs Burns' observations meanwhile
8.w: New central chest pain is potentially life-threatening and needs immediate registered nurse assessment and escalation. Mrs Burns still needs a post-fall assessment, but interim observations can be delegated to a competent healthcare assistant until Tariq reviews her (P5.5 prioritisation, delegation and assignment of care; Code 11). Two steps: prioritise, then delegate appropriately.

n.0: Mrs Burns needs assessment, but a potential acute coronary syndrome takes priority over a fall in a patient who reports feeling well.
n.1: Families are not a substitute for clinical observation, and this delays Mr Lee's assessment.
n.2: Recording an ECG may be within a trained assistant's role, but Tariq should assess the patient with chest pain himself first.

8.q: Callum, a district nurse, mentions that his car has broken down. The son of a patient he visits offers to lend him £500 to repair it until payday. What should Callum do?
o: Accept the loan and declare it to his manager
Decline the loan and keep the relationship professional
Accept the loan and repay it in full on payday
Accept a smaller amount as a gift in place of a loan
8.w: Code 21.2: never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them. Code 21.3 requires honesty and integrity in financial dealings.

n.0: Declaring it does not make it acceptable; loans from people close to patients are prohibited by Code 21.2.
n.2: Code 21.2 says never ask for or accept loans from anyone in your care or anyone close to them, even if repaid.
n.3: A cash gift of this kind is not trivial and breaches Code 21.1.

8.q: A health visitor explains early weight change to a new father. Which statement about weight in the first weeks of life is accurate?
o: Most babies have regained their birth weight by 3 weeks of age
Most babies regain their birth weight by 6 weeks of age
Weight loss usually continues for about 2 weeks before gain begins
Babies should not lose any weight if feeding is going well
8.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.1.1: it is common for infants to lose some weight in the early days, this usually stops after about 3 or 4 days, and most have returned to birth weight by 3 weeks. Not regaining birth weight by 3 weeks is a trigger for assessment (rec 1.1.4).

n.1: Six weeks is too late; regaining birth weight is expected by 3 weeks.
n.2: Early weight loss usually stops after 3 or 4 days, not 2 weeks.
n.3: Some early weight loss is common and expected even when feeding goes well.

8.q: The husband of a woman on a medical ward has started texting Rhys, her nurse, on his personal mobile, asking for updates late at night. Rhys gave him the number to arrange a visit. What should Rhys do?
o: Block the number without explaining his reasons to the husband
Reply with brief updates as the husband is her next of kin
Explain the boundary, give the ward number and tell the nurse in charge
Reply to messages during his shifts and switch off his phone at home
8.w: Proficiency P1.13: develop, manage and maintain appropriate relationships with people, their families and carers. Code 20.6 boundaries; Code 5 confidentiality; Code 8.2 keep colleagues informed.

n.0: Blocking without explanation damages the therapeutic relationship and leaves the husband without a proper contact route.
n.1: Next of kin status does not authorise sharing without her consent, and personal phone contact blurs boundaries.
n.3: Continuing private messaging keeps an unprofessional channel open and risks confidentiality.

8.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
8.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

8.q: A surgical registrar asks Priya, a registered nurse, to obtain Mrs Kaur's signature on a consent form for a laparoscopic procedure tomorrow. Priya has never seen this operation and does not know its specific risks or alternatives. What should Priya do?
o: Read the consent form aloud and witness Mrs Kaur's signature
Decline and ask the registrar to take consent from Mrs Kaur
Ask Mrs Kaur whether she has any questions before she signs
Obtain the signature and ask the registrar to explain risks later
8.w: Valid consent needs the person to be informed of material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 13 requires nurses to work within the limits of their competence, asking a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it (13.3). Priya cannot give that information, so the clinician who can should seek consent.

n.0: Reading the form does not allow Priya to answer questions about risks and alternatives she does not know.
n.2: Priya could not answer Mrs Kaur's questions about this operation's risks, so her consent would not be properly informed.
n.3: A signature obtained before the risks are explained does not show informed consent; the form is evidence, not consent itself.

8.q: Martina, a staff nurse, has just finished three consecutive 12-hour night shifts and feels exhausted. The ward manager phones asking her to work an extra day shift starting in four hours because of sickness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the shift and ask a colleague to second-check her medicines
Accept a shorter shift and leave as soon as cover can be found
Accept the shift and plan to rest during her break in the afternoon
Decline the shift, explaining that fatigue would make her practice unsafe
8.w: Fatigue is a key human factor that impairs judgement and increases error. Code 20.9 requires registrants to maintain the level of health needed to carry out their role, and Code 19.1 requires them to take measures to reduce mistakes. Martina should explain the safety risk so the manager can seek other cover (P5.2).

n.0: A second check does not make an exhausted nurse safe across all her tasks on a full shift.
n.1: Working even part of the shift while exhausted creates the same risk, and the time cover arrives is uncertain.
n.2: A short break does not offset the fatigue from three night shifts; she would still start the shift unsafe.

8.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
8.q: Ella, aged 10, has abdominal pain after surgery. She says her pain is '7 out of 10', but her mother thinks she is exaggerating because she is chatting with friends. What should the nurse do?
o: Wait until Ella looks distressed before giving analgesia
Score Ella's pain on the FLACC scale instead
Use the mother's estimate, because she knows Ella best
Accept Ella's self-report and act on it, then reassess
8.w: Self-report is the preferred measure of pain when a child can give it; children may use distraction or socialising to cope, so behaviour can underestimate pain. The nurse should believe and act on Ella's score, give prescribed analgesia and reassess (P4.8; AnnexB.3.5).

n.0: Waiting for visible distress leaves pain untreated and ignores her report.
n.1: FLACC is for children who cannot self-report and is validated up to 7 years.
n.2: Parents' views help, but a capable child's own report takes priority.

8.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
8.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

8.q: Frances, 84, has a sacral pressure ulcer. A routine wound swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. The ulcer has no increased pain, redness, heat or exudate, and she has no fever. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat the swab daily until it shows no growth
Start systemic antibiotics because the swab is positive
Apply a topical antiseptic routinely to the ulcer
Continue current care without starting antibiotics
8.w: NICE CG179: do not offer systemic antibiotics to adults based on positive wound cultures without clinical evidence of infection, and do not routinely use topical antiseptics or antimicrobials on pressure ulcers. Wounds are commonly colonised.

n.0: Repeated swabs of a colonised wound are unhelpful and do not guide care.
n.1: Systemic antibiotics without clinical infection contribute to resistance (NICE NG15).
n.2: CG179 advises against routine topical antiseptics on pressure ulcers.

8.q: Jade, 14, has a suspected appendix abscess and needs IV antibiotics and a drain. The surgeon assesses her as Gillick competent and she consents. Her mother, who has parental responsibility, objects because she wants a second opinion first. What is the legal position?
o: The mother's objection overrides Jade's consent while Jade is under 16
Treatment needs the agreement of both Jade and her mother
Treatment must wait for a court order because the two disagree
Jade's consent is valid and treatment can proceed
8.w: When a child under 16 is Gillick competent and consents, that consent is valid and treatment can proceed even if a parent disagrees (Gillick 1986; NSPCC Learning). Staff should still try to involve and support the mother.

n.0: A parent cannot veto the valid consent of a Gillick competent child to treatment in her interests.
n.1: The competent child's consent is sufficient; joint agreement is good practice, not a legal requirement.
n.2: A court is needed for refusals of life-sustaining treatment or genuine disputes over a child lacking competence, not to confirm a competent child's consent.

8.q: Gary, 52, tells the nurse he is thinking of paying for a private 'full body' screening scan because 'the NHS does not screen for enough things'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: NHS programmes are offered where benefits are judged to outweigh harms
Private screening tests are more accurate than NHS screening tests
All private screening tests are approved by the UK National Screening Committee
Each GP practice chooses which screening tests to offer its patients
8.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): the UK National Screening Committee advises the NHS on which screening programmes to offer and recommends screening only when the benefits to the group offered outweigh the harms; some commercial tests are not recommended because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms.

n.1: There is no basis for this; some private tests are not recommended because benefits may not outweigh harms.
n.2: Some private tests are not recommended by the UK NSC.
n.3: The UK NSC advises the NHS in all four nations on which screening programmes to offer.

8.q: A nurse is planning patient information for an outpatient clinic and wants to account for health literacy across the local population. Which statement about health literacy in England is supported by Public Health England evidence?
o: Up to 61% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health literacy is measured by a person's highest school qualification
Difficulty understanding health information mainly affects people over 80
About 10% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
8.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): a Public Health England report found that up to 61% of the English working-age population do not routinely understand the health and wellbeing information they are given. Health literacy (WHO) is the personal characteristics and social resources needed to access, understand, appraise and use information to make health decisions.

n.1: Health literacy is the ability to access, understand, appraise and use information, not a qualification level.
n.2: Low health literacy is common across working-age adults, not mainly in the oldest age groups.
n.3: The figure is far higher; PHE found up to 61% of the working-age population struggle.

8.q: Mrs Anita Rao, 68, is admitted for elective surgery. She is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. Her 12-year-old grandson has come with her and offers to interpret. What should the admitting nurse do?
o: Record and flag her need for a BSL interpreter and arrange one to attend
Rely on lip reading by facing Mrs Rao and speaking slowly and clearly
Accept the grandson's offer, as Mrs Rao is comfortable with him interpreting
Use written notes for the admission, as she can read English well
8.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs arising from disability or sensory loss. A qualified BSL interpreter ensures accurate information and valid consent; children should not be used to interpret clinical information (Code 7.2; P7.9).

n.1: Lip reading is unreliable for complex clinical information and is not her preferred communication method.
n.2: A child interpreter may mistranslate clinical information and is placed in an inappropriate role, risking invalid consent.
n.3: Written English may not be fully accessible to a first-language BSL user, and the standard requires her preferred format.

8.q: Mr Long's NEWS2 is 7. The nurse calls the junior doctor using SBAR, who says he will come 'when he can' in about two hours. What should the nurse do next?
o: Escalate now to a senior or the critical care outreach team
Record the call in the notes and hand it over to the next shift
Call the junior doctor again in one hour for an update
Wait for the junior doctor and repeat observations hourly
8.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): score 7 or more requires emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies and continuous monitoring. Code 16.1 escalate concerns; Annexe A 1.9.

n.1: Recording is needed, but the patient needs urgent senior review now.
n.2: Delaying further escalation for an hour is unsafe at this score.
n.3: A NEWS2 of 7 needs emergency assessment; waiting two hours is unsafe.
