8.q: Practitioners are writing the section of Maya's EHC plan that records her views. Maya, 14, has cerebral palsy and communicates with an eye-gaze device. How should her views be recorded, according to NICE NG213?
o: In professional language so the plan is clear to services
As a summary by her teacher, who knows her well
In her own words through her device, without rewriting them
As a summary of her views written by her parents
8.w: NICE NG213 Disabled children and young people up to 25 with severe complex needs (2022, updated 2023) rec 1.4.13: preserve the child or young person's voice: use their preferred communication format, use their own words (or the equivalent if they do not communicate verbally) and do not rewrite what they have said; rec 1.4.8 makes clear which parts are their contributions.

n.0: Rewriting Maya's views in professional language loses her voice, which NG213 says not to do.
n.1: A teacher's summary replaces Maya's own words with another person's interpretation.
n.3: Parents' views are recorded too, but they do not replace Maya's own contribution.

8.q: Your close colleague, going through a divorce, asks you not to mention that she has given several time-critical medicines over an hour late this week. She promises it will stop. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree to keep it confidential if she promises to improve
Offer support but explain you must tell the nurse in charge
Give her time-critical medicines for her so the delays stop
Report her to the NMC without speaking to anyone locally
8.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but this must never compromise patient safety. Code 16.1: raise and escalate safety concerns; 19.1 reduce harm.

n.0: Code 8.7 says support must not compromise patient safety; late time-critical medicines need escalating.
n.2: Covering for her hides the problem and leaves the risk unmanaged.
n.3: Local escalation and support should come first; referral is not the immediate proportionate step.

8.q: Daniel, 13, is to have planned spinal surgery next month. Which approach to preparation best suits his stage of development?
o: Give detailed information, invite his questions and involve him in decisions
Speak mainly with his parents and let them decide how much to tell him
Prepare him on the morning of surgery to avoid weeks of worry
Use doll play to act out the operation with him and his younger sister
8.w: Adolescents can think abstractly and want detailed, honest information, privacy and a say in decisions about their care. Preparation well ahead, with time for questions (and a pre-admission visit if available), supports autonomy and reduces anxiety (P4.3; T2 play therapy and preparation).

n.1: Excluding a 13-year-old from information about his own surgery ignores his developing autonomy.
n.2: A last-minute explanation suits toddlers, not an adolescent facing major planned surgery.
n.3: Doll play suits younger children and may feel patronising to an adolescent.

8.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
8.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

8.q: Dennis, 70, has a deep laceration to his forearm from a fall on the ward. Blood is spurting and soaking through the dressing despite firm direct pressure. You have called for help. What should be done next?
o: Elevate the arm and wait for the bleeding to stop
Apply an ice pack directly to the wound site
Apply a tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound
Remove the soaked dressing and press on a new one
8.w: RCUK first aid 2025: use direct pressure and a haemostatic dressing; apply a tourniquet as soon as possible for life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure, 5-7 cm above the injury and not over a joint, recording the time applied.

n.0: Elevation is not part of the RCUK 2025 escalating approach (pressure, haemostatic dressing, tourniquet) and waiting delays control.
n.1: Ice does not control arterial bleeding.
n.3: Removing the dressing disturbs clot formation; pressure is maintained and escalated.

8.q: Mr Booth, 58, has type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide. Before lunch he is sweaty and shaky but alert and able to swallow. His capillary blood glucose is 3.3 mmol/L. What should the nurse do first?
o: Withhold his gliclazide and recheck at the next meal
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give his lunch now and recheck the glucose in 1 hour
Give 15-20 g of glucose tablets by mouth and recheck
8.w: RCUK First aid guidelines 2025: treat hypoglycaemia when capillary glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L; if awake and able to swallow give 15-20 g glucose or dextrose tablets by mouth, repeat the measurement after treatment (repeat treatment if no improvement after 15 minutes), then give a snack once recovered.

n.0: Medication review may follow, but the low glucose needs treating now.
n.1: He is alert and can swallow; 999 and the recovery position are for an unresponsive person.
n.2: A meal acts too slowly; quick-acting glucose is needed first, then a longer-acting snack.

8.q: Iris, 70, dies on a general ward. She was on the NHS Organ Donor Register as wanting to donate. Her husband asks the nurse whether her wish to donate can still be met now that she has died on the ward. Which response is accurate?
o: The ward nurse can remove the corneas before transfer to the mortuary
Donation is not possible because she did not die in intensive care
Organs can be retrieved from the ward if it is within 24 hours of death
Tissue such as corneas may still be donated, up to 24 hours after death
8.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): organ donation is possible only from intensive care units and emergency departments and is organised before death; whole-body and tissue donation is possible after death, and cornea donation can take place up to 24 hours after death in hospitals, hospices and funeral homes.

n.0: Ward nurses do not retrieve tissue; donation is arranged with the specialist donation service.
n.1: This is true for organs, but tissue donation, including corneas, remains possible after death.
n.2: Organ donation is organised before death from intensive care or emergency departments; it cannot be arranged after a ward death.

8.q: Gloria, 72, has been prescribed oral nutritional supplements twice daily. On the ward round you notice the supplement bottles are left unopened on her table each day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to bring in food from home and stop recording intake
Stop the supplements because she clearly does not want them
Sign the chart for the supplements because they were supplied
Explore why with her and review the plan with the dietitian
8.w: Effective nutrition support requires monitoring that it is actually taken (NICE CG32 monitoring). Explore reasons (taste, fullness, opening the bottle, timing) and review with Gloria and the dietitian. Recording a supplement as taken when it was not would be inaccurate (Code 10.3).

n.0: Food from home may help, but intake must still be monitored and recorded.
n.1: Stopping without exploring reasons or involving the dietitian may leave her malnourished.
n.2: Recording unopened supplements as given falsifies the record.

8.q: A registered nurse is reviewing four recent deaths on a care of older people ward. All were verified, and none involved suspicious circumstances. Which death should be referred to the coroner?
o: Bill, 74, who died an expected death in a hospice from motor neurone disease
Harold, 79, who died an expected death from confirmed COVID-19
Edith, 88, who died five days after a hip fracture from a fall at home
Joan, 91, who died an expected death from heart failure under her GP
8.w: RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024), Appendix 1 (Ministry of Justice): refer to the coroner where the death may have been caused by violence, trauma or physical injury, whether intentional or otherwise, among other criteria. A notifiable disease such as COVID-19 is not a reason to refer.

n.0: An expected death from a diagnosed progressive illness is not, on these facts, reportable to the coroner.
n.1: A notifiable infectious disease such as COVID-19 is not, by itself, a reason to refer a death to the coroner.
n.3: An expected death from a known natural cause with an attending practitioner does not need coroner referral.

8.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
8.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

8.q: Harold, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids. Overnight he becomes breathless with RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, crackles at both lung bases and new ankle swelling. His fluid balance is positive 2,300 mL over 24 hours. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the infusion rate to correct the dehydration
Give a prescribed diuretic before informing anyone
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Continue the infusion and recheck in 4 hours
8.w: Breathlessness, crackles, oedema and a large positive balance suggest fluid overload. Stop the infusion, sit him upright, give oxygen to target and escalate urgently: NEWS2 RR 26 = 3 and SpO2 92% = 2 gives at least 5 (RCP 2017). CG174 asks for fluid mismanagement to be reported as an incident.

n.0: More fluid worsens overload.
n.1: Treatment decisions need urgent medical review; giving a diuretic first delays escalation.
n.3: Continuing the infusion worsens overload and 4 hours is too long.

8.q: Sophie is 22 weeks pregnant. A scan has shown that her baby has a life-limiting condition and she plans to continue the pregnancy. When does NICE NG61 advise that discussions about an Advance Care Plan should begin?
o: After the baby reaches 28 days old and leaves neonatal care
During the pregnancy, with the right professionals involved
Once the baby has been born and assessed by a neonatologist
When the baby is first admitted to hospital after birth
8.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions: begin discussing an Advance Care Plan with parents during the pregnancy if there is an antenatal diagnosis of a life-limiting condition, considering who should take part (for example obstetric, neonatal and palliative care teams).

n.0: Waiting four weeks after birth misses planning for birth and the neonatal period.
n.2: Waiting until birth leaves no plan in place for decisions at delivery.
n.3: A first admission may be an emergency, which is too late for planning.

8.q: Mr Grant, 72, has COPD and is admitted with breathlessness. His SpO2 is 89% on air. No target saturation range has been prescribed or documented. A colleague says to use NEWS2 SpO2 Scale 2 because he has COPD. What should the nurse do?
o: Use Scale 2, because a diagnosis of COPD is sufficient
Use Scale 1 and ask the medical team to prescribe a target range
Use Scale 2 and give oxygen to reach 94-98% saturations
Leave the SpO2 parameter unscored until a target range is prescribed
8.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): Scale 2 (target 88-92%) is for people with hypercapnic respiratory failure and is used when a clinician has prescribed that target. Until then Scale 1 applies (89% scores 3), and the team should be asked to set a target.

n.0: COPD alone does not authorise Scale 2; it must be prescribed by a clinician.
n.2: Scale 2 corresponds to a target of 88-92%, not 94-98%.
n.3: Leaving the parameter unscored gives a falsely low NEWS2 and delays escalation.

8.q: Mrs Leila Hassan, 71, is recovering from a hip fracture. She lives in a first-floor flat and is worried about managing her bath and kitchen safely at home. Which professional is best placed to assess her for equipment and adaptations?
o: A district nursing sister
An occupational therapist
A hospital social worker
A community physiotherapist
8.w: Occupational therapists assess a person's ability to carry out activities of daily living and recommend equipment and home adaptations, often through a home visit (P5.4; NICE NG249 recommends home hazard assessment ideally by an occupational therapist).

n.0: District nurses provide nursing care at home but are not the lead for daily living equipment assessment.
n.2: Social workers coordinate care and support arrangements but do not assess for equipment.
n.3: Physiotherapists focus on mobility, strength and exercise rather than assessing the home environment for equipment.

8.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
8.q: Ellie, aged 18 months, has a fever with some amber features but no diagnosis has been reached. The doctor decides she can go home. What must the nurse ensure before discharge?
o: A plan for her parents to measure her temperature hourly overnight
A safety net, with written warning signs and how to get help
A clinic appointment in 2 weeks to recheck her temperature
A prescription for regular paracetamol and ibuprofen for 5 days
8.w: NICE NG143: if any amber features are present and no diagnosis has been reached, provide a safety net (verbal and/or written information on warning symptoms and how to access further care, arranged follow-up, or liaison with other professionals) or refer to specialist care. Parents should check the child during the night and seek help if concerned.

n.0: Hourly temperatures are not required and do not tell parents what to do if their child worsens.
n.2: A 2-week follow-up is too late to act as a safety net for an acute febrile illness.
n.3: Regular combined antipyretics are not recommended; they are given for distress, one at a time.

8.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
8.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

8.q: Ben, a staff nurse on a respiratory ward, has developed red, cracked skin across the backs of both hands after several weeks of frequent hand hygiene. He asks his ward manager for advice. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Use soap and water instead of handrub for routine care until his hands heal
Seek occupational health advice and use his own emollient regularly, including on breaks
Apply hand cream from the communal tub in the staff room after each patient contact
Wear non-sterile gloves for routine care tasks so his skin is protected
8.w: NIPCM ch 1.2 skin care: dry hands thoroughly, use an emollient hand cream regularly (for example during breaks and off duty), do not use communal tubs, and staff with skin problems should seek advice from occupational health or their GP. Damaged skin harbours organisms and may need further intervention or reporting.

n.0: Alcohol handrub is recommended for routine hand hygiene and is generally less drying than repeated soap and water.
n.2: NIPCM advises against communal tubs of hand cream because they can become contaminated.
n.3: Gloves are not recommended where no body fluid exposure is anticipated; overuse increases infection risk and does not replace hand hygiene.

8.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
8.q: Chloe, aged 11, weighs 38 kg and has suspected sepsis needing an IV fluid bolus. What is the correct bolus volume according to NICE NG254?
o: 380 mL over less than 10 minutes
250 mL over less than 10 minutes
500 mL over 15 minutes
760 mL over 30 minutes
8.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.9.2: for people under 16, give 10 mL/kg of glucose-free crystalloid over less than 10 minutes, up to a maximum bolus of 250 mL. 10 mL x 38 kg = 380 mL, which is capped at 250 mL.

n.0: 380 mL is the calculated 10 mL/kg volume, but it exceeds the 250 mL maximum.
n.2: 500 mL is the adult bolus volume and exceeds the paediatric maximum.
n.3: 760 mL is 20 mL/kg and far above the maximum bolus.

8.q: Zara, 4, has been fitting for 12 minutes at nursery. The nursery nurse gave buccal midazolam from Zara's plan 8 minutes ago and called 999 straight afterwards. Zara is still convulsing and the ambulance is 5 minutes away. Her plan allows a second dose. What should happen now?
o: Give a second dose once the ambulance crew arrive
Give oral levetiracetam from her daily medicines
Wait, as one benzodiazepine dose is the limit outside hospital
Give the second dose of benzodiazepine set out in her plan
8.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.7-7.1.8: if status does not respond to the first dose, call emergency services, and continue to follow the individualised plan or give a second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first.

n.0: Waiting for the crew adds further delay when the plan already allows a second dose now.
n.1: Nothing should be given by mouth to a convulsing child, and oral maintenance doses do not stop status epilepticus.
n.2: NG217 allows a second benzodiazepine dose 5-10 minutes after the first when the plan says so.

8.q: Femi, a nurse on a medical ward, notices that her neighbour has been admitted to another ward in the trust. She has access to the electronic record system and is curious about the diagnosis. She is not involved in the neighbour's care. What applies?
o: She may view it if she later offers support as a friend
She may view it if she does not share what she reads
Viewing the record breaches the need-to-know principle
She may view it because she has trust login access
8.w: Caldicott principle 4: access to personal confidential data should be on a strict need-to-know basis. Having system access does not create a right to view records of people not in your care; this also breaches Code 5.1.

n.0: Personal support as a friend is not a care purpose that justifies access.
n.1: Accessing the record without a care purpose is itself the breach, whether or not it is shared.
n.3: System access is given for care purposes; it does not authorise curiosity viewing.

8.q: Zara, 3, needs urgent but not life-threatening surgery. Her two mothers were civil partners when Zara was conceived through licensed fertility clinic treatment. The birth mother is abroad and cannot be reached; Zara's other mother, who is named on the birth certificate, is present. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Treat Zara under the emergency necessity principle without anyone's consent
Apply to court for an order, as the non-birth mother has no automatic parental responsibility
Obtain consent from the other mother, who is a legal parent with parental responsibility
Delay surgery until the birth mother can be reached to give consent
8.w: Under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008, a woman in a civil partnership with the birth mother at the time of licensed treatment is the child's second female parent, and she has parental responsibility (Children Act 1989 s2(1A)). Her consent is valid.

n.0: Necessity applies when no one with authority to consent is available; a parent with PR is present.
n.1: No court order is needed: the second female parent holds PR automatically in these circumstances.
n.3: Both legal parents hold PR here, so waiting for the birth mother would cause unnecessary delay to urgent surgery.

8.q: A health visitor reviews Kacper, 3. He has extensive untreated dental decay, has missed his last four hospital appointments, is often seen in dirty clothes in winter without a coat, and his weight has fallen from the 25th to below the 2nd centile. Which category of abuse does Working Together 2026 use for this pattern?
o: Physical abuse
Neglect
Fabricated or induced illness
Emotional abuse
8.w: Working Together 2026 defines neglect as the persistent failure to meet a child's basic physical and/or psychological needs, likely to result in serious impairment of health or development, including failing to provide adequate food and clothing or to ensure access to appropriate medical care.

n.0: There is no inflicted injury described.
n.2: FII involves a carer fabricating or inducing illness; here care is being omitted.
n.3: Emotional abuse is persistent emotional maltreatment; this pattern is failure to meet physical and health needs.

8.q: Pauline, 67, has a fine-bore nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. Her morning medicines are due through the tube. The tube was placed and confirmed yesterday. What check should the nurse make before giving them?
o: Inject air and listen over the stomach for a 'whoosh'
Test an aspirate and confirm a pH of 5.5 or below
Check the tube is not coiled by looking in her mouth
Test an aspirate with blue litmus paper for a colour change
8.w: NICE CG32 monitoring and NHS patient safety alerts on nasogastric tubes: confirm gastric placement before each use by testing an aspirate with CE-marked pH paper, accepting pH 5.5 or below; if no aspirate or pH above 5.5, do not use the tube and escalate (X-ray may be needed). A misplaced tube used for feeding is a Never Event.

n.0: The 'whoosh' test is unreliable and must not be used to confirm placement.
n.2: A mouth check may find coiling, but it does not confirm the tip is in the stomach.
n.3: Litmus paper is not sensitive enough to confirm gastric placement.

8.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
8.q: Ruby, aged 6, has suspected sepsis with high risk criteria. Her venous lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. She has had antibiotics. What else does NICE NG254 recommend?
o: Consider a fluid bolus and recheck her lactate in 4 hours
Give oral fluids and repeat her observations every hour
Start maintenance fluids and review on the next ward round
Give a fluid bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care
8.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.7.5: for children under 12 with suspected sepsis, any high risk criteria and lactate over 4 mmol/L, give an IV fluid bolus without delay (within 1 hour) and refer to a critical care specialist or team to review management, including central access and inotropes.

n.0: 'Consider a bolus' applies when lactate is below 2 mmol/L; above 4, a bolus is given and critical care involved.
n.1: Oral fluids are not adequate resuscitation for a child with high risk sepsis and a raised lactate.
n.2: Maintenance fluids do not treat shock, and waiting for a ward round delays critical care.

8.q: Imogen, a staff nurse, sees a colleague starting to move Mr Price, 84, from bed to chair using an under-arm drag lift. His care plan states that he must be hoisted. What should Imogen do?
o: Ask her colleague to stop, help hoist Mr Price, then discuss it privately
Help her colleague complete the transfer and mention it to the ward manager later
Speak to her colleague about it privately at the end of the shift
Report the colleague on the incident system without speaking to her about it
8.w: Code 16 requires acting without delay if there is a risk to patient safety. Imogen should stop the unsafe practice first, ensure Mr Price is moved safely according to his care plan, and then challenge constructively in private, agreeing any learning needs (P5.9 challenge and give constructive feedback about care delivered by others). Two steps: make safe, then feedback.

n.1: Joining an unsafe technique exposes Mr Price and both staff to injury.
n.2: Waiting until later allows the unsafe transfer to continue now.
n.3: Reporting may be appropriate, but the immediate risk must be stopped first and a direct conversation supports learning.

8.q: Sam, 26, has a learning disability and often hits out in the noisy dining room at mealtimes. The team wants to use positive behaviour support. What should they do first?
o: Assess what triggers the behaviour and what it achieves
Increase his sedation before every mealtime
Use restraint whenever he begins to hit out
Withdraw meals in the dining room as a planned consequence
8.w: Annexe A 3.9: positive behaviour support approaches. PBS uses functional assessment to understand behaviour and changes the environment proactively.

n.1: Medication as first response is not PBS and may cause harm.
n.2: Restraint is reactive; PBS starts with understanding the function of behaviour.
n.3: Punishment is not part of PBS and may breach his rights.

8.q: At the end of a shift, the nurse is evaluating Mrs Dunn's care plan for pain after a hip fracture. Which entry best documents her progress?
o: Pain management ongoing; patient seems a lot more comfortable this afternoon.
Patient complained of pain all morning but is settled now.
14:30 Pain 7/10 moving at 12:00; 3/10 at 13:00 after oxycodone. Plan continued.
Analgesia given as prescribed. Continue current plan as per care plan.
8.w: Code 10.1-10.4: complete records accurately at the time, attributing, dating and timing entries without speculation. P3.15 requires documenting progress against goals; a timed, measured pain score before and after the intervention shows whether the plan is working.

n.0: 'Seems more comfortable' gives no measurement and is open to interpretation.
n.1: 'Complained' is judgemental, and the entry gives no times, scores or interventions.
n.3: This records an action but not its effect, so progress cannot be evaluated.

8.q: Dorothy, 86, has advanced dementia. For three days she has spat out her anticonvulsant and pushed staff away at medicine rounds. Her son suggests hiding it in her tea. What is the nurse's most appropriate first step?
o: Assess her capacity to make this specific decision about the medicine
Arrange for the medicine to be given by injection instead
Hide the medicine in her tea, as she has a diagnosis of dementia
Stop the anticonvulsant, as she is repeatedly refusing it
8.w: The MCA 2005 (ss1-3) requires a capacity assessment that is decision-specific and time-specific; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. Only if she lacks capacity can a best interests decision about covert administration follow (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21).

n.1: Changing the route needs a prescriber and does not address capacity or consent.
n.2: A diagnosis does not prove lack of capacity (MCA s2(3)); covert use also needs a best interests process.
n.3: Stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures; the refusal needs assessment, not unilateral cessation.

8.q: Amir, 8, is subject to a full care order and lives with foster carers. He needs a minor surgical procedure. His mother visits and asks who now holds parental responsibility for him. Which answer is correct under the Children Act 1989?
o: The mother, as a care order leaves parental responsibility unchanged
The local authority, as the care order ended the mother's responsibility
The foster carers, as they now provide Amir's day-to-day care
The mother and the local authority, which shares it under the order
8.w: Under s33 of the Children Act 1989 a care order gives the local authority parental responsibility, which it shares with the parents; the local authority may limit how far a parent exercises theirs. The mother keeps PR.

n.0: The care order does change the position: the local authority acquires PR alongside the parents.
n.1: A care order does not remove the mother's PR; it is shared, although the local authority may restrict its exercise.
n.2: Foster carers do not acquire PR through a placement; they act under delegated authority from the local authority.

8.q: A nurse in an NHS trust's children's emergency department is unsure whether a toddler's injuries warrant a referral and wants expert safeguarding advice from within the trust. Under Working Together 2026, whose role is it to provide this advice in a provider organisation?
o: The trust's Caldicott Guardian for patient data
The Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO)
The trust's named nurse for safeguarding children
The designated nurse for safeguarding children at the ICB
8.w: Working Together 2026 says NHS trusts should identify a named doctor and a named nurse (named professionals) who promote good practice, give advice and expertise to colleagues and support safeguarding within the provider. Designated professionals work at strategic level across the ICB area.

n.0: The Caldicott Guardian oversees use of confidential information, not clinical safeguarding decisions.
n.1: The LADO manages allegations against people who work with children.
n.3: Designated professionals provide strategic leadership across the health system in the area, not routine case advice within one trust.

8.q: A district nurse visits Mr Shaw, 68, whose wife died recently. He has given his dog to a neighbour, written letters to his children and says calmly that 'everything is sorted now'. He denies any physical symptoms. How should the nurse interpret these signs?
o: They are warning signs of suicidal intent needing direct enquiry
They suggest early dementia, so a memory screen is the priority
They show he is adjusting well and needs routine follow-up
They suggest normal grief, so a bereavement leaflet is enough
8.w: Giving away possessions, putting affairs in order and sudden calm after loss can signal suicidal intent (NMC Annexe B 1.1.6: recognise signs of self-harm and suicidal ideation). NICE NG225 supports asking about suicidal thoughts and acting on immediate safety concerns.

n.1: Nothing suggests cognitive decline; the behaviour points to risk of suicide.
n.2: Settling affairs after recent bereavement with sudden calm is a recognised warning sign, not evidence of adjustment.
n.3: A leaflet does not address possible suicidal intent, which needs direct enquiry.

8.q: Ronald, 80, is prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch, changed every 72 hours. The new patch is due today. His previous patch is on his upper left chest. What is the correct way to apply the new patch?
o: Apply the new patch to the same area once the old one has been removed
Remove the old patch and apply the new one to a different area of skin
Apply the new patch, then remove the old one at the next 72-hour change
Apply the new patch over the old one to maintain a steady dose
8.w: For transdermal patches the old patch is removed before the new one is applied, sites are rotated to reduce skin irritation, and the patch goes on clean, dry, hairless skin (AnnexB.11.8). Leaving an old fentanyl patch in place causes opioid toxicity.

n.0: Reusing the same site raises the risk of skin irritation and altered absorption.
n.2: Leaving the old patch for another 72 hours doubles the dose for that period.
n.3: Two patches at once would double the fentanyl dose and risk respiratory depression.

8.q: Ava, 2, weighs 12 kg and is prescribed oral morphine for post-operative pain. The ward guideline gives 200 micrograms/kg per dose. The prescription reads 'morphine oral 24 mg'. What should the nurse do?
o: Withhold it and ask the prescriber to review the dose
Give half the dose now and the remainder in 1 hour
Give the dose, as morphine needs vary between children
Give 2.4 mg, then ask the prescriber to amend the chart
8.w: 200 micrograms/kg x 12 kg = 2400 micrograms = 2.4 mg, so 24 mg is ten times the expected dose. The nurse must not give it, should contact the prescriber to amend it and report the near miss (NMC Code standard 18 on administering medicines and 19.1 on near misses; local incident reporting).

n.1: Splitting a ten-fold overdose still gives five times the safe dose within the hour.
n.2: A ten-fold opioid overdose risks respiratory arrest; variation in need does not justify it.
n.3: The nurse cannot give a dose that differs from the prescription; the prescriber must rewrite it first.

8.q: Single rooms are full on a respiratory ward. Two patients with the same confirmed respiratory virus are to be cohorted in a bay. Under current NIPCM guidance, what is the minimum separation between their beds?
o: At least 0.5 metres between the bed spaces
At least 3 metres between the bed spaces
At least 2 metres between the bed spaces
At least 1 metre between the bed spaces
8.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 states cohorted infectious patients should be separated by at least 3 feet (1 metre) with the door closed. Droplet precautions use at least 1 metre; the 2 metres introduced during COVID-19 has reverted to 1 metre in all areas.

n.0: Half a metre is below the 1 metre minimum for separation in a cohort.
n.1: 3 metres exceeds the NIPCM standard; the distance given is 3 feet, which is about 1 metre.
n.2: 2 metres was a COVID-19 measure that NIPCM says has returned to 1 metre.

9.q: Mrs Turner, 72, had a hip replacement two days ago. Her son tells the nurse at visiting time that his mother 'seems confused and is seeing things on the curtains', which started this afternoon. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the son to stay with her to settle her for the night
Note it and ask the night staff to see if it continues
Reassure the son that this is common after an anaesthetic
Assess her for delirium and record the reported change
9.w: NICE CG103 recs 1.3.1 and 1.5.1-1.5.2: recent changes or fluctuations (including hallucinations) may be reported by relatives and should prompt assessment with an appropriate tool; changes must be documented.

n.0: Family presence can help, but it does not replace assessment of a new change.
n.1: Deferring to night staff delays assessment of an acute change.
n.2: Dismissing a new change risks missing delirium and its cause.

9.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

9.q: Samuel, 79, is in the last days of life. Yesterday a trial of subcutaneous fluids was started because he was thirsty and slightly confused. Today the nurse notes new crackles at both lung bases and increasing ankle swelling. He is more breathless. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 'as required' midazolam for breathlessness and continue the fluids
Increase the infusion rate because his thirst is still present
Continue the fluids and reassess them at tomorrow's daily review
Reduce or stop the fluids and inform the team of signs of fluid overload
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.9: for a person started on clinically assisted hydration, monitor at least every 12 hours for benefit or harm; continue if there is clinical benefit and reduce or stop it if there are signs of possible harm such as fluid overload, or if the person no longer wants it.

n.0: Sedating him without removing the cause of the overload is not appropriate; the fluids are causing harm.
n.1: Increasing fluid would worsen the overload; thirst is managed with mouth care and sips (rec 1.4.2).
n.2: NG31 rec 1.4.9 says reduce or stop clinically assisted hydration if there are signs of harm such as fluid overload.

9.q: Finn, 8 months, is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms orally. The stock is digoxin elixir 50 micrograms per mL. What volume should be given?
o: 0.8 mL
9.w: Volume = 62.5 micrograms / 50 micrograms per mL = 1.25 mL. Keep dose and stock in the same unit (micrograms) to avoid ten-fold and thousand-fold errors.

n.0: 0.125 mL is a ten-fold under-dose.
n.2: 0.8 mL comes from inverting the calculation (50 / 62.5).
n.3: 12.5 mL is a ten-fold overdose from a decimal slip.

9.q: Mr Dunn, 66, is going home on a new medicine. He says he 'doesn't get on with reading' and has left his leaflet unopened. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explain in plain words with pictures, then use teach-back
Explain it once in full medical terms to be accurate
Ask the pharmacist to post a copy of the leaflet to him
Give him a second copy of the leaflet in larger print
9.w: Proficiency P2.10: provide information in accessible ways; Annexe A 2.2 clear language and appropriate materials; Annexe A 2.6 repetition and positive reinforcement; Code 7.4 check understanding.

n.1: Medical terms reduce understanding; Code 7.1 requires terms people can understand.
n.2: Posting the same written information will not help him understand it.
n.3: Larger print does not address difficulty with reading.

9.q: You are preparing to redress Stan's surgical wound using aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT). Which principle is central to ANTT?
o: Completing the dressing within 5 minutes
Protecting key parts and key sites from touch
Cleaning the wound with an antiseptic each time
Wearing sterile gloves for every dressing change
9.w: ANTT is based on identifying and protecting key parts (for example the inside of the dressing) and key sites (the wound) by not touching them directly or indirectly, with hand hygiene and an aseptic field. Glove choice depends on whether key parts must be touched.

n.0: Speed is not the defining principle of ANTT.
n.2: Routine antiseptic cleansing is not a principle of ANTT and can harm tissue.
n.3: Sterile gloves are needed when key parts must be touched; non-sterile gloves are used otherwise.

9.q: A nurse is admitting four people to an acute medical unit. Using the risk factors in NICE CG103, which person is at increased risk of developing delirium and should be observed for it?
o: Mr Green, 45, admitted for a planned endoscopy
Mrs Young, 78, admitted with a urinary infection
Ms Black, 30, admitted with a simple ankle fracture
Mr White, 52, admitted for blood pressure review
9.w: NICE CG103 (updated 2023) lists risk factors including age 65 or over, past or present cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness. Mrs Young is 78, so she should be observed at least daily for indicators of delirium.

n.0: At 45 and admitted for a planned procedure, Mr Green has none of the CG103 risk factors described.
n.2: An ankle fracture is not a CG103 risk factor; current hip fracture is.
n.3: At 52 with no listed risk factor, Mr White is not identified as at risk by CG103.

9.q: Ruth, 64, has chronic kidney disease and symptomatic anaemia with a haemoglobin of 68 g/L. She is not bleeding and does not have acute coronary syndrome. The doctor plans a red cell transfusion. In line with NICE NG24, what is the recommended approach?
o: Transfuse 1 unit, then reassess and check haemoglobin
Transfuse until haemoglobin reaches at least 110 g/L
Transfuse 2 units, then check haemoglobin the next day
Transfuse 3 units to avoid repeated cannulation
9.w: NICE NG24 (updated 2026): use a restrictive threshold of 70 g/L with a target of 70-90 g/L after transfusion, and consider single-unit transfusions for adults without active bleeding, clinically reassessing and checking haemoglobin after each unit before giving more.

n.1: 110 g/L is well above the NG24 post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L.
n.2: Two units without reassessment risks overtransfusion and circulatory overload.
n.3: Multiple units without reassessment conflicts with single-unit transfusion and raises overload risk.

9.q: Chloe, 14, is admitted to a general paediatric ward overnight after taking an overdose of paracetamol. She is medically stable on treatment. According to NICE NG225, which arrangement should be in place while she is on the ward?
o: Joint daily review by paediatric and children's mental health teams
A mental health review once she is medically fit for discharge
A weekly multidisciplinary meeting led by her GP and school nurse
Transfer to an adult mental health ward for assessment
9.w: NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022) rec 1.7.24: children and young people admitted to a paediatric ward after self-harm should have 24-hour access to CAMHS/CYPMHS or age-appropriate liaison psychiatry, a joint daily review by paediatric and mental health teams, daily family access and regular MDT meetings.

n.1: Mental health input starts during the admission, with joint daily review, not at discharge.
n.2: NG225 specifies regular MDT meetings between the paediatric team and mental health services, not weekly GP-led meetings.
n.3: An adult ward is not age-appropriate; NG225 keeps her on the paediatric ward with CYPMHS input.

9.q: Amira, 12, is in hospital after an appendicectomy. She shows the nurse messages from someone she met in an online game who says he is 14, asks her to keep their chats secret, move to a private app and send photos in her pyjamas. What should the nurse do?
o: Advise Amira to block the contact and reassure her parents
Tell Amira to stop using online games while in hospital
Recognise possible grooming and follow safeguarding procedures
Ask the contact directly through the app to confirm his age
9.w: Requests for secrecy, moving to a private platform and requests for images are signs of online grooming, which Working Together 2026 includes within child sexual abuse. The nurse should follow safeguarding procedures, preserve the messages and involve police (for example via a CEOP report) as advised.

n.0: Blocking the contact loses evidence and does not address possible abuse of Amira or others.
n.1: Restricting game use does not protect her or address the grooming.
n.3: Contacting the suspect could alert him and is not a nurse's role.

9.q: Single rooms are full on a respiratory ward. Two patients with the same confirmed respiratory virus are to be cohorted in a bay. Under current NIPCM guidance, what is the minimum separation between their beds?
o: At least 0.5 metres between the bed spaces
At least 3 metres between the bed spaces
At least 2 metres between the bed spaces
At least 1 metre between the bed spaces
9.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 states cohorted infectious patients should be separated by at least 3 feet (1 metre) with the door closed. Droplet precautions use at least 1 metre; the 2 metres introduced during COVID-19 has reverted to 1 metre in all areas.

n.0: Half a metre is below the 1 metre minimum for separation in a cohort.
n.1: 3 metres exceeds the NIPCM standard; the distance given is 3 feet, which is about 1 metre.
n.2: 2 metres was a COVID-19 measure that NIPCM says has returned to 1 metre.

9.q: Ayla, 8 months, is breastfed and has diarrhoea for a day. She is alert, feeding and has no signs of dehydration. Her mother wants to stop breastfeeding and give diluted apple juice instead. What should the nurse advise?
o: Give flat cola between breastfeeds to replace sugar and salt
Continue breastfeeding and offer extra fluids such as ORS
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give diluted apple juice
Change to diluted formula until the diarrhoea has stopped
9.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s: continue breastfeeding and other milk feeds, encourage fluid intake, and discourage fruit juices and carbonated drinks; offer ORS as supplemental fluid if at increased risk of dehydration.

n.0: Carbonated drinks are discouraged because their sugar and low sodium can worsen diarrhoea.
n.2: CG84 says continue breastfeeding and discourage fruit juice, which can worsen diarrhoea.
n.3: Diluting milk feeds is not recommended; full-strength milk is given.

9.q: A journalist telephones a medical ward asking how a well-known footballer admitted that morning is doing. The admission has already been reported on local news. The nurse who answers is the most senior person on the ward. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Confirm that he is a patient but share no clinical details
Decline to comment and refer the caller to the communications team
Give a brief general update, as the admission is already public
Ask the patient's consultant to call the journalist back later
9.w: Code 21.6: cooperate with the media only when appropriate, always protecting the confidentiality and dignity of people receiving care. Code 5.1 respects privacy; trust communications teams handle media enquiries with the patient's consent.

n.0: Confirming that someone is a patient is itself a disclosure of confidential information (Code 5).
n.2: Media reports do not remove the duty of confidentiality (Code 5.1); no information should be shared without consent and agreed process.
n.3: Passing the request to a clinician bypasses the trust's media process; media contact goes through the communications team.

9.q: At 22:00 two registered nurses phone in sick on a 30-bed ward with three acutely unwell patients. The nurse in charge has one registered nurse and two healthcare assistants. What is the priority action?
o: Escalate to the site manager now and request extra staff
Ask the healthcare assistants to give the evening medicines
Complete an incident report at the end of the shift
Reallocate patients and report the shortfall at the morning huddle
9.w: Proficiency P6.2: understand the relationship between safe staffing, skill mix, safety and quality and escalate concerns. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt escalation of risks; an incident report follows.

n.1: Delegating medicines beyond competence adds risk (Code 11.1) and does not solve the staffing gap.
n.2: Reporting is needed but does not resolve the immediate risk; escalation comes first.
n.3: Waiting until morning leaves an unsafe skill mix all night; it needs escalating now.

9.q: On a medical ward, Mrs Hall's daughter asks who can prescribe a new laxative for her mother this afternoon. The doctors are busy in clinic. Which team member could prescribe it?
o: The ward pharmacy technician during the medicines round
A registered nursing associate with three years' experience
Any registered nurse following the doctor's verbal agreement
A registered nurse with a recorded prescribing qualification
9.w: Only nurses and midwives with a recorded prescribing qualification on the NMC register can prescribe; nursing associates do not prescribe (FACTS S-CODE, Code 18). Knowing the scope of practice of each team member is part of P5.4.

n.0: Pharmacy technicians support medicines management but do not prescribe.
n.1: Nursing associates are not able to prescribe, whatever their experience.
n.2: A registered nurse without a prescribing qualification cannot prescribe, even with a doctor's verbal agreement.

9.q: Gwen, 70, is in the last days of life with metastatic cancer and new bone pain. She has not taken opioids before. The team agree to start subcutaneous morphine for symptom control, and the nurse is planning her care. Which approach to dosing is recommended?
o: Wait until her pain is severe before giving the first dose of morphine
Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start at the top of the prescribed range so that she is comfortable quickly
Give a loading dose by intramuscular injection, then change to subcutaneous
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.7 and 1.5.8: for people starting treatment who have not previously had medicines for symptom management, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing symptoms at least daily.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.11 asks for pain to be managed promptly and effectively once identified.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.7 recommends starting with the lowest effective dose for people not previously given symptom-control medicines.
n.3: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.5.5).

9.q: A nurse is planning patient information for an outpatient clinic and wants to account for health literacy across the local population. Which statement about health literacy in England is supported by Public Health England evidence?
o: Up to 61% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health literacy is measured by a person's highest school qualification
Difficulty understanding health information mainly affects people over 80
About 10% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
9.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): a Public Health England report found that up to 61% of the English working-age population do not routinely understand the health and wellbeing information they are given. Health literacy (WHO) is the personal characteristics and social resources needed to access, understand, appraise and use information to make health decisions.

n.1: Health literacy is the ability to access, understand, appraise and use information, not a qualification level.
n.2: Low health literacy is common across working-age adults, not mainly in the oldest age groups.
n.3: The figure is far higher; PHE found up to 61% of the working-age population struggle.

9.q: Joanne is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and is preparing to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she show over the three-year period?
o: 900 hours, including 450 for each registration
675 hours, as half of the second registration counts
1,350 hours, including 450 for each registration
450 hours across both registrations combined
9.w: NMC revalidation, practice hours (page updated 26/05/2021): 450 hours for one registration, 900 hours for nurse and midwife (450 each), 1,350 for triple registration.

n.1: There is no pro rata reduction; each registration needs its own 450 hours.
n.2: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as nurse, midwife and nursing associate.
n.3: 450 hours is the figure for a single registration; dual nurse and midwife registration requires 900.

9.q: Finley, aged 18 months, is admitted with faltering growth. The nurse needs to measure him for plotting on a UK-WHO growth chart. Which measurement should be taken?
o: Head circumference, which replaces length after 12 months
Mid-upper arm circumference, because he is under 5
Standing height, because he can walk independently
Supine length, because he is under 2 years old
9.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.2: weigh the child and measure length from birth to 2 years old, or height if aged over 2 years, then plot current and previous measurements on the UK-WHO growth charts (AnnexB.2.6: measuring weight and height).

n.0: Head circumference is a separate measure and does not replace length.
n.1: Mid-upper arm circumference is a nutritional screening tool, not the measurement used to assess linear growth on UK-WHO charts.
n.2: Standing height is used over 2 years; walking ability does not change the method below that age.

9.q: Mrs Cole, 76, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. She tells the nurse that her main wish is to be able to get to the bathroom by herself before she goes home. Which care plan goal best reflects a person-centred, evaluable plan?
o: She will walk to the bathroom with her frame and one helper by Friday
Staff will encourage Mrs Cole to mobilise as much as possible
Mrs Cole's mobility will be improved during her stay on the stroke unit
Mrs Cole will be independent in all activities before discharge
9.w: NMC proficiency P3.5 requires person-centred, evidence-based plans with agreed goals. A good goal is centred on the person's own priority, specific, measurable and time-bound, so progress can be evaluated (P3.15).

n.1: This describes a staff action, not an outcome for Mrs Cole.
n.2: 'Improved mobility' is vague, with no measure or timescale to evaluate against.
n.3: Full independence in all activities is not her stated goal and is unlikely to be realistic or measurable.

9.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
9.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

9.q: Kofi, 72, has a NEWS2 of 6. You have completed an ABCDE assessment, given oxygen and called the doctor using SBAR. The doctor will arrive in 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate next action?
o: Hand over to the next shift that he has been reviewed
Leave him to rest and record observations again in 4 hours
Repeat the ABCDE assessment to check his response to interventions
Start the oral antibiotics left on his drug chart from yesterday
9.w: ABCDE is cyclical: after each intervention reassess from A. A NEWS2 of 5 or more requires at least hourly monitoring, and any deterioration should trigger re-escalation (RCP 2017 chart 4).

n.0: He has not yet been reviewed, so this handover would be inaccurate and unsafe.
n.1: A NEWS2 of 5-6 requires at least hourly observations, not 4-hourly.
n.3: Oral antibiotics from yesterday are not a response to an acute deterioration and need medical review.

9.q: Mr Peter Clarke, 73, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. He can wash his face and upper body himself, although it takes him 20 minutes. A healthcare assistant suggests washing him to save time. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Agree for weekdays and let Mr Clarke wash himself at weekends when it is quieter
Ask the occupational therapist to decide whether Mr Clarke should wash himself
Agree, as it reduces the risk that Mr Clarke becomes tired before therapy
Encourage Mr Clarke to wash what he can, with prompts and help where needed
9.w: Nurses support people to maintain independence and avoid unnecessary interventions (P7.8). Doing for a person what they can do for themselves reduces function and dignity; rehabilitation depends on practice with support where needed (Code 1.2 fundamentals of care; Code 2).

n.0: Inconsistent practice slows recovery and is driven by staff convenience.
n.1: The occupational therapist may advise, but supporting independence in daily care is part of the nurse's role now.
n.2: Fatigue can be managed through planning; removing the activity undermines his rehabilitation.

9.q: Evie, aged 7, has been diagnosed with leukaemia. Her parents tell the nurse that her brother Sam, 5, has started wetting the bed and asking whether he will get ill too. Which nursing response best reflects family-centred care?
o: Include Sam, with honest age-appropriate information and play support
Advise the parents to keep Sam away from the ward to protect him from worry
Suggest the parents wait until Sam is older before talking about Evie's illness
Refer Sam to his GP for investigation of the new bed wetting
9.w: Family-centred care recognises that a child's illness affects the whole family, including siblings, who may feel anxious, jealous or responsible. Honest, age-appropriate information, involvement in visits and play specialist support help siblings cope (P3.4, P4.2).

n.1: Excluding Sam is likely to increase his anxiety and fantasies about the illness.
n.2: Delaying explanation leaves a worried child without support at a time of change.
n.3: New bed wetting here is a likely response to family stress; a medical referral alone misses his emotional needs.

9.q: Ben is unsure whether his worry about a care home's practice is a whistleblowing matter and wants free, confidential, independent advice before acting. Which source does NMC guidance suggest?
o: Protect, the independent whistleblowing charity
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
NHS Resolution, the NHS litigation authority
Healthwatch, the local patient voice organisation
9.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance lists Protect (independent whistleblowing charity), professional bodies and trade unions as sources of advice.

n.1: The Ombudsman handles unresolved complaints about services; it does not advise staff on whistleblowing.
n.2: NHS Resolution handles clinical negligence claims, not staff advice on raising concerns.
n.3: Healthwatch gathers public views on services rather than giving staff whistleblowing advice.

9.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
9.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

9.q: Rose, 79, rings her bell repeatedly at night. When you answer she says she is uncomfortable, cold and needs the toilet. Her pain score is 1 out of 10. What is the best approach to help her rest?
o: Meet her comfort and toileting needs and plan regular night checks
Explain that the bell is for emergencies and move it out of her reach
Give her a sedative to help her sleep without disturbing others
Close the door to her side room so that she is not disturbed
9.w: Annexe B 3.1 and 3.6: assess and meet comfort needs such as warmth, toileting and positioning, which are common barriers to sleep. Intentional rounding at intervals can reduce unmet need and calls.

n.1: Removing the call bell is unsafe and a breach of dignity and safety.
n.2: Sedation does not address her unmet needs and increases falls risk.
n.3: Closing the door does not meet her needs and reduces observation.

9.q: Nurses on a surgical ward want to check whether pain scores are reassessed within 30 minutes of giving analgesia, as their trust policy requires. They plan to review 40 recent patient records against this requirement. What type of activity is this?
o: Service evaluation, because it describes current care with no standard
Research, because it collects data from patient records
A PDSA cycle, because it tests a change to practice on a small scale
Clinical audit, because it measures care against a set standard
9.w: Clinical audit is a quality improvement cycle that measures the effectiveness of care against agreed standards and acts to bring practice in line with them (HQIP definition). Here an existing policy standard is being measured, so it is audit (P6.4, P6.7).

n.0: Service evaluation describes current care without reference to a standard; this project has a defined standard.
n.1: Research generates new knowledge, for example by testing a hypothesis; reviewing records against an existing standard is not research.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; no change is being tested here, only current practice measured.

9.q: Ella, 9, tells a nurse that her 14-year-old cousin makes her touch him when he babysits. A colleague says that because both are children this is 'experimenting' and not abuse. Which response reflects Working Together 2026?
o: Treat it as experimentation and advise the parents to supervise
Wait for a second disclosure before deciding whether it is abuse
Refer it as child sexual abuse; both children may need help
Refer the 14-year-old to the police and take no action for Ella
9.w: Working Together 2026 recognises that child sexual abuse can be perpetrated by other children. A 14-year-old coercing a 9-year-old is harmful sexual behaviour and child sexual abuse; Ella needs protection and the older child also needs a safeguarding assessment.

n.0: The age and power gap and coercion make this abuse, not developmentally normal experimentation.
n.1: A single disclosure is enough to act; waiting leaves Ella at risk.
n.3: Ella is the victim and needs a safeguarding response; the police may be involved, but referral to children's social care is required.

9.q: Jade, 14, has a suspected appendix abscess and needs IV antibiotics and a drain. The surgeon assesses her as Gillick competent and she consents. Her mother, who has parental responsibility, objects because she wants a second opinion first. What is the legal position?
o: The mother's objection overrides Jade's consent while Jade is under 16
Treatment needs the agreement of both Jade and her mother
Treatment must wait for a court order because the two disagree
Jade's consent is valid and treatment can proceed
9.w: When a child under 16 is Gillick competent and consents, that consent is valid and treatment can proceed even if a parent disagrees (Gillick 1986; NSPCC Learning). Staff should still try to involve and support the mother.

n.0: A parent cannot veto the valid consent of a Gillick competent child to treatment in her interests.
n.1: The competent child's consent is sufficient; joint agreement is good practice, not a legal requirement.
n.2: A court is needed for refusals of life-sustaining treatment or genuine disputes over a child lacking competence, not to confirm a competent child's consent.

9.q: Mr Shah, 69, has motor neurone disease. He shows the nurse a document he wrote and signed refusing mechanical ventilation. It was witnessed but contains no statement that it applies even if his life is at risk. He now lacks capacity and is in respiratory failure. What is the status of the document?
o: It is not valid because it was not drafted by a solicitor
It is not valid as a refusal of this life-sustaining treatment
It is valid because it is written, signed and witnessed
It is valid because his family confirm these were his wishes
9.w: MCA 2005 s25(5)-(6): an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed, witnessed and include a statement by the person that it is to apply even if life is at risk. Without that statement it does not apply to ventilation, although it must still inform the best interests decision.

n.0: There is no requirement for a solicitor to draft an advance decision.
n.2: Writing, signature and witness are necessary but not sufficient; the life-at-risk statement is missing.
n.3: Family confirmation cannot supply a missing statutory formality.

9.q: Jamie, 3, weighs 14 kg and is prescribed IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg once daily. The nurse is checking the prescription before preparing the dose. What dose should be given?
o: 49 mg
980 mg
9.8 mg
98 mg
9.w: Weight-based dosing: 7 mg/kg x 14 kg = 98 mg. Children's doses are calculated from a current weight in kilograms and checked against the BNF for Children.

n.0: 49 mg is half the dose (3.5 mg/kg) and would under-treat infection.
n.1: 980 mg is a ten-fold overdose, the characteristic paediatric error.
n.2: 9.8 mg is a ten-fold under-dose from a misplaced decimal point.

9.q: A doctor needs to tell Mrs Ibrahim, 70, who speaks Somali and limited English, that her husband has died in intensive care. Her adult niece is with her. What is the most appropriate way to communicate?
o: Wait until her son arrives to translate later that day
Use a professional Somali interpreter for the conversation
Give the news in simple English and check she understands
Ask the niece to interpret, as she is family and will support her
9.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; reliance on family is strongly discouraged. Code 7.2 meet language needs; Annexe A 2.9.

n.0: Delaying the news without reason causes distress; an interpreter can be arranged now.
n.2: Simple English risks misunderstanding when news is this serious.
n.3: Relying on family is discouraged; the niece is also grieving and may filter the news.

9.q: A practice nurse is assessing Sami, 18 months, who has a fever and is irritable. His skin is dark brown and the nurse cannot see any rash on his limbs or trunk. According to NICE NG240, where else should she check for petechiae?
o: The conjunctivae
The scalp hairline
The tongue
The soles of the feet
9.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) rec 1.1.12: check all over the body including nappy areas, and look for petechiae in the conjunctivae because rashes can be hard to detect on brown, black or tanned skin.

n.1: The scalp is not a site NG240 highlights; dense hair makes petechiae harder to see.
n.2: NG240 does not name the tongue; the conjunctivae are specified.
n.3: The soles are checked as part of the whole body, but NG240 names the conjunctivae as the site to check on darker skin.

9.q: Lauren is leading a test of a new structured handover sheet on one night shift. The test has finished and she is now comparing the number of omitted items with what the team predicted. Which stage of the PDSA cycle is this?
o: Plan
Act
Do
Study
9.w: In Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA), Plan sets the objective and predictions, Do carries out the test and collects data, Study analyses the results and compares them with predictions, and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (NHS England PDSA guidance; P6.4).

n.0: Plan is where the objective, prediction and data collection are agreed before the test.
n.1: Act follows Study and decides what to do next with the change.
n.2: Do is the stage of carrying out the test and recording data and observations.

9.q: A nurse joining a care home finds that Ada, 90, has been given her medicines covertly for 10 months. The best interests decision and management plan are filed, but there is no record of any review since. What should the nurse do?
o: Continue, as a plan is in place and signed
Ask Ada's daughter to confirm she still agrees with the plan
Stop all covert medicines until the GP's next visit
Arrange a review of the plan with the multidisciplinary team
9.w: Covert administration requires a documented management plan that is reviewed regularly (NICE SC1 1.15; RPS/RCN 2019 paras 21-23). Ada's capacity, the need for each medicine and the method should be reconsidered by the team, including the prescriber and pharmacist.

n.0: A plan without review may be out of date; review is a required safeguard.
n.1: Family views are part of the review, but the daughter cannot authorise continuation alone.
n.2: Abruptly stopping all medicines could cause harm; a prompt review is needed instead.

9.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
9.q: A student nurse asks how the FLACC pain scale is scored. Which description is correct?
o: Five categories each scored 0 to 3, giving a total of 0 to 15
Five categories each scored 0 to 2, giving a total of 0 to 10
Six faces scored 0 to 10, chosen by the child
Four categories each scored 0 to 2, giving a total of 0 to 8
9.w: FLACC scores five behaviours (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability), each from 0 to 2, giving a total from 0 to 10 (Merkel et al. 1997).

n.0: Each FLACC item is scored 0 to 2, not 0 to 3.
n.2: Six faces chosen by the child describes the Wong-Baker FACES self-report scale.
n.3: FLACC has five categories, not four.

9.q: Jordan, 16, is brought to the emergency department heavily intoxicated with a 3 cm scalp laceration. He is not bleeding actively and is otherwise stable, but cannot currently weigh up information about suturing. He is expected to sober up within a few hours. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Wait until he regains capacity, as the wound can safely be closed later
Contact his parents for consent and suture once they agree
Suture now, as a 16-year-old's consent is presumed under FLRA s8
Suture now in his best interests, as he lacks capacity at present
9.w: Under the MCA 2005 s4(3), a best interests decision must consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and whether the decision can wait until then. A stable laceration can be closed safely within hours, so waiting respects Jordan's own decision.

n.1: Seeking parental consent bypasses Jordan's right to decide when he will shortly be able to.
n.2: FLRA s8 makes a 16-year-old's actual consent effective; it does not presume consent when he cannot give it.
n.3: Lack of capacity now does not justify acting if the decision can safely wait for him to regain it.

9.q: Ray, 58, smokes, drinks about 30 units a week and takes little exercise. He tells the nurse he wants to be healthier but feels overwhelmed by everything he 'should' change. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise him to stop smoking and drinking on the same day
Tell him to start with alcohol, as it carries the greatest risk
Give leaflets on all three topics and review him in six months
Ask which change he feels most motivated to tackle first
9.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) rec 8: tailor interventions by assessing the person's behaviour, capability, context and how motivated they are to change; if many behaviours need to change, assess which one or ones the person is most motivated to tackle. NMC Annexe A 2.7: assess motivation and capacity for behaviour change.

n.0: Tackling several behaviours at once when he feels overwhelmed may reduce his chance of success; PH49 asks which he is most motivated to change.
n.1: Choosing for him ignores his motivation; PH49 recommends assessing which behaviour he is most motivated to tackle.
n.2: Leaflets without a plan miss the chance to agree goals; PH49 recommends goals, action plans and planned review.

9.q: Rosa reviews feedback and notices she spends less time explaining care to patients who speak English with a strong accent, assuming they will not understand. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Offer these patients an interpreter in place of her explanation
Ask colleagues to explain care to these patients for her
Continue as before, as shorter explanations reduce confusion
Recognise this as possible unconscious bias and reflect on it
9.w: Annexe A 1.7: be aware of your own unconscious bias in communication. Code 1.3 avoid assumptions; Code 9.2 reflect on feedback to improve practice.

n.0: An accent does not mean an interpreter is needed; offering one by default is another assumption.
n.1: Passing the task on avoids addressing her own bias and its effect on communication.
n.2: This keeps an assumption that denies patients information; Code 1.3 says avoid assumptions.

9.q: Ben, a newly registered nurse, is asked to clean up after a patient's commode using a chlorine-releasing product he has not used before. A domestic assistant tells him the solution works better if he makes it twice as strong. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make up a stronger solution as advised, wearing gloves and an apron
Follow the COSHH assessment and data sheet for dilution and PPE
Mix the product with detergent to clean and disinfect in one step
Decant the solution into a spare spray bottle so it is easy to use
9.w: The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 require employers to assess hazardous substances and set control measures, and employees to follow them. The product's COSHH assessment and safety data sheet state the correct dilution, ventilation and PPE (HSE, COSHH basics; Code 19).

n.0: Making the solution stronger than specified increases exposure to a hazardous substance; PPE does not make an uncontrolled concentration safe.
n.2: Mixing chlorine-releasing agents with other chemicals can release toxic gases; products are used as the COSHH assessment directs.
n.3: Decanting into an unlabelled or wrongly labelled container breaks the controls and leaves others unaware of the hazard.

9.q: Nurse Holly has been asked to support a doctor who will tell Mr Pearce, 61, that his biopsy shows cancer. Which preparation is most appropriate?
o: Tell Mr Pearce the result first so the doctor can focus on treatment
Arrange a private room and hand her bleep to a colleague
Ask a relative to break the news before the doctor arrives
Use the bay with curtains drawn to save time
9.w: Annexe A 2.9: engage in difficult conversations including breaking bad news. Code 1.1 dignity, 5.1 privacy and 2.6 respond compassionately to distress.

n.0: Delivering the diagnosis outside the planned conversation risks giving it without support.
n.2: Results should be given by the clinical team, with the patient's consent to involve others.
n.3: Curtains do not give privacy; a private room protects dignity and confidentiality.

9.q: A ward is running an improvement project to discharge more patients before midday. The team is already measuring the percentage of discharges before 12:00. Which additional measure would act as a balancing measure?
o: Number of patients discharged before 12:00 each day
Average time that discharge letters are completed
Number of take-home prescriptions ready the evening before
Readmission rate within 30 days of discharge
9.w: Balancing measures check whether improving one part of a system causes problems elsewhere. Rushing discharges could increase readmissions, so 30-day readmission is a balancing measure. The other options are outcome or process measures for the same aim (Model for Improvement measures: outcome, process, balancing; P6.4, P6.7). Two steps: classify each measure, then identify the one that detects unintended harm.

n.0: This is the outcome measure itself, restated as a count.
n.1: Discharge letter timing is a process measure that supports the aim, not a check for unintended harm.
n.2: Prescriptions ready in advance is a process measure on the route to earlier discharge.

9.q: Ava, aged 4, is receiving chemotherapy for leukaemia and is severely immunosuppressed. Her parents ask about her annual flu vaccine. What is the correct advice?
o: Give inactivated flu vaccine by injection, because the nasal vaccine is live
Give the nasal vaccine but delay it until her blood counts recover
Avoid any flu vaccine until chemotherapy has finished
Give the nasal live vaccine as usual, as it is the routine childhood product
9.w: The childhood flu programme uses live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV, nasal). The UKHSA schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used; live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression (P2.11; T2 pathogenesis and immunology).

n.1: LAIV remains contraindicated while she is severely immunosuppressed on treatment.
n.2: Children in clinical risk groups need flu protection; the inactivated vaccine can be given.
n.3: A live vaccine can cause disease in a severely immunosuppressed child.

9.q: Daniel, 8, needs a blood test after a febrile illness. The nurse assesses that he does not understand the reasons, risks or alternatives. He says he does not want 'the needle'. His mother, who has parental responsibility, is present. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: His mother can consent, with Daniel involved as far as he understands
The test should wait until Daniel himself is able to give consent
Daniel's refusal must be followed because he has expressed a clear wish
His mother's consent is needed in writing before the test can go ahead
9.w: A child who is not competent for the decision cannot give or refuse consent; a person with parental responsibility consents. The child's views should still be sought and respected as far as possible (UNCRC Article 12), with preparation and distraction.

n.1: Delaying a needed test until an 8-year-old becomes competent is not in his interests.
n.2: A child who lacks competence for the decision cannot give a legally decisive refusal; his views are considered, not binding.
n.3: Written consent is not a legal requirement for a blood test; verbal consent from his mother is valid.

9.q: Ada, 88, has been sleeping poorly. She dozes most of the afternoon, is woken for observations at 02:00 and 06:00, and has a NEWS2 of 0. She says she is tired all day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Review her observation times with the team to protect her sleep
Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative for her to take at night
Wake her more often in the afternoon so that she sleeps at night
Leave her plan unchanged, as observations have to be done at night
9.w: With a NEWS2 of 0 the minimum frequency is 12-hourly (RCP 2017), so night-time waking may be avoidable. Reviewing the care plan to cluster care and protect sleep supports rest (Annexe B 3.1, 3.6).

n.1: Sedatives are not first line and increase falls risk in older people.
n.2: Repeatedly waking her during the day adds fatigue rather than addressing the night-time disturbance.
n.3: Observation timing is a clinical decision and can be reviewed when the score is 0.
