9.q: Winston, 69, has COPD with hypercapnia and is prescribed a salbutamol nebuliser. His target saturation is 88-92%. How should the nebuliser be driven?
o: By oxygen at 6-8 L/min for the whole nebulisation
By compressed air, with oxygen by nasal cannulae if needed
By oxygen at 2 L/min to reduce the risk of hypercapnia
By oxygen at 15 L/min through a reservoir mask
9.w: BTS oxygen guideline: in people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, nebulisers should be air-driven, with supplemental oxygen given by nasal cannulae to keep saturation at 88-92%.

n.0: Prolonged oxygen-driven nebulisation risks hypercapnia in this group.
n.2: 2 L/min is too low to nebulise the drug effectively.
n.3: A reservoir mask delivers high-concentration oxygen and is not a nebuliser driver.

9.q: Mr Booth, 58, has type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide. Before lunch he is sweaty and shaky but alert and able to swallow. His capillary blood glucose is 3.3 mmol/L. What should the nurse do first?
o: Withhold his gliclazide and recheck at the next meal
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give his lunch now and recheck the glucose in 1 hour
Give 15-20 g of glucose tablets by mouth and recheck
9.w: RCUK First aid guidelines 2025: treat hypoglycaemia when capillary glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L; if awake and able to swallow give 15-20 g glucose or dextrose tablets by mouth, repeat the measurement after treatment (repeat treatment if no improvement after 15 minutes), then give a snack once recovered.

n.0: Medication review may follow, but the low glucose needs treating now.
n.1: He is alert and can swallow; 999 and the recovery position are for an unresponsive person.
n.2: A meal acts too slowly; quick-acting glucose is needed first, then a longer-acting snack.

9.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
9.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

9.q: Four babies were born at term on the same day. Which baby has a recognised risk factor that means blood glucose monitoring should start before the second feed?
o: Dev, who was born after a labour of 14 hours
Cara, whose mother had an epidural in labour
Ava, whose mother took labetalol in the third trimester
Ben, born by planned caesarean section under spinal
9.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024): risk factors for impaired metabolic adaptation include fetal growth restriction (birth weight below the 2nd centile), maternal diabetes and maternal beta-blockers in the third trimester or at birth. At-risk babies have glucose measured before the second feed (2-4 hours after birth).

n.0: A 14-hour labour is not a BAPM risk factor.
n.1: Maternal epidural is not a BAPM risk factor.
n.3: Caesarean birth is not a BAPM risk factor for neonatal hypoglycaemia.

9.q: Kieran, 45, is shouting in a corridor after being told his discharge is delayed. He is pacing and red-faced but has not threatened anyone. Which approach is the best first step?
o: Call security to remove him from the ward straight away
Stand close and tell him firmly to lower his voice immediately
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and acknowledge his frustration
Walk away and leave him until he has calmed himself down
9.w: De-escalation (Annexe A 3.5; NICE NG10) is the first-line response to agitation: a calm, non-threatening stance at a safe distance, active listening and acknowledging feelings, offering choices and reducing stimulation. Restrictive options are a last resort.

n.0: Removal by security is restrictive and premature when de-escalation has not been tried.
n.1: Standing close and issuing commands can feel threatening and escalate the situation.
n.3: Leaving an agitated person unsupported misses the chance to de-escalate and to keep others safe.

9.q: Children's social care starts a Family Help assessment for Ollie, 6, after a nurse's referral about neglect. His father asks the nurse how long the assessment can take. Under Working Together 2026, what is the maximum time from referral to a decision on the assessment?
o: 35 working days from the point of referral
45 working days from the point of referral
10 working days from the point of referral
15 working days from the point of referral
9.w: Working Together 2026 states that the time from referral to the decision at the end of the assessment should be no longer than 45 working days; if it exceeds this, the lead practitioner should record the reasons.

n.0: 35 working days is not a Working Together timescale.
n.2: Ten working days is the core group timescale after an initial child protection conference.
n.3: Fifteen working days is the timescale for an initial child protection conference after the strategy discussion.

9.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
9.q: Amelia, aged 2 weeks, is brought to the children's emergency department because she feels hot. Which method should the nurse use to measure her temperature?
o: An electronic thermometer in the axilla
A forehead chemical strip thermometer
A chemical dot thermometer under the tongue
An infra-red tympanic thermometer
9.w: NICE NG143: in infants under 4 weeks, measure body temperature with an electronic thermometer in the axilla. From 4 weeks to 5 years, an electronic or chemical dot thermometer in the axilla or an infra-red tympanic thermometer can be used (AnnexB.4.8).

n.1: NG143 says forehead chemical thermometers are unreliable and should not be used by healthcare professionals.
n.2: The oral route is not used routinely in children aged 0 to 5 years.
n.3: Tympanic thermometers are an option from 4 weeks of age, not in a 2-week-old.

9.q: A ward manager wants to check whether patients' falls risk assessments are completed within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires, by reviewing 50 sets of notes. How should this project be classified?
o: Research, which needs NHS research ethics committee review
Health surveillance, which tracks outbreaks and health threats
Service evaluation, which judges a service without a standard
Clinical audit, which measures practice against a set standard
9.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (October 2022): clinical audit answers 'Does this service reach a predetermined standard?', uses care already in use and does not require REC review.

n.0: It tests no hypothesis and seeks no generalisable knowledge; it compares practice with an existing standard.
n.1: Surveillance monitors threats to population health, not compliance with a ward policy.
n.2: Service evaluation does not measure against a predetermined standard; this project does.

9.q: Finley, 8, has a confirmed diagnosis of asthma. He has symptoms three nights a week and uses his reliever most days. He takes no other asthma treatment. According to NICE NG245, what should be offered first as maintenance therapy?
o: Paediatric high-dose inhaled corticosteroid with SABA as needed
Regular montelukast with SABA as needed
Paediatric low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with SABA as needed
SABA as needed with no regular preventer medicine
9.w: NICE NG245 Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN, November 2024): for children aged 5-11 with newly diagnosed asthma, offer a twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS with SABA as needed; MART is the next step if control is not achieved.

n.0: High-dose ICS is reserved for specialist-led care after lower steps fail; it is not the starting dose.
n.1: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a later add-on option, not initial maintenance for a 5-11 year old.
n.3: Reliever-only treatment leaves airway inflammation untreated and SABA over-use is linked to severe attacks (MHRA 2025).

9.q: Grace, 7, is dying at a children's hospice. She takes small sips of water but can no longer drink much. Her parents ask whether she needs a drip. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start IV fluids now, as dying children need full hydration to be comfortable
Support sips and mouth care; discuss if a drip is in her best interests
Stop offering drinks, as sipping fluids may cause her more discomfort
Pass a nasogastric tube so she can have full maintenance fluids
9.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions recs 1.3.48-1.3.51: encourage and support the child to drink if she wants to and is able, continue lip and mouth care, and discuss with the family whether enteral or IV fluids are in her best interests, as they may be a burden and may change the place of care.

n.0: NG61 says IV fluids may be a burden for a dying child; starting them is a best interests decision, not routine.
n.2: NG61 says encourage and support drinking if she wants to and is able.
n.3: A nasogastric tube is a best interests decision discussed with the family, not routine.

9.q: During a ward teaching session on transmission-based precautions, a student nurse asks which route of transmission is responsible for most cross-infection in care settings, including spread via equipment and the patient's surroundings. Which answer is correct?
o: Airborne transmission via aerosols
Droplet transmission over short distances
Blood-borne transmission via sharps injuries
Contact transmission, direct or indirect
9.w: NIPCM ch 2 defines contact precautions as preventing spread by direct contact with the patient or indirectly from the immediate care environment, including care equipment, and states this is the most common route of cross-infection transmission.

n.0: Airborne spread applies to a smaller group of organisms such as measles and TB.
n.1: Droplet spread is important for respiratory pathogens but NIPCM names contact as the most common route.
n.2: Sharps injuries carry blood-borne virus risk to staff, but are not the main route of cross-infection between patients.

9.q: Aiden, aged 2, needs a nasogastric tube passed. A health play specialist is not available. Which distraction is most suited to his age?
o: Blowing and popping bubbles or watching a light-up toy
Counting backwards from 100 in his head
Guided imagery about his favourite holiday
Explaining the anatomy of the nose using a diagram
9.w: Distraction should match developmental stage: toddlers respond to simple, sensory, attention-grabbing activities such as bubbles, light-up or musical toys and songs (AnnexA.3.8 distraction and diversion strategies).

n.1: Counting backwards from 100 is beyond a 2-year-old's ability.
n.2: Guided imagery needs abstract thinking suited to older children and adolescents.
n.3: A diagram is a preparation tool for older school-age children, not a distraction for a toddler.

9.q: Freya, 2, is on a children's ward with confirmed bacterial meningitis. She is now haemodynamically stable and drinking. A junior doctor suggests restricting her fluids to two-thirds of maintenance. According to NICE NG240, what is the best response?
o: Restrict to two-thirds maintenance for the first 48 hours
Restrict to half maintenance and give mannitol
Give her normal maintenance fluids by mouth, unrestricted
Give maintenance as IV fluids and stop oral intake
9.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) recs 1.9.1-1.9.2: do not routinely restrict fluid intake below maintenance in bacterial meningitis; give maintenance fluids orally or enterally if tolerated. Osmotic agents are not routine.

n.0: Routine fluid restriction is not recommended; it risks under-perfusion.
n.1: Mannitol is considered only for raised intracranial pressure with herniation concerns, and fluid restriction is not routine.
n.3: NG240 prefers oral or enteral maintenance when tolerated, and Freya is drinking.

9.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity and peripheral vascular disease. After a full explanation of the risks, he declines a recommended below-knee amputation, saying he would rather take his chances. The team thinks this is an unwise choice. Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies most directly?
o: Making an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Any act done for a person must be in their best interests
The less restrictive option must be considered first
All practicable steps must be taken to help the person decide
9.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Mr Pearce has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

n.1: Best interests (s1(5)) applies to acts for people who lack capacity; Mr Pearce has capacity.
n.2: The less restrictive principle (s1(6)) applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.
n.3: Supporting decision-making (s1(3)) has already been met by the full explanation; the issue now is respecting an unwise choice.

9.q: In a nursing home, the GP reviews Hilda, 88, by video call and decides to reduce her bisoprolol dose from tomorrow. The GP cannot visit to amend the medication administration record (MAR). Under RPS/RCN guidance, how should the change be communicated?
o: By a message passed on by Hilda's daughter after the call
By a secure electronic message from the GP, with records updated
By the nurse amending the MAR from her notes of the call
By a text message from the GP to the nurse's personal mobile phone
9.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20.2: if the prescriber cannot issue a new prescription or amend the chart, the changes are communicated by an appropriately secure electronic method and the patient's records are updated.

n.0: A relayed message from a relative is not a direction from the prescriber.
n.2: Without the prescriber's written or secure electronic confirmation, the nurse would be altering a prescription.
n.3: A personal phone is not a secure, auditable route for prescribing information.

9.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
9.q: Jess, aged 8, has acute asthma. Earlier, wheeze was heard throughout her chest. Now she is too breathless to talk, her SpO2 is 90%, and on auscultation the nurse hears very little air entry and almost no wheeze. What does this finding mean?
o: A silent chest, a life-threatening sign that needs an emergency call
Normal breath sounds now her wheeze has stopped
Her bronchospasm is resolving, so nebulisers can be spaced out
Mucus plugging that will clear with chest physiotherapy
9.w: Reduced air entry with little or no wheeze in a breathless child (silent chest) shows very poor air movement and is listed as a life-threatening feature of acute asthma in children in the BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244); RCUK 2025 also lists diminished air entry as decompensated respiratory failure. It needs immediate senior help.

n.1: Breath sounds are not normal; air entry is greatly reduced.
n.2: Loss of wheeze here reflects too little air movement, not improvement; she cannot talk and is hypoxic.
n.3: Physiotherapy is not the treatment for life-threatening asthma.

9.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
9.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

9.q: A children's nurse is completing a psychosocial assessment for Jordan, 14, who has frequent minor injuries. Which finding would most strongly raise concern about county lines exploitation?
o: Repeated missing episodes and trips to another city
A new group of older friends from his football club
Spending long evenings playing online games at home
Falling grades during his exam year at school
9.w: Repeated missing episodes and unexplained travel to other areas are key county lines indicators, as children are used to move drugs and money between areas (Working Together 2026, child criminal exploitation).

n.1: New friends through an organised club are not in themselves an exploitation indicator.
n.2: Online gaming alone is not an indicator of criminal exploitation.
n.3: Falling grades are non-specific and common in adolescence.

9.q: Beryl, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score to decide whether she needs falls prevention. What does NICE NG249 (2025) recommend?
o: Offer an assessment if she falls again on the ward
Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and plan
Complete the prediction tool and act on a high score
Use the prediction tool weekly to monitor her risk
9.w: NICE NG249 (2025): do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Offer all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over (or 50-64 at higher risk) a comprehensive, multifactorial falls assessment and management plan.

n.0: She already qualifies for assessment as an inpatient aged 65 or over.
n.2: NG249 advises against using prediction tools to identify risk.
n.3: Repeating a prediction tool does not make it a valid basis for care.

9.q: Maya, 14, weighs 58 kg and has reached puberty. She has anaphylaxis with wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg after an IV antibiotic on the adolescent ward. Which IM adrenaline dose (1 mg/mL) is appropriate?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
1 mg (1 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
9.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): over 12 years the IM dose is 500 micrograms (0.5 mL), with 300 micrograms reserved for a child who is small or prepubertal. Maya is 58 kg and pubertal.

n.0: 150 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6 months to 6 years.
n.2: 1 mg IM is double the recommended maximum single IM dose.
n.3: 300 micrograms suits a 6-12 year old or a small, prepubertal over-12; Maya is neither.

9.q: Olivia, 23, has a learning disability and is anxious about her admission. During a ward round several staff discuss her care at the bedside using medical terms, talking over her. Which action best role-models person-centred care?
o: Continue the round and explain the plan to her carer afterwards
Speak to her directly in plain language and include her in the discussion
Give her a leaflet about her condition after the ward round finishes
Ask the team to discuss her care at the nurses' station instead
9.w: P4.1 asks nurses to role-model person-centred care. Code 2.1-2.3 and 7.1-7.3: work in partnership, encourage people to be involved in decisions, and use terms people can understand, making reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: Talking to her carer instead excludes her from decisions about her own care.
n.2: A leaflet afterwards does not involve her in the discussion and may not be accessible.
n.3: Moving the discussion away removes her from decisions that concern her.

9.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, is on day 2 after a hip replacement. Her daughter tells the nurse her mother 'is not making sense today' and keeps asking where she is, which is new. Her other observations are within normal ranges. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck her level of consciousness at the next routine set
Record new confusion as scoring 3 and inform the medical team
Record her as Alert, as she is awake and talking with her daughter
Reassure the daughter that this is normal after hip surgery
9.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): new confusion (C on ACVPU) scores 3. A single parameter scoring 3 requires at least hourly monitoring and the RN informing the medical team. NICE CG103 also asks that changes reported by relatives prompt delirium assessment.

n.0: New confusion scores 3 and needs action now, not at the next routine check.
n.2: Being awake and talking does not make a newly confused person 'Alert' on ACVPU.
n.3: New confusion is not an expected finding and may signal delirium, sepsis or other illness.

9.q: Leon, 39, stopped smoking three months ago with support. He tells the nurse he is worried he will start again at a family wedding next month, where many guests smoke. What is the most appropriate support?
o: Help him make an 'if-then' plan for moments when he is tempted
Advise him to avoid weddings and other social events for a year
Close his episode of care, as his quit attempt is now complete
Reassure him that relapse is rare once three months have passed
9.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) recs 6 and 10: interventions should address relapse and recognise that it is common; help people maintain change by giving them well-rehearsed action plans such as 'if-then' plans, social support and feedback and monitoring for at least 1 year.

n.1: Avoiding all social contact is unrealistic and removes social support that helps people maintain change.
n.2: PH49 rec 10 recommends feedback and monitoring for at least a year to help maintain change.
n.3: PH49 recognises that relapse is common and asks for interventions to address it.

9.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
9.q: Ellie, aged 3, has gastroenteritis. Her mother asks when she can go back to nursery. What advice is correct?
o: When her stools have become fully formed again
Once she has gone 24 hours without any vomiting
48 hours after her last diarrhoea or vomiting
After she finishes a 5-day course of ORS at home
9.w: NICE CG84: children should not attend school or other childcare facilities while they have diarrhoea or vomiting caused by gastroenteritis, and should not go back until at least 48 hours after the last episode. Handwashing with soap and water is the most important measure to prevent spread.

n.0: Stool consistency is not the measure; the rule is 48 hours after the last episode.
n.1: 24 hours is too short; the exclusion period is 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting.
n.3: ORS is used for rehydration as needed, not as a fixed course linked to return.

9.q: Maya, 18 months, is prescribed oral paracetamol suspension. The nurse finds that the only syringes in the clean utility room are IV (Luer) syringes. What should the nurse use to measure and give the dose?
o: A Luer syringe with the tip removed after drawing up
A Luer IV syringe, labelled clearly as 'for oral use'
A 5 mL medicine spoon instead of any syringe
An oral or enteral syringe from another ward or pharmacy
9.w: National patient safety guidance requires oral liquids to be measured and given with oral or enteral (ENFit) syringes, which cannot connect to IV devices, to prevent wrong-route administration. Spoons are inaccurate for small paediatric volumes.

n.0: Altering a syringe does not remove the wrong-route risk and is unsafe practice.
n.1: A labelled Luer syringe can still be connected to an IV line, causing a wrong-route error.
n.2: A spoon is inaccurate for a measured paediatric dose and spills easily.

9.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

9.q: Grace has worked as a registered nurse in Manchester and is moving to a post in Glasgow. She asks her manager which statute governs decisions for adults who lack capacity once she is practising in Scotland, as Code 4.3 requires her to follow the law where she practises. Which statute should the manager name?
o: Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003
Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000
Mental Capacity Act 2005
9.w: Capacity law is devolved. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies in England and Wales; in Scotland decisions for adults lacking capacity fall under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000. Code 4.3 requires registrants to keep to the mental capacity law of the country in which they practise.

n.0: The 2003 Scottish Act concerns compulsory care and treatment for mental disorder, not general decisions for adults lacking capacity.
n.1: The 2019 Act amends the MCA 2005 in England and Wales to create the Liberty Protection Safeguards, which are not in force.
n.3: The MCA 2005 covers England and Wales, so it would not govern Grace's practice in Glasgow.

9.q: Imogen, a staff nurse, sees a colleague starting to move Mr Price, 84, from bed to chair using an under-arm drag lift. His care plan states that he must be hoisted. What should Imogen do?
o: Ask her colleague to stop, help hoist Mr Price, then discuss it privately
Help her colleague complete the transfer and mention it to the ward manager later
Speak to her colleague about it privately at the end of the shift
Report the colleague on the incident system without speaking to her about it
9.w: Code 16 requires acting without delay if there is a risk to patient safety. Imogen should stop the unsafe practice first, ensure Mr Price is moved safely according to his care plan, and then challenge constructively in private, agreeing any learning needs (P5.9 challenge and give constructive feedback about care delivered by others). Two steps: make safe, then feedback.

n.1: Joining an unsafe technique exposes Mr Price and both staff to injury.
n.2: Waiting until later allows the unsafe transfer to continue now.
n.3: Reporting may be appropriate, but the immediate risk must be stopped first and a direct conversation supports learning.

9.q: You are performing chest compressions on Alan, 60, who has collapsed in a hospital car park. According to RCUK 2025, what compression depth and rate are correct for an adult?
o: 5-6 cm at 100-120 per minute
6-7 cm at 80-100 per minute
4-5 cm at 100-120 per minute
5-6 cm at 120-140 per minute
9.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: compress on the lower half of the sternum to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, at 100-120 per minute, allowing full recoil.

n.1: 6-7 cm is too deep and 80-100 per minute is too slow.
n.2: 4-5 cm is too shallow for an adult.
n.3: 120-140 per minute is faster than the recommended maximum of 120.

9.q: A GP practice nurse in England identifies that a parent's alcohol use may be affecting her 6-year-old patient's care. The nurse wonders whether the s16LA information sharing duty applies to primary care. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to health staff on a child protection plan
It applies to local authorities and the police, not health
It applies to NHS trusts, but not to GP practices
It applies to providers including GPs and dentists
9.w: The statutory guidance states the duty applies to section 11 organisations (including ICBs, NHS trusts and the police), designated education and childcare agencies, and providers delivering services for them, which includes GPs, dentists and other primary care providers.

n.0: The duty is not limited to children with a child protection plan.
n.1: Health bodies such as ICBs and NHS trusts are relevant persons under the duty.
n.2: GPs and other primary care providers are expressly included.

9.q: After inserting a peripheral cannula into the hand of Agnes, 88, the nurse needs to secure and cover the site. Which type of dressing is recommended so that the site can be inspected?
o: A sterile hydrocolloid dressing over the hub
A sterile gauze dressing and crepe bandage
Non-sterile adhesive tape over a gauze square
A sterile transparent semipermeable dressing
9.w: Vascular access device care (NICE CG139 and the IPC facts sheet) uses a sterile, transparent, semipermeable membrane dressing so the insertion site can be observed for signs of infection or phlebitis without removing it.

n.0: Hydrocolloid dressings are for wounds; they are opaque and not designed for cannula sites.
n.1: A bandage over gauze prevents regular inspection of the insertion site.
n.2: Non-sterile tape and gauze hide the site and are not a sterile covering for a Key-Site.

9.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke and cannot speak clearly. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. Before anyone concludes he lacks capacity, what should the nurse do?
o: Wait for his speech to recover fully before discussing the move
Record that he lacks capacity because he cannot speak clearly
Ask his wife to make the decision as she knows his wishes best
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy input
9.w: MCA 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means, so aids and specialist input should be tried.

n.0: Delaying indefinitely is not required; the duty is to take practicable steps to support his decision now.
n.1: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; s3(1)(d) covers any means.
n.2: His wife cannot decide for him unless she holds a relevant LPA; the first step is to support him to decide.

9.q: Sophie is 22 weeks pregnant. A scan has shown that her baby has a life-limiting condition and she plans to continue the pregnancy. When does NICE NG61 advise that discussions about an Advance Care Plan should begin?
o: After the baby reaches 28 days old and leaves neonatal care
During the pregnancy, with the right professionals involved
Once the baby has been born and assessed by a neonatologist
When the baby is first admitted to hospital after birth
9.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions: begin discussing an Advance Care Plan with parents during the pregnancy if there is an antenatal diagnosis of a life-limiting condition, considering who should take part (for example obstetric, neonatal and palliative care teams).

n.0: Waiting four weeks after birth misses planning for birth and the neonatal period.
n.2: Waiting until birth leaves no plan in place for decisions at delivery.
n.3: A first admission may be an emergency, which is too late for planning.

9.q: Before a short handover, Graham, a staff nurse, needs to ask a healthcare assistant to monitor Mr Okafor, 70, who had a hypotensive episode earlier. Which instruction is clearest?
o: 'Please check Mr Okafor's BP and pulse at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is under 100.'
'Please keep an eye on Mr Okafor this afternoon and let me know how he gets on.'
'Please do the usual observations on everyone in bay 2, including Mr Okafor, this afternoon.'
'Please do Mr Okafor's observations when you have time and tell me if anything looks off.'
9.w: AnnexA.1.11 requires clear verbal, digital or written information and instructions when delegating or handing over. An instruction stating what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when removes ambiguity (Code 11.2; AnnexA.4.1.2).

n.1: 'Keep an eye on' does not specify what to measure, when, or what to report.
n.2: A general bay instruction does not flag Mr Okafor's specific risk or what to report.
n.3: There is no time set or threshold for reporting; 'anything off' depends on the assistant's interpretation.

9.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for alcohol intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She refuses to let staff contact anyone. Under the Children Act 2004 s16LA duty in force since 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
o: Seek Kerry's consent again and share the information if she agrees
Share once a safeguarding threshold has been reached
Record the concern and share if it happens again
Share the relevant information with children's social care now
9.w: Children Act 2004 s16LA (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, in force 30 September 2026) requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, without a threshold and without needing consent, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child. A young child alone at home needs immediate action.

n.0: Consent is not required under s16LA, and waiting for it delays protection of a child at immediate risk.
n.1: s16LA sets no threshold; the information is relevant to his safety and must be shared.
n.2: A 3-year-old alone at home is at immediate risk; waiting for a repeat leaves him unprotected.

9.q: Mr Daly, 80, has capacity. When the nurse begins to explain his scan results, he says, "I don't want the details. Just tell my daughter." What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain the results fully, as he has a legal right to know them all
Respect his wish, check what he wants to know and his consent to share
Tell his daughter everything and give him no information himself
Delay the conversation until he is ready for all the details
9.w: Code 2.4: respect the level to which people want to be involved in decisions about their care. Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows, with consent.

n.0: Code 2.4 requires respect for the level of involvement he wants.
n.2: He should be asked what he does want to know, and his consent confirmed first.
n.3: He has stated his wish now; delaying ignores it.

9.q: Eileen, 76, is prescribed morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously. The ward stocks morphine sulfate 10 mg in 1 mL ampoules. A second nurse witnesses throughout. Which controlled drugs register entry correctly records the dose and the remainder?
o: 2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.4 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.6 mL) discarded, both signatures
2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) returned to the CD cupboard
2.5 mg (2.5 mL) given; ampoule recorded as used with no remainder
9.w: Volume = 2.5 / 10 x 1 = 0.25 mL, leaving 7.5 mg (0.75 mL). NICE NG46: for CDs left over after administration, record the amount disposed of and the signatures of the person disposing and any witness. Opened ampoules are not returned to stock.

n.1: 0.4 mL contains 4 mg, so the volume is wrong for a 2.5 mg dose.
n.2: Opened ampoules cannot be returned to stock; the remainder is disposed of and recorded.
n.3: 2.5 mL exceeds the 1 mL ampoule and would be a tenfold miscalculation.

9.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
9.q: Leo, aged 2, has had a fever for 6 days. He has red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips and a rash. His mother says the GP thought it was a virus. What should the nurse consider?
o: Kawasaki disease, because fever has lasted 5 days or more
Scarlet fever, needing oral antibiotics at home
A viral illness that will resolve without assessment
Measles, needing isolation and no further assessment
9.w: NICE NG143: fever lasting 5 days or longer is an amber feature, and the clinician should assess for Kawasaki disease (fever with conjunctival injection without discharge, red cracked lips or strawberry tongue, rash, changes in hands and feet, neck lymph nodes). Early treatment reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysm (NHS, Kawasaki disease).

n.1: Scarlet fever is possible in children with fever and rash, but 6 days of fever with non-purulent red eyes and cracked lips points to Kawasaki disease, which needs specialist assessment.
n.2: Fever for 5 days or more is amber and should not be assumed viral.
n.3: Measles needs isolation, but this pattern does not fit as well, and any prolonged fever still needs assessment.

9.q: During a multidisciplinary meeting about Ellie, 5, who is ready for discharge, a manager suggests postponing a decision about where she should live for several months to 'see how things settle'. The children's nurse wants to challenge this using the Children Act 1989. Which principle is most relevant?
o: A court should make an order when it is better than making none
Delay in deciding is likely to prejudice the child's welfare
Local authorities must work in partnership with parents
Parental responsibility is shared between both parents
9.w: Section 1(2) of the Children Act 1989 sets the 'no delay' principle: any delay in determining a question about a child's upbringing is likely to prejudice the child's welfare. Open-ended postponement directly conflicts with it.

n.0: The no-order principle (s1(5)) stops unnecessary orders; it does not address postponing a decision.
n.2: Partnership with parents is good practice but does not answer the risk caused by delay.
n.3: Shared parental responsibility concerns who can make decisions, not the timing of decisions.

9.q: Blood from a dislodged cannula has spilled onto the hard floor beside the bed of Thomas, 66. Spill granules are available. The nurse has put on non-sterile gloves and an apron. What should the nurse do next?
o: Cover with paper towels and apply 70% alcohol to the towels
Apply 1,000 ppm chlorine solution and mop the area straight away
Wipe it up with paper towels and clean the area with detergent
Apply chlorine-releasing granules and leave for the contact time
9.w: NIPCM appendix 9: for blood or high-risk body fluid spills apply chlorine-releasing granules (or towels soaked in 10,000 ppm available chlorine), follow the contact time (or 3 minutes), discard the waste as healthcare waste, then wash with detergent and dry.

n.0: Alcohol is not the NIPCM agent for blood spills.
n.1: 1,000 ppm is for urine, faeces or vomit spills; blood needs granules or 10,000 ppm, with contact time.
n.2: Detergent alone does not disinfect a blood spill, which may contain blood-borne viruses.

9.q: A red cell transfusion for Graham, 66, started at 14:00. Baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate were recorded at 13:30 and were normal. According to BSH guidance, when should the next set of observations be taken?
o: At 14:30, 30 minutes after the start
At 15:00, 1 hour after the start
At 14:15, 15 minutes after the start
At the end of the unit, within 60 minutes
9.w: BSH (2017) observations: baseline no more than 60 minutes before starting, then pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, and again no more than 60 minutes after the end. Severe reactions often occur early in the unit.

n.0: The BSH timepoint is 15 minutes, not 30.
n.1: Waiting an hour misses the early period when serious reactions usually start.
n.3: End-of-unit observations are needed, but an observation at 15 minutes comes first.

9.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
9.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

9.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which abbreviation practice best supports safe record keeping when documenting medicines and care in the notes. Which approach should she follow?
o: Write terms in full unless the trust approves the abbreviation
Use abbreviations for drug names to save time in busy shifts
Use the abbreviations she learned during her training abroad
Use any abbreviation that colleagues on the ward understand
9.w: Code 10.4: records must be clearly written and not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. Annexe A 1.8 accurate, clear, legible records.

n.1: Abbreviating drug names risks medication errors and breaches Code 10.4.
n.2: Abbreviations vary between countries and may not be understood here.
n.3: Local shorthand may be misread by others; Code 10.4 says no unnecessary abbreviations.

9.q: A practice nurse invites people with a BMI over 40 to an intensive weight-management programme rather than offering it to the whole practice population. Which advantage is associated with this high-risk approach?
o: It tackles the social influences on behaviour in the wider community
Those invited are often more motivated, as their personal risk is high
It removes the need to assess each person's individual risk factors
It brings the largest fall in disease across the whole population
9.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the high-risk approach may be more cost-effective than population-wide approaches and targets people who are more motivated to change their behaviour; the population approach achieves risk reduction at population level. NICE PH49 (2014) rec 9: high-intensity interventions for people at high risk, for example a BMI over 40.

n.0: Addressing social influences on the whole community is a feature of the population approach.
n.2: A high-risk approach depends on identifying individuals by assessing their risk.
n.3: A large fall in total disease is the strength of the population approach, not a high-risk approach.

9.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
9.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

9.q: Maddie, 6, has cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency. Her mother says Maddie has greasy, foul-smelling stools and is not gaining weight. Maddie takes her pancreatic enzyme capsules only with breakfast. What advice should the nurse give, with the dietitian?
o: Stop the enzymes for a week to see if her stools change
Give a double dose of enzymes with breakfast only
Give enzymes with every fat-containing meal and snack
Reduce the fat in her diet so that she needs fewer enzymes
9.w: NICE NG78 Cystic fibrosis: diagnosis and management recs 1.7.2 and 1.7.6: offer oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and adjust the dose to minimise malabsorption; enzymes are taken with all fat-containing meals, snacks and milk drinks. Calorie intake is increased, not reduced.

n.0: Stopping enzymes would worsen malabsorption and weight loss.
n.1: Enzymes act on the food eaten at that time; a large breakfast dose does not cover later meals.
n.3: Children with CF need high-energy diets; reducing fat worsens faltering growth.

9.q: Mrs Ahmed, 66, has capacity and care needs after a stroke. She discloses that her husband sometimes slaps her but says she does not want any action taken. Nobody else lives in the home. Following the statutory guidance, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a safeguarding referral but do not let her know it has been made
Share her disclosure with relevant professionals via the safeguarding lead
Report her husband directly to the police against her wishes
Respect her wishes, taking no further action and making no record
9.w: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.92: if an adult with capacity does not want action taken, this does not preclude sharing information with relevant professional colleagues to assess risk and check she is not being coerced. It is good practice to tell her this is being done unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Para 14.92 says she should normally be told, unless telling her would increase the risk; nothing suggests that here.
n.2: Police involvement against her wishes is not the first step without a wider risk or public interest; colleagues should first assess the risk.
n.3: Her wishes carry great weight, but para 14.92 allows information to be shared with professional colleagues, and the disclosure must be recorded.

9.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
9.q: Kai, aged 2, is 4 hours after hernia repair. He is grimacing, kicking, arching, crying steadily and hard to console. His FLACC score is 8. Analgesia is prescribed. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck the FLACC score in 4 hours before taking action
Give the prescribed analgesia and reassess once it has had time to work
Use distraction and comfort measures and avoid medicines at his age
Ask his parents to settle him and record the score as behaviour
9.w: Two steps: interpret, then act. A FLACC score of 7 to 10 indicates severe pain. The nurse should give the prescribed analgesia promptly, use comfort and distraction alongside, and reassess pain after the medicine has had time to work to judge whether it is effective (AnnexB.3.5; P4.8).

n.0: Waiting 4 hours leaves severe pain untreated.
n.2: Distraction helps, but severe post-operative pain needs analgesia; age 2 is no reason to withhold prescribed medicines.
n.3: Labelling the score as behaviour ignores severe pain that needs treatment.

9.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
9.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

9.q: Ruth, 85, has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible but no bone, tendon or muscle is exposed. Using the international NPIAP-EPUAP classification, which category is this?
o: Category 2
Suspected deep tissue injury
Category 3
Category 4
9.w: NPIAP-EPUAP classification (used per NICE CG179): category 3 is full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible but bone, tendon or muscle not exposed. Category 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle; category 2 is partial-thickness loss.

n.0: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss of dermis, such as a shallow open wound or blister.
n.1: Suspected deep tissue injury is an area of purple or maroon intact skin or a blood-filled blister.
n.3: Category 4 involves exposed bone, tendon or muscle.

9.q: A practice nurse in England plans to share concerns about Leo, 5, with children's social care under the s16LA duty. She intends to share whether or not his father agrees. How should she approach the conversation with the father?
o: Leave him uninformed, as the duty does not require openness
Ask for his consent, then withhold if he refuses it
Ask for his consent, then share anyway if he refuses it
Explain openly what will be shared and why, not asking consent
9.w: The statutory guidance says that where the lawful basis is public task or legal obligation, practitioners should avoid seeking consent if they intend to share anyway, and should not imply that the family's agreement decides the matter. Where safe, they should be open and transparent about what is shared and why.

n.0: Practitioners should be transparent with families where it is safe to do so.
n.1: Lack of consent is not a reason to withhold information under the duty.
n.2: Seeking consent that will then be overridden is misleading and is discouraged by the guidance.

9.q: After treating Kiran, 12, for hypoglycaemia with 15 g of glucose tablets, the nurse plans the next step. Kiran has type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections, and his next meal is 2 hours away. When should his capillary glucose be rechecked?
o: After 1 hour
After 30 minutes
Within 15 minutes
At his next meal
9.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.89: recheck blood glucose within 15 minutes (fast-acting glucose should act within 5-15 minutes) and give more if still low; then complex carbohydrate as his meal is not imminent.

n.0: One hour is far too long to leave a possible ongoing hypo.
n.1: Thirty minutes leaves a persistent hypo untreated for too long.
n.3: Waiting 2 hours risks recurrent or worsening hypoglycaemia.

9.q: Callum, 15, has type 1 diabetes and has been admitted twice with DKA this year. His parents say he used to manage well but now skips insulin when out with friends. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask his parents to take over all his insulin injections until he is 18
Warn Callum firmly that further admissions will lead to a safeguarding referral
Arrange for him to move to the adult diabetes service now to promote independence
Speak with Callum alone, explore what gets in the way, and plan goals with him
9.w: Adolescence brings a drive for autonomy, peer influence and risk taking, and adherence often falls. A non-judgemental conversation alone with the young person, exploring barriers (for example embarrassment in front of friends) and agreeing realistic goals, supports self-management and health behaviour change (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Removing all responsibility undermines developing independence and is unlikely to be accepted by a 15-year-old.
n.1: Threats are not a therapeutic approach and may further reduce engagement.
n.2: Transition is planned gradually (NICE NG43), not used as a response to poor adherence.

9.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
9.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

10.q: Finn, 8 months, is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms orally. The stock is digoxin elixir 50 micrograms per mL. What volume should be given?
o: 0.8 mL
10.w: Volume = 62.5 micrograms / 50 micrograms per mL = 1.25 mL. Keep dose and stock in the same unit (micrograms) to avoid ten-fold and thousand-fold errors.

n.0: 0.125 mL is a ten-fold under-dose.
n.2: 0.8 mL comes from inverting the calculation (50 / 62.5).
n.3: 12.5 mL is a ten-fold overdose from a decimal slip.

10.q: A nurse is recording a 12-lead ECG for Mr Ford, 76, who is cold and shivering. The trace has a wandering, fuzzy baseline in several leads. What is the best way to improve the recording?
o: Accept the trace, as shivering does not affect how it is interpreted
Warm him, help him relax and lie still, then check electrode contact
Increase the paper speed and record the trace again at once
Record the trace with him standing to reduce the shivering
10.w: Muscle tremor, movement and poor electrode contact cause artefact. Making the person warm, comfortable and still, usually lying or semi-recumbent, with clean dry skin and good electrode contact, gives an interpretable trace (Annexe B 2.3).

n.0: Artefact can mimic or hide abnormalities, so the trace may not be interpretable.
n.2: Changing paper speed alters the appearance of the trace and does not remove tremor artefact.
n.3: Standing increases muscle activity and movement; ECGs are recorded with the person at rest.

10.q: Amina, 15, attends a sexual health clinic in England with painful periods. During the consultation she tells the nurse that she was 'cut' when she was 7 during a family visit abroad. What must the nurse do under the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
o: Seek Amina's consent before reporting, as she is 15 and competent
Report the case to the police personally, usually by calling 101
Inform the clinic's safeguarding lead, who will make the police report
Refer Amina to children's social care, who will decide whether to inform the police
10.w: Section 5B of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 requires regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales to report to the police when a girl under 18 discloses that FGM has been carried out on her. Home Office procedural information recommends reporting by calling 101; the duty is personal and does not require consent.

n.0: The duty applies regardless of consent, and complying with it does not breach confidentiality.
n.2: The duty is personal to the professional who hears the disclosure and cannot be transferred to a safeguarding lead.
n.3: A social care referral is good practice alongside, but the legal duty is a report to the police.

10.q: At 03:00 Mr Fry, 58, recently diagnosed with motor neurone disease, is awake and tearful and says, "What's the point of carrying on?" What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reassure him that things will look brighter in the morning light
Offer him a sleeping tablet so that he can rest
Tell him the doctor will talk it through with him on the ward round
Sit with him, explore his meaning and ask about self-harm thoughts
10.w: Proficiency P1.12: support people who are emotionally vulnerable; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; Code 17.1 protect people at risk. NICE NG225: assess and support with a safety plan, not risk tools.

n.0: False reassurance dismisses possible suicidal thoughts that need exploring.
n.1: Sedation does not address his distress or assess his safety.
n.2: Delaying leaves a possibly at-risk person unsupported now.

10.q: A nurse is giving Hana, aged 12 weeks, her routine injections. Which site should be used for the intramuscular vaccines?
o: The ventrogluteal site of the hip
The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
The anterolateral aspect of the thigh
The dorsogluteal muscle of the buttock
10.w: The UKHSA schedule lists the thigh as the usual site for the 8, 12 and 16 week injections; intramuscular vaccines go into the anterolateral thigh in infants, with the deltoid or thigh used from 1 year.

n.0: The ventrogluteal site is not a recommended site for routine infant vaccines.
n.1: The deltoid is too small in young infants; the upper arm is used from around 1 year.
n.3: The buttock is not recommended for vaccines because of fat depth and sciatic nerve risk.

10.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
10.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

10.q: Two weeks after discharge from an acute mental health unit, a former patient messages Sam, his named nurse, asking to meet for coffee to say thank you. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Meet in a public place as the patient has been discharged
Accept if the patient's care coordinator agrees to it
Decline the invitation and keep contact professional
Meet once with a colleague present to say goodbye
10.w: Code 20.5-20.6: do not take advantage of vulnerability; stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past.

n.0: Code 20.6 boundaries extend to people who have been in your care in the past.
n.1: Another professional's agreement does not change the boundary set by Code 20.6.
n.3: A social meeting, even accompanied, blurs the professional relationship with a former patient.

10.q: Grace, aged 18 months, was born in September 2024. Her mother asks why her older son, born in March 2024, did not have an appointment at this age. What is the correct explanation?
o: It is a catch-up appointment for children who missed the 1-year vaccines
Children born from 1 July 2024 are given a BCG vaccine at the 18-month visit
Children born from 1 July 2024 get a 4th 6-in-1 and 2nd MMRV at 18 months
It is an appointment to give the HPV vaccine early to girls born after July 2024
10.w: UKHSA routine schedule (from 1 September 2026): children born on or after 1 July 2024 are offered a fourth 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) and a second MMRV at 18 months; those born on or before 30 June 2024 have no 18-month appointment.

n.0: It is a routine appointment for a whole birth cohort, not a catch-up for missed vaccines.
n.1: BCG is a selective vaccine given within 28 days of birth to at-risk infants.
n.3: HPV is given at 12 to 13 years to boys and girls, not at 18 months.

10.q: Frank, 63, is prescribed oral morphine solution 2.5-5 mg as required every 2 hours for pain. He had 2.5 mg 4 hours ago with little effect and now rates his pain 8/10. He is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 2.5 mg now and repeat it in 30 minutes if needed
Give 7.5 mg, as the previous 2.5 mg dose was ineffective
Withhold the dose until the doctor increases the prescription
Give 5 mg, the top of the prescribed range, and reassess
10.w: Titration within a prescribed range is a nurse's decision based on assessment (AnnexB.11.5). The previous dose was ineffective, he is not sedated and 2 hours have passed, so the higher dose within the range is appropriate, with reassessment of pain, sedation and respiratory rate.

n.0: Repeating at 30 minutes breaches the 2-hourly minimum interval.
n.1: 7.5 mg exceeds the prescribed range, which the nurse cannot change.
n.2: A suitable dose is available within the range; withholding leaves him in pain.

10.q: Charlie, a mental health nurse in England, asks in October 2026 whether the Mental Health Act 2025 has replaced the 1983 Act for detentions on his ward. Which statement is correct?
o: The 2025 Act received Royal Assent, but most provisions are not yet in force
The 2025 Act applies to new detentions; the 1983 Act applies to existing ones
The 2025 Act is still a Bill and has not yet completed its parliamentary stages
The 2025 Act is fully in force and has replaced the 1983 Act in England
10.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions (including changes to sections 3 and 4) were not in force at October 2026. The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended remains the current law for detention (BUILD-PLAN unsettled law note; P7.4 implications of current and future health policy).

n.1: There is no rule of this kind; detentions continue under the 1983 Act as amended until provisions are commenced.
n.2: The Act completed its passage and received Royal Assent in December 2025.
n.3: Most provisions of the 2025 Act await commencement, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies.

10.q: Alfred, 86, has delirium and MRSA and is nursed in a single room. With the door closed he becomes distressed and has twice tried to climb out of bed. The healthcare support worker suggests propping the door open. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the door closed and increase checks on Alfred to hourly
Move Alfred back to the open bay where staff can see him
Prop the door open and mention the change at the next handover
Document a risk assessment and agree the door plan with the IPC team
10.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: isolation room doors should remain closed, and if this is not possible a documented risk assessment is needed, with IPC team advice on precautions. Alfred's falls risk and distress must be balanced against transmission risk.

n.0: Hourly checks do not address the falls risk and distress that the closed door is causing.
n.1: Moving him to a bay exposes other patients to MRSA without IPC team assessment.
n.2: Changing isolation conditions needs a documented risk assessment, not an informal handover note.

10.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
10.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

10.q: Ms Grey, 34, has symptoms of a urinary tract infection and needs a urine sample sent for culture. She is independent and mobile. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after passing it
Discard the first part of the stream and collect the midstream urine
Collect the last few drops of urine at the end of passing it
Collect the first part of the urine stream into a clean pot
10.w: A clean-catch midstream specimen reduces contamination by skin and urethral organisms. The first part of the stream is discarded and the midstream portion collected into a sterile container, labelled and sent promptly (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Urine from the toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
n.2: The end of the stream is not the midstream sample required for culture.
n.3: First-catch urine carries urethral and skin organisms that contaminate a culture; it is the sample used for chlamydia testing, not for MSU culture.

10.q: Kenneth, 68, lives in England and asks the practice nurse what the NHS bowel cancer screening programme will offer him. He has no bowel symptoms. Which answer is accurate?
o: A home test kit every 2 years
A home test kit every year
A colonoscopy every 5 years
A one-off camera test at age 70
10.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): everyone aged 50 to 74 is offered a bowel cancer screening home test kit every 2 years; people aged 75 or over can ask for a kit every 2 years.

n.1: The bowel screening kit is sent every 2 years, not annually.
n.2: Colonoscopy is a diagnostic test offered after a positive screening result, not the routine screen.
n.3: The current programme offers a home test kit every 2 years from 50 to 74.

10.q: A CDOP reviews the deaths of three infants in its area that involved co-sleeping after parental alcohol use. The panel recommends a local safer sleep campaign. What is the main purpose of the CDOP review, as described in Working Together 2026?
o: Independent scrutiny to find modifiable factors and prevent deaths
Determination of the medical cause of death in place of the coroner
Investigation of the deaths to decide whether criminal charges should follow
Disciplinary review of practitioners involved in each child's care
10.w: The CDOP review is the final, independent scrutiny of a child's death by professionals with no responsibility for the child during life. It aims to identify modifiable factors that could be altered to prevent future deaths and to share learning, including with the National Child Mortality Database.

n.1: The coroner retains responsibility for inquests into the cause of death.
n.2: Criminal investigation is the responsibility of the police and CPS.
n.3: CDOP reviews are for learning, not for disciplining individuals.

10.q: A GP practice annual report states that on 1 April 2026, 850 of its 12,000 registered adults were living with diagnosed type 2 diabetes. A student nurse on placement asks what this figure measures. Which term is correct?
o: Prevalence
Relative risk
Life expectancy
Incidence
10.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: prevalence is the total number of existing cases in a population at a point in time (point prevalence) or over a period; incidence counts new cases. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2.

n.1: Relative risk compares the risk of an outcome between an exposed and an unexposed group.
n.2: Life expectancy estimates average years of life remaining and is unrelated to this count.
n.3: Incidence counts new cases over a period; this figure counts everyone currently living with the condition.

10.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
10.q: Freddie, aged 4 months, is found unresponsive in his cot and breathing noisily. The nurse calls for help and opens his airway. How should his head be positioned?
o: Turned to one side, with the neck extended over a pillow
In the neutral position, with the head level and face parallel to the bed
Flexed forward slightly, with the chin resting down towards the chest
Fully extended, with the head tilted back as far as it will go
10.w: Infants have a large occiput and a short neck, and the soft trachea is easily compressed by over-extension. RCUK paediatric life support: open an infant's airway with the head in the neutral position and chin lift; children need a slightly more extended 'sniffing' position (T2 physiological differences; AnnexB.2.7).

n.0: Turning and extending over a pillow does not open the airway and over-extends the neck.
n.2: Flexion pushes the chin to the chest and obstructs the airway, which the large occiput already tends to do.
n.3: Over-extension kinks the soft infant trachea and can obstruct the airway.

10.q: Yusuf, 50, is prescribed co-amoxiclav 1.2 g by slow intravenous injection over 3 to 4 minutes via his peripheral cannula. The second check is complete. The ward is busy and his maintenance fluids are running. How should the nurse give the dose?
o: Add it to the maintenance fluid bag and let it run in with the fluids
Flush to confirm patency, give over 3 to 4 minutes, then flush again
Give it by rapid push over 30 seconds, then flush with saline
Give it without a flush, as the cannula was used this morning
10.w: Safe IV administration via a vascular access device (AnnexB.11.9; NICE CG139 flushing with 0.9% sodium chloride): check patency and the site with a flush, give the drug at the prescribed rate, observe for reactions, then flush to clear the line.

n.0: Adding drugs to a bag changes the prescribed route and rate and risks incompatibility.
n.2: Giving faster than prescribed risks adverse reactions and does not follow the prescription.
n.3: Patency must be checked before each use; a morning flush does not confirm current patency.

10.q: While a nurse changes his dressing, Kai, 10, says, 'I'll tell you something about my uncle, but you have to promise not to tell anyone.' What is the best response?
o: 'Please wait while I fetch the safeguarding lead to hear it with me.'
'You should tell your mum about this rather than tell me.'
'I promise, you can tell me anything and it will stay between us.'
'I can't promise that, but I'll share it with people who can help.'
10.w: Practitioners must not promise secrecy to a child, but should keep the child talking and explain honestly that information may be shared with people who can help, then listen, record in the child's words and follow safeguarding procedures.

n.0: Pausing to fetch someone may shut down the disclosure; the nurse should listen now and escalate afterwards.
n.1: Redirecting him may stop a disclosure; the uncle may be someone the mother cannot protect him from.
n.2: A promise of secrecy cannot be kept if Kai discloses harm and would break his trust.

10.q: A newly qualified nurse on a children's ward has a concern that a 15-year-old patient may be being radicalised by an older relative. She is unsure who to contact within her NHS trust for specialist advice. Who is the most appropriate person?
o: The trust's Prevent lead
The counter-terrorism police unit
The Local Authority Designated Officer
The chair of the local Channel panel
10.w: NHS trusts have a Prevent lead who advises staff and handles Prevent concerns alongside the safeguarding team, using the notice, check, share approach before any referral.

n.1: Police contact is for immediate risk; specialist advice in the trust comes from the Prevent lead.
n.2: The LADO handles allegations against people who work with children.
n.3: Channel panels consider referrals once made; they are not the first point of advice within a trust.

10.q: Before a transfer, Rosa checks the mobile hoist on her ward. The examination label shows that its last thorough examination under LOLER was eight months ago, and no examination scheme with different intervals is displayed. What should Rosa do?
o: Use the hoist, because lifting equipment is examined every 12 months
Take the hoist out of use, report it and use another hoist that is in date
Carry out a visual pre-use check and continue if the hoist looks sound
Use the hoist for this transfer and report the overdue date at handover
10.w: Under LOLER 1998, lifting equipment and accessories used for lifting people must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months (other lifting equipment every 12 months) unless an examination scheme sets other intervals. A hoist overdue for examination should not be used to lift a person and should be reported (HSE, Thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment).

n.0: The 12-month interval applies to lifting equipment that is not used to lift people; patient hoists fall under the 6-month interval.
n.2: A pre-use check is good practice but does not replace the thorough examination by a competent person that LOLER requires.
n.3: Knowingly using equipment that is overdue for its statutory examination puts the patient at risk; the problem must be dealt with before the transfer.

10.q: Marion, 85, lives in a care home and has had diarrhoea for 3 days. Staff say she has been drinking very little and seems more tired than usual. You are assessing her hydration status on admission. Which combination of findings most suggests dehydration?
o: Ankle oedema, crackles in the lungs and weight gain
Dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and tachycardia
Moist mouth, pale dilute urine and normal skin turgor
Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and polyuria
10.w: Dehydration commonly presents with dry mucous membranes, thirst, reduced and concentrated urine, tachycardia and postural hypotension (Annexe B 5.4). CG174 indicators of fluid need include HR over 90 and systolic under 100.

n.0: Oedema, crackles and weight gain suggest fluid overload.
n.2: A moist mouth and pale dilute urine suggest adequate hydration.
n.3: Raised BP and bounding pulse do not indicate dehydration.

10.q: Agency nurse Paul's electronic record login has expired. A permanent colleague offers him her smartcard so he can document his care until IT resets his access. What should Paul do?
o: Use her card and add his own name at the start of each entry
Use her card and ask her to check his entries afterwards
Wait until his access returns and write all entries then
Decline and use the approved paper back-up until access returns
10.w: Code 10.4: attribute entries to yourself; Code 10.5: keep records secure. Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely; P1.15 digital skills for safe practice.

n.0: Entries would still be attributed to her login, breaching Code 10.4 and information security.
n.1: Her checking does not correct the false attribution of entries to her.
n.2: Delaying documentation risks missing information; Code 10.1 requires timely records.

10.q: Sidney, 76, has fallen twice in the past year at home and could not get up without help after the second fall. His GP practice nurse sees him for a routine review. What does NICE NG249 recommend?
o: Refer him for a bone scan without other assessment
Offer him a comprehensive falls assessment and management
Give him a leaflet on falls and review him in a year
Advise him to stay in his chair to avoid further falls
10.w: NICE NG249: in the community, offer a comprehensive falls assessment and management to people who have fallen in the past year and meet any criterion, such as being unable to get up independently or having 2 or more falls in the year. Sidney meets both.

n.0: Osteoporosis risk is part of the assessment, but not the whole of it.
n.2: A leaflet alone does not meet his assessed needs.
n.3: Reducing activity increases deconditioning and falls risk; exercise programmes are recommended.

10.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
10.q: Ellie, aged 3 months, is admitted with bronchiolitis. The nurse hears a short noise at the end of each breath out and sees her nostrils flaring. What does the noise most likely indicate?
o: Normal breathing sounds in a young infant
Wheeze, a sign that the illness is improving
Grunting, a sign of severe respiratory distress
Stridor from narrowing of the upper airway
10.w: Grunting is a noise on expiration as the infant breathes out against a partly closed glottis to keep alveoli open; it signals severe respiratory distress (NICE NG9 and NG143 list grunting as a red feature; RCUK 2025 Table 2). Escalate urgently.

n.0: Grunting is not a normal infant sound and indicates significant distress.
n.1: Wheeze is a musical sound on expiration and does not mean improvement.
n.3: Stridor is a harsh sound mainly on breathing in, from upper airway narrowing.

10.q: A health visitor sees Noor, 3 months, at home and notices a small bruise on her thigh. Her mother, who is attentive and has no previous concerns, says it happened when she fastened the car seat buckle. Under the local bruising protocol, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise the mother to take Noor to the GP if more bruises appear
Refer Noor for urgent paediatric assessment under the protocol
Ask the mother to photograph the bruise daily for one week
Accept the explanation, as the mother is caring and it is plausible
10.w: Bruising protocols for non-mobile infants apply to any bruise however small, and irrespective of the explanation or how caring the parent appears. The infant needs paediatric assessment and children's social care involvement to exclude abuse and medical causes such as a bleeding disorder.

n.0: Waiting for further bruising risks further harm.
n.2: Monitoring photographs delays the urgent assessment the protocol requires.
n.3: Judging the parent's character is not a safe basis for not referring a non-mobile infant with a bruise.

10.q: Ruby, 19 months, moves around by bottom shuffling and does not yet walk. She can pull to stand briefly. Her father also bottom shuffled and walked at 22 months. Ruby's other development is normal. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Advise a baby walker to encourage her to bear weight and step
Note the family history and arrange a review for when she reaches 3 years
Reassure and recheck at the 2-year review because shufflers often walk late
Refer for assessment because she is not walking at 18 months
10.w: Not walking by 18 months (corrected for gestational age) is one of the delayed motor milestones listed in NICE NG62 rec 1.3.5, and rec 1.3.6 advises referring all children with delayed motor milestones to a child development service for further assessment. Bottom shufflers and children with a family history often walk later, but assessment confirms the normal variant and excludes causes such as cerebral palsy or a muscle disorder, rather than assuming one.

n.0: Baby walkers do not help children learn to walk and carry a risk of injury, so they are not advised.
n.1: Waiting until 3 years would delay assessment of a red flag by well over a year.
n.2: Bottom shuffling makes late walking more likely but does not remove the need to assess a child not walking at 18 months; waiting another 5 months delays diagnosis if there is a cause.
