10.q: Priya is 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She asks the practice nurse when she will first meet a health visitor under the Healthy Child Programme in England. What is the correct answer?
o: At the new baby review about 10 to 14 days after the birth
At an antenatal review from 28 weeks of pregnancy
At the 6 to 8 week review, alongside the baby's physical examination
At the 12-month review, when development is first checked
10.w: The Healthy Child Programme in England has five mandated health visitor reviews: antenatal (from 28 weeks), new birth, 6 to 8 weeks, 12 months (9 to 15 months) and 2 to 2.5 years. Health visitors first make contact in pregnancy, around 28 weeks, through an antenatal review, ideally face to face at home (DHSC/OHID, Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme, Part 2, Feb 2026).

n.0: The new baby review is the second mandated contact, not the first.
n.2: The 6 to 8 week review comes later, after the antenatal and new birth reviews.
n.3: The 12-month review is the fourth mandated contact.

10.q: Frank, 68, has COPD and pneumonia. Two days ago the team thought he was dying and started an end of life care plan. Today he is more alert, has eaten some breakfast and his breathing is easier. The doctors disagree about whether he is still dying. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue the end of life care plan unchanged, as improvement is often brief
Seek advice from the specialist palliative care team about the uncertainty
Request daily full blood counts and renal function to clarify his prognosis
Stop the end of life care plan and restart all of his previous medicines
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.7: seek advice from colleagues with more experience of end of life care when there is a high level of uncertainty, for example conflicting signs, about whether a person is dying, stabilising or may recover. Rec 1.1.3: improvement could indicate stabilising or recovery.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.1.3 warns that improvement may mean the person is stabilising or recovering, so the plan cannot simply continue unchanged.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.1.4 advises avoiding investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last days of life.
n.3: Reversing all care without a shared review is premature; the guidance is to seek experienced advice when the picture is uncertain.

10.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 72, has capacity and a leg ulcer. When the nurse arrives to change the dressing she says firmly that she does not want it done today because she is tired. The dressing is not urgent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Change the dressing gently because it is in her best interests
Respect her decision, explore her reasons and record the refusal
Ask her daughter to persuade her to accept the dressing change
Assess her capacity because she is refusing recommended care
10.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment. Mrs Adeyemi has capacity, so her refusal is valid. The nurse should explore why, explain any consequences, offer another time and document the refusal.

n.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity (MCA s4); treating a capacitous person against her refusal is unlawful.
n.2: Using a relative to pressure her undermines the voluntariness of any later consent.
n.3: Refusing care is not evidence of incapacity; MCA s1(4) says an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity, and capacity is presumed.

10.q: A nurse researcher wants to understand what living with a new stoma is like for young adults, in their own words. Which research approach is most suitable?
o: A qualitative design using in-depth interviews
A randomised controlled trial of stoma care products
A retrospective audit of stoma complication rates
A cross-sectional survey using closed questions
10.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022) recognises qualitative research approaches; interviews explore meaning and experience. Proficiency P1.7: understand research methods to critically analyse findings.

n.1: An RCT compares interventions; it does not explore lived experience.
n.2: An audit measures practice against a standard, not personal experience.
n.3: Closed questions limit responses and do not capture experience in people's own words.

10.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
10.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

10.q: Pauline, 73, has an MRSA-colonised leg ulcer. The nurse removes a dressing heavily soaked with wound exudate. In an acute hospital in England, which waste stream should the used dressing go into?
o: Yellow and black striped offensive waste bag
Orange bag for infectious clinical waste
Black domestic waste bag
Purple bag for cytotoxic waste
10.w: NIPCM ch 1.9 (HTM 07-01): clinical waste that is infectious, for example from a patient known or suspected to be infected or colonised, goes in a UN-approved orange bag. Offensive (tiger) waste is for non-infectious waste containing body fluids.

n.0: Tiger bags are for offensive waste that is not infectious; this dressing is from a colonised wound.
n.2: Domestic bags are for non-healthcare general waste, not soiled dressings.
n.3: Purple is for waste contaminated with cytotoxic or cytostatic medicines.

10.q: At 07:30 the ward medicines refrigerator display reads 11°C and the overnight maximum recorded is 13°C. It contains insulin pens and influenza vaccines. Yesterday's readings were within range. What should the nurse do?
o: Quarantine the contents, report it, and seek pharmacy advice before use
Move the items to another fridge and use them as normal
Discard all the contents immediately into the pharmaceutical waste bin
Turn the thermostat down and recheck the temperature tomorrow
10.w: Medicines such as insulin and vaccines are stored at 2-8°C (Green Book ch 3 cold chain). After a temperature excursion, the stock is quarantined in a working fridge and not used until pharmacy (or the vaccine manufacturer via pharmacy) advises; the excursion is reported and recorded (AnnexB.11.11).

n.1: Using stock after an excursion without advice risks giving ineffective vaccines or insulin.
n.2: Some stock may be usable after assessment; discarding everything without advice wastes medicines.
n.3: Adjusting the dial does not address whether the exposed stock is still safe.

10.q: Amira, 10, had anaphylaxis with hypotension and has received IM adrenaline. Her breathing is now quiet and unlaboured, but her blood pressure is still low and she feels faint. She asks to stand up and walk to the toilet. How should the nurse position her?
o: Keep her lying flat with her legs raised
Place her in the recovery position on her side
Help her to walk slowly to the toilet
Sit her upright in a chair beside the bed
10.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): avoid sudden changes in posture. A patient with cardiovascular instability is kept flat, with or without legs raised, to maximise venous return; standing or sitting up has been linked to cardiovascular collapse and death.

n.1: The recovery position is for an unconscious patient who is breathing; Amira is conscious and needs maximal venous return.
n.2: Standing and walking reduce venous return and have been associated with fatal collapse in anaphylaxis.
n.3: A semi-recumbent or sitting position suits predominantly respiratory symptoms; Amira's problem is hypotension.

10.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
10.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

10.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
10.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

10.q: Jade, 14, has a suspected appendix abscess and needs IV antibiotics and a drain. The surgeon assesses her as Gillick competent and she consents. Her mother, who has parental responsibility, objects because she wants a second opinion first. What is the legal position?
o: The mother's objection overrides Jade's consent while Jade is under 16
Treatment needs the agreement of both Jade and her mother
Treatment must wait for a court order because the two disagree
Jade's consent is valid and treatment can proceed
10.w: When a child under 16 is Gillick competent and consents, that consent is valid and treatment can proceed even if a parent disagrees (Gillick 1986; NSPCC Learning). Staff should still try to involve and support the mother.

n.0: A parent cannot veto the valid consent of a Gillick competent child to treatment in her interests.
n.1: The competent child's consent is sufficient; joint agreement is good practice, not a legal requirement.
n.2: A court is needed for refusals of life-sustaining treatment or genuine disputes over a child lacking competence, not to confirm a competent child's consent.

10.q: Callum, 15, has type 1 diabetes and has been admitted twice with DKA this year. His parents say he used to manage well but now skips insulin when out with friends. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask his parents to take over all his insulin injections until he is 18
Warn Callum firmly that further admissions will lead to a safeguarding referral
Arrange for him to move to the adult diabetes service now to promote independence
Speak with Callum alone, explore what gets in the way, and plan goals with him
10.w: Adolescence brings a drive for autonomy, peer influence and risk taking, and adherence often falls. A non-judgemental conversation alone with the young person, exploring barriers (for example embarrassment in front of friends) and agreeing realistic goals, supports self-management and health behaviour change (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Removing all responsibility undermines developing independence and is unlikely to be accepted by a 15-year-old.
n.1: Threats are not a therapeutic approach and may further reduce engagement.
n.2: Transition is planned gradually (NICE NG43), not used as a response to poor adherence.

10.q: Patricia, 73, lives in England and has had regular breast screening. She asks the practice nurse why she has not received an invitation since she turned 71. Which response is accurate?
o: Invitations stop after 70, but she can refer herself for screening
Women over 70 are invited every 5 years instead of every 3 years
Breast screening ends at 70 because no benefit remains after that age
She needs a GP referral to a breast clinic to be screened
10.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): breast screening is offered to women aged 50 to 70; women over 70 can self-refer.

n.1: Routine invitations are for women aged 50 to 70; after 70 screening is by self-referral.
n.2: Women over 70 can still self-refer; screening is available to them on request.
n.3: A breast clinic referral is for symptoms; screening after 70 is by self-referral.

10.q: Which contemporary tool is most widely used in UK adult care settings to screen for malnutrition?
o: The Braden scale for predicting risk
The 4AT rapid assessment test
The Waterlow risk assessment score
The 'MUST' screening tool
10.w: 'MUST' (BAPEN) combines BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect to give a low, medium or high risk of malnutrition, with a management plan for each (Annexe B 5.2).

n.0: Braden assesses pressure ulcer risk.
n.1: The 4AT screens for delirium.
n.2: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

10.q: Daisy, 10 months, has a fever and is being assessed for a urinary tract infection on the children's assessment unit. Her mother suggests putting a cotton wool ball inside Daisy's nappy to collect urine. Which method should the nurse use first?
o: A gauze pad in the nappy
A suprapubic aspirate
A cotton wool ball in the nappy
A clean catch urine sample
10.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022): use a clean catch wherever possible; if not possible use urine collection pads per manufacturer's instructions. Do not use cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels. Catheter or suprapubic aspiration only if non-invasive methods are not possible.

n.0: NG224 says do not use gauze to collect urine.
n.1: Suprapubic aspiration is invasive and used when non-invasive methods are not possible.
n.2: NG224 says do not use cotton wool balls to collect urine; fibres contaminate the sample.

10.q: A student nurse on a children's ward asks for an example of an UNLICENSED medicine, as opposed to an off-label one. Which example should the nurse give?
o: A licensed adult tablet prescribed for a child aged 8
An oral liquid 'special' made because no licensed liquid exists
A licensed IV antibiotic given at a higher dose than the licence
A licensed medicine used for a different indication
10.w: An unlicensed medicine has no UK marketing authorisation, such as a 'special' made by a manufacturing unit or an imported product. Off-label use is a licensed medicine used outside its licence (age, dose, route or indication).

n.0: A licensed tablet used outside its licensed age range is off-label, not unlicensed.
n.2: A licensed product given at an unlicensed dose is off-label use.
n.3: Using a licensed medicine for a different indication is off-label use.

10.q: A nurse is about to take blood for a full blood count and urea and electrolytes from Mrs Ellis, 66. She has a peripheral cannula in her left forearm with an IV infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride running. Which site is most appropriate?
o: The cannula itself, after briefly pausing the infusion
Her left antecubital fossa, above the cannula
A vein in her right arm, away from the infusion
A vein in the back of her left hand, below the cannula
10.w: Blood taken from a limb with an infusion running can be diluted or contaminated by the fluid, giving falsely altered results (for example sodium, potassium or glucose). The opposite arm should be used (Annexe B 2.2).

n.0: Sampling from an infusing cannula risks contaminated results and is not the most appropriate choice here.
n.1: Sampling above an infusion on the same arm risks contamination with the infused fluid.
n.3: The same limb is still affected by the infusion; the opposite arm is preferred.

10.q: George, 71, has known COPD with previous hypercapnic respiratory failure. He arrives breathless with SpO2 84% on air. Blood gas results are awaited. What target saturation range is appropriate?
10.w: BTS guideline: for people with known COPD or other risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure, aim for 88-92% pending blood gas results; NEWS2 Scale 2 is then used if this target is prescribed (RCP 2017).

n.0: 85-88% leaves him below the recommended lower limit of 88%.
n.1: 92-95% overshoots the 88-92% target for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.2: 94-98% risks worsening hypercapnia in someone with previous hypercapnic failure.

10.q: Mrs Dean, 49, has just eaten an orange and asks the nurse to check her blood glucose. The nurse plans to use the side of her fingertip. What should the nurse do before taking the sample?
o: Squeeze the finger firmly to produce a large drop
Ask her to wash and dry her hands
Clean her finger with an alcohol wipe and test while still wet
Use the first drop from the centre of the fingertip pad
10.w: Sugar residue on the skin, for example from fruit, can give a falsely high capillary glucose reading. Washing and drying the hands with warm water removes residue and improves blood flow (Annexe B 2.10: measure and interpret blood glucose).

n.0: Firm squeezing dilutes the drop with tissue fluid and can give an inaccurate result.
n.2: Testing through wet alcohol can dilute the sample and alter the reading.
n.3: The pad is more painful and the problem of sugar on the skin remains.

10.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
10.q: A nurse is assessing the circulation of Ava, aged 3, during an ABCDE assessment. How should central capillary refill time be measured and interpreted?
o: Press on the forehead for 10 seconds; normal is under 4 seconds
Press on the sternum for 5 seconds; normal is 2 seconds or less
Press on the sole of the foot for 5 seconds; normal is 3 seconds or less
Press on a fingertip for 2 seconds; normal is under 5 seconds
10.w: Central capillary refill is measured by pressing on the sternum for 5 seconds and timing the return of colour; 2 seconds or less is normal, and 3 seconds or more is an amber sign in NICE NG143 (AnnexB.2.8: circulatory assessment).

n.0: The forehead is not the recommended site, and 4 seconds would be abnormal.
n.2: A peripheral site is affected by temperature; 3 seconds or more is abnormal (NG143 amber).
n.3: Two seconds of pressure is too short, and under 5 seconds is far too long a normal limit.

10.q: Chloe, 12, has been accommodated by the local authority under section 20 of the Children Act 1989 with her parents' agreement while her mother receives inpatient treatment. She now lives with a foster carer and needs a minor procedure. Who holds parental responsibility for Chloe?
o: The foster carer, who acquires it for the length of the placement
The local authority and her parents jointly, as under a care order
The local authority, which acquired it when Chloe was accommodated
Her parents, who keep parental responsibility during accommodation
10.w: Section 20 accommodation is voluntary. The local authority does not acquire parental responsibility; the parents keep it and can remove the child (Children Act 1989 s20). Consent should come from a parent with PR, or from Chloe if competent for the decision.

n.0: Foster carers do not acquire PR through a placement.
n.1: Shared PR with the local authority is the effect of a care order, which Chloe is not subject to.
n.2: The local authority gains PR under a care order (s33), not under voluntary s20 accommodation.

10.q: Kayla, 30, had a psychosocial assessment in an emergency department after self-harm and is discharged home. The team remains concerned about her safety. According to NICE NG225, within what time should initial aftercare be provided?
o: Within 14 days, at a routine outpatient clinic
Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment
Within 7 days of the psychosocial assessment
Within 24 hours of arriving at the department
10.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.10.2: if there are ongoing safety concerns after self-harm, the responsible team should provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment.

n.0: A routine 14-day appointment is far later than NG225 recommends when safety concerns persist.
n.2: 7 days is longer than the 48-hour aftercare window in NG225.
n.3: The timing runs from the psychosocial assessment, and the interval is 48 hours.

10.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
10.q: Kai, aged 2, is 4 hours after hernia repair. He is grimacing, kicking, arching, crying steadily and hard to console. His FLACC score is 8. Analgesia is prescribed. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck the FLACC score in 4 hours before taking action
Give the prescribed analgesia and reassess once it has had time to work
Use distraction and comfort measures and avoid medicines at his age
Ask his parents to settle him and record the score as behaviour
10.w: Two steps: interpret, then act. A FLACC score of 7 to 10 indicates severe pain. The nurse should give the prescribed analgesia promptly, use comfort and distraction alongside, and reassess pain after the medicine has had time to work to judge whether it is effective (AnnexB.3.5; P4.8).

n.0: Waiting 4 hours leaves severe pain untreated.
n.2: Distraction helps, but severe post-operative pain needs analgesia; age 2 is no reason to withhold prescribed medicines.
n.3: Labelling the score as behaviour ignores severe pain that needs treatment.

10.q: Hugh, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to be moved from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
o: Lift him under the arms with two staff members
Use a drag lift with one person on each side
Use a hoist with an assessed sling
Ask him to stand and pivot using a frame
10.w: Annexe B 7.2-7.3: use moving and handling equipment for people with impaired mobility. A person who cannot bear weight needs a hoist with a correctly sized and assessed sling, operated by trained staff per the handling plan. Underarm drag lifts injure patients and staff.

n.0: Lifting under the arms is a drag lift, which risks shoulder injury to him and back injury to staff.
n.1: A drag lift is an unsafe technique and not part of contemporary practice.
n.3: He cannot bear weight, so a standing pivot transfer is unsafe.

10.q: Oscar, 6, is having a convulsive seizure on the children's ward that has lasted 5 minutes. He has a working IV cannula, the resuscitation trolley is at the bedside and he has no individual emergency plan. Which first-line treatment does NICE NG217 recommend?
o: IV levetiracetam
IV lorazepam
Rectal diazepam
Buccal midazolam
10.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.3: without an individualised plan, give buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, or IV lorazepam if IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available, as they are here.

n.0: Levetiracetam is the second-line treatment after two benzodiazepine doses.
n.2: Rectal diazepam is a community alternative and is slower than IV lorazepam when IV access exists.
n.3: Buccal midazolam is the first-line community option; with IV access and resuscitation facilities NG217 advises IV lorazepam.

10.q: On a medical ward, Mrs Hall's daughter asks who can prescribe a new laxative for her mother this afternoon. The doctors are busy in clinic. Which team member could prescribe it?
o: The ward pharmacy technician during the medicines round
A registered nursing associate with three years' experience
Any registered nurse following the doctor's verbal agreement
A registered nurse with a recorded prescribing qualification
10.w: Only nurses and midwives with a recorded prescribing qualification on the NMC register can prescribe; nursing associates do not prescribe (FACTS S-CODE, Code 18). Knowing the scope of practice of each team member is part of P5.4.

n.0: Pharmacy technicians support medicines management but do not prescribe.
n.1: Nursing associates are not able to prescribe, whatever their experience.
n.2: A registered nurse without a prescribing qualification cannot prescribe, even with a doctor's verbal agreement.

10.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
10.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

10.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
10.q: Ali, 7 months, has bronchiolitis and is on oxygen. His saturations have been 91 to 92%. He becomes quiet and floppy; his heart rate falls from 170 to 55 beats/min and he has poor perfusion despite effective bag-mask ventilation by the team. What should happen next?
o: Start chest compressions
Recheck the heart rate in 5 minutes
Give a fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg
Increase the oxygen and observe
10.w: Two steps: recognise that bradycardia in a hypoxic infant is pre-terminal, then act. RCUK 2025: start chest compressions if the heart rate is below 60 beats/min with poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation.

n.1: Waiting 5 minutes in a pre-arrest state risks cardiac arrest.
n.2: Fluids do not treat hypoxic bradycardia; compressions are needed when HR is below 60 with poor perfusion despite ventilation.
n.3: Oxygen and ventilation are already being given; the criteria for compressions are met.

10.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing patients' names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has most directly been breached?
o: Accuracy (keeping data up to date)
Storage limitation (retention periods)
Purpose limitation (use for stated purposes)
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
10.w: UK GDPR Article 5 requires personal data to be processed securely, protecting against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5 also requires records to be kept securely.

n.0: Nothing suggests the content is inaccurate; the problem is security.
n.1: Storage limitation concerns keeping data no longer than necessary, not leaving it unsecured.
n.2: Purpose limitation concerns using data for the purpose it was collected; handover is a legitimate purpose.

10.q: Winifred, 86, lives alone and takes 12 regular medicines from three prescribers. She has fallen twice this month and her daughter reports increasing daytime drowsiness. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the community nurse's most appropriate action?
o: Request a structured medication review with her GP and pharmacist
Spread her doses across the day to reduce side effects
Advise her daughter to buy a pill organiser for the medicines
Stop the medicines most likely to cause drowsiness and falls
10.w: Polypharmacy with falls and drowsiness is a trigger for a structured medication review (NICE NG5 medicines optimisation; P4.15). Prescribers and pharmacists can review the indication, risks and benefits of each medicine together with Winifred.

n.1: Retiming doses without review may cause errors and does not address inappropriate medicines.
n.2: A pill organiser may help adherence but does not address why she is falling.
n.3: Stopping medicines is a prescribing decision and abrupt withdrawal can cause harm.

10.q: Nadia, 44, is seen by a district nurse at home. She has a chest infection, says she has not passed urine for 20 hours, and her systolic BP is 88 mmHg. Under NICE NG253 (2025) community criteria, what should the nurse do?
o: Advise her to increase oral fluids and recheck tomorrow
Take a urine sample and await the culture result
Ask the GP to review her within the next 24 hours
Arrange emergency transfer to hospital by 999 ambulance
10.w: NG253 table 1 (community): not passing urine for 18 hours and systolic BP 90 mmHg or less are each high-risk criteria. High risk outside hospital needs emergency transfer, usually by 999 ambulance.

n.0: Oral fluids and next-day review leave a high-risk person at home.
n.1: Waiting for culture results delays emergency assessment.
n.2: A routine GP review in 24 hours is far too slow for high-risk sepsis criteria.

10.q: Megan, 17, has advanced cystic fibrosis and capacity. She tells her nurse she wants to make a legally binding advance decision refusing invasive ventilation in the future. What should the nurse explain?
o: She can make a binding advance decision now, as the MCA applies from 16
Advance decisions start at 18, so her wishes go in a care plan
An advance decision requires her parents' signature as she is a minor
An advance decision is valid if witnessed by two registered professionals
10.w: Section 24 of the MCA 2005 allows a person aged 18 or over to make an advance decision to refuse treatment. Megan's wishes should be recorded in an advance care plan and will strongly inform best interests decisions; NICE NG61 supports advance care planning for young people.

n.0: Most of the MCA applies from 16, but advance decisions (and lasting powers of attorney) require the person to be 18.
n.2: Parental signatures cannot make a binding advance decision for a minor.
n.3: Witnessing is a formality for life-sustaining refusals by adults; it does not make a 17-year-old's decision valid.

10.q: A covert administration plan for Sidney, 88, states that his dispersible aspirin and liquid antibiotic may be mixed with food on pharmacist advice. The nurse plans to stir them into his full bowl of porridge, which he often leaves half-eaten. What is the best approach?
o: Mix them into the whole bowl so they are well disguised
Mix them into the porridge and give the rest with lunch
Mix them into a small amount of the advised food first
Mix them into his tea, which he usually finishes
10.w: The covert plan details how each medicine is given, with pharmacist advice (RPS/RCN 2019; NICE SC1). Using a small amount of the advised food, offered first, makes it more likely that the full dose is taken; mixing into a large portion risks a partial dose.

n.0: If he leaves half the bowl he receives only part of the dose.
n.1: Splitting a dose across meals is not in the plan and makes the dose taken uncertain.
n.3: Changing the vehicle to tea departs from the agreed plan and pharmacist advice on compatibility.

10.q: Before discharge, a nurse helps Sophie, 27, who self-harms, to develop a safety plan. Which description of the safety plan best follows NICE NG225?
o: Written with and agreed by Sophie, and held by her
Written by the team, then shared with Sophie's family
Written by Sophie, without input from services or family
Written by the nurse, kept in the notes for professionals
10.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.17 and 1.11.7-1.11.8: a safety plan should be written with and agreed by the person, held by the person, and shared with family and professionals as the person decides. It covers means of self-harm, triggers, coping strategies, supportive contacts, service contact details and keeping the environment safe.

n.1: A plan written for her and shared without her agreement is not collaborative.
n.2: NG225 describes developing the plan in collaboration with services and, as appropriate, family and carers.
n.3: A plan held by professionals is not accessible to Sophie at a time of crisis.

10.q: Leo, 4, attends the children's emergency department with an asthma attack. He can say only two or three words per breath. His SpO2 is 91% in air, heart rate 150 and respiratory rate 46. He is alert, pink and has audible wheeze throughout. How should the nurse classify this attack?
o: Moderate asthma exacerbation
Acute severe asthma
Near-fatal asthma
Life-threatening asthma
10.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): acute severe in a child aged 1-5 = cannot complete sentences, SpO2 < 92%, HR > 140, RR > 40. Life-threatening needs SpO2 < 92% plus a feature such as silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion or confusion, none of which Leo has.

n.0: Moderate asthma means talking in sentences with SpO2 of 92% or more; Leo cannot finish sentences and his SpO2 is 91%.
n.2: Near-fatal asthma is defined by raised PaCO2 or the need for ventilation, which is not described.
n.3: Leo is alert, pink and wheezy with good air entry; life-threatening features such as silent chest or exhaustion are absent.

10.q: Ivy, 85, has confirmed norovirus and her bed linen is soiled with diarrhoea. The healthcare support worker strips the bed. How should the soiled linen be handled?
o: Roll it up and seal it in a water-soluble bag inside an impermeable bag
Shake it out over the bin, then put it in a red-tagged bag at the bedside
Rinse off the faeces in the sluice, then place it in the used linen bag
Place it on the chair while remaking the bed, then bag it as used linen
10.w: NIPCM ch 1.7: infectious linen is not sorted or rinsed but rolled together and sealed in a water-soluble (alginate) bag, then placed in an impermeable bag immediately on removal, secured and tagged before leaving the area.

n.1: Shaking linen disperses organisms into the environment.
n.2: NIPCM says used linen must not be rinsed, and linen from an infectious patient is infectious, not used, linen.
n.3: Used linen must not be placed on floors or other surfaces such as chairs.

10.q: You observe Jake, a first-year student nurse, using alcohol-based handrub. He applies a small amount, rubs his palms together for about 10 seconds, misses his thumbs and fingertips, and wipes the residue on his tunic. What feedback is most appropriate?
o: Apply a second dose and rub palms for a further 10 seconds
Cover all surfaces, including thumbs and fingertips, for 20 to 30 seconds until dry
Rinse the handrub off under running water after 15 seconds of firm rubbing
Rub all hand surfaces for 40 to 60 seconds, then dry them with a paper towel
10.w: The WHO handrub technique adopted in NIPCM appendix 2 covers all surfaces of the hands, including thumbs and fingertips, and takes 20 to 30 seconds, with hands left to dry naturally. 40 to 60 seconds is the duration for handwashing with soap and water.

n.0: A second dose rubbed on the palms still misses the thumbs and fingertips that he omitted.
n.2: Handrub is not rinsed off; rinsing removes the product before it has acted.
n.3: 40 to 60 seconds is the handwash duration; handrub is rubbed until dry and is not towel-dried.

10.q: Which of the following child deaths requires a joint agency response under Working Together 2026?
o: A 4-month-old found dead in his cot with no immediately apparent cause
A 10-year-old who dies on a ward from known end-stage cancer
A 2-year-old with a known cardiac condition who dies after planned surgery
A 15-year-old with cystic fibrosis who dies in hospital as anticipated
10.w: A joint agency response is required where a child's death is or could be due to external causes; is sudden with no immediately apparent cause (including sudden unexpected death in infancy); occurs in custody or under the Mental Health Act; raises suspicion of not being natural; or is a stillbirth with no health professional present (Working Together 2026, para 449).

n.1: An expected death from a known condition does not meet the joint agency response criteria.
n.2: A death following planned treatment for a known condition is reviewed through the usual process, unless other concerns arise.
n.3: An anticipated death from a known condition does not meet the criteria.

10.q: Joanne is the first health professional at a road traffic collision and is passing information to the ambulance control room using the M/ETHANE structure. What does the 'H' in M/ETHANE stand for?
o: Hospital
Head injuries
Hazards
Help needed
10.w: M/ETHANE (JESIP joint doctrine): Major incident declared or standby; Exact location; Type of incident; Hazards (present and potential); Access routes; Number of casualties; Emergency services present and required (P6.12).

n.0: The receiving hospital is decided by the ambulance service; it is not an M/ETHANE heading.
n.1: Injury types inform casualty numbers and severity but are not the 'H' heading.
n.3: Resources needed are reported under 'Emergency services', not 'H'.

10.q: Lily, 6, has a life-limiting neurodegenerative condition. A newly qualified nurse sees 'Advance Care Plan' in her notes and assumes this means Lily is not for resuscitation. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: An Advance Care Plan is the same document as a DNACPR order
An Advance Care Plan is a legal order made by the family court
An Advance Care Plan applies once Lily is in the last days of life
An Advance Care Plan covers wishes and care; it is not a DNACPR order
10.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.14: all children with life-limiting conditions should have an Advance Care Plan in their record (wishes, place of care, management of life-threatening events) and it should not be confused with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order. Resuscitate unless a DNACPR order is in place.

n.0: NG61 says the Advance Care Plan should not be confused with a DNACPR order.
n.1: An Advance Care Plan is agreed with the child and family and the team, not made by a court.
n.2: Advance Care Planning starts early and is reviewed regularly, not only in the last days.

10.q: Marcus Bell, 66, is on a surgical ward. His observations are: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on air, BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, alert, temperature 37.2°C. His NEWS2 total is 3. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Increase observations to at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat the observations in 4 hours and escalate if the total rises
Continue 4 to 6 hourly observations as the total score is below 5
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
10.w: A respiratory rate of 26/min scores 3 in a single parameter (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Chart 1). A score of 3 in any one parameter triggers a low-medium clinical risk response: minimum 1-hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team, who decide whether escalation is needed (Chart 4). Two steps: calculate the parameter score, then apply the single-parameter rule.

n.1: Four-hourly review delays recognition of deterioration when a single parameter is already scoring 3.
n.2: The aggregate of 3 is low, but a single red score of 3 overrides this and requires at least hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.3: Emergency critical care assessment is the response to an aggregate of 7 or more; this is an urgent ward-based response.

10.q: A nurse on placement with the local public health team reads a report stating that 120 people in a town of 100,000 were newly diagnosed with tuberculosis between January and December 2025. Which epidemiological measure does this figure describe?
o: Prevalence
Mortality rate
Case fatality rate
Incidence
10.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: incidence is the number of new cases of a disease arising in a population over a given period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases at a point or over a period. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2 (epidemiology).

n.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or period, not only the new cases arising in the year.
n.1: A mortality rate counts deaths in a population, not new diagnoses.
n.2: Case fatality is the proportion of people with a disease who die from it.

10.q: On a children's ward, staff hear a mother repeatedly call her 7-year-old son 'disgusting' and 'a baby' in front of other families because he wets the bed, and tell him he will be sent away if it happens again. Which category of abuse does this most closely fit?
o: Emotional abuse
Child criminal exploitation
Neglect
Physical abuse
10.w: Working Together 2026 describes emotional abuse as persistent emotional maltreatment causing severe effects on emotional development, including making a child feel worthless or unloved, imposing developmentally inappropriate expectations, and threats. A pattern of humiliation and threats of abandonment fits.

n.1: Criminal exploitation is coercing a child into crime, which is not described.
n.2: Neglect is failure to meet basic needs; this is active emotional maltreatment.
n.3: No physical harm is described.

10.q: Wendy, 60, develops stridor, facial swelling and a blotchy rash after a wasp sting in the hospital garden. A colleague has called for help and brought the emergency box with adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Where should you inject the intramuscular adrenaline?
o: Deltoid muscle of the non-dominant arm
Anterolateral middle third of the thigh
Subcutaneous tissue of the abdomen
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
10.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline: IM adrenaline is given into the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh, which gives reliable absorption.

n.0: The deltoid is not the recommended site for anaphylaxis.
n.2: Subcutaneous injection gives slower, less reliable absorption.
n.3: The buttock is not recommended and risks injection into fat or the sciatic area.

10.q: Ellie qualified six weeks ago. At the start of a night shift she is told she will be the only registered nurse for 28 patients on an unfamiliar ward, and has never taken charge. What should she do first?
o: Accept the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Raise her concerns at once with the person in charge and record it
Leave the ward and return to her own ward for safety
Accept the shift and phone her own ward manager at home
10.w: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 and NMC Raising concerns guidance support escalation and keeping a record.

n.0: Delaying until the morning leaves patients at risk; Code 16.2 requires her to raise concerns immediately.
n.2: Leaving abandons patients; she must raise the concern so safe cover is arranged.
n.3: Her absent manager cannot change tonight's staffing; the site lead or person in charge must be told now.

10.q: Ali, 66, had a colostomy formed 2 days ago. On inspection the stoma is dark purple-black and dry. It was red and moist yesterday. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a smaller appliance to reduce swelling
Clean it with antiseptic and recheck in 24 hours
Record it as a normal post-operative change
Report it urgently to the surgical team
10.w: A healthy stoma is moist and red or pink. A dusky, purple or black stoma suggests ischaemia or necrosis and needs urgent surgical review (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: A tight appliance could worsen ischaemia.
n.1: Antiseptic does not address ischaemia, and waiting 24 hours risks necrosis progressing.
n.2: This is not a normal change; a healthy stoma stays moist and red.

10.q: Jamal, a first-year student nurse, is visibly upset after caring for a patient who died unexpectedly on his shift. Later that day his practice supervisor, Helen, has time to talk. What is the most helpful approach?
o: Invite him to talk through the event and reflect on his feelings and learning
Ask him to write a reflective account for his portfolio before his next shift
Reassure him that he will get used to deaths with more experience
Suggest he takes the rest of the week off and speaks to occupational health
10.w: Supervisors encourage colleagues and students to reflect on practice (AnnexA.4.1.4) and support their wellbeing. A supportive conversation that explores feelings and learning helps the student process the event, with further support offered if needed (P5.8 promote reflection).

n.1: Written reflection may help later, but setting a task first misses the need for supportive discussion now.
n.2: This dismisses his distress and does not support reflection.
n.3: Some students need time off or occupational health input, but the first step is to listen and explore with him.

10.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
10.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

10.q: On a children's ward in England, the nurse is caring for Lily, 15, who needs a decision about a minor procedure. A student nurse asks whether the Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs this decision. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to children of any age if parents agree
Its powers generally apply to people aged 16 and over
Its powers apply to people aged 18 and over
It applies to anyone over 12 who is in hospital
10.w: MCA 2005 s2(5): the powers under the Act do not generally apply to a person under 16 (subject to s18(3), which concerns property). Decisions for Lily follow the law on children's consent and parental responsibility.

n.0: Parental agreement does not bring a child under 16 within the MCA.
n.2: The MCA starts at 16, not 18; it covers 16 and 17 year olds.
n.3: There is no age-12 threshold in the MCA; s2(5) sets 16.

10.q: Walter, 79, has a ReSPECT form recommending ward-based treatment but not admission to intensive care. He becomes acutely unwell and cannot express his views. A student nurse asks what status the ReSPECT form has. Which statement is correct?
o: Its recommendations guide the clinicians present but are not legally binding
It is a legally binding refusal of treatment that clinicians must follow
It replaces the need for clinicians to assess what treatment would benefit him
It becomes valid once Walter has also registered a lasting power of attorney
10.w: Resuscitation Council UK (ReSPECT; RCUK 2025 Ethics guidelines): ReSPECT creates personalised recommendations for a future emergency in which the person cannot make or express choices. Preferences and recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; the final decision rests with clinicians present unless a legally binding document applies.

n.1: RCUK states ReSPECT recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; only documents such as a valid ADRT are binding.
n.2: Clinicians still make treatment decisions at the time, using the recommendations to inform them.
n.3: A ReSPECT form does not depend on an LPA; it records recommendations from conversations with the person and clinicians.

10.q: Noah, 4, is in the last days of life on a children's ward. His breathing has become irregular and noisy, his hands and feet are cold and mottled and he has stopped feeding. His parents ask why the nurse is not taking blood pressure every hour. What should the nurse explain?
o: He may die within days; gentle, non-invasive checks keep him comfortable
Observations are stopped because Noah no longer needs nursing care
Hourly blood pressure will now restart so that any change is detected
These signs are a reaction to his medicines, which will be stopped
10.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.3.57: changes in breathing pattern, impaired peripheral perfusion and loss of interest in food or drink are common in the last hours or days of life; monitor these non-invasively as far as possible while continuing comfort care.

n.1: Nursing care continues; it is focused on comfort rather than routine observations.
n.2: Hourly blood pressure disturbs a dying child and does not change his care; NG61 advises monitoring the signs of dying non-invasively as far as possible.
n.3: These are recognised signs of approaching death, not a medicine reaction.

10.q: Ivy, 84, now has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to decide where she lives or how she is cared for. Some years ago, with capacity, she wrote a signed letter saying she would like to be cared for at home and prefers baths to showers. How should staff treat this letter?
o: As having no weight now that she lacks capacity to confirm her wishes
As a legally binding instruction that must be followed in the same way as an ADRT
As a statement of her wishes that must be considered in best interests decisions
As binding once her GP has countersigned it and placed it in her record
10.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4(6)(a): in deciding best interests, consider so far as reasonably ascertainable the person's past and present wishes and feelings, in particular any relevant written statement made when they had capacity. An advance statement of this kind is considered but is not legally binding, unlike a valid and applicable ADRT (ss24-26).

n.0: MCA s4(6)(a) requires decision makers to consider past wishes, in particular relevant written statements made with capacity.
n.1: A statement of wishes and preferences is not legally binding; only a valid, applicable ADRT binds staff to a refusal of treatment.
n.3: A GP signature does not convert a statement of wishes into a binding document.

10.q: A laboratory scientist phones the ward with a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L for Mr Shaw. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to take this result?
o: Ask the laboratory to email the result to the doctor directly
Remember it and tell the doctor at the next ward round
Write it on the handover sheet for the night team to act on
Write it down, read it back, then tell the doctor at once
10.w: Annexe A 1.9 and 1.11: share verbal information clearly. Writing a telephoned result down and reading it back confirms it was heard correctly, and a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L needs the doctor told at once (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.0: Email may not be seen promptly; the nurse must act on it now.
n.1: Relying on memory risks error, and waiting delays urgent treatment.
n.2: A critical result needs immediate action, not handover.

10.q: Toby, 4, develops stridor, wheeze and widespread hives 10 minutes after eating a cashew at a children's day unit. His respiratory rate is 44 and his lips are swelling. The nurse has 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline. What IM dose should be given?
o: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
50 micrograms (0.05 mL)
10.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral thigh: 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms (0.15 mL); 6-12 years 300 micrograms; over 12 years 500 micrograms; under 6 months 100-150 micrograms.

n.0: 500 micrograms is the dose for over 12s and adults.
n.1: 300 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6-12 years; Toby is 4.
n.3: 50 micrograms is below every RCUK age band; under-dosing delays reversal of airway swelling.

10.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
10.q: Sophie, aged 4, is on high-flow nasal oxygen for bronchiolitis. A newly qualified nurse is unsure how to score oxygen delivery on the national PEWS. What is correct?
o: High flow scores 2 because it is given by nasal cannula
High flow scores the maximum of 4 for oxygen delivery
High flow is recorded but not scored, like temperature
High flow scores 0 because the saturations are normal
10.w: The national PEWS charts state that high flow, BiPAP and CPAP score the maximum of 4 on oxygen delivery, reflecting the level of respiratory support needed.

n.0: The method of delivery does not reduce the score; high flow scores the maximum.
n.2: Oxygen delivery is a scored parameter, unlike temperature.
n.3: Normal saturations on support do not cancel the oxygen delivery score.

10.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

10.q: Josh, 16, has moderate to severe depression and has not responded to 6 sessions of CBT. After multidisciplinary review he starts fluoxetine alongside continuing therapy. His mother asks how closely he will be monitored. What does NICE NG134 suggest?
o: A review at 6 weeks, when the medicine will be fully effective
Weekly contact with Josh and his parents for the first 4 weeks
Monthly contact for 3 months, then 3-monthly reviews
A review when he next attends his CBT session
10.w: NICE NG134 Depression in children and young people: antidepressants for moderate to severe depression are offered in combination with a concurrent psychological therapy, and specific arrangements are made for careful monitoring of adverse reactions and mental state, for example weekly contact with the young person and parents for the first 4 weeks.

n.0: Six weeks is too long to wait, because suicidal thoughts and agitation can emerge early in treatment.
n.2: Monthly contact is less frequent than NG134 suggests for the first 4 weeks.
n.3: Therapy sessions alone do not provide the specific monitoring for adverse drug reactions.

10.q: Over two months, Zara has noticed her usually cheerful colleague has become withdrawn, irritable with patients and has had several short-term absences. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Speak to her privately, voice concern and signpost support
Avoid raising it in case it causes her more stress
Suggest she takes annual leave to recover from stress
Report her absence pattern to the ward manager at once
10.w: Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to health. Code 8.7 support colleagues; escalate if patient safety becomes affected.

n.1: Avoiding the issue fails to support a colleague showing signs of vulnerability (P1.5).
n.2: Advising leave without understanding the problem may not meet her needs.
n.3: Raising it with the manager may follow, but a supportive conversation is the appropriate first step when there is no immediate safety risk.

10.q: For a week, Sean, a staff nurse, has noticed that a colleague often takes long breaks, leaving her bay without registered nurse cover. Two call bells went unanswered yesterday. Which approach is most appropriate for Sean to take?
o: Talk to her privately, describe what he has seen and its effect on patients
Report her to the ward manager without discussing the matter with her first
Mention the long breaks during the safety huddle so the whole team is aware
Cover her bay himself during her breaks to make sure that patients are safe
10.w: Effective confrontation is private, specific and focused on behaviour and its impact on patients, inviting the other person's view and agreeing a solution. Escalation follows if the problem continues (AnnexA.4.2.4 appropriate and effective confrontation strategies; Code 8 and 16).

n.1: Escalation may be needed later, but a direct conversation is the proportionate first step.
n.2: Raising an individual's behaviour in front of the team is humiliating and may provoke defensiveness.
n.3: Covering for her hides the problem and stretches his own care.

10.q: Maya, 18 months, is prescribed oral paracetamol suspension. The nurse finds that the only syringes in the clean utility room are IV (Luer) syringes. What should the nurse use to measure and give the dose?
o: A Luer syringe with the tip removed after drawing up
A Luer IV syringe, labelled clearly as 'for oral use'
A 5 mL medicine spoon instead of any syringe
An oral or enteral syringe from another ward or pharmacy
10.w: National patient safety guidance requires oral liquids to be measured and given with oral or enteral (ENFit) syringes, which cannot connect to IV devices, to prevent wrong-route administration. Spoons are inaccurate for small paediatric volumes.

n.0: Altering a syringe does not remove the wrong-route risk and is unsafe practice.
n.1: A labelled Luer syringe can still be connected to an IV line, causing a wrong-route error.
n.2: A spoon is inaccurate for a measured paediatric dose and spills easily.

10.q: Mr Daly, 80, has capacity. When the nurse begins to explain his scan results, he says, "I don't want the details. Just tell my daughter." What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain the results fully, as he has a legal right to know them all
Respect his wish, check what he wants to know and his consent to share
Tell his daughter everything and give him no information himself
Delay the conversation until he is ready for all the details
10.w: Code 2.4: respect the level to which people want to be involved in decisions about their care. Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows, with consent.

n.0: Code 2.4 requires respect for the level of involvement he wants.
n.2: He should be asked what he does want to know, and his consent confirmed first.
n.3: He has stated his wish now; delaying ignores it.

10.q: Maisie, 7 months, was admitted with bronchiolitis. For the last 4 hours, including a sleep, her SpO2 has stayed at 93-95% in air. She is feeding adequately and her breathing is settling. Her parents ask about going home. What does NICE NG9 advise?
o: She should complete a course of antibiotics before discharge
She can go home with safety-netting advice for her parents
She should stay for 24 hours with saturations of 95% or more
She should stay until her cough has fully resolved
10.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): discharge when clinically stable, taking adequate oral fluids and maintaining SpO2 above 90% in air (6 weeks and over) for 4 hours including a period of sleep, with safety-netting (cough may last up to 3 weeks).

n.0: NG9 says do not use antibiotics in bronchiolitis.
n.2: NG9 requires 4 hours above 90% including sleep, not 24 hours at 95%.
n.3: The cough resolves within 3 weeks in 90%; waiting for it to stop is not a discharge criterion.

10.q: During a late shift on an adult surgical ward, a healthcare assistant tells Ruby, the nurse in charge, that Mr Peter Grant, 70, asked for analgesia 45 minutes ago and has still not received it because both nurses in his bay are busy. What should Ruby do?
o: Complete an incident report at the end of the shift and continue with the current allocation
Record the delay in Mr Grant's notes and discuss the bay workload at the next team meeting
Arrange for Mr Grant's analgesia to be given now and escalate the red flag on staffing
Ask the healthcare assistant to tell Mr Grant that a nurse will come once the bay is quieter
10.w: NICE SG1 Safe staffing for nursing in adult inpatient wards (2014) lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief as a nursing red flag. A red flag should prompt an immediate escalation response by the registered nurse in charge, for example allocating additional staff (rec 1.4.3, Box 2). Mr Grant's pain is dealt with first.

n.0: Reporting is useful but does not relieve his pain or address the staffing problem now.
n.1: Documenting and deferring discussion does not meet the immediate escalation response that SG1 requires.
n.3: This prolongs his pain and treats a recognised red flag as routine.

10.q: Simon, 38, has anaphylaxis after an iodinated contrast injection in the radiology department. The nurse opens the emergency drug box, which contains several adrenaline preparations. Which preparation should be drawn up for his intramuscular injection?
o: 5 mg/mL (1 in 200)
10 micrograms/mL (1 in 100,000)
100 micrograms/mL (1 in 10,000)
10.w: RCUK: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses the 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) preparation, for example 0.5 mL = 500 micrograms in an adult.

n.0: 5 mg/mL is not a standard adrenaline preparation for anaphylaxis.
n.1: 1 in 100,000 is a dilution used by specialists for IV infusion, not IM.
n.2: 1 in 10,000 is the IV preparation used in cardiac arrest, not for IM anaphylaxis treatment.

10.q: A ward team wants the strongest evidence on whether a new dressing reduces infection in surgical wounds. Which type of study gives the highest level of evidence for this question?
o: An expert consensus opinion paper from specialists
A single large randomised controlled trial
A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
A large prospective cohort study of patients
10.w: Oxford CEBM levels of evidence (therapy): level 1a is a systematic review of randomised controlled trials; expert opinion is level 5. Code 6.1 requires evidence-based information.

n.0: Expert opinion is the lowest level in evidence hierarchies such as the Oxford CEBM levels.
n.1: A well-designed RCT is strong evidence but ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
n.3: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs for treatment effects.

10.q: Tony, 70, is on a fluid balance chart. Over 24 hours his intake is 1,200 mL oral and 1,000 mL IV. His output is 1,400 mL urine and 300 mL from a nasogastric tube. What is his fluid balance?
o: Positive 800 mL
Positive 500 mL
Negative 200 mL
Negative 500 mL

n.0: Positive 800 mL omits the 300 mL nasogastric loss.
n.2: Negative 200 mL does not match the totals recorded.
n.3: Negative 500 mL reverses intake and output.

10.q: Bryony, 39, is nil by mouth after surgery. Her observations are stable and her prescription is for 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. The nurse is setting up the infusion and will ask a colleague to check it. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 166 mL/h on the volumetric pump
125 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.5 mL/h on the volumetric pump
80 mL/h on the volumetric pump
10.w: Rate (mL/h) = volume / time = 1,000 mL / 8 h = 125 mL/h. Accurate dosage calculation is a patient safety proficiency (P4.14) and the setting should be checked against the prescription.

n.0: 166 mL/h corresponds to 6 hours, not 8.
n.2: 12.5 mL/h is a decimal place error, a tenfold underinfusion.
n.3: 80 mL/h would deliver 1,000 mL over 12.5 hours.

10.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
10.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

10.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
10.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

10.q: Sami, 9, has anaphylaxis after a bee sting during a hospital open day. The nurse has drawn up 300 micrograms of adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Where should it be injected?
o: Intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh
Intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle
Intramuscularly into the dorsogluteal muscle
Subcutaneously into the abdomen
10.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): give IM adrenaline early into the anterolateral thigh, which gives reliable absorption in children and adults.

n.1: The deltoid is a smaller muscle with less reliable absorption; RCUK specifies the anterolateral thigh.
n.2: The buttock carries a risk of sciatic nerve injury and slower absorption; RCUK specifies the thigh.
n.3: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less predictable than IM in a shocked child.

10.q: Tom, 17, has complex needs and does not meet the criteria for any specialist adult health service. His children's team is planning his transition. Whose involvement does NICE NG43 describe as critical?
o: The local pharmacy
His GP
The adult A&E department
His school SENCO
10.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.3.9: if a young person does not meet the criteria for specialist adult health services, involving the GP in transition planning is absolutely critical.

n.0: The pharmacy supplies medicines but does not take on ongoing care coordination.
n.2: A&E provides emergency care, not ongoing coordination.
n.3: The SENCO supports education, but NG43 names the GP as critical where no adult specialist service exists.

10.q: Sam, 26, has a learning disability and often hits out in the noisy dining room at mealtimes. The team wants to use positive behaviour support. What should they do first?
o: Assess what triggers the behaviour and what it achieves
Increase his sedation before every mealtime
Use restraint whenever he begins to hit out
Withdraw meals in the dining room as a planned consequence
10.w: Annexe A 3.9: positive behaviour support approaches. PBS uses functional assessment to understand behaviour and changes the environment proactively.

n.1: Medication as first response is not PBS and may cause harm.
n.2: Restraint is reactive; PBS starts with understanding the function of behaviour.
n.3: Punishment is not part of PBS and may breach his rights.

10.q: A nurse has completed a detailed physical assessment of Mr Rees, 75, who is admitted after a fall at home. She has recorded his observations, skin, mobility and continence. Which further area is most needed to make the assessment holistic before discharge planning?
o: A second set of skin checks by another registered nurse
His social circumstances, support at home and his own priorities
A full list of every past hospital admission he has had
A full repeat of his observations before the end of the day shift
10.w: Holistic assessment (P3.1, P3.4) combines physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs and the person's own goals. After a fall at home, his living situation, support and priorities are central to safe planning, and NICE NG249 includes a home hazard assessment.

n.0: A second skin check adds to the physical assessment already completed.
n.2: An exhaustive admission history adds little compared with his current social and support needs.
n.3: Repeat observations are part of physical monitoring, not the missing holistic domain.

11.q: Ben, 4, has just been diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive condition. Genetic testing shows his mother is a carrier and his father is unaffected. His parents ask about the risk for a future son. What is the chance that a future son will be affected?
o: 1 in 2
1 in 4
Nil, as his father is unaffected
1 in 8
11.w: X-linked recessive inheritance: a carrier mother passes her affected X to half of her children. Each son has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected; each daughter a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier.

n.1: 1 in 4 is the chance across ALL children (sons and daughters) of an affected son, not the chance for a son.
n.2: Sons inherit their X chromosome from the mother, so the father's status does not protect a son.
n.3: 1 in 8 does not apply to any child of a carrier mother.

11.q: On a busy surgical ward, a doctor asks Holly, a staff nurse, to get a healthcare assistant to give a prescribed dose of intravenous antibiotic so that it is not late. The healthcare assistant has not been trained in IV administration. What should Holly do?
o: Delay the dose until the evening medicines round, when more nurses are on duty
Give the IV dose herself or arrange for another competent registrant to give it
Delegate the IV dose and supervise the healthcare assistant closely at the bedside
Ask the doctor to give the dose, as the healthcare assistant is not trained
11.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence. An untrained healthcare assistant cannot safely give IV medicines, so the dose must be given by a competent registrant without undue delay (Code 18.1; P5.4 roles and scope of practice of team members).

n.0: Delaying a prescribed antibiotic risks harm when a competent nurse can give it now.
n.2: Supervision does not make delegation appropriate when the person lacks the training and competence for the task.
n.3: The doctor could give it, but medicine administration is within Holly's own role; passing it back adds delay without a reason.

11.q: Ellie, 18, moved to the adult cystic fibrosis service three months ago and has not attended her last two appointments. The adult team cannot reach her by phone. What does NICE NG43 advise?
o: Discharge her back to the GP as she has not engaged
Try to contact Ellie and family, follow up and involve the GP
Refer her back to children's services as she is not ready
Send her a letter and wait for her to rebook
11.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.4.1: if a young person does not attend or engage after transfer, adult health and social care, working within safeguarding protocols, should try to contact the young person and family, follow them up and involve other professionals including the GP.

n.0: Discharging after non-attendance leaves a young person with a serious condition without specialist care.
n.2: NG43 rec 1.4.2 refers a young person who does not engage back to the named worker, not to children's services.
n.3: A letter and passive wait does not meet the active follow-up NG43 requires.

11.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
11.q: Ella, aged 1 month, is admitted with poor feeding. Her respiratory rate is 72 breaths/min and heart rate 150 beats/min. She is not crying. Which interpretation is correct?
o: Her heart rate is within range and her breathing is rapid
Her heart rate is raised and her breathing is normal
Both values are within normal limits for a 1-month-old
Both values are raised and she needs immediate review
11.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1): at 1 month, the approximate normal respiratory rate is 25 to 60 breaths/min and heart rate 110 to 180 beats/min. A respiratory rate of 72 is above range (tachypnoea), while a heart rate of 150 is within range and below the NICE NG143 amber threshold of 160 for infants under 12 months.

n.1: A heart rate of 150 is within the 110 to 180 range at 1 month, and it is the breathing rate that is raised.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 72 is above the upper limit of 60 at 1 month.
n.3: A heart rate of 150 is within range at 1 month; the abnormal value is the respiratory rate.

11.q: Four patients on an elderly care ward have laboratory-confirmed norovirus. All single rooms are occupied. The IPC team agrees a cohort bay. Which plan for the cohort is most appropriate?
o: Place them together in one bay with the door closed and dedicated equipment
Place them together with a neutropenic patient who also has diarrhoea
Place them with two patients who have diarrhoea that is not yet confirmed
Keep each in their current bay with curtains drawn and contact precautions
11.w: NIPCM ch 2.1-2.2: cohorting is considered when single rooms are short and two or more patients have the same confirmed infection; doors stay closed and reusable equipment is dedicated to the cohort area. Immunosuppressed patients and those with different or unconfirmed infections must not be mixed in.

n.1: NIPCM states patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes, such as those who are immunosuppressed, must not be cohorted with others.
n.2: Unconfirmed diarrhoea may be a different infection; cohorts are formed from patients with the same confirmed infection.
n.3: Leaving infected patients in mixed bays exposes susceptible patients; curtains do not contain norovirus.

11.q: Julie, 58, has motor neurone disease and full capacity. She tells the specialist nurse she wants to make an advance decision refusing mechanical ventilation in the future, even if her life is at risk. In England, what is needed for this refusal to be valid and applicable to life-sustaining treatment?
o: Signed by her GP and registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Written, signed and witnessed, stating it applies even if her life is at risk
Written down and then confirmed in writing by her next of kin
Recorded verbally in her notes and countersigned by two registered nurses
11.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss24-25: a person aged 18 or over with capacity may make an advance decision to refuse treatment. For life-sustaining treatment it must be in writing, signed by the person (or by another in their presence and by their direction), signed by a witness, and contain a statement that it applies even if life is at risk.

n.0: Registration with the Office of the Public Guardian applies to lasting powers of attorney, not advance decisions; no GP signature is required.
n.2: Next of kin confirmation is not a legal requirement; Julie's signature, a witness and the 'even if life is at risk' statement are.
n.3: A verbal advance decision can refuse other treatment, but a refusal of life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed and witnessed (MCA s25(5)-(6)).

11.q: Before a transfer, Rosa checks the mobile hoist on her ward. The examination label shows that its last thorough examination under LOLER was eight months ago, and no examination scheme with different intervals is displayed. What should Rosa do?
o: Use the hoist, because lifting equipment is examined every 12 months
Take the hoist out of use, report it and use another hoist that is in date
Carry out a visual pre-use check and continue if the hoist looks sound
Use the hoist for this transfer and report the overdue date at handover
11.w: Under LOLER 1998, lifting equipment and accessories used for lifting people must be thoroughly examined at least every 6 months (other lifting equipment every 12 months) unless an examination scheme sets other intervals. A hoist overdue for examination should not be used to lift a person and should be reported (HSE, Thorough examinations and inspections of lifting equipment).

n.0: The 12-month interval applies to lifting equipment that is not used to lift people; patient hoists fall under the 6-month interval.
n.2: A pre-use check is good practice but does not replace the thorough examination by a competent person that LOLER requires.
n.3: Knowingly using equipment that is overdue for its statutory examination puts the patient at risk; the problem must be dealt with before the transfer.

11.q: At the start of an early shift, Nina, a staff nurse, is allocated four patients on a medical ward. Which patient should she see first?
o: Mr Ali, 66, whose insulin is due with breakfast in 45 minutes
Mrs Dunn, 74, whose respiratory rate is 28/min, SpO2 89% and who is newly confused
Ms Reid, 52, who reports post-operative pain of 5/10, last analgesia 3 hours ago
Mr Shaw, 59, who is to be discharged today and needs his discharge letter
11.w: Prioritisation uses an ABCDE approach and early warning scores: Mrs Dunn has a respiratory rate of 28 (scores 3), SpO2 89% (scores 3) and new confusion (scores 3) on NEWS2 (RCP 2017), indicating possible life-threatening deterioration needing immediate assessment and escalation (P5.5 lead and manage care of a group of people with prioritisation).

n.0: Time-critical insulin matters, but there are 45 minutes before it is due and he is not unwell.
n.2: Her pain needs prompt attention, possibly by another team member, but is not life-threatening.
n.3: Discharge paperwork can safely wait while a deteriorating patient is assessed.

11.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
11.q: Ali, 7 months, has bronchiolitis and is on oxygen. His saturations have been 91 to 92%. He becomes quiet and floppy; his heart rate falls from 170 to 55 beats/min and he has poor perfusion despite effective bag-mask ventilation by the team. What should happen next?
o: Start chest compressions
Recheck the heart rate in 5 minutes
Give a fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg
Increase the oxygen and observe
11.w: Two steps: recognise that bradycardia in a hypoxic infant is pre-terminal, then act. RCUK 2025: start chest compressions if the heart rate is below 60 beats/min with poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation.

n.1: Waiting 5 minutes in a pre-arrest state risks cardiac arrest.
n.2: Fluids do not treat hypoxic bradycardia; compressions are needed when HR is below 60 with poor perfusion despite ventilation.
n.3: Oxygen and ventilation are already being given; the criteria for compressions are met.
