11.q: Before entering the room of Margaret, 71, who has influenza and needs help to wash, Ade gathers an apron, a fluid-resistant surgical mask, goggles and non-sterile gloves. In which order should Ade put this equipment on?
o: Mask, eye protection, gloves, then apron
Apron, mask, eye protection, then gloves
Apron, gloves, eye protection, then mask
Gloves, apron, mask, then eye protection
11.w: NIPCM appendix 6 sets the order for putting on PPE as apron or gown, FRSM or respirator, eye protection, then gloves. Gloves go on last so that they are not contaminated while the other items are adjusted.

n.0: The apron goes on first; putting it on last means pulling it over gloves and face protection.
n.2: The mask is fitted before eye protection and gloves; adjusting a mask with gloved hands risks contamination.
n.3: Putting gloves on first means they touch the apron ties, mask and goggles while fitting them.

11.q: Ms Okoro, 24, has type 1 diabetes and has been vomiting since last night. Her urinalysis shows glucose 3+ and ketones 3+. She is breathing quickly and her capillary glucose is 22.6 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage oral fluids and recheck her urine in 4 hours
Check her blood ketones and inform the doctor urgently
Record the results and send the urine for culture
Give her usual insulin dose and recheck in the morning
11.w: High glucose with heavy ketonuria, vomiting and rapid breathing in type 1 diabetes suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency. The nurse should check capillary blood ketones per local protocol and escalate urgently (P3.11, P3.12; Annexe B 2.10).

n.0: Oral fluids and a 4-hour recheck delay treatment of possible ketoacidosis.
n.2: Culture does not address the immediate danger shown by the results.
n.3: Her usual dose does not treat ketoacidosis, and waiting until morning is unsafe.

11.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
11.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

11.q: Ben, a theatre nurse, has developed persistent back pain that is making patient transfers difficult. He has not told anyone. Which action best reflects his professional responsibility for his own health?
o: Wait until his annual appraisal to mention the problem
Seek occupational health advice and discuss adjustments
Take regular painkillers and keep doing transfers as before
Avoid transfers by swapping tasks with colleagues informally
11.w: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role. Proficiency P1.6: take responsibility for a healthy lifestyle to maintain fitness for practice; Code 19.4 personal precautions.

n.0: Waiting delays support; Code 20.9 requires maintaining the health needed for the role now.
n.2: Masking symptoms risks harm to himself and patients and does not address fitness for his role.
n.3: Informal swaps hide the problem and may leave the team short of safe handlers.

11.q: Nurse Sara notices she has written the wrong blood pressure value in a patient's paper observation chart. What is the correct way to correct the entry?
o: Write the right value over the top of the wrong one
Cover the entry with correction fluid and rewrite it neatly
Tear out the page and copy the chart onto a new sheet
Strike through once, keep it legible, then sign, date and time
11.w: Code 10.3-10.4: complete records accurately without falsification, attribute entries and date and time them. Annexe A 1.8: write accurate, clear, legible records.

n.0: Overwriting makes both values illegible and unattributed.
n.1: Obscuring the original entry could be seen as falsification and makes the change untraceable (Code 10.3).
n.2: Removing pages destroys part of the record and breaches Code 10.3.

11.q: During a multidisciplinary meeting about Ellie, 5, who is ready for discharge, a manager suggests postponing a decision about where she should live for several months to 'see how things settle'. The children's nurse wants to challenge this using the Children Act 1989. Which principle is most relevant?
o: A court should make an order when it is better than making none
Delay in deciding is likely to prejudice the child's welfare
Local authorities must work in partnership with parents
Parental responsibility is shared between both parents
11.w: Section 1(2) of the Children Act 1989 sets the 'no delay' principle: any delay in determining a question about a child's upbringing is likely to prejudice the child's welfare. Open-ended postponement directly conflicts with it.

n.0: The no-order principle (s1(5)) stops unnecessary orders; it does not address postponing a decision.
n.2: Partnership with parents is good practice but does not answer the risk caused by delay.
n.3: Shared parental responsibility concerns who can make decisions, not the timing of decisions.

11.q: Jacob, 5 months, has bronchiolitis. He is becoming tired with feeds and is now taking about half his usual milk. His parents ask what will help. According to NICE NG9, which intervention is recommended?
o: A short course of oral prednisolone
Nebulised salbutamol via face mask
Nasogastric or orogastric fluids
Nebulised 3% hypertonic saline
11.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): give fluids by nasogastric or orogastric tube if a child cannot take enough fluid by mouth; consider IV isotonic fluids if NG/OG is not tolerated or respiratory failure is impending.

n.0: NG9 says do not use corticosteroids in bronchiolitis.
n.1: NG9 says do not use salbutamol in bronchiolitis.
n.3: NG9 says do not use hypertonic saline in bronchiolitis.

11.q: Ruth, a staff nurse, is writing a referral to a dietitian for Mrs Smith, 63, who has lost weight after bowel surgery. The electronic record includes her full medical history, including a termination of pregnancy 30 years ago. What should Ruth include in the referral?
o: The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything except the termination of pregnancy
Her full medical history so the dietitian has the whole picture
A summary written after asking her family
11.w: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data. UK GDPR data minimisation also requires data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. Only information relevant to nutrition should be shared.

n.1: Removing one sensitive item still shares other irrelevant data; relevance, not sensitivity, decides what is sent.
n.2: Sending the full history exceeds what the dietitian needs and breaches the minimum necessary principle.
n.3: Families are not a source for a clinical referral, and involving them without consent breaches confidentiality.

11.q: Vincent, 48, attends the practice nurse for a wound dressing. While checking his record, the nurse sees he smokes 20 cigarettes a day. They have about a minute before the next patient. Which approach reflects very brief advice on smoking?
o: Ask about smoking and advise him to cut down gradually by himself
Ask, advise that medicines plus specialist support work best, and offer referral
Explain the diseases caused by smoking in detail over the next 20 minutes
Wait until he says he is ready to quit before raising the topic of smoking
11.w: NCSCT Very Brief Advice on smoking; NICE NG209 (2021, updated 2025): very brief advice is Ask (record smoking status), Advise (the best way to stop is with a combination of medication and specialist support) and Act (offer referral to local stop smoking support); it takes about 30 seconds.

n.0: VBA advises that the most effective way to stop is medication combined with specialist behavioural support, not quitting unaided.
n.2: Very brief advice takes about 30 seconds; a long lecture is not the VBA model and is not feasible here.
n.3: VBA is offered to everyone who smokes at every opportunity, whatever their stated readiness.

11.q: A CDOP reviews the deaths of three infants in its area that involved co-sleeping after parental alcohol use. The panel recommends a local safer sleep campaign. What is the main purpose of the CDOP review, as described in Working Together 2026?
o: Independent scrutiny to find modifiable factors and prevent deaths
Determination of the medical cause of death in place of the coroner
Investigation of the deaths to decide whether criminal charges should follow
Disciplinary review of practitioners involved in each child's care
11.w: The CDOP review is the final, independent scrutiny of a child's death by professionals with no responsibility for the child during life. It aims to identify modifiable factors that could be altered to prevent future deaths and to share learning, including with the National Child Mortality Database.

n.1: The coroner retains responsibility for inquests into the cause of death.
n.2: Criminal investigation is the responsibility of the police and CPS.
n.3: CDOP reviews are for learning, not for disciplining individuals.

11.q: Mason, 6, weighs 21 kg and is in cardiac arrest in a hospital outpatient area. CPR is in progress and an AED arrives. It has a paediatric mode and child pads are available. How should the AED be used?
o: Paediatric mode, with pads front and back of the chest
Adult mode, with pads on the front and back of the chest
Paediatric mode, with pads attached once the arrest team arrives
Adult mode, with pads below the right clavicle and left side
11.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: use the paediatric (attenuated) mode under 25 kg (about 8 years), with pads anteroposterior in smaller children (one left of the sternum, one between the scapulae). Adult mode is used above 25 kg.

n.1: Mason is under 25 kg and paediatric mode is available, so the attenuated energy should be used.
n.2: The AED should be attached as soon as it arrives so the rhythm can be analysed; waiting for the team delays any shock.
n.3: Adult mode and sternal-apical pads are for children over 25 kg or adults; Mason weighs 21 kg.

11.q: Mrs Ivy Turner, 86, is admitted with a chest infection and has urinary incontinence at night. A colleague suggests inserting a urinary catheter so her bed stays dry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Insert the catheter and review it after one week
Use continence pads overnight until she is discharged
Insert the catheter overnight and remove it each morning
Carry out a continence assessment and plan alternatives
11.w: Catheters carry risks of infection and loss of continence function and should not be used for staff convenience. A continence assessment identifies causes and less invasive options such as prompted toileting (P7.8 avoid unnecessary interventions; NICE CG139 urinary catheter use only after considering alternatives).

n.0: Catheterising for convenience exposes her to infection risk without a clinical indication.
n.1: Pads without a continence assessment leave the cause unidentified and may reduce continence and dignity.
n.2: Repeated insertion increases infection and trauma risk and is not a continence plan.

11.q: Mr Doyle, 55, tells his community mental health nurse that he has been saving his prescribed tablets and has a large supply at home, as he 'might need them one day'. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Remove the tablets from his home while he is out of the room
Tell his GP to reduce his prescription at the next medication review
Note his comment in the record and review it at the next visit
Discuss removing the tablets with him and agree a plan to keep him safe
11.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.7.1: establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them with therapeutic collaboration or negotiation to keep the person safe. A stockpile with this comment is an immediate safety concern needing collaborative action and escalation.

n.0: Covert removal undermines trust; NG225 describes collaborative negotiation, not unilateral action.
n.1: Waiting for a future review leaves the means available now.
n.2: Delaying to the next visit fails to act on an immediate safety concern.

11.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
11.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

11.q: Ms Ruiz, 59, has hepatic encephalopathy. She is drowsy and confused in the evenings but alert and orientated most mornings. A non-urgent decision is needed about whether she wants to join a clinical trial. When is it most appropriate to assess her capacity for this decision?
o: In the evening, so the assessment reflects her worst state
In the morning, when she is usually at her most alert
After discharge, once her condition has fully resolved
At any time, since capacity is a fixed state
11.w: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific (MCA 2005 s2(1), 'at the material time'), and s1(3) requires all practicable steps to help the person decide. Choosing the time when she is most alert supports her to make the decision herself.

n.0: Assessing at her worst ignores the duty to take practicable steps to help her decide.
n.2: Delaying until full recovery is unnecessary when she has lucid periods now in which she may be able to decide.
n.3: Capacity can fluctuate; s2(2) recognises that an impairment may be temporary.

11.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
11.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

11.q: Sophie, 15, has severe anorexia nervosa and has been admitted to a paediatric ward for medical stabilisation and refeeding. Which blood result is the priority to monitor closely in the first days of refeeding?
o: Serum cholesterol
HbA1c
Serum phosphate
Serum amylase
11.w: NICE NG69 Eating disorders and RCPsych MEED guidance (2022): staff must recognise and manage refeeding syndrome, in which phosphate (with potassium and magnesium) falls as feeding restarts, risking cardiac and respiratory failure; electrolytes are monitored closely in the first days.

n.0: Cholesterol may be abnormal in anorexia but does not signal refeeding syndrome.
n.1: HbA1c reflects glucose control over months and does not detect refeeding syndrome.
n.3: Amylase does not reflect the electrolyte shifts of refeeding syndrome.

11.q: Bilal, aged 3, is admitted with pneumonia. His mother speaks little English. His 11-year-old sister offers to interpret while the nurse takes a history. What should the nurse do?
o: Use simple English and gestures to complete the history
Ask a bilingual cleaner from the ward to interpret
Accept the sister's offer, because she knows the family best
Thank the sister and arrange a professional interpreter
11.w: Children should not be used to interpret: it places an inappropriate burden on them and risks inaccurate or filtered information. A professional interpreter (face to face, telephone or video) ensures accurate, confidential communication with the family (P3.4; NHS England guidance on interpreting).

n.0: Simple English and gestures are not enough for an accurate clinical history.
n.1: An untrained member of staff may interpret inaccurately and the family's confidentiality is not protected.
n.2: Using a child as an interpreter is inappropriate and risks errors and distress for the child.

11.q: Agnes, 79, has type 2 diabetes with reduced sensation in her feet. Her toenails are long and thickened, and she asks you to cut them during her bath. What is the most appropriate action?
o: File her nails down after soaking her feet for 20 minutes
Explain the risk and refer her to the podiatry service
Ask a healthcare support worker to cut them carefully
Cut her nails straight across with sterile nail clippers
11.w: People with diabetes and reduced sensation are at high risk of foot ulceration from minor trauma, so thickened nails should be cut by a podiatrist. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during nail care.

n.0: Prolonged soaking softens skin and can cause maceration in a person with diabetes.
n.2: Delegating a task that needs specialist assessment does not reduce the risk.
n.3: Cutting thickened nails in a person with diabetic neuropathy risks injury and ulceration.

11.q: In a nursing home, the GP reviews Hilda, 88, by video call and decides to reduce her bisoprolol dose from tomorrow. The GP cannot visit to amend the medication administration record (MAR). Under RPS/RCN guidance, how should the change be communicated?
o: By a message passed on by Hilda's daughter after the call
By a secure electronic message from the GP, with records updated
By the nurse amending the MAR from her notes of the call
By a text message from the GP to the nurse's personal mobile phone
11.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 20.2: if the prescriber cannot issue a new prescription or amend the chart, the changes are communicated by an appropriately secure electronic method and the patient's records are updated.

n.0: A relayed message from a relative is not a direction from the prescriber.
n.2: Without the prescriber's written or secure electronic confirmation, the nurse would be altering a prescription.
n.3: A personal phone is not a secure, auditable route for prescribing information.

11.q: Mia, 10, is on the paediatric intensive care unit after an infection. She is stable, not bleeding and has no cyanotic heart disease. Her Hb is 76 g/L. The team asks whether she meets the BSH threshold for a red cell transfusion. What is the answer?
o: Yes, the usual threshold in stable children is 80 g/L
No, the usual threshold in stable children is 70 g/L
No, the usual threshold in stable children is 60 g/L
Yes, the usual threshold in stable children is 90 g/L
11.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) section 3.2.1: use an Hb threshold of 70 g/L pre-transfusion in stable non-cyanotic children (1B); a higher threshold may be considered if unstable or symptomatic.

n.0: 80 g/L is not the BSH threshold for stable non-cyanotic children.
n.2: Mia does not need transfusion, but the BSH threshold is 70 g/L, not 60 g/L.
n.3: 90 g/L is a liberal threshold not supported for stable children.

11.q: Lucy, 16, needs an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy under sedation to investigate weight loss. She has capacity and consents. A student nurse asks whether her consent covers a diagnostic test and the sedation, because the Family Law Reform Act refers to 'treatment'. What should the nurse explain?
o: Section 8 covers the test, but sedation needs separate parental consent
Section 8 covers the endoscopy once she has been assessed as Gillick competent
Section 8 covers treatment, so her mother must consent to diagnostic tests
Section 8 includes diagnostic procedures and anaesthesia ancillary to them
11.w: FLRA 1969 s8(2) states that 'surgical, medical or dental treatment' includes any procedure undertaken for the purposes of diagnosis, and that the section applies to procedures such as anaesthetic which are ancillary to treatment.

n.0: Anaesthesia and similar ancillary procedures are expressly covered by s8(2).
n.1: Gillick applies under 16; at 16 Lucy's consent is effective under s8 and she is presumed to have capacity.
n.2: Diagnostic procedures are expressly included in s8(2), so parental consent is not needed.

11.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
11.q: Oliver, aged 6 weeks, has a temperature of 38.2°C measured in the axilla. He is feeding a little less than usual but is pink and alert. Using the NICE traffic light system, how should he be categorised?
o: Amber, because his temperature is still below 39°C
Red, as he is under 3 months with a fever of 38°C or more
Green, because he is alert and pink and still feeding well
Amber, because his feeding has reduced from his usual
11.w: NICE NG143: a child aged under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher is in the red (high risk) group, whatever other features are present, and needs urgent assessment. Infants this young cannot be judged reliably on appearance.

n.0: The 39°C threshold applies to babies aged 3 to 6 months; under 3 months, 38°C or more is red.
n.2: Appearing well does not lower the risk category for an infant under 3 months with fever.
n.3: Reduced feeding is an amber feature, but his age and temperature already place him in red.

11.q: Martin, 66, is eating lunch in a ward day room when he clutches his throat. He is coughing forcefully, red in the face and can speak a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between his shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Lie him on the floor and start chest compressions
11.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): with an effective cough (mild obstruction), encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration to an ineffective cough or until the obstruction is relieved.

n.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough in a conscious person.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts follow back blows when the cough is ineffective.
n.3: CPR is started if the person becomes unconscious.

11.q: Thomas, 71, has advanced lung cancer and full capacity. The registrar decides that CPR would not be in his interests and plans to complete a DNACPR form. The registrar tells the nurse they will not mention it to Thomas because 'it might upset him'. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Remind the registrar that Thomas should be consulted unless it would cause him harm
Ask Thomas's wife to decide whether he should be told about the decision
Accept the plan, as DNACPR decisions are a medical matter that need no discussion
Record the DNACPR now and plan to tell Thomas at next week's ward round
11.w: R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals NHS FT [2014] EWCA Civ 822: Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions, and there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Lord Dyson MR (para 54) said doctors should be wary of being too ready to exclude patients from the process on the grounds that their involvement is likely to distress them; a belief that discussion would cause distress is unlikely to be enough unless the distress is likely to cause harm (para 56).

n.1: Thomas has capacity; his wife cannot decide what he is told about his own care.
n.2: R (Tracey) [2014] held there is a presumption the patient will be consulted, and warned against excluding patients because the discussion may distress them.
n.3: Delaying the conversation until after the decision is recorded still breaches the duty to consult him first.

11.q: Ali, 66, had a colostomy formed 2 days ago. On inspection the stoma is dark purple-black and dry. It was red and moist yesterday. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a smaller appliance to reduce swelling
Clean it with antiseptic and recheck in 24 hours
Record it as a normal post-operative change
Report it urgently to the surgical team
11.w: A healthy stoma is moist and red or pink. A dusky, purple or black stoma suggests ischaemia or necrosis and needs urgent surgical review (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: A tight appliance could worsen ischaemia.
n.1: Antiseptic does not address ischaemia, and waiting 24 hours risks necrosis progressing.
n.2: This is not a normal change; a healthy stoma stays moist and red.

11.q: You are performing chest compressions on Alan, 60, who has collapsed in a hospital car park. According to RCUK 2025, what compression depth and rate are correct for an adult?
o: 5-6 cm at 100-120 per minute
6-7 cm at 80-100 per minute
4-5 cm at 100-120 per minute
5-6 cm at 120-140 per minute
11.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: compress on the lower half of the sternum to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, at 100-120 per minute, allowing full recoil.

n.1: 6-7 cm is too deep and 80-100 per minute is too slow.
n.2: 4-5 cm is too shallow for an adult.
n.3: 120-140 per minute is faster than the recommended maximum of 120.

11.q: A children's nurse inserting a urinary catheter for Maryam, 9, after surgery notices genital appearances that she believes show FGM. She has not had specialist FGM training and is unsure of the type. What should she do?
o: Report to the police, as the duty applies once signs appear to show FGM
Report once a doctor's diagnosis of FGM is recorded in the notes
Ask a gynaecologist to examine Maryam and confirm the type of FGM first
Record the findings and ask the parents whether FGM has been carried out
11.w: Under the procedural information, the duty applies at the point a professional sees physical signs that appear to show FGM in the course of their work. A full clinical diagnosis is not required, and no further examination should be carried out for the purpose of confirming it.

n.1: A medical diagnosis is not required before the duty applies.
n.2: An examination solely to confirm FGM should not be carried out; the duty applies on what was observed.
n.3: Asking the parents first may put Maryam at risk and does not discharge the duty.

11.q: A new wound treatment costs £30,000 more per patient than standard care and produces 1.5 more QALYs per patient. Using NICE's standard threshold in force since April 2026, what is the incremental cost per QALY and how does it compare?
o: £30,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, within the threshold range
£20,000 per QALY, below the threshold range
£45,000 per QALY, above the threshold range
11.w: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = extra cost / extra QALYs = £30,000 / 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY. This is below the standard range of £25,000-£35,000 per QALY, so the treatment would usually be considered cost-effective (P7.3). Two steps: calculate, then compare with the current threshold.

n.0: This ignores the QALY gain and uses the extra cost alone.
n.1: The calculation is right, but £20,000 is below the current £25,000-£35,000 range, not within it.
n.3: This multiplies cost by QALYs instead of dividing.

11.q: Practitioners are writing the section of Maya's EHC plan that records her views. Maya, 14, has cerebral palsy and communicates with an eye-gaze device. How should her views be recorded, according to NICE NG213?
o: In professional language so the plan is clear to services
As a summary by her teacher, who knows her well
In her own words through her device, without rewriting them
As a summary of her views written by her parents
11.w: NICE NG213 Disabled children and young people up to 25 with severe complex needs (2022, updated 2023) rec 1.4.13: preserve the child or young person's voice: use their preferred communication format, use their own words (or the equivalent if they do not communicate verbally) and do not rewrite what they have said; rec 1.4.8 makes clear which parts are their contributions.

n.0: Rewriting Maya's views in professional language loses her voice, which NG213 says not to do.
n.1: A teacher's summary replaces Maya's own words with another person's interpretation.
n.3: Parents' views are recorded too, but they do not replace Maya's own contribution.

11.q: Leo, 3, attends the emergency department with several bruises. His father says he is 'always falling over'. Which distribution of bruising is most suggestive of non-accidental injury in a mobile toddler?
o: A bruise on the centre of the forehead
Grazes and bruising on the palms and elbows
Bruises over both shins and knees
Bruises on both ears and the side of the neck
11.w: Accidental bruises in mobile children typically occur over bony prominences at the front of the body (shins, knees, forehead). NICE CG89 lists bruising on non-bony parts of the body or face, including the ears, neck, cheeks and buttocks, as a reason to suspect maltreatment.

n.0: Forehead bruises over bone are common from falls in toddlers.
n.1: Palm and elbow injuries are typical of falls onto outstretched hands.
n.2: Shin and knee bruises are typical accidental injuries in mobile toddlers.

11.q: A hospital is reviewing how it meets the Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605). Which patient's need falls within the scope of the standard?
o: A patient whose first language is Romanian
A patient who wants a copy of their clinic letter
A Deaf patient who uses British Sign Language
A patient who prefers appointments by email
11.w: Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025): covers information and communication needs relating to disability, impairment or sensory loss, through six stages: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review.

n.0: Language needs without a disability are met through interpreting services, not the AIS.
n.1: Receiving copies is an access right, not an AIS communication need.
n.3: A general preference unrelated to disability or sensory loss is outside the AIS.

11.q: Gwen, 70, is in the last days of life with metastatic cancer and new bone pain. She has not taken opioids before. The team agree to start subcutaneous morphine for symptom control, and the nurse is planning her care. Which approach to dosing is recommended?
o: Wait until her pain is severe before giving the first dose of morphine
Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start at the top of the prescribed range so that she is comfortable quickly
Give a loading dose by intramuscular injection, then change to subcutaneous
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.7 and 1.5.8: for people starting treatment who have not previously had medicines for symptom management, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing symptoms at least daily.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.11 asks for pain to be managed promptly and effectively once identified.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.7 recommends starting with the lowest effective dose for people not previously given symptom-control medicines.
n.3: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.5.5).

11.q: Kofi, 72, has a NEWS2 of 6. You have completed an ABCDE assessment, given oxygen and called the doctor using SBAR. The doctor will arrive in 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate next action?
o: Hand over to the next shift that he has been reviewed
Leave him to rest and record observations again in 4 hours
Repeat the ABCDE assessment to check his response to interventions
Start the oral antibiotics left on his drug chart from yesterday
11.w: ABCDE is cyclical: after each intervention reassess from A. A NEWS2 of 5 or more requires at least hourly monitoring, and any deterioration should trigger re-escalation (RCP 2017 chart 4).

n.0: He has not yet been reviewed, so this handover would be inaccurate and unsafe.
n.1: A NEWS2 of 5-6 requires at least hourly observations, not 4-hourly.
n.3: Oral antibiotics from yesterday are not a response to an acute deterioration and need medical review.

11.q: Dolores, 88, is frail and drowsy after a stroke. She has a dry, coated tongue and cracked lips, takes nothing by mouth and has an unsafe swallow. Which oral care plan is most appropriate?
o: Daily chlorhexidine mouthwash rinses by mouth
Lemon and glycerine swabs every two hours
Gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip balm
Mouth care whenever her relatives request it
11.w: People who are nil by mouth and drowsy need frequent oral assessment and gentle care with a soft toothbrush, moistening and lip care. Lemon and glycerine dry the mouth further and mouthwashes risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow (Annexe B 4.5; NICE NG31 advises frequent mouth and lip care).

n.0: Rinses she cannot spit out risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow.
n.1: Lemon and glycerine swabs dry the mucosa further and can damage teeth.
n.3: Oral care is a planned nursing intervention based on assessment, not on request.

11.q: Baby Isaac was born at 38 weeks. His mother takes labetalol for hypertension in pregnancy. Isaac breastfed at 40 minutes old. At 3 hours, before the second feed, his blood glucose is 1.6 mmol/L. He is alert, warm and showing feeding cues. Which action does the BAPM framework support?
o: Give 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg with a supported breastfeed
Give formula at 150 mL/kg/day and recheck glucose in 6 hours
Continue feeding with no further glucose checks
Start IV 10% glucose before the next feed
11.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice points 16 and 18: if the first pre-feed glucose is 1.0-1.9 mmol/L with no abnormal signs (Flowchart B), buccal 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg may be given alongside feeding support, with repeat measurement.

n.1: Formula volumes in the first 24 hours are 40-60 mL/kg/day, and a 6-hour wait is too long.
n.2: A baby at risk with glucose of 1.6 mmol/L needs treatment and repeat measurement.
n.3: IV glucose is for severe (below 1.0 mmol/L) or persistent hypoglycaemia, or abnormal signs, after medical review.

11.q: Eric, 58, has a PEG tube. His paracetamol oral suspension, baclofen liquid and a dispersible aspirin tablet are due at 12:00. His feed is running. How should the nurse give these medicines?
o: Give all three, then flush once with water at the end
Give each separately, flushing with water before, between and after
Add the three medicines into the feed bag to run with the feed
Mix all three in one enteral syringe and give them together
11.w: For enteral tubes, each medicine is given separately in a suitable liquid or dispersed form via an enteral syringe, with the tube flushed with water before, between and after each medicine to prevent interactions and blockage (AnnexB.11.9; RPS/RCN references the NEWT guidelines). The feed is paused while medicines are given.

n.0: Without flushing between medicines they may interact in the tube and block it.
n.2: Adding medicines to feed risks incompatibility and unpredictable dosing if the feed stops.
n.3: Mixing medicines can cause physical or chemical incompatibilities and tube blockage.

11.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
11.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

11.q: Dorothy, 86, has advanced dementia. For three days she has spat out her anticonvulsant and pushed staff away at medicine rounds. Her son suggests hiding it in her tea. What is the nurse's most appropriate first step?
o: Assess her capacity to make this specific decision about the medicine
Arrange for the medicine to be given by injection instead
Hide the medicine in her tea, as she has a diagnosis of dementia
Stop the anticonvulsant, as she is repeatedly refusing it
11.w: The MCA 2005 (ss1-3) requires a capacity assessment that is decision-specific and time-specific; a diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. Only if she lacks capacity can a best interests decision about covert administration follow (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21).

n.1: Changing the route needs a prescriber and does not address capacity or consent.
n.2: A diagnosis does not prove lack of capacity (MCA s2(3)); covert use also needs a best interests process.
n.3: Stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures; the refusal needs assessment, not unilateral cessation.

11.q: A ward nurse tells the trust's safeguarding lead that a 13-year-old patient disclosed FGM to her during a dressing change. The safeguarding lead says she will phone the police herself so that the nurse can return to her busy shift. What is the correct position?
o: The safeguarding lead can report, as a regulated professional in the same trust
The safeguarding lead must report, as the nurse is not trained in FGM
The nurse must make the report herself, as the duty cannot be transferred
Either can report, as both are regulated professionals in the trust
11.w: The mandatory reporting duty is a personal duty: the professional who receives the disclosure must make the report, and the responsibility cannot be transferred. The nurse should still involve the safeguarding lead for support and wider safeguarding action.

n.0: Working in the same trust does not allow the duty to be passed to another person.
n.1: Training level does not change who holds the duty.
n.3: Being regulated in the same trust does not allow the duty to be shared or passed on; it stays with the nurse who heard the disclosure.

11.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
11.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

11.q: A ward manager has designed a new bedside safety checklist and wants every ward in the hospital to start using it next Monday. Arjun, the ward's quality improvement lead, is asked for advice. Which approach best reflects improvement methodology?
o: Pilot it on one ward for a year before deciding whether to use it more widely
Introduce it on all wards on Monday and audit compliance in six months
Test it with a few patients on one ward, measure, adapt and then scale up
Ask each ward manager to decide whether to adopt the checklist locally
11.w: The Model for Improvement uses rapid, small-scale PDSA cycles: test a change with a few patients or one shift, measure the effect, adapt, and build up to wider implementation once it works. This limits risk and builds learning and ownership (NHS England improvement guidance; P6.4, P6.6).

n.0: A single year-long pilot is slow; PDSA relies on short, repeated cycles that allow rapid adaptation.
n.1: Hospital-wide launch without testing risks spreading an untested change, and a six-month delay in measurement slows learning.
n.3: Leaving adoption to individual choice produces inconsistent practice without any evidence that the checklist works.

11.q: Mr Kaye, 61, is on a cardiac monitor. The monitor alarms and shows a chaotic trace resembling ventricular fibrillation. The nurse looks across and sees Mr Kaye sitting up, talking and brushing his teeth. What should the nurse do first?
o: Go to him, assess him and check the electrodes and leads
Put out a cardiac arrest call and bring the defibrillator
Silence the alarm and review the monitor trace later
Give a precordial thump to restore a normal rhythm
11.w: Monitor traces must be interpreted with the patient. Movement such as tooth brushing commonly causes artefact resembling VF. The nurse should assess him directly and check electrode contact; a cardiac arrest is confirmed by assessing the patient (RCUK 2025), not by the monitor alone.

n.1: He is conscious and talking, so he is not in cardiac arrest.
n.2: Silencing without assessing the patient risks missing a genuine problem.
n.3: A precordial thump is not indicated in a conscious person and is not a response to artefact.

11.q: Daniel, 13, is to have planned spinal surgery next month. Which approach to preparation best suits his stage of development?
o: Give detailed information, invite his questions and involve him in decisions
Speak mainly with his parents and let them decide how much to tell him
Prepare him on the morning of surgery to avoid weeks of worry
Use doll play to act out the operation with him and his younger sister
11.w: Adolescents can think abstractly and want detailed, honest information, privacy and a say in decisions about their care. Preparation well ahead, with time for questions (and a pre-admission visit if available), supports autonomy and reduces anxiety (P4.3; T2 play therapy and preparation).

n.1: Excluding a 13-year-old from information about his own surgery ignores his developing autonomy.
n.2: A last-minute explanation suits toddlers, not an adolescent facing major planned surgery.
n.3: Doll play suits younger children and may feel patronising to an adolescent.

11.q: Finn, 6, is admitted with asthma. He tells the nurse he hides under his bed when his dad shouts at his mum and hits her, and he has started wetting the bed again. Finn has no injuries. How is Finn best described for safeguarding purposes?
o: He is a victim of domestic abuse in his own right
He is at risk of neglect, as his mother is unable to protect him
He is not a victim, as he has not himself been physically harmed
He is a child in need, as he has a long-term health condition
11.w: Section 3 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 recognises a child who sees or hears, or experiences the effects of, domestic abuse and is related to either party as a victim in their own right. Working Together 2026 includes seeing or hearing the ill-treatment of another within emotional abuse. A safeguarding referral is needed.

n.1: Labelling the non-abusing mother as neglectful misdirects the response; the harm arises from the father's abuse.
n.2: Physical injury is not required; witnessing domestic abuse is harm in itself.
n.3: Asthma may make him a child in need, but the safeguarding issue here is domestic abuse.

11.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
11.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

11.q: Sofia, 9, has a two-month history of night cough and wheeze. Her GP suspects asthma and refers her to the practice nurse for objective testing under NICE NG245. Which test should be done first?
o: Peak flow variability recorded over 2 weeks
Bronchial challenge testing with methacholine
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO)
Skin prick testing to house dust mite
11.w: NICE NG245 Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN, November 2024): in children aged 5-11, measure FeNO first (35 ppb or more supports asthma); if not confirmed, do spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, then peak flow variability.

n.0: Peak flow variability is a later step in the NG245 diagnostic sequence for 5-11 year olds.
n.1: Bronchial challenge is a specialist test used when earlier tests are inconclusive.
n.3: Skin prick testing identifies sensitisation but does not diagnose asthma.

11.q: A urinal has been knocked over, spilling urine across the floor of a bay. The urine contains no visible blood. The nurse wears gloves and an apron. Which approach to managing this spill is correct?
o: Sprinkle chlorine-releasing granules directly on the urine
Pour 10,000 ppm chlorine solution directly on the urine first
Soak up with paper towels, then clean with 1,000 ppm chlorine
Leave it for the domestic team to clean at the next routine round
11.w: NIPCM appendix 9: do not use a chlorine-releasing agent directly on a urine spill (it can release chlorine gas). Soak up with disposable paper towels (a gelling agent may be used), then decontaminate with 1,000 ppm available chlorine or a combined detergent and chlorine product, then wash and dry.

n.0: Granules are for blood and high-risk body fluids; on urine they risk releasing chlorine gas.
n.1: Chlorine must not be applied directly to urine, and 10,000 ppm is the blood-spill strength.
n.3: Spills are treated immediately by trained staff, not left as a slip and infection hazard.

11.q: Mary, 74, had a hip replacement 8 hours ago. She has not passed urine since surgery, says she needs to go but cannot, and has lower abdominal discomfort. Which action is most appropriate first?
o: Restrict her fluids until she passes urine
Give her a laxative to relieve the discomfort
Insert a catheter without discussing it with her
Assess her bladder volume with a bladder scanner
11.w: Annexe B 6.4: recognise and respond to retention. A bladder scan assesses residual volume to guide whether catheterisation is needed, which is then performed with her consent and in line with local policy.

n.0: Restricting fluids does not treat retention and risks dehydration.
n.1: A laxative does not address urinary retention.
n.2: Catheterisation needs assessment and valid consent (Code 4.2).

11.q: At the end of a shift, which item is most important for Nurse Ben to include when handing over Mrs Webb, 77?
o: Her IV antibiotic is due at 18:00; her NEWS2 rose to 4
She was admitted four days ago from her own home
She enjoyed her lunch and watched television all afternoon
Her daughter visited during the afternoon
11.w: Annexe A 1.11: provide clear information when handing over care. Code 10.2 identify risks and problems; Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed.

n.1: Admission date is less urgent than outstanding care and deterioration.
n.2: Social details matter less than risks and time-critical care.
n.3: Visitor details are not the priority for safe handover.

11.q: Harper, 3 months, was born at term and has no underlying conditions. She is admitted with bronchiolitis. She is feeding about 80% of her usual amount and her SpO2 has been 91% in air for the last hour, with mild recession. What should the nurse do about oxygen?
o: Keep monitoring her in air; oxygen is not yet indicated
Start oxygen to keep her saturations at 94-98%
Start oxygen because her saturations are below 92%
Start nasal high-flow oxygen to reduce her work of breathing
11.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): give supplemental oxygen if SpO2 is persistently below 90% in children aged 6 weeks and over (below 92% under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions). Harper is 3 months, otherwise well, at 91%.

n.1: A 94-98% target is used in other acute illness; NG9 sets a lower threshold of 90% for bronchiolitis from 6 weeks.
n.2: 92% is the threshold for babies under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions; Harper is 3 months and otherwise well.
n.3: High-flow or CPAP is for impending respiratory failure; Harper has mild recession and acceptable saturations.

11.q: Agnes, 55, has received her cervical screening invitation. She tells the nurse she has heard mixed things about screening and is unsure whether to go. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that cervical screening is compulsory for women of her age group
Advise her that screening prevents every case of cervical cancer
Give balanced information on benefits and limits, and support her choice
Book her test now and explain the details at her appointment
11.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): deciding whether to have screening is a personal choice; benefits (early detection, preventing some deaths) are weighed against risks and limitations (false positives and negatives, anxiety, difficult decisions). Code 4.2: make sure informed consent is obtained.

n.0: Screening is a personal choice; NHS screening is offered, not mandated.
n.1: Screening tests are not 100% accurate; this overstates the benefit and is misleading.
n.3: Booking before she has decided bypasses informed choice.

11.q: Aiden, aged 2, needs a nasogastric tube passed. A health play specialist is not available. Which distraction is most suited to his age?
o: Blowing and popping bubbles or watching a light-up toy
Counting backwards from 100 in his head
Guided imagery about his favourite holiday
Explaining the anatomy of the nose using a diagram
11.w: Distraction should match developmental stage: toddlers respond to simple, sensory, attention-grabbing activities such as bubbles, light-up or musical toys and songs (AnnexA.3.8 distraction and diversion strategies).

n.1: Counting backwards from 100 is beyond a 2-year-old's ability.
n.2: Guided imagery needs abstract thinking suited to older children and adolescents.
n.3: A diagram is a preparation tool for older school-age children, not a distraction for a toddler.

11.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
11.q: Kian, aged 2, has a temperature of 38.9°C. He responds normally to his parents but is not smiling. Respiratory rate is 46, SpO2 96% in air, heart rate 135 and capillary refill 2 seconds. Which NICE traffic light feature is present?
o: An SpO2 of 96% in air, which is an amber feature
A respiratory rate above 40, amber when over 12 months
No amber features, so he is in the green category
A heart rate above the amber threshold for his age
11.w: Two steps: compare each value with the NG143 table, then classify. A respiratory rate above 40 breaths/min in a child over 12 months is amber; not smiling is also amber (reduced response to social cues). His heart rate (amber threshold above 140 at 2 to 5 years), SpO2 (amber at 95% or less) and capillary refill are not amber.

n.0: The amber SpO2 threshold is 95% or less in air; 96% is not amber.
n.2: He has amber features (respiratory rate and not smiling), so he is not green.
n.3: The NG143 amber heart rate threshold at 2 to 5 years is above 140; his is 135.

11.q: Patricia, 73, lives in England and has had regular breast screening. She asks the practice nurse why she has not received an invitation since she turned 71. Which response is accurate?
o: Invitations stop after 70, but she can refer herself for screening
Women over 70 are invited every 5 years instead of every 3 years
Breast screening ends at 70 because no benefit remains after that age
She needs a GP referral to a breast clinic to be screened
11.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): breast screening is offered to women aged 50 to 70; women over 70 can self-refer.

n.1: Routine invitations are for women aged 50 to 70; after 70 screening is by self-referral.
n.2: Women over 70 can still self-refer; screening is available to them on request.
n.3: A breast clinic referral is for symptoms; screening after 70 is by self-referral.

11.q: During a morning shift, Grace, a staff nurse, slips on a wet floor in the sluice and fractures her wrist. She is taken to the emergency department. The ward manager is the responsible person under RIDDOR 2013. How should this injury be reported?
o: To the HSE without delay and within 10 days, as it is a specified injury
To the HSE within 15 days, as it happened in a clinical area
Through the local incident system, as staff injuries are not reportable
To the HSE within 15 days, if Grace is off work for more than seven days
11.w: A fracture other than to fingers, thumbs or toes is a specified injury under RIDDOR 2013. Specified injuries and work-related deaths must be reported to the HSE without delay, and within 10 days. The incident should also be recorded on the local system (HSE, RIDDOR: when do I report).

n.1: The 15-day deadline is for over-7-day incapacitation, and the location of the accident does not decide the timescale.
n.2: Work-related injuries to employees are exactly what RIDDOR covers; local reporting is needed in addition to, not instead of, the RIDDOR report.
n.3: The over-7-day rule applies to injuries that are not specified injuries; a wrist fracture is reportable whatever the length of absence.

11.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
11.q: Ruby, aged 4, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She is quiet. Heart rate is 165 beats/min, capillary refill time 4 seconds, and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. A student says the normal blood pressure is reassuring. What is the best response?
o: Disagree, because low blood pressure is a late sign in children
Agree, because a normal blood pressure shows her circulation is coping
Disagree, because her breathing rate is a better guide than her pulse
Agree, but ask for the blood pressure to be rechecked in an hour
11.w: Children compensate for circulatory failure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so blood pressure stays normal until late; hypotension signals decompensation and risk of arrest (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill already indicate compensated shock needing urgent escalation.

n.1: Blood pressure is maintained in compensated shock, so a normal reading does not rule it out.
n.2: Breathing rate matters, but here her heart rate and capillary refill show compensated shock; no single sign outranks the others.
n.3: Waiting an hour delays treatment of compensated shock.

11.q: Ivan, 72, has COPD and is prescribed salbutamol 2 puffs via a pressurised metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. He tells the nurse he usually sprays both puffs into the spacer and then takes one big breath. What should the nurse advise?
o: Spray one puff and breathe it in, then repeat for the second
Spray both puffs together, then take several slow breaths
Spray one puff, wait a full minute, then breathe it in
Spray both puffs together, then take one breath and hold it
11.w: With a spacer, one actuation is given at a time and inhaled straight away (by a slow deep breath or several tidal breaths), then the process is repeated for the next puff after shaking (AnnexB.11.8). Multiple actuations into the spacer reduce the dose delivered.

n.1: Firing two puffs together causes the drug to stick to the spacer walls, reducing the dose reaching the lungs.
n.2: Delaying inhalation lets the drug settle on the spacer walls.
n.3: This repeats his current error of firing both puffs into the spacer at once.

11.q: Sam, 34, died after an incident on a surgical ward that the trust accepts is a notifiable safety incident. Under regulation 20, who should the trust notify about the incident?
o: Sam's GP, who will discuss the incident with the family
The CQC, which notifies families on the trust's behalf
A person lawfully acting on Sam's behalf, such as next of kin
The coroner, who will then decide whether to inform the family
11.w: Reg 20(7): the relevant person is the service user or, on their death, a person lawfully acting on their behalf (also if under 16 and not competent, or 16 or over and lacking capacity).

n.0: The GP is not the relevant person; reg 20 notification goes to the person acting on Sam's behalf.
n.1: The CQC regulates compliance but does not notify relevant persons for providers.
n.3: Coroner referral is a separate duty; reg 20 requires the relevant person to be notified.

11.q: In October 2026 a community children's nurse in England is worried that Noah, 7, is often hungry and tired at clinic. She plans to share this with his school's designated safeguarding lead so they can offer support. Noah's mother refuses consent. What is the correct position?
o: The nurse must wait until concerns reach the threshold for a referral
The nurse should share the information, as consent is not required under s16LA
The nurse needs the mother's consent before sharing, as there is no s47 enquiry
The nurse can share once a court has authorised disclosure to the school
11.w: From 30 September 2026, s16LA of the Children Act 2004 requires relevant persons to share information that may help another relevant person safeguard or promote a child's welfare. Consent is not required and lack of consent is not a reason to withhold (statutory guidance, September 2026). The nurse should usually tell the mother what is being shared and why, unless that would put Noah at risk.

n.0: No statutory threshold has to be met before the duty applies; it covers early help and unmet needs.
n.2: Consent is not required under the duty, and sharing is not limited to s47 enquiries.
n.3: No court authorisation is needed; the duty itself requires sharing.

11.q: Fred, 72, has crusting around both eyelids after a viral illness. You are asked to clean his eyes. Which technique is correct?
o: Use one swab for each eye, wiping back and forth across the lid
Use one swab for both eyes, wiping from outer to inner corner
Use a fresh swab for each eye, wiping from inner to outer corner
Use a dry cotton bud inside the lower lid to remove crusts
11.w: Eye care principles: use sterile saline and a separate swab for each eye, wiping once from the inner canthus outward, so that debris and infection are not carried into the tear duct or the other eye (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wiping back and forth reintroduces debris to the eye.
n.1: Sharing a swab and wiping inward risks cross-infection and moving debris into the tear duct.
n.3: Inserting a cotton bud inside the lid risks corneal injury.

11.q: Kenneth, 68, lives in England and asks the practice nurse what the NHS bowel cancer screening programme will offer him. He has no bowel symptoms. Which answer is accurate?
o: A home test kit every 2 years
A home test kit every year
A colonoscopy every 5 years
A one-off camera test at age 70
11.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): everyone aged 50 to 74 is offered a bowel cancer screening home test kit every 2 years; people aged 75 or over can ask for a kit every 2 years.

n.1: The bowel screening kit is sent every 2 years, not annually.
n.2: Colonoscopy is a diagnostic test offered after a positive screening result, not the routine screen.
n.3: The current programme offers a home test kit every 2 years from 50 to 74.

11.q: Which is the correct order of the phases of wound healing?
o: Inflammation, haemostasis, maturation, proliferation
Proliferation, haemostasis, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, proliferation, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation
11.w: Wounds heal through overlapping phases: haemostasis (clotting), inflammation (clearing debris and bacteria), proliferation (granulation tissue and epithelialisation) and maturation or remodelling (collagen reorganisation, which can last months).

n.0: Haemostasis comes first, and proliferation precedes maturation.
n.1: Proliferation follows inflammation; it does not begin the process.
n.2: Inflammation precedes proliferation, not the other way round.

11.q: Rania, 6, has a fever and vomiting but no urinary symptoms. A dipstick on her clean catch urine is positive for leukocyte esterase and negative for nitrite. According to NICE NG224, what should happen?
o: Repeat the dipstick test on a fresh sample in 1 week
Treat as asymptomatic bacteriuria with no further action
Start antibiotics for a UTI straight away
Send urine for culture and look for another cause of fever
11.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) Table 2: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative = send for microscopy and culture; do not give antibiotics unless there is good clinical evidence of UTI. A positive leukocyte result may reflect infection elsewhere.

n.0: A one-week delay leaves a febrile child without a diagnosis.
n.1: Rania is febrile and unwell, so this is not asymptomatic, and culture is needed.
n.2: Antibiotics are withheld unless there is good clinical evidence of UTI, which Rania lacks.

11.q: Mrs Shah, 58, asks a practice nurse whether a herbal supplement she has bought online will help her blood pressure alongside her prescribed amlodipine. The nurse is unsure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her that nurses cannot discuss non-prescribed products
Check a reliable source or the pharmacist before advising her
Advise her that herbal products are natural and safe to take
Advise her to stop the amlodipine while she tries the supplement
11.w: Code 6.1: information or advice must be evidence-based, including about health products; Code 18.3: check compatibility with other treatment, including over-the-counter medicines; Code 13.3 seek help when unsure.

n.0: Code 18.3 expects compatibility with other treatments, including over-the-counter products, to be checked.
n.2: This is not evidence-based and ignores possible interactions (Code 6.1, 18.3).
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review could be harmful and is outside the nurse's evidence base.

11.q: Maeve, 79, has dementia and lacks capacity. When she had capacity she made a written, signed and witnessed advance decision refusing antipsychotic medication. The team confirms it is valid and applicable. She is now refusing a newly prescribed antipsychotic. Her family ask for it to be given covertly. What applies?
o: Respect the advance decision and do not give the antipsychotic
Give it covertly, as a best interests meeting overrides the advance decision
Give it covertly until a court decides on the advance decision
Give it covertly if her family and the GP both agree
11.w: Under the MCA 2005 ss24-26, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same effect as a capacitous refusal and binds professionals. Best interests decisions cannot override it, so the antipsychotic cannot be given, covertly or otherwise.

n.1: A best interests decision cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision.
n.2: Treatment may be given to prevent serious deterioration while a court decides on validity, but here validity is confirmed.
n.3: Family and GP agreement does not override a binding advance refusal.

11.q: A medical ward has one free single room. The nurse in charge must decide which of four patients should move into it. Applying NIPCM single-room prioritisation, which patient should be moved first?
o: Edith, 92, who is frail and has been admitted with a hip fracture
Ann, 66, with pneumonia, a dry cough and on day 4 of antibiotics
Derek, 70, with vomiting and diarrhoea and suspected norovirus
Kevin, 59, with leg cellulitis fully contained by a dry dressing
11.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 flags diarrhoea and vomiting as a cross-infection risk and directs that single rooms are prioritised for infectious patients most likely to transmit to others; norovirus spreads rapidly in bays. Prioritisation is reviewed daily with IPC team input.

n.0: Frailty raises Edith's risk of acquiring infection, but she is not an infection source needing isolation.
n.1: Ann is on treatment with a dry cough and poses a lower transmission risk than active vomiting and diarrhoea.
n.3: Contained, dressed cellulitis presents a low transmission risk with standard precautions.

11.q: Ethan, 7, is autistic and is admitted for elective surgery tomorrow. His father says Ethan becomes very distressed by noise, bright lights and unexpected changes. Which plan best reflects reasonable adjustments for Ethan?
o: A bay near the nurses' station so staff can observe him closely
A quiet side room, visual timetable and his father's routines
Admission to the general paediatric bay with other children
Sedation on arrival so that he does not become distressed
11.w: The Equality Act 2010 (s20) requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people, including autistic children. Adjustments include a quiet environment, preparation with visual supports, predictable routines and using the family's knowledge of the child (NG213 person-centred care; NHS reasonable adjustment guidance).

n.0: A busy area near the nurses' station increases noise, light and interruptions that distress Ethan.
n.2: A busy general bay increases sensory overload and unpredictability.
n.3: Routine sedation is a restrictive intervention that does not address his needs and needs a clinical indication.

11.q: Mr Price, 79, was alert this morning. At 14:00 his eyes are closed and he opens them and answers when the nurse speaks to him, but then drifts off again. His other observations are unchanged from earlier. How should his level of consciousness be recorded and scored on NEWS2?
o: V on ACVPU, scoring 1
V on ACVPU, scoring 3
A on ACVPU, scoring 0
P on ACVPU, scoring 3
11.w: ACVPU: Alert, new Confusion, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive. He responds to voice, so V. NEWS2 Chart 1 scores any of C, V, P or U as 3, which also triggers at least hourly monitoring and informing the medical team.

n.0: V is correct, but any score other than Alert scores 3 on NEWS2, not 1.
n.2: He is not alert, as his eyes are closed until he is spoken to.
n.3: He responds to voice, so a pain stimulus was not needed; P overstates the level.

11.q: Ruby, 6, has lost weight over three weeks, is drinking constantly and has started wetting the bed again. At a GP practice her capillary glucose is 19 mmol/L. She is alert and not vomiting. What should happen next?
o: Same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team
Routine paediatric outpatient referral within 2 weeks
Repeat capillary glucose at the practice in 48 hours
Fasting glucose test booked for next week
11.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.1.2: refer children and young people with suspected type 1 diabetes immediately (on the same day) to a multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team, because DKA can develop quickly.

n.1: A routine referral is too slow for suspected type 1 diabetes.
n.2: Delaying 48 hours risks progression to DKA.
n.3: Waiting a week for a fasting test risks DKA; NG18 requires same-day referral.

11.q: Grace, 52, has chronic osteoarthritis pain. She asks how she can manage flare-ups at home alongside her prescribed paracetamol. Which advice is most appropriate to support self-management?
o: Take her husband's leftover codeine tablets for bad days
Double her paracetamol dose on days when the pain is worse
Rest in bed until the pain fully settles after each flare-up
Pace activities and use local heat alongside regular analgesia
11.w: Self-management of long-term pain combines pacing, gentle activity and non-drug measures such as heat with analgesia taken as prescribed (P4.5, P4.8). Medicine doses must not exceed the prescription or licensed maximum.

n.0: Taking medicines prescribed for someone else is unsafe and unlawful for prescription-only medicines.
n.1: Doubling paracetamol risks exceeding the maximum daily dose and liver toxicity.
n.2: Prolonged bed rest worsens stiffness and deconditioning in osteoarthritis.

11.q: A charge nurse asks what a basic business case for funding two additional healthcare assistant posts should contain. Which content is most appropriate?
o: Last year's off-duty rotas to show how often extra shifts were filled
A list of the staff who support the request, with their signatures
The problem, the options considered, their costs and the expected benefits
Details of recent incidents including the patients' names and dates of birth
11.w: A business case explains why change is needed, the options (including doing nothing), costs, expected benefits to patients and the organisation, and how success will be measured (P7.12). Evidence should be anonymised to protect confidentiality (Code 5).

n.0: Past rotas may support part of the argument but are not the core content of a business case.
n.1: Support from colleagues does not show need, cost or benefit.
n.3: Identifiable patient information is not needed and would breach confidentiality; anonymised data should be used.

11.q: Mr Evans, 77, is being discharged home with a new leg ulcer that will need daily dressings from the district nursing team. The ward nurse hesitates to send details of his wound and medicines, worried about breaching confidentiality. Which Caldicott principle best guides her?
o: Inform patients and service users about how their information is used
Sharing for individual care matters as much as protecting confidentiality
Use the minimum necessary personal confidential data for each purpose
Access to personal confidential data should be on a strict need-to-know basis
11.w: Caldicott principle 7 (National Data Guardian, 2020): the duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect patient confidentiality. Sharing with the district nurses supports his direct care.

n.0: Informing patients (principle 8) is good practice but does not resolve her concern about sharing for direct care.
n.2: Minimum necessary data (principle 3) shapes how much is shared, but the nurse's hesitation is about whether to share at all.
n.3: Need-to-know access (principle 4) limits who sees data; the district nurses clearly need to know.

11.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
11.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

11.q: Albert, 85, dies at home with his wife present at 02:10. The community nurse arrives at 03:30 and completes verification of his expected death at 03:45. His wife asks what time will be recorded as the time of death. What should the nurse tell her?
o: 03:30, when the nurse arrived at the house
02:10, when she noticed that he had stopped breathing
The time the doctor completes the death certificate
03:45, when verification of death was completed
11.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the time of verification is recognised as the official time of death and is recorded when verification is completed, not when the death is first reported. Families should be advised there may be a difference between the time of the last breath and the official time of death.

n.0: Arrival time is not the time of death; it is recorded when verification is completed.
n.1: The guidance says families should be told that the time of the last breath may differ from the official time of death.
n.2: The MCCD is completed later by a medical practitioner; the official time of death is the time of verification.

11.q: Ethan, 14, attends a clinic with his mother. The nurse wants to complete a psychosocial assessment. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask Ethan to fill in a questionnaire and pass it to his mother to check
See Ethan alone for part of the visit and explain confidentiality limits
See Ethan with his mother throughout so she can add any missing detail
Ask his mother to answer the questions because Ethan is still under 16
11.w: Good adolescent practice is to see the young person on their own for part of the consultation and to explain at the start what will stay confidential and when information may need to be shared to keep them or others safe (NICE NG204 rec 1.5.2 offer young people time on their own; Doukrou and Segal 2018, HEEADSSS). This respects developing autonomy (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Passing his answers to his mother breaches the confidence he would expect and discourages honest answers.
n.2: Young people are less likely to disclose risks such as substance use or self-harm in front of a parent.
n.3: Young people under 16 can give their own history, and a parent may not know about many psychosocial risks.

11.q: Grace, aged 18 months, was born in September 2024. Her mother asks why her older son, born in March 2024, did not have an appointment at this age. What is the correct explanation?
o: It is a catch-up appointment for children who missed the 1-year vaccines
Children born from 1 July 2024 are given a BCG vaccine at the 18-month visit
Children born from 1 July 2024 get a 4th 6-in-1 and 2nd MMRV at 18 months
It is an appointment to give the HPV vaccine early to girls born after July 2024
11.w: UKHSA routine schedule (from 1 September 2026): children born on or after 1 July 2024 are offered a fourth 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) and a second MMRV at 18 months; those born on or before 30 June 2024 have no 18-month appointment.

n.0: It is a routine appointment for a whole birth cohort, not a catch-up for missed vaccines.
n.1: BCG is a selective vaccine given within 28 days of birth to at-risk infants.
n.3: HPV is given at 12 to 13 years to boys and girls, not at 18 months.

11.q: Leanne, a staff nurse, is asked by the nurse in charge to remove a patient's chest drain because the doctors are busy. Leanne has read about the procedure but has never been trained or assessed in it. What should Leanne do first?
o: Watch an online video of the procedure and then remove the drain
Remove the drain with the nurse in charge talking her through it
Remove the drain and record that she did so on the instruction given
Explain she is untrained and ask a competent practitioner to do it
11.w: Code 13.3: ask for help from a suitably qualified professional for any procedure beyond your competence; 13.5: complete training first; 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Safe evidence-based practice in procedures (P1.20) depends on this.

n.0: Self-directed viewing is not training or assessment; Code 13.5 requires the necessary training before a new role or procedure.
n.1: Verbal guidance from someone not supervising hands-on does not make her competent; she would be practising beyond her competence (Code 13.3).
n.2: Being instructed does not transfer accountability; each registrant is accountable for working within competence (Code 13).

11.q: Mrs Dean, 49, has just eaten an orange and asks the nurse to check her blood glucose. The nurse plans to use the side of her fingertip. What should the nurse do before taking the sample?
o: Squeeze the finger firmly to produce a large drop
Ask her to wash and dry her hands
Clean her finger with an alcohol wipe and test while still wet
Use the first drop from the centre of the fingertip pad
11.w: Sugar residue on the skin, for example from fruit, can give a falsely high capillary glucose reading. Washing and drying the hands with warm water removes residue and improves blood flow (Annexe B 2.10: measure and interpret blood glucose).

n.0: Firm squeezing dilutes the drop with tissue fluid and can give an inaccurate result.
n.2: Testing through wet alcohol can dilute the sample and alter the reading.
n.3: The pad is more painful and the problem of sugar on the skin remains.

11.q: Mr Patel, 59, needs an unplanned return to theatre after a swab was left in his abdomen during surgery in an NHS hospital. He recovers fully within two weeks. How should this incident be classified for the statutory duty of candour?
o: A notifiable safety incident involving moderate harm
A near miss, as he made a full recovery
A notifiable safety incident involving severe harm
No harm, as the recovery took under 28 days
11.w: Reg 20 and CQC guidance: moderate harm includes harm requiring a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery, and significant but not permanent harm. Moderate harm makes it a notifiable safety incident for a health service body.

n.1: Harm occurred; an unplanned return to surgery is a listed example of moderate harm.
n.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of function; his recovery was full.
n.3: The 28-day period applies to prolonged psychological harm and pain, not to moderate harm requiring extra treatment.

11.q: Mrs Ellis, 81, has advanced heart failure and full capacity. A doctor completes a DNACPR form overnight and asks the nurse not to mention it to her because 'it will only upset her'. Mrs Ellis has said she wants to be involved in all decisions. Which statement best reflects the legal position?
o: She should be consulted unless this is likely to cause her physical or psychological harm
She should be told once the decision has been reviewed by a second consultant
She need not be told because a DNACPR decision is a clinical decision for the doctor
Her husband should be told instead, as the decision affects the whole family
