11.w: In R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014] EWCA Civ 822, the Court of Appeal held that Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions and that there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Possible upset is not enough.

n.1: A second opinion does not replace the duty to consult her before the notice is placed; delaying her involvement is not lawful on these facts.
n.2: Tracey held that although CPR is a clinical decision, the patient must be involved and consulted; the clinical nature of the decision does not remove that duty.
n.3: Mrs Ellis has capacity, so the duty to consult is owed to her; informing her husband in her place breaches her Article 8 rights and confidentiality.

11.q: Ellie, 15, attends a sexual health clinic and asks a nurse for the contraceptive pill. She does not want her parents to know. The nurse wants to use the framework that applies specifically to giving contraceptive advice and treatment to under-16s without parental knowledge. Which framework applies?
o: The Bolam test for a responsible body of opinion
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 test of capacity
Section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969
The Fraser guidelines
11.w: Lord Fraser's guidelines in Gillick set the conditions under which a practitioner may give contraceptive advice or treatment to an under-16 without parental knowledge; since Axon (2006) they are also applied to STI treatment and termination.

n.0: Bolam concerns the standard of care in negligence, not consent for a minor.
n.1: The MCA 2005 applies from age 16; Ellie is 15.
n.2: FLRA 1969 s8 gives 16 and 17-year-olds the right to consent, so it does not apply to Ellie.

11.q: At 21:00 Yusuf arrives to take charge of a 24-bed ward for the night. One registered nurse has phoned in sick and no replacement has been found, leaving Yusuf as the only registered nurse with three healthcare assistants. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the shift and complete an incident report at the end of the night describing it
Start the shift and allocate the medicines round to the most senior healthcare assistant
Escalate immediately to the site manager, as fewer than two registered nurses is a red flag
Ask the day staff to stay until midnight and then manage the remainder of the shift himself
11.w: NICE SG1 Box 2 lists fewer than 2 registered nurses present on a ward during any shift as a nursing red flag, which requires an immediate escalation response. Code 16.1 and 25.1 require prompt action on risks to safety and effective management of staff and resources.

n.0: Reporting after the shift leaves the risk unmanaged throughout the night.
n.1: Healthcare assistants cannot be delegated tasks outside their competence, such as a full registered nurse medicines round (Code 11.1).
n.3: A short extension by tired day staff does not solve the shortfall for most of the night and bypasses escalation.

11.q: Jade believes her ward manager is altering staffing records to hide unfilled shifts. She does not feel able to raise this with the manager herself. What is the most appropriate step?
o: Raise it with the manager's own staff at the next team meeting
Raise it with the designated person named in the trust's policy
Post her concerns on a professional social media group
Wait until she has more evidence before telling anyone
11.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance: if you cannot raise the concern with your line manager, stage 2 is the designated person in your organisation (for example a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian). Code 16.1.

n.0: Discussing it with peers does not escalate it to someone able to act.
n.2: Public posting bypasses proper channels and risks confidentiality; NMC guidance uses internal and regulatory routes.
n.3: Code standard 16 requires her to act without delay; she does not need proof to raise a concern.

11.q: Bridget, 58, is due to have her first red cell transfusion before surgery. She asks the nurse what she should know about it. According to NICE NG24, which information should the nurse include?
o: That she will be able to give blood herself once she has recovered
That she will no longer be eligible to donate blood after a transfusion
That she cannot refuse once the transfusion has been prescribed
That a transfusion has no risks if the bedside checks are completed
11.w: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2: give verbal and written information on the reason for transfusion, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, that the person is no longer eligible to donate blood, and encourage questions; document the discussion (1.14.3).

n.0: NG24 states people who have had a transfusion are no longer eligible to donate blood.
n.2: A person with capacity may refuse a transfusion; consent remains her decision.
n.3: Transfusion carries risks that must be explained even with correct checks.

11.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
11.q: Lucy, aged 11, has a sprained ankle. Her father asks whether he can give her aspirin at home, as that is what he takes. What should the nurse advise?
o: Aspirin is safe for sprains when it is taken with food
Aspirin can be given for up to 3 days and then stopped
Aspirin is safe at half the adult dose for children over 10
Do not give aspirin under 16 unless prescribed; use paracetamol
11.w: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless prescribed by a doctor (for example in Kawasaki disease), because of the risk of Reye's syndrome (NHS). Paracetamol or ibuprofen are suitable for a sprain.

n.0: Taking aspirin with food reduces stomach upset but does not remove the risk of Reye's syndrome.
n.1: Short courses still carry the risk; aspirin is avoided in under-16s unless prescribed.
n.2: There is no half-dose exception; aspirin is avoided in under-16s unless prescribed.

11.q: Tara, 22, tells the nurse, "I always fail at everything." The nurse asks her to list examples that support and contradict this thought. Which technique is this?
o: A cognitive behavioural therapy method
A motivational interviewing technique
A distraction and diversion technique
A reminiscence therapy based technique
11.w: Annexe A 3.6: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques. Examining evidence for and against an unhelpful thought is cognitive restructuring.

n.1: MI explores ambivalence about change, not evidence for thoughts.
n.2: Distraction moves attention away; this examines the thought directly.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories for wellbeing, not testing thoughts.

11.q: Mr Albert King, 81, has heart failure, type 2 diabetes, COPD and osteoarthritis. He takes 14 different medicines and has had two falls this month. The community nurse visits. What is the most appropriate next step to address his complex needs?
o: Remove the medicines he finds hardest to swallow from his list
Advise him to stop his diuretic on days when he feels dizzy
Request a structured medication review with his GP or pharmacist
Refer him to the falls clinic and leave the medicines unchanged
11.w: Polypharmacy with multiple long-term conditions increases the risk of falls and adverse effects. A structured medication review, including psychotropic and cardiovascular drugs, is part of falls assessment (NICE NG249; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; P7.5 comorbidities and complex needs).

n.0: Nurses without prescribing responsibility for him must not stop prescribed medicines on swallowing difficulty alone; the issue needs review.
n.1: Advising him to stop a diuretic without prescriber review risks fluid overload.
n.3: A falls referral is reasonable, but leaving medicines unreviewed ignores a likely contributing factor.

11.q: Noah, 12, is autistic and has a learning disability. He has been banging his head and is more distressed than usual for two days. Staff at his school say it is 'just his autism'. What should the community children's nurse do first?
o: Increase his behaviour support plan and review in a month
Assess for a physical cause such as toothache or constipation
Advise the school to use a helmet and continue as usual
Refer him to CAMHS for a medication review
11.w: Diagnostic overshadowing (attributing new behaviour to a person's autism or learning disability) leads to missed physical illness. A change in behaviour may communicate pain or illness, so a physical assessment comes first (P3.7: recognise complex needs; NHS reasonable adjustments).

n.0: Changing the behaviour plan without assessment risks missing a treatable physical cause.
n.2: A helmet protects him but does not find the cause of a new change in behaviour.
n.3: Medication review comes after physical causes have been excluded.

11.q: Vera, 81, is recovering from pneumonia and is keen to return home. She can wash her face and upper body slowly but tires easily. A healthcare support worker suggests giving her a full bed bath to save time. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Postpone her wash until she can manage it without help
Set her up to wash what she can and help with the rest
Give her a full bed bath so that she can rest afterwards
Ask her daughter to wash her during the afternoon visit
11.w: Annexe B 4.3: assist with washing and dressing in a way that promotes independence. Encouraging Vera to do what she can, with help for the rest, maintains her abilities and dignity and supports her goal of going home (Code 1.2, 2.1).

n.0: Postponing hygiene leaves her needs unmet and risks skin problems.
n.2: A full bed bath removes the independence she needs to regain.
n.3: Hygiene is a fundamental of care that the nursing team is responsible for providing.

11.q: A newly qualified nurse asks why the Human Rights Act 1998 matters to everyday practice on an NHS children's ward. Which statement is accurate?
o: It applies to adults, while the UNCRC governs NHS care of children
It applies to disputes between private individuals rather than to the NHS
It applies once a case has reached the European Court of Human Rights
It requires NHS bodies to act compatibly with Convention rights
11.w: Section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority, including NHS bodies and staff acting for them, to act incompatibly with Convention rights. Rights such as Articles 2, 3, 8 and 14 apply to children as well as adults.

n.0: Convention rights apply to everyone, including children; the UNCRC is not directly enforceable in English courts.
n.1: The Act's main duty is on public authorities, which include NHS trusts.
n.2: The Act lets rights be enforced in UK courts without going to Strasbourg first.

12.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
12.q: Ella, aged 1 month, is admitted with poor feeding. Her respiratory rate is 72 breaths/min and heart rate 150 beats/min. She is not crying. Which interpretation is correct?
o: Her heart rate is within range and her breathing is rapid
Her heart rate is raised and her breathing is normal
Both values are within normal limits for a 1-month-old
Both values are raised and she needs immediate review
12.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1): at 1 month, the approximate normal respiratory rate is 25 to 60 breaths/min and heart rate 110 to 180 beats/min. A respiratory rate of 72 is above range (tachypnoea), while a heart rate of 150 is within range and below the NICE NG143 amber threshold of 160 for infants under 12 months.

n.1: A heart rate of 150 is within the 110 to 180 range at 1 month, and it is the breathing rate that is raised.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 72 is above the upper limit of 60 at 1 month.
n.3: A heart rate of 150 is within range at 1 month; the abnormal value is the respiratory rate.

12.q: Jason, 26, attends the emergency department for the third time this year with injuries after drinking heavily. He tells the nurse that as a child he lived with domestic violence and that his father misused alcohol. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to use this information?
o: Refer him to children's social care about what happened in his childhood
Tell him his drinking is a choice that is unrelated to his childhood
Recognise that early adversity may underlie his current risks, and offer support
Treat his injuries and avoid discussing his past, as it is not relevant now
12.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): adults with 4+ ACEs were more likely to be high-risk drinkers and victims of violence. NMC P2.6: understand the importance of early years and childhood experiences on later physical, mental and behavioural health and wellbeing.

n.0: Jason is an adult; children's social care is for current concerns about children.
n.1: This is dismissive and contradicts evidence linking ACEs with high-risk drinking.
n.3: The ACE evidence links childhood adversity with health-harming behaviours, so it is relevant to his care.

12.q: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should admit a new patient. Patients and visitors nearby are watching. Lorna is the nurse in charge. What should Lorna do first?
o: Admit the new patient herself so that the disagreement is no longer relevant
Calmly ask them both to step into the office and talk the issue through there
Tell both nurses firmly that they will each be reported to the ward manager
Leave them to resolve it between themselves, as they are both experienced nurses
12.w: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and the team's professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3 calm presence when dealing with conflict; Code 20.1 and 20.3). The admission can then be allocated clearly.

n.0: Taking the task herself avoids the conflict without addressing it and adds to her workload.
n.2: Threatening sanctions in public escalates the conflict and does not resolve the allocation.
n.3: A public argument is affecting patients now; the nurse in charge needs to intervene.

12.q: Zara, 3, needs urgent but not life-threatening surgery. Her two mothers were civil partners when Zara was conceived through licensed fertility clinic treatment. The birth mother is abroad and cannot be reached; Zara's other mother, who is named on the birth certificate, is present. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Treat Zara under the emergency necessity principle without anyone's consent
Apply to court for an order, as the non-birth mother has no automatic parental responsibility
Obtain consent from the other mother, who is a legal parent with parental responsibility
Delay surgery until the birth mother can be reached to give consent
12.w: Under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008, a woman in a civil partnership with the birth mother at the time of licensed treatment is the child's second female parent, and she has parental responsibility (Children Act 1989 s2(1A)). Her consent is valid.

n.0: Necessity applies when no one with authority to consent is available; a parent with PR is present.
n.1: No court order is needed: the second female parent holds PR automatically in these circumstances.
n.3: Both legal parents hold PR here, so waiting for the birth mother would cause unnecessary delay to urgent surgery.

12.q: Kwame, 64, has motor neurone disease and is now thought to be in his last days. The team are deciding who should talk with him about his prognosis. He knows the ward sister well and trusts her, and she has experience of these conversations. According to NICE NG31, what should guide the choice of professional?
o: Their seniority and grade within the treating medical team
Which professional the family would prefer to lead the conversation
Which professional first made the diagnosis of his condition
Their competence and confidence, and their rapport with the person
12.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.2.2: identify the most appropriate available multiprofessional team member to explain the dying person's prognosis, based on the professional's competence and confidence and their rapport with the person.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.2.2 does not base the choice on grade; a senior doctor without rapport may not be the most appropriate person.
n.1: Family views matter, but NG31 rec 1.2.2 bases the choice on the professional's competence, confidence and rapport with the person.
n.2: The diagnosing clinician is not the NG31 criterion; competence, confidence and rapport are.

12.q: A practice nurse is assessing Sami, 18 months, who has a fever and is irritable. His skin is dark brown and the nurse cannot see any rash on his limbs or trunk. According to NICE NG240, where else should she check for petechiae?
o: The conjunctivae
The scalp hairline
The tongue
The soles of the feet
12.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) rec 1.1.12: check all over the body including nappy areas, and look for petechiae in the conjunctivae because rashes can be hard to detect on brown, black or tanned skin.

n.1: The scalp is not a site NG240 highlights; dense hair makes petechiae harder to see.
n.2: NG240 does not name the tongue; the conjunctivae are specified.
n.3: The soles are checked as part of the whole body, but NG240 names the conjunctivae as the site to check on darker skin.

12.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
12.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

12.q: Mr Brennan, 74, was assessed last month as lacking capacity to manage his complex investments. Today he tells the nurse he would like fish rather than chicken for lunch and wants to wear his own clothes. Which statement is correct?
o: His financial attorney should make these choices on his behalf
He lacks capacity for all decisions until a new assessment is completed
He can choose his lunch but not his clothing without an assessment
He may be able to make these decisions, as capacity is decision-specific
12.w: MCA 2005 s2(1): lack of capacity relates to a specific matter at the material time. Being unable to manage complex investments says nothing about everyday choices, which he is presumed able to make (s1(2)).

n.0: A property and financial affairs attorney has no authority over personal welfare choices such as food or clothing.
n.1: Incapacity is not global; a finding about one decision does not transfer to others.
n.2: There is no basis for treating clothing differently from food; both are everyday choices he is presumed able to make.

12.q: Krishna, 64, is a Hindu man on an acute ward. During his assessment he asks for a female nurse not to wash him and to wash with running water rather than a bowl. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record his preferences in the care plan and arrange care to meet them
Ask his family to come in and do all his washing during visiting time
Tell him staffing makes it difficult and he will be washed by whoever is free
Explain that a bowl wash is the standard ward practice for every patient
12.w: Code 1.1, 4.1 and Annexe B 3.4: treat people as individuals and respect their cultural and religious preferences in personal care, documenting them so that care can be arranged to meet them where possible.

n.1: Families may help if they wish, but care remains the nurse's responsibility.
n.2: Dismissing his preference fails to respect his dignity and beliefs.
n.3: Standard practice should adapt to individual needs where reasonably possible.

12.q: Within 24 hours, three patients in the same six-bed bay on an elderly care ward develop sudden vomiting and diarrhoea. None was admitted with these symptoms. What should the nurse in charge do first?
o: Phone UKHSA directly to notify a notifiable disease
Send stool samples and wait for results before reporting
Inform the IPC team promptly about a possible outbreak
Report it at the weekly ward governance meeting
12.w: Two or more linked cases in the same area suggest an outbreak (P2.12, communicable disease surveillance). The IPC team should be informed promptly so that bay closure, isolation and sampling can be coordinated (NIPCM ch 2.1); the IPC team leads outbreak management and liaises with the UKHSA health protection team where needed.

n.0: Statutory notification is the registered medical practitioner's duty; the nurse in charge's first step in a ward outbreak is the IPC team, who coordinate control measures and any health protection liaison.
n.1: Samples are needed, but waiting for results before reporting delays outbreak control.
n.3: A weekly meeting delays control measures while the infection spreads.

12.q: For a week, Sean, a staff nurse, has noticed that a colleague often takes long breaks, leaving her bay without registered nurse cover. Two call bells went unanswered yesterday. Which approach is most appropriate for Sean to take?
o: Talk to her privately, describe what he has seen and its effect on patients
Report her to the ward manager without discussing the matter with her first
Mention the long breaks during the safety huddle so the whole team is aware
Cover her bay himself during her breaks to make sure that patients are safe
12.w: Effective confrontation is private, specific and focused on behaviour and its impact on patients, inviting the other person's view and agreeing a solution. Escalation follows if the problem continues (AnnexA.4.2.4 appropriate and effective confrontation strategies; Code 8 and 16).

n.1: Escalation may be needed later, but a direct conversation is the proportionate first step.
n.2: Raising an individual's behaviour in front of the team is humiliating and may provoke defensiveness.
n.3: Covering for her hides the problem and stretches his own care.

12.q: Mrs Cole, 76, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. She tells the nurse that her main wish is to be able to get to the bathroom by herself before she goes home. Which care plan goal best reflects a person-centred, evaluable plan?
o: She will walk to the bathroom with her frame and one helper by Friday
Staff will encourage Mrs Cole to mobilise as much as possible
Mrs Cole's mobility will be improved during her stay on the stroke unit
Mrs Cole will be independent in all activities before discharge
12.w: NMC proficiency P3.5 requires person-centred, evidence-based plans with agreed goals. A good goal is centred on the person's own priority, specific, measurable and time-bound, so progress can be evaluated (P3.15).

n.1: This describes a staff action, not an outcome for Mrs Cole.
n.2: 'Improved mobility' is vague, with no measure or timescale to evaluate against.
n.3: Full independence in all activities is not her stated goal and is unlikely to be realistic or measurable.

12.q: For three weeks the call bells in one bay on Kemi's ward have failed intermittently. Each failure has been reported as an incident, but estates staff say a full replacement needs trust funding. What is the most appropriate next step for Kemi as the nurse in charge?
o: Move patients who cannot use a call bell to beds nearer the nurses' station each shift
Keep reporting each failure as an incident until the estates team replaces the system
Write to the local newspaper about the delay to replacing the call bell system
Escalate to the ward manager so the risk can be assessed and added to the risk register
12.w: A persistent risk that cannot be fixed at ward level should be escalated so it is formally assessed, recorded on the organisation's risk register with an owner and controls, and reviewed (P6.3 local and national frameworks for managing and reporting risk; Code 16.1 and 25.1). Interim measures continue alongside escalation.

n.0: Moving patients is a sensible interim control but does not get the underlying risk managed or funded.
n.1: Incident reports record events; they do not on their own place a known, ongoing risk under managed review with an owner.
n.2: Going to the media before using internal escalation routes is not consistent with NMC raising concerns guidance.

12.q: Ellie, 5, is having a cannula inserted tomorrow. Today the play specialist uses a doll with a cannula to show Ellie what will happen and let her practise on it. Which approach is this?
o: Distraction and diversion
Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Therapeutic play
12.w: Annexe A 3.7: play therapy. Therapeutic play prepares children for procedures and helps them express feelings.

n.0: Distraction is used during the procedure; this prepares her beforehand.
n.1: CBT addresses thoughts and behaviour; this uses play to prepare.
n.2: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and goals.

12.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
12.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

12.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
12.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

12.q: During a ward teaching session on transmission-based precautions, a student nurse asks which route of transmission is responsible for most cross-infection in care settings, including spread via equipment and the patient's surroundings. Which answer is correct?
o: Airborne transmission via aerosols
Droplet transmission over short distances
Blood-borne transmission via sharps injuries
Contact transmission, direct or indirect
12.w: NIPCM ch 2 defines contact precautions as preventing spread by direct contact with the patient or indirectly from the immediate care environment, including care equipment, and states this is the most common route of cross-infection transmission.

n.0: Airborne spread applies to a smaller group of organisms such as measles and TB.
n.1: Droplet spread is important for respiratory pathogens but NIPCM names contact as the most common route.
n.2: Sharps injuries carry blood-borne virus risk to staff, but are not the main route of cross-infection between patients.

12.q: Jordan, 12, has cystic fibrosis and is in Year 7. His mother asks the children's CF nurse when they should start planning his move to adult services. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
o: From his 16th birthday
From Year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest
Once the adult team accepts the referral
In the 6 months before his 18th birthday
12.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.2.1: start planning for adulthood from Year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest, or immediately if a young person enters children's services close to the point of transfer.

n.0: Sixteen is later than NG43 advises; planning starts by Year 9.
n.2: Planning starts long before referral; it prepares the young person for the move.
n.3: Six months before 18 is far too late for gradual, developmentally appropriate planning.

12.q: Phyllis, 85, on a medical ward, has had three episodes of loose, watery stool (Bristol type 7) since this morning with no obvious cause. She started antibiotics 5 days ago. What is the priority action?
o: Wait for two more episodes before sending a sample
Give her prescribed loperamide and continue to monitor her
Move her nearer the toilet in the shared bay
Isolate her in a single room and send a stool sample
12.w: Unexplained diarrhoea, especially after antibiotics, may be infective (for example C. difficile). Isolate promptly in a single room with contact precautions, send a stool sample, and use soap and water for hand hygiene (NIPCM; Annexe B 6.4).

n.0: Delay increases the risk of spread and delays diagnosis.
n.1: Antidiarrhoeals can be harmful in suspected C. difficile and do not reduce spread.
n.2: Staying in a shared bay risks transmission to other patients.

12.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
12.q: Sophie, aged 18 months, has gastroenteritis. Which finding is a red flag sign that she is at increased risk of progressing to shock (NICE CG84)?
o: She has had three loose stools today
Her eyes appear sunken
She is thirsty and drinking eagerly
Her temperature is 37.9°C
12.w: NICE CG84 Table 1: red flag symptoms and signs of clinical dehydration include appearing unwell or deteriorating, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnoea and reduced skin turgor. Children with red flags need ORS only (no other oral fluids) and closer monitoring.

n.0: Loose stools are expected in gastroenteritis; their number alone is not a red flag sign.
n.2: Thirst is a feature of dehydration but not one of the red flag signs.
n.3: A mild fever is common in gastroenteritis and is not a dehydration red flag.

12.q: Fatima, 45, is admitted for an elective procedure. She asks that only female staff provide her intimate personal care because of her religious beliefs. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree to her request if her religion is recorded on the notes
Arrange female staff for her personal care where possible
Explain that personal care will be given by whoever is on duty that shift
Ask her to bring a female relative to give her personal care
12.w: Proficiency P1.14: provide non-discriminatory, person-centred, sensitive care reflecting people's values, beliefs and culture. Code 1.3 and 2.4; religion or belief is a protected characteristic (Equality Act s4).

n.0: Respecting a preference does not depend on paperwork; it should be accommodated where possible now.
n.2: This disregards her beliefs; P1.14 requires care that reflects people's values, beliefs and culture.
n.3: This shifts care onto family and may not be safe or what she wants.

12.q: Maya, 14, weighs 58 kg and has reached puberty. She has anaphylaxis with wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg after an IV antibiotic on the adolescent ward. Which IM adrenaline dose (1 mg/mL) is appropriate?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
1 mg (1 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
12.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): over 12 years the IM dose is 500 micrograms (0.5 mL), with 300 micrograms reserved for a child who is small or prepubertal. Maya is 58 kg and pubertal.

n.0: 150 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6 months to 6 years.
n.2: 1 mg IM is double the recommended maximum single IM dose.
n.3: 300 micrograms suits a 6-12 year old or a small, prepubertal over-12; Maya is neither.

12.q: Bernard, 74, has COPD with a prescribed target saturation of 88-92%, and his chart uses SpO2 Scale 2. He is on 2 L/min oxygen with SpO2 91%. RR 20, BP 132/84, pulse 88, alert, temperature 37.0°C. What is his NEWS2?
12.w: On Scale 2, SpO2 88-92% scores 0. Supplemental oxygen scores 2. RR 12-20, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert and temperature 36.1-38.0 all score 0. Total = 2 (RCP NEWS2 2017).

n.0: 0 omits the 2 points for supplemental oxygen.
n.1: 3 adds a point for SpO2, but 88-92% scores 0 on Scale 2.
n.2: 5 applies Scale 1 (91% = 3) to a patient with a prescribed 88-92% target.

12.q: Ms Grey, 34, has symptoms of a urinary tract infection and needs a urine sample sent for culture. She is independent and mobile. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after passing it
Discard the first part of the stream and collect the midstream urine
Collect the last few drops of urine at the end of passing it
Collect the first part of the urine stream into a clean pot
12.w: A clean-catch midstream specimen reduces contamination by skin and urethral organisms. The first part of the stream is discarded and the midstream portion collected into a sterile container, labelled and sent promptly (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Urine from the toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
n.2: The end of the stream is not the midstream sample required for culture.
n.3: First-catch urine carries urethral and skin organisms that contaminate a culture; it is the sample used for chlamydia testing, not for MSU culture.

12.q: At the end of a shift, which item is most important for Nurse Ben to include when handing over Mrs Webb, 77?
o: Her IV antibiotic is due at 18:00; her NEWS2 rose to 4
She was admitted four days ago from her own home
She enjoyed her lunch and watched television all afternoon
Her daughter visited during the afternoon
12.w: Annexe A 1.11: provide clear information when handing over care. Code 10.2 identify risks and problems; Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed.

n.1: Admission date is less urgent than outstanding care and deterioration.
n.2: Social details matter less than risks and time-critical care.
n.3: Visitor details are not the priority for safe handover.

12.q: Toby, 4, develops stridor, wheeze and widespread hives 10 minutes after eating a cashew at a children's day unit. His respiratory rate is 44 and his lips are swelling. The nurse has 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline. What IM dose should be given?
o: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
50 micrograms (0.05 mL)
12.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral thigh: 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms (0.15 mL); 6-12 years 300 micrograms; over 12 years 500 micrograms; under 6 months 100-150 micrograms.

n.0: 500 micrograms is the dose for over 12s and adults.
n.1: 300 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6-12 years; Toby is 4.
n.3: 50 micrograms is below every RCUK age band; under-dosing delays reversal of airway swelling.

12.q: Ruth, a staff nurse, is writing a referral to a dietitian for Mrs Smith, 63, who has lost weight after bowel surgery. The electronic record includes her full medical history, including a termination of pregnancy 30 years ago. What should Ruth include in the referral?
o: The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything except the termination of pregnancy
Her full medical history so the dietitian has the whole picture
A summary written after asking her family
12.w: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data. UK GDPR data minimisation also requires data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. Only information relevant to nutrition should be shared.

n.1: Removing one sensitive item still shares other irrelevant data; relevance, not sensitivity, decides what is sent.
n.2: Sending the full history exceeds what the dietitian needs and breaches the minimum necessary principle.
n.3: Families are not a source for a clinical referral, and involving them without consent breaches confidentiality.

12.q: Before the ambulance service arrives, off-duty nurse Imran stops at a multi-vehicle collision on a dual carriageway. Traffic is still moving past and one car is leaking fuel. Several people appear injured. What should Imran do first?
o: Start assessing the nearest injured person in the car that is leaking fuel
Check that the scene is safe, then call 999 and describe the incident clearly
Move all the injured people away from the vehicles to the hard shoulder
Leave the scene, as he is off duty and is not covered by trust indemnity
12.w: Code 15.1-15.3: offer help in an emergency within the limits of your knowledge and competence, taking account of your own safety. Scene safety comes first, then early alert to emergency services with clear information (the M/ETHANE structure) so the right response is sent (P6.12).

n.0: Approaching a leaking vehicle beside moving traffic before assessing danger risks creating another casualty.
n.2: Moving injured people without assessment can worsen injuries and exposes Imran to traffic.
n.3: The Code expects registrants to offer help in emergencies outside work, within competence and safety.

12.q: A staff nurse uses a public social media profile that states she is a registered nurse at the local hospital. Which post would most clearly breach the Code?
o: Sharing the NHS flu vaccination campaign with her followers
Celebrating her own nursing graduation with a family photo
Posting a link to an NMC consultation on the Code
Urging followers, as a nurse, to vote for a political party
12.w: Code 21.5: never use your status as a registered professional to promote causes that are not related to health. Code 20.7 also cautions against expressing personal political beliefs inappropriately.

n.0: Promoting a public health message is related to health and supports Code 3.1.
n.1: A personal photo with no patient information does not breach the Code.
n.2: Sharing professional regulatory information is not a breach.

12.q: Amira, 12, is in hospital after an appendicectomy. She shows the nurse messages from someone she met in an online game who says he is 14, asks her to keep their chats secret, move to a private app and send photos in her pyjamas. What should the nurse do?
o: Advise Amira to block the contact and reassure her parents
Tell Amira to stop using online games while in hospital
Recognise possible grooming and follow safeguarding procedures
Ask the contact directly through the app to confirm his age
12.w: Requests for secrecy, moving to a private platform and requests for images are signs of online grooming, which Working Together 2026 includes within child sexual abuse. The nurse should follow safeguarding procedures, preserve the messages and involve police (for example via a CEOP report) as advised.

n.0: Blocking the contact loses evidence and does not address possible abuse of Amira or others.
n.1: Restricting game use does not protect her or address the grooming.
n.3: Contacting the suspect could alert him and is not a nurse's role.

12.q: Fatima, 57, is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has no history of lung disease and her SpO2 is 90% on air. What target oxygen saturation range should be prescribed?
12.w: BTS oxygen guideline and NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.10.1: the target for most acutely ill adults is 94-98%.

n.0: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some people with COPD.
n.2: 92-96% is not the standard BTS adult target range.
n.3: Aiming for 98-100% risks hyperoxaemia; BTS notes higher saturations are associated with harm.

12.q: Mr Kapoor, 67, has capacity and has told Hayley, his nurse, that he does not want the proposed amputation and would prefer palliative wound care. On the ward round the surgeon starts to describe the operation date without asking his views. What should Hayley do?
o: Say that Mr Kapoor has shared views about the operation and invite him to explain them
Record Mr Kapoor's wishes in his nursing notes once the ward round has finished
Wait until after the ward round and then ask Mr Kapoor whether he has changed his mind
Tell the surgeon that Mr Kapoor has asked her to cancel the operation on his behalf
12.w: Advocacy means making sure the person's own voice is heard in decisions about their care (AnnexA.4.2.6.3; Code 3.4 act as an advocate for the vulnerable; Code 2.5 respect the right to refuse treatment). Inviting Mr Kapoor to speak supports his autonomy without speaking over him (MCA 2005 s1 principles).

n.1: Recording his wishes is necessary but does not ensure they are heard in the decision being made now.
n.2: Waiting allows a decision to be made without him; he has already expressed his wishes.
n.3: Hayley should not overstate or speak for him when he can speak for himself.

12.q: Sami, 9, has anaphylaxis after a bee sting during a hospital open day. The nurse has drawn up 300 micrograms of adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Where should it be injected?
o: Intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh
Intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle
Intramuscularly into the dorsogluteal muscle
Subcutaneously into the abdomen
12.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): give IM adrenaline early into the anterolateral thigh, which gives reliable absorption in children and adults.

n.1: The deltoid is a smaller muscle with less reliable absorption; RCUK specifies the anterolateral thigh.
n.2: The buttock carries a risk of sciatic nerve injury and slower absorption; RCUK specifies the thigh.
n.3: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less predictable than IM in a shocked child.

12.q: The son of Betty Walsh, 88, approaches Daniel, the nurse in charge, upset that his mother waited over an hour for pain relief this morning. He says he wants to complain. What is the most appropriate response from Daniel?
o: Ask him to put the complaint in writing before discussing it any further
Listen, apologise for the wait, check her pain now and explain how to complain
Explain that the ward was short-staffed, so the delay was nobody's fault
Move Mrs Walsh to another bay so that the complaint does not affect her care
12.w: Code 24.1-24.2: never let a complaint affect the care provided, and use complaints as a form of feedback to reflect and improve. Listening, apologising, dealing with the immediate need and explaining the complaints process is a compassionate, open response (Code 14; P6.9).

n.0: Complaints can be made verbally; insisting on writing first is obstructive and delays resolution.
n.2: Explaining causes can follow, but opening with a defence dismisses his concern and does not address his mother's pain now.
n.3: Moving her does not address the complaint or her pain and may itself disrupt her care.

12.q: A company representative gives a ward manager a single-site study of 20 patients, funded by the company, with no control group, reporting that its new catheter reduces infections. The manager wants to switch at once. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Switch now, as published evidence shows a clear benefit
Appraise the study's limits and seek stronger evidence first
Reject the product, as industry-funded studies are invalid
Switch now and audit infection rates after six months
12.w: Proficiency P1.7-P1.8: critically analyse research findings and think critically when applying evidence. Code 6.1 information must be evidence-based; small uncontrolled studies sit low in evidence hierarchies.

n.0: A small, uncontrolled, industry-funded study has a high risk of bias and does not justify a change alone.
n.2: Funding source raises the risk of bias but does not automatically invalidate a study; appraisal is needed.
n.3: Auditing after a change does not replace appraising whether the evidence supports the change.

12.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
12.q: Lucy, aged 11, has a sprained ankle. Her father asks whether he can give her aspirin at home, as that is what he takes. What should the nurse advise?
o: Aspirin is safe for sprains when it is taken with food
Aspirin can be given for up to 3 days and then stopped
Aspirin is safe at half the adult dose for children over 10
Do not give aspirin under 16 unless prescribed; use paracetamol
12.w: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless prescribed by a doctor (for example in Kawasaki disease), because of the risk of Reye's syndrome (NHS). Paracetamol or ibuprofen are suitable for a sprain.

n.0: Taking aspirin with food reduces stomach upset but does not remove the risk of Reye's syndrome.
n.1: Short courses still carry the risk; aspirin is avoided in under-16s unless prescribed.
n.2: There is no half-dose exception; aspirin is avoided in under-16s unless prescribed.

12.q: Nora, 80, is dying from heart failure in a nursing home. Tonight she has become restless, keeps pulling at her sheets and is groaning. She last passed urine 10 hours ago and her lower abdomen looks swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the GP to prescribe an antipsychotic for terminal delirium
Ask a relative to sit with her and see whether she settles overnight
Give the prescribed 'as required' midazolam to settle her agitation
Assess her for urinary retention and pain before giving sedation
12.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.11 and 1.5.23: agitation in isolation is sometimes associated with unrelieved pain or a full bladder or rectum; treat reversible causes of pain such as urinary retention before considering benzodiazepines or antipsychotics.

n.0: An antipsychotic is considered for delirium only after reversible causes such as urinary retention are explored (recs 1.5.25 and 1.5.27).
n.1: Company can help, but it leaves a likely full bladder untreated; reversible causes should be assessed first.
n.2: Sedation first would mask a reversible cause; NG31 rec 1.5.23 says agitation may reflect a full bladder or unrelieved pain.

12.q: A practice nurse in England plans to share concerns about Leo, 5, with children's social care under the s16LA duty. She intends to share whether or not his father agrees. How should she approach the conversation with the father?
o: Leave him uninformed, as the duty does not require openness
Ask for his consent, then withhold if he refuses it
Ask for his consent, then share anyway if he refuses it
Explain openly what will be shared and why, not asking consent
12.w: The statutory guidance says that where the lawful basis is public task or legal obligation, practitioners should avoid seeking consent if they intend to share anyway, and should not imply that the family's agreement decides the matter. Where safe, they should be open and transparent about what is shared and why.

n.0: Practitioners should be transparent with families where it is safe to do so.
n.1: Lack of consent is not a reason to withhold information under the duty.
n.2: Seeking consent that will then be overridden is misleading and is discouraged by the guidance.

12.q: Frank Ellis, 74, uses a walking frame and fell once at home last month. He has capacity and wants to walk to the day room for lunch. His daughter asks the nurse to keep him in his chair so he cannot fall again. Which response best reflects positive risk management?
o: Let Mr Ellis walk to the day room after he signs a disclaimer accepting the risk of falling
Arrange for him to use a wheelchair to reach the day room until physiotherapy can review him
Agree with the daughter and keep him seated at lunchtimes until he is discharged home
Agree a plan with Mr Ellis for supervised walking with his frame and record the discussion
12.w: Positive risk management weighs benefits and harms with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so they can do what matters to them, rather than removing all activity (P6.10 risk management versus risk aversion). Mr Ellis has capacity, so his decision is respected (MCA 2005 s1), and the plan and discussion are documented (Code 10).

n.0: A disclaimer does not manage the risk or remove the nurse's duty of care; it replaces planning with paperwork.
n.1: Using a wheelchair when he can walk with his frame reduces independence and mobility without a clinical reason.
n.2: Keeping him seated is risk aversion: it removes activity he values, causes deconditioning and overrides the choice of a person with capacity.

12.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is concerned that a planned reduction in local district nursing posts will affect housebound patients. He wants to use his professional knowledge to influence the decision. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Refuse to accept new referrals until the reduction in posts is withdrawn
Share named patients' stories with a local newspaper to raise awareness
Write to his MP with anonymised evidence about the impact on care
Tell his patients during home visits that they should vote against the council
12.w: Political awareness and influence are part of the nurse's role (P7.13; P5.12). Engaging with elected representatives using anonymised evidence is legitimate, while the Code requires confidentiality (Code 5) and that personal political views are not expressed inappropriately to people in his care (Code 20.7).

n.0: Refusing referrals puts patients at risk and is not a professional way to influence policy.
n.1: Sharing identifiable patient information breaches confidentiality (Code 5).
n.3: Expressing personal political views to patients during care breaches Code 20.7.

12.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
12.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

12.q: Children's social care starts a Family Help assessment for Ollie, 6, after a nurse's referral about neglect. His father asks the nurse how long the assessment can take. Under Working Together 2026, what is the maximum time from referral to a decision on the assessment?
o: 35 working days from the point of referral
45 working days from the point of referral
10 working days from the point of referral
15 working days from the point of referral
12.w: Working Together 2026 states that the time from referral to the decision at the end of the assessment should be no longer than 45 working days; if it exceeds this, the lead practitioner should record the reasons.

n.0: 35 working days is not a Working Together timescale.
n.2: Ten working days is the core group timescale after an initial child protection conference.
n.3: Fifteen working days is the timescale for an initial child protection conference after the strategy discussion.

12.q: Mr Dunn, 66, is going home on a new medicine. He says he 'doesn't get on with reading' and has left his leaflet unopened. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explain in plain words with pictures, then use teach-back
Explain it once in full medical terms to be accurate
Ask the pharmacist to post a copy of the leaflet to him
Give him a second copy of the leaflet in larger print
12.w: Proficiency P2.10: provide information in accessible ways; Annexe A 2.2 clear language and appropriate materials; Annexe A 2.6 repetition and positive reinforcement; Code 7.4 check understanding.

n.1: Medical terms reduce understanding; Code 7.1 requires terms people can understand.
n.2: Posting the same written information will not help him understand it.
n.3: Larger print does not address difficulty with reading.

12.q: Ruby, 19 months, moves around by bottom shuffling and does not yet walk. She can pull to stand briefly. Her father also bottom shuffled and walked at 22 months. Ruby's other development is normal. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Advise a baby walker to encourage her to bear weight and step
Note the family history and arrange a review for when she reaches 3 years
Reassure and recheck at the 2-year review because shufflers often walk late
Refer for assessment because she is not walking at 18 months
12.w: Not walking by 18 months (corrected for gestational age) is one of the delayed motor milestones listed in NICE NG62 rec 1.3.5, and rec 1.3.6 advises referring all children with delayed motor milestones to a child development service for further assessment. Bottom shufflers and children with a family history often walk later, but assessment confirms the normal variant and excludes causes such as cerebral palsy or a muscle disorder, rather than assuming one.

n.0: Baby walkers do not help children learn to walk and carry a risk of injury, so they are not advised.
n.1: Waiting until 3 years would delay assessment of a red flag by well over a year.
n.2: Bottom shuffling makes late walking more likely but does not remove the need to assess a child not walking at 18 months; waiting another 5 months delays diagnosis if there is a cause.

12.q: Imogen, a staff nurse, sees a colleague starting to move Mr Price, 84, from bed to chair using an under-arm drag lift. His care plan states that he must be hoisted. What should Imogen do?
o: Ask her colleague to stop, help hoist Mr Price, then discuss it privately
Help her colleague complete the transfer and mention it to the ward manager later
Speak to her colleague about it privately at the end of the shift
Report the colleague on the incident system without speaking to her about it
12.w: Code 16 requires acting without delay if there is a risk to patient safety. Imogen should stop the unsafe practice first, ensure Mr Price is moved safely according to his care plan, and then challenge constructively in private, agreeing any learning needs (P5.9 challenge and give constructive feedback about care delivered by others). Two steps: make safe, then feedback.

n.1: Joining an unsafe technique exposes Mr Price and both staff to injury.
n.2: Waiting until later allows the unsafe transfer to continue now.
n.3: Reporting may be appropriate, but the immediate risk must be stopped first and a direct conversation supports learning.

12.q: Derek, 59, has a history of alcohol misuse. He has eaten almost nothing for 7 days and his BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Nutrition support is planned. Using NICE CG32 criteria, what is his refeeding risk and the appropriate starting approach?
o: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Low risk: start at full requirements of 25-35 kcal/kg/day
Moderate risk: start at 50% of requirements without thiamin
No risk: offer normal ward meals without any monitoring
12.w: NICE CG32: high refeeding risk includes two or more of BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little or no intake for over 5 days, or alcohol misuse. Derek has three. Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly, and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days, with electrolyte monitoring.

n.1: Full requirements in a high-risk person can precipitate refeeding syndrome.
n.2: He meets the high-risk criteria, and thiamin is needed.
n.3: Unmonitored feeding ignores his high refeeding risk.

12.q: Mr Moore, 83, has delirium. He is shouting, pulling at his cannula and swinging his arms at staff. No one has been hurt yet. What should the nurse do first?
o: Request haloperidol as the first step to calm him down quickly
Restrain his arms so the cannula is not pulled out
Ask security to stay with him until he settles down
Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and look for causes
12.w: NICE CG103: if a person with delirium is distressed or a risk to themselves or others, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation; consider short-term haloperidol if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate. Underlying causes such as pain, retention or hypoxia should be sought (Annexe B 1.1.5).

n.0: Medication is considered when de-escalation fails or is inappropriate, not as the first step.
n.1: Physical restraint is a last resort and may worsen agitation and delirium.
n.2: Security presence is restrictive and does not address his distress or its cause.

12.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
12.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

12.q: Callum, 15, has type 1 diabetes and has been admitted twice with DKA this year. His parents say he used to manage well but now skips insulin when out with friends. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask his parents to take over all his insulin injections until he is 18
Warn Callum firmly that further admissions will lead to a safeguarding referral
Arrange for him to move to the adult diabetes service now to promote independence
Speak with Callum alone, explore what gets in the way, and plan goals with him
12.w: Adolescence brings a drive for autonomy, peer influence and risk taking, and adherence often falls. A non-judgemental conversation alone with the young person, exploring barriers (for example embarrassment in front of friends) and agreeing realistic goals, supports self-management and health behaviour change (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Removing all responsibility undermines developing independence and is unlikely to be accepted by a 15-year-old.
n.1: Threats are not a therapeutic approach and may further reduce engagement.
n.2: Transition is planned gradually (NICE NG43), not used as a response to poor adherence.

12.q: A nurse is deciding whether to share information about Yasmin, 13, who is living in a refuge with her mother after fleeing domestic abuse. Under the s16LA statutory guidance, in which circumstance may the nurse decide not to share particular information?
o: When Yasmin's father, who has parental responsibility, objects
When the family has not given consent to the sharing
When sharing would be more detrimental to Yasmin than not sharing
When the nurse feels uncomfortable about the possible consequences
12.w: The duty does not apply in extremely limited circumstances where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing, for example where disclosing a refuge address would place the child at immediate risk (statutory guidance, Limitation: detriment to the child). Other relevant information should still be shared and the decision recorded.

n.0: Parental objection is not a reason to withhold under the duty.
n.1: Lack of consent is expressly not a reason to withhold.
n.3: Practitioner discomfort is not a reason to withhold; the guidance says seek prompt advice instead.

12.q: During the morning medication round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the drug trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. Several injections are still due. What should Lewis do with the full container?
o: Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Leave it open and start a second container beside it on the trolley
Press the contents down to make room for the remaining needles
Use it until it is completely full, then seal it before lunch
12.w: NIPCM ch 1.9: sharps containers must be disposed of when the manufacturer's fill line is reached, labelled with point of origin and dates of assembly and disposal, and use the temporary closure when not in use.

n.1: A full container left open is a sharps hazard; it should be locked and removed.
n.2: Pushing down sharps risks a needlestick injury and overfills the container.
n.3: Filling past the fill line risks protruding sharps and injury.

12.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity and peripheral vascular disease. After a full explanation of the risks, he declines a recommended below-knee amputation, saying he would rather take his chances. The team thinks this is an unwise choice. Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies most directly?
o: Making an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Any act done for a person must be in their best interests
The less restrictive option must be considered first
All practicable steps must be taken to help the person decide
12.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Mr Pearce has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

n.1: Best interests (s1(5)) applies to acts for people who lack capacity; Mr Pearce has capacity.
n.2: The less restrictive principle (s1(6)) applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.
n.3: Supporting decision-making (s1(3)) has already been met by the full explanation; the issue now is respecting an unwise choice.

12.q: A laboratory scientist phones the ward with a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L for Mr Shaw. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to take this result?
o: Ask the laboratory to email the result to the doctor directly
Remember it and tell the doctor at the next ward round
Write it on the handover sheet for the night team to act on
Write it down, read it back, then tell the doctor at once
12.w: Annexe A 1.9 and 1.11: share verbal information clearly. Writing a telephoned result down and reading it back confirms it was heard correctly, and a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L needs the doctor told at once (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.0: Email may not be seen promptly; the nurse must act on it now.
n.1: Relying on memory risks error, and waiting delays urgent treatment.
n.2: A critical result needs immediate action, not handover.

12.q: Ella, 9, has moderate DKA and is not shocked. She received a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 minutes and her IV deficit and maintenance fluids started 40 minutes ago. The registrar asks when the insulin infusion should begin. What does BSPED advise?
o: Start the infusion 1-2 hours after IV fluids began, with no bolus
Start the infusion at the same time as the first fluid bolus
Give an insulin bolus now, then start the infusion
Wait until her pH is above 7.3 before starting any insulin
12.w: BSPED DKA guideline (2021): start IV insulin infusion 1-2 hours after beginning IV fluids, at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour, and do not give an insulin bolus, because early insulin and boluses may increase the risk of cerebral oedema.

n.1: Insulin started with the first fluids is linked to higher cerebral oedema risk; BSPED delays it 1-2 hours.
n.2: BSPED says do not give bolus doses of insulin.
n.3: Insulin is needed to switch off ketone production; waiting for pH to normalise would prolong DKA.

12.q: Mr Bello, 30, gave verbal consent for a urinary catheter to be inserted. Partway through, he becomes distressed and says, 'Stop, I don't want this any more.' The nurse is concerned that his bladder is still full. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the procedure, then discuss his concerns and the options
Finish quickly because stopping now would cause more discomfort
Continue, because consent was obtained before the procedure began
Pause, then restart once a colleague is present to reassure him
12.w: Consent is ongoing and a person with capacity may withdraw it at any point (Code 2.5 and 4.2). The nurse should stop, explore his worries, explain the risks of not proceeding and agree a plan with him, then document the discussion.

n.1: Completing a procedure after consent is withdrawn is treatment without consent, however brief.
n.2: Earlier consent does not continue once it has been withdrawn by a person with capacity.
n.3: Restarting without fresh consent overrides his refusal; a colleague's presence does not supply consent.

12.q: Baby Isaac was born at 38 weeks. His mother takes labetalol for hypertension in pregnancy. Isaac breastfed at 40 minutes old. At 3 hours, before the second feed, his blood glucose is 1.6 mmol/L. He is alert, warm and showing feeding cues. Which action does the BAPM framework support?
o: Give 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg with a supported breastfeed
Give formula at 150 mL/kg/day and recheck glucose in 6 hours
Continue feeding with no further glucose checks
Start IV 10% glucose before the next feed
12.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice points 16 and 18: if the first pre-feed glucose is 1.0-1.9 mmol/L with no abnormal signs (Flowchart B), buccal 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg may be given alongside feeding support, with repeat measurement.

n.1: Formula volumes in the first 24 hours are 40-60 mL/kg/day, and a 6-hour wait is too long.
n.2: A baby at risk with glucose of 1.6 mmol/L needs treatment and repeat measurement.
n.3: IV glucose is for severe (below 1.0 mmol/L) or persistent hypoglycaemia, or abnormal signs, after medical review.

12.q: A practice nurse invites people with a BMI over 40 to an intensive weight-management programme rather than offering it to the whole practice population. Which advantage is associated with this high-risk approach?
o: It tackles the social influences on behaviour in the wider community
Those invited are often more motivated, as their personal risk is high
It removes the need to assess each person's individual risk factors
It brings the largest fall in disease across the whole population
12.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: Epidemiological basis for preventive strategies: the high-risk approach may be more cost-effective than population-wide approaches and targets people who are more motivated to change their behaviour; the population approach achieves risk reduction at population level. NICE PH49 (2014) rec 9: high-intensity interventions for people at high risk, for example a BMI over 40.

n.0: Addressing social influences on the whole community is a feature of the population approach.
n.2: A high-risk approach depends on identifying individuals by assessing their risk.
n.3: A large fall in total disease is the strength of the population approach, not a high-risk approach.

12.q: Isla, 9, has a fever and a sore throat. At an urgent treatment centre her father says he gave her one of his aspirin tablets last night and asks if he can continue. What should the nurse advise?
o: Stop the aspirin and use paracetamol or ibuprofen if she is distressed
Continue the aspirin, as the restriction applies under 5s
Give the aspirin with food to protect her stomach
Continue the aspirin at half the adult dose until the fever settles
12.w: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless prescribed by a doctor (for example for Kawasaki disease) because of the risk of Reye's syndrome. NICE NG143: use paracetamol or ibuprofen if a febrile child is distressed.

n.1: The aspirin restriction applies to all children under 16, not only under 5s.
n.2: Food protects the stomach but does not address the Reye's syndrome risk.
n.3: A reduced dose does not remove the Reye's syndrome risk in under 16s.

12.q: Priya is 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She asks the practice nurse when she will first meet a health visitor under the Healthy Child Programme in England. What is the correct answer?
o: At the new baby review about 10 to 14 days after the birth
At an antenatal review from 28 weeks of pregnancy
At the 6 to 8 week review, alongside the baby's physical examination
At the 12-month review, when development is first checked
12.w: The Healthy Child Programme in England has five mandated health visitor reviews: antenatal (from 28 weeks), new birth, 6 to 8 weeks, 12 months (9 to 15 months) and 2 to 2.5 years. Health visitors first make contact in pregnancy, around 28 weeks, through an antenatal review, ideally face to face at home (DHSC/OHID, Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme, Part 2, Feb 2026).

n.0: The new baby review is the second mandated contact, not the first.
n.2: The 6 to 8 week review comes later, after the antenatal and new birth reviews.
n.3: The 12-month review is the fourth mandated contact.

12.q: Pharmacy has not yet collected four out-of-date diamorphine ampoules from a ward's CD cupboard. A nurse suggests destroying them in a denaturing kit with another registered nurse to tidy the cupboard before an audit. What is the correct action?
o: Destroy them in a denaturing kit with a second registered nurse
Keep them segregated and recorded until an authorised witness attends
Destroy them and record it once the ward manager has countersigned
Return them to pharmacy in the sealed internal post
12.w: NICE NG46: stock Schedule 2 controlled drugs may only be destroyed in the presence of an authorised witness (for example someone appointed by the CD accountable officer). Until then they stay in the CD cupboard, clearly segregated and recorded.

n.0: A colleague who is not an authorised witness cannot witness destruction of stock Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: A ward manager is not an authorised witness by virtue of the role, and recording after the event does not fix this.
n.3: Internal post is not a secure, auditable transport route for Schedule 2 CDs.

12.q: Kyle, a staff nurse, notices that Bev, a healthcare assistant, has become quiet and withdrawn since a relative criticised her in front of colleagues. Bev's care remains of a good standard. What is the most appropriate way for Kyle to support and motivate her?
o: Give Bev lighter tasks for the next few shifts so that she can recover
Speak with Bev privately, acknowledge her good care and ask how she is
Report Bev's change in mood to the ward manager for a formal welfare review
Tell Bev that complaints are part of the job and she should not take it personally
12.w: Leaders guide, support and motivate others (P5.6) and the Code asks registrants to work cooperatively and support the staff they are responsible for (Code 8, 25.2). Specific recognition and a private, supportive conversation help restore confidence and show that her work is valued.

n.0: Changing her work without discussion may suggest a lack of confidence in her.
n.2: Escalating to a formal process before talking with her is disproportionate.
n.3: Dismissing her feelings is unsupportive and unlikely to restore motivation.

12.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
12.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

12.q: Ethan, 7, is autistic and is admitted for elective surgery tomorrow. His father says Ethan becomes very distressed by noise, bright lights and unexpected changes. Which plan best reflects reasonable adjustments for Ethan?
o: A bay near the nurses' station so staff can observe him closely
A quiet side room, visual timetable and his father's routines
Admission to the general paediatric bay with other children
Sedation on arrival so that he does not become distressed
12.w: The Equality Act 2010 (s20) requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people, including autistic children. Adjustments include a quiet environment, preparation with visual supports, predictable routines and using the family's knowledge of the child (NG213 person-centred care; NHS reasonable adjustment guidance).

n.0: A busy area near the nurses' station increases noise, light and interruptions that distress Ethan.
n.2: A busy general bay increases sensory overload and unpredictability.
n.3: Routine sedation is a restrictive intervention that does not address his needs and needs a clinical indication.

12.q: Sunita, 59, is admitted to a surgical ward for elective knee surgery. She is mobile, has no history of pressure damage and her skin is intact. The ward has several types of support surface available. According to NICE CG179, which mattress should she be given?
o: High-specification foam mattress
Sheepskin mattress topper
Water-filled mattress overlay
Standard hospital foam mattress
12.w: NICE CG179: use a high-specification foam mattress for all adults admitted to secondary care, and consider a dynamic support surface if one is not sufficient for those at high risk.

n.1: Sheepskins are not the recommended pressure-redistributing surface for adults.
n.2: Water-filled overlays are not the CG179 standard support surface.
n.3: A standard foam mattress does not meet the CG179 recommendation.

12.q: Mrs Gill, 87, has delirium and lacks capacity to understand her risk of falling. At night she repeatedly tries to climb out of bed and is unsteady. A healthcare assistant suggests putting the bed rails up. Which action best follows the least restrictive principle?
o: Request a sedative to help her stay in bed at night
Raise both bed rails while she is asleep at night
Tuck the sheets in tightly so she cannot get out
Use a low bed with a crash mat and closer observation
12.w: MCA 2005 s1(6): before acting, consider whether the purpose can be achieved as effectively in a way less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom of action. A low bed, crash mat and closer observation reduce injury risk without confining her; rails may increase harm if she climbs over them.

n.0: Sedation to keep her in bed is chemical restraint and may worsen delirium and falls risk.
n.1: Bed rails restrict her movement and may increase the height and severity of a fall if she climbs over them.
n.2: Tucking sheets to prevent her leaving bed is a form of restraint and risks entrapment.

12.q: Before Leo's 2 to 2.5 year review, the health visiting team sends his parents a questionnaire about his communication, motor, problem-solving and personal-social skills. What is this tool?
o: The Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3)
The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ)
The Schedule of Growing Skills (SGS II)
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale
12.w: Parents are sent the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3) to complete before the 9 to 12 month and 2 to 2.5 year reviews (NHS, baby reviews; Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme 2026 also names ASQ for the 12-month and 2 to 2.5 year reviews).

n.1: The SDQ is a behavioural screening questionnaire for older children, not the standard tool at these reviews.
n.2: The SGS II is a professional-administered developmental assessment, not the parent questionnaire sent before reviews.
n.3: The Edinburgh scale screens parents for postnatal depression, not child development.

12.q: Phyllis, 92, dies peacefully in a nursing home. Her death was expected and a DNACPR discussion is documented. The registered nurse, who is trained and competent, begins verification of death. For how long, at minimum, should Phyllis be observed to establish irreversible cardiorespiratory arrest?
o: 10 minutes
1 minute
2 minutes
5 minutes
12.w: Hospice UK/RCN, Care after death: Registered Nurse Verification of Expected Adult Death (6th edition, 2024): observe for a minimum of five minutes to establish irreversible cardiorespiratory arrest; any spontaneous return of cardiac or respiratory activity prompts a further five minutes of observation.

n.0: Ten minutes is longer than required; a further 5 minutes is needed only if spontaneous activity returns.
n.1: One minute is the minimum time for checking the absence of a central pulse and of heart sounds, within the longer observation period.
n.2: Two minutes is shorter than the minimum observation period set in the RNVoEAD guidance.

12.q: A children's ward in England introduces a rule limiting parents to two hours of visiting a day to reduce noise. The parents of Lola, 2, who is distressed when they leave, complain that this breaches their human rights. Which article of the Human Rights Act 1998 is most directly engaged?
o: Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 2, the right to life
Article 8, respect for private and family life
12.w: Article 8 (Schedule 1, Human Rights Act 1998) protects respect for private and family life. A blanket restriction separating a young child from her parents engages it; as a qualified right, any interference must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

n.0: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, which the visiting rule does not involve.
n.1: Article 3 is engaged by serious ill-treatment; a visiting rule is better analysed as an interference with family life.
n.2: Article 2 concerns the protection of life, not family contact.

12.q: On admission, Gemma, 35, lists citalopram as her only regular medicine. When asked about other products, she says she has been taking St John's wort from a health food shop for low mood. What should the nurse do?
o: Record it as a herbal product that needs no further review or action
Remove it from her locker and dispose of it in the sharps bin
