Record it and inform the prescriber, as it interacts with citalopram
Advise her to double her citalopram dose instead of using it
12.w: Medicines reconciliation includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5; P4.15). St John's wort taken with an SSRI such as citalopram increases the risk of serotonin syndrome and interacts with many other drugs, so it is documented and the prescriber or pharmacist informed.

n.0: Herbal products can cause significant interactions and must be reviewed.
n.1: Patients' own products are not removed without consent, and sharps bins are not for medicines.
n.3: Changing a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision and could cause toxicity.

12.q: Which communication tool is widely used in UK healthcare to structure an urgent telephone escalation to a doctor about a deteriorating person?
o: SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan
PDSA: plan, do, study, act
SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, timed
SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation
12.w: SBAR is the standard structured tool used across the NHS for escalation, giving the listener the situation, relevant background, the nurse's assessment and a clear recommendation or request (Annexe A 4.2.6.2 appropriate escalation).

n.0: SOAP is a format for documenting a clinical encounter, not for escalation calls.
n.1: PDSA is the Model for Improvement cycle used in quality improvement.
n.2: SMART describes how to write goals or objectives.

12.q: Freddie, 2, weighs 12 kg and has had gastroenteritis for two days. He has dry mucous membranes and is passing less urine, but he is alert with normal skin turgor and capillary refill. The plan is oral rehydration solution (ORS) for clinical dehydration. What volume should be given for rehydration?
o: 1200 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance
600 mL over 24 hours, including maintenance
120 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance
600 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance
12.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s: for clinical dehydration without red flags give low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, in small frequent amounts. 50 mL/kg x 12 kg = 600 mL.

n.0: 1200 mL is 100 mL/kg, the IV deficit used for a child who was shocked at presentation.
n.1: Spreading 600 mL over 24 hours as total intake ignores maintenance and corrects the deficit too slowly.
n.2: 120 mL is 10 mL/kg, far below the CG84 rehydration volume.

12.q: Lily, 6, has a life-limiting neurodegenerative condition. A newly qualified nurse sees 'Advance Care Plan' in her notes and assumes this means Lily is not for resuscitation. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: An Advance Care Plan is the same document as a DNACPR order
An Advance Care Plan is a legal order made by the family court
An Advance Care Plan applies once Lily is in the last days of life
An Advance Care Plan covers wishes and care; it is not a DNACPR order
12.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.14: all children with life-limiting conditions should have an Advance Care Plan in their record (wishes, place of care, management of life-threatening events) and it should not be confused with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order. Resuscitate unless a DNACPR order is in place.

n.0: NG61 says the Advance Care Plan should not be confused with a DNACPR order.
n.1: An Advance Care Plan is agreed with the child and family and the team, not made by a court.
n.2: Advance Care Planning starts early and is reviewed regularly, not only in the last days.

12.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
12.q: Leo, aged 9, is on a children's ward. He has two moderate to high risk criteria for sepsis and no high risk criteria. Blood tests including lactate have been taken. What does NICE NG254 advise about review and antibiotics?
o: Review on the next ward round, with antibiotics if fever persists
Antibiotics within 1 hour and an urgent critical care referral
Review results within 1 hour; antibiotic decision within 3 hours
Discharge home with safety-netting advice if his lactate is normal
12.w: NICE NG254 (recs 1.7.12 to 1.7.14): with 2 or more moderate to high risk criteria, carry out blood tests and arrange clinician review of the condition and venous lactate results within 1 hour; if lactate is 2 mmol/L or lower and no definitive condition is found, reassess and decide on antibiotics within 3 hours. Lactate over 2 means treating as high risk.

n.0: Waiting for a ward round misses the 1-hour review and 3-hour decision times.
n.1: Antibiotics within 1 hour and critical care referral are for high risk criteria with a raised lactate.
n.3: A normal lactate does not end assessment; the child still needs review and an antibiotic decision.

12.q: At a 6 to 8 week review, Kezia's mother says she has felt low and tearful most days for the past month and no longer enjoys things. Her baby is feeding and growing well. What should the health visitor do?
o: Advise her to rest more and ask her partner to do night feeds
Focus the review on the baby and suggest she mentions it to her GP if it continues
Reassure her that 'baby blues' are common and usually settle by 6 months
Explore her mood further, assess risk and arrange prompt assessment
12.w: Health visitors should routinely enquire about parents' physical and mental health at postnatal reviews (Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme 2026, using the NICE antenatal and postnatal mental health approach). Low mood and loss of interest for a month go beyond baby blues (which settle within about 2 weeks) and suggest possible postnatal depression, so further assessment, including risk, and prompt referral are needed (P2.6: early years and parental wellbeing).

n.0: Practical advice alone does not assess or treat possible depression.
n.1: Parental mental health is part of the review and affects the baby's development, so it should be addressed now.
n.2: Baby blues settle within the first couple of weeks; symptoms for a month need assessment, not reassurance.

12.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
12.q: Poppy, aged 2, has a fever of 38.7°C and is playing happily. Her mother asks whether she should give paracetamol and ibuprofen together to bring the temperature down. What is the best advice?
o: Give both alternately every 2 hours until her temperature is normal
Give one medicine if Poppy becomes distressed, not both together
Give paracetamol now to prevent a febrile seizure, even if she is happy
Give both together, as this brings the temperature down fastest
12.w: NICE NG143: consider paracetamol or ibuprofen if the child appears distressed, not solely to reduce body temperature. Do not give both at the same time; consider alternating only if distress persists or recurs before the next dose is due. Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures.

n.0: Alternating is considered only for persistent distress, and the aim is comfort, not a normal temperature.
n.2: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures and are not given for temperature in a happy child.
n.3: NG143 advises against giving both agents simultaneously.

12.q: Which entry in a patient's nursing notes best meets the Code's requirements for record keeping?
o: Pt fell again, prob drunk as usual. Dr aware, all fine, will watch. JL
Afternoon: patient found on floor but appears OK. Will monitor. Nurse
14:30 Patient on floor, probably slipped on wet floor, unhurt and settled
14:30 Found on floor by bed. Alert, uninjured. Dr Khan informed. J Lee, RN
12.w: Code 10.4: attribute entries to yourself, clearly written, dated and timed, without unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation; Code 10.2 record steps taken.

n.0: This includes speculation and judgemental language and lacks a time (Code 10.4).
n.1: No exact time, vague content and not attributed to a named person.
n.2: The cause is speculation, it is not attributed and no escalation is recorded.

12.q: A GP practice annual report states that on 1 April 2026, 850 of its 12,000 registered adults were living with diagnosed type 2 diabetes. A student nurse on placement asks what this figure measures. Which term is correct?
o: Prevalence
Relative risk
Life expectancy
Incidence
12.w: Faculty of Public Health, HealthKnowledge: prevalence is the total number of existing cases in a population at a point in time (point prevalence) or over a period; incidence counts new cases. NMC Standards of proficiency P2.2.

n.1: Relative risk compares the risk of an outcome between an exposed and an unexposed group.
n.2: Life expectancy estimates average years of life remaining and is unrelated to this count.
n.3: Incidence counts new cases over a period; this figure counts everyone currently living with the condition.

12.q: Ethan, 10, attends a day surgery unit with his stepfather, who has been married to Ethan's mother for four years and lives with them. There is no court order or formal agreement in place. The stepfather asks to sign the consent form for an elective hernia repair. What is the correct position?
o: He would first need to adopt Ethan to hold parental responsibility
He holds parental responsibility after living with Ethan for three years
He lacks parental responsibility without a section 4A agreement or court order
He holds parental responsibility because he is married to Ethan's mother
12.w: Under s4A of the Children Act 1989 a step-parent married to (or the civil partner of) a parent with PR can acquire parental responsibility by agreement with the parents who have PR or by court order. Marriage alone does not confer it.

n.0: Adoption would give PR, but it is not needed: a s4A agreement or order is sufficient.
n.1: A period of living together does not confer PR; an agreement or order is required.
n.3: Marriage to the mother does not give a step-parent PR automatically.

12.q: Ben, 13, was assessed as Gillick competent to consent to a plaster cast for a minor fracture last month. He is now being considered for spinal surgery with significant risks and a long recovery. His father asks whether the earlier assessment means Ben can consent to the spinal surgery. What should the nurse explain?
o: Competence for surgery is assessed by the father, who holds parental responsibility
The earlier assessment applies to all treatment until he turns 16
Competence for major surgery is presumed from the age of 13
Competence is decision-specific, so it must be assessed for this decision
12.w: Gillick competence is decision-specific: a child may be competent for a simple decision but not for a complex, higher-risk one. Ben's understanding of the spinal surgery, its risks, alternatives and consequences must be assessed afresh.

n.0: Competence is assessed by the clinician seeking consent, not by a parent.
n.1: A previous assessment for a simpler decision does not carry over to a more complex one.
n.2: There is no presumption of competence under 16; it must be demonstrated for each decision.

12.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
12.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

12.q: Freya, 10, has complex needs and a gastrostomy. Her school wants teaching assistants to give her feeds. According to NICE NG213, what should be in place before staff carry out this delegated clinical task?
o: Written consent from Freya's parents for each feed given
A registered nurse present in school for every feed
Parents attending school to give every feed themselves
Training and assessed competence for the staff giving feeds
12.w: NICE NG213 Disabled children and young people up to 25 with severe complex needs (2022, updated 2023): people carrying out delegated clinical tasks should be trained and assessed as competent, and the EHC plan should state who is responsible for providing support and the level of expertise needed (recs 1.4.11 and 1.15.24-1.15.25).

n.0: Per-feed written consent is not required; the agreed plan and competence of staff are what matter.
n.1: Delegated tasks are designed so trained, competent non-registered staff can carry them out.
n.2: Requiring parents to attend for every feed would restrict Freya's education and family life.

12.q: Reviewing the night's charts, Nurse Hana sees that a healthcare assistant recorded hourly observations for a patient who was off the ward in theatre for three of those hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Mention it informally to the healthcare assistant next week
Amend the entries herself so the chart is accurate
Leave it, as the patient has now returned safely
Escalate it to the nurse in charge straight away
12.w: Code 10.3: complete records without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to these requirements. Code 16.1 escalate concerns.

n.0: Falsified observations are a safety concern; Code 10.3 requires immediate action.
n.1: Altering another person's entries is itself inappropriate; the concern must be escalated.
n.2: The patient's safety now does not remove the falsification; it must be acted upon.

12.q: Lola, 6, weighs 21 kg and has type 1 diabetes. At home she is drowsy and cannot swallow safely; her glucose meter reads 2.2 mmol/L. Her mother has a glucagon kit and phones the community children's nurse. What dose of IM glucagon should be given?
o: 2 mg
500 micrograms
250 micrograms
1 mg
12.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.91: IM glucagon 500 micrograms for children under 8 years or under 25 kg; 1 mg if over 8 years or 25 kg or more. Seek medical help if no response within 10 minutes.

n.0: 2 mg exceeds every NG18 dose.
n.2: 250 micrograms is below the NG18 dose.
n.3: 1 mg is for children over 8 years or weighing 25 kg or more; Lola is 6 and 21 kg.

12.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
12.q: Ruby, aged 4, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She is quiet. Heart rate is 165 beats/min, capillary refill time 4 seconds, and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. A student says the normal blood pressure is reassuring. What is the best response?
o: Disagree, because low blood pressure is a late sign in children
Agree, because a normal blood pressure shows her circulation is coping
Disagree, because her breathing rate is a better guide than her pulse
Agree, but ask for the blood pressure to be rechecked in an hour
12.w: Children compensate for circulatory failure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so blood pressure stays normal until late; hypotension signals decompensation and risk of arrest (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill already indicate compensated shock needing urgent escalation.

n.1: Blood pressure is maintained in compensated shock, so a normal reading does not rule it out.
n.2: Breathing rate matters, but here her heart rate and capillary refill show compensated shock; no single sign outranks the others.
n.3: Waiting an hour delays treatment of compensated shock.

12.q: Stanley, 83, has a nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. The tube was confirmed in the stomach by X-ray yesterday and is secured at 60 cm at the nostril. He needs medicines, flushes and feeds today. Under NICE CG32, when must the tube position be confirmed?
o: Before the first feed of each day
When the person reports discomfort
After placement and before each use
After placement and then once a day
12.w: NICE CG32 rec 1.7.17: confirm the position of all nasogastric tubes after placement and before each use (each feed, flush or medicine) by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary.

n.0: A single check at the start misses later displacement from coughing, vomiting or movement.
n.1: Displacement may cause no symptoms, so checks cannot wait for discomfort.
n.3: Daily checks miss displacement between uses.

12.q: Bryony, 39, is nil by mouth after surgery. Her observations are stable and her prescription is for 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours via a volumetric infusion pump. The nurse is setting up the infusion and will ask a colleague to check it. At what rate should the pump be set?
o: 166 mL/h on the volumetric pump
125 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.5 mL/h on the volumetric pump
80 mL/h on the volumetric pump
12.w: Rate (mL/h) = volume / time = 1,000 mL / 8 h = 125 mL/h. Accurate dosage calculation is a patient safety proficiency (P4.14) and the setting should be checked against the prescription.

n.0: 166 mL/h corresponds to 6 hours, not 8.
n.2: 12.5 mL/h is a decimal place error, a tenfold underinfusion.
n.3: 80 mL/h would deliver 1,000 mL over 12.5 hours.

12.q: Ella, 9, tells a nurse that her 14-year-old cousin makes her touch him when he babysits. A colleague says that because both are children this is 'experimenting' and not abuse. Which response reflects Working Together 2026?
o: Treat it as experimentation and advise the parents to supervise
Wait for a second disclosure before deciding whether it is abuse
Refer it as child sexual abuse; both children may need help
Refer the 14-year-old to the police and take no action for Ella
12.w: Working Together 2026 recognises that child sexual abuse can be perpetrated by other children. A 14-year-old coercing a 9-year-old is harmful sexual behaviour and child sexual abuse; Ella needs protection and the older child also needs a safeguarding assessment.

n.0: The age and power gap and coercion make this abuse, not developmentally normal experimentation.
n.1: A single disclosure is enough to act; waiting leaves Ella at risk.
n.3: Ella is the victim and needs a safeguarding response; the police may be involved, but referral to children's social care is required.

12.q: Iris, 70, dies on a general ward. She was on the NHS Organ Donor Register as wanting to donate. Her husband asks the nurse whether her wish to donate can still be met now that she has died on the ward. Which response is accurate?
o: The ward nurse can remove the corneas before transfer to the mortuary
Donation is not possible because she did not die in intensive care
Organs can be retrieved from the ward if it is within 24 hours of death
Tissue such as corneas may still be donated, up to 24 hours after death
12.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): organ donation is possible only from intensive care units and emergency departments and is organised before death; whole-body and tissue donation is possible after death, and cornea donation can take place up to 24 hours after death in hospitals, hospices and funeral homes.

n.0: Ward nurses do not retrieve tissue; donation is arranged with the specialist donation service.
n.1: This is true for organs, but tissue donation, including corneas, remains possible after death.
n.2: Organ donation is organised before death from intensive care or emergency departments; it cannot be arranged after a ward death.

12.q: A urinal has been knocked over, spilling urine across the floor of a bay. The urine contains no visible blood. The nurse wears gloves and an apron. Which approach to managing this spill is correct?
o: Sprinkle chlorine-releasing granules directly on the urine
Pour 10,000 ppm chlorine solution directly on the urine first
Soak up with paper towels, then clean with 1,000 ppm chlorine
Leave it for the domestic team to clean at the next routine round
12.w: NIPCM appendix 9: do not use a chlorine-releasing agent directly on a urine spill (it can release chlorine gas). Soak up with disposable paper towels (a gelling agent may be used), then decontaminate with 1,000 ppm available chlorine or a combined detergent and chlorine product, then wash and dry.

n.0: Granules are for blood and high-risk body fluids; on urine they risk releasing chlorine gas.
n.1: Chlorine must not be applied directly to urine, and 10,000 ppm is the blood-spill strength.
n.3: Spills are treated immediately by trained staff, not left as a slip and infection hazard.

12.q: A school nurse must share information about Oliver, 9, with children's social care. Some of the information includes old, unverified allegations about his mother's past and labels such as 'chaotic family'. How should the nurse share in line with the s16LA guidance?
o: Withhold everything until each allegation has been verified
Share all historical material so the full picture is passed on
Share what is relevant, avoiding labels and untested allegations
Share the allegations, but remove Oliver's name from the report
12.w: The statutory guidance asks practitioners to consider relevance and to mitigate harm by limiting information, avoiding stigmatising language, identity labels, historical narrative and untested allegations unless strictly relevant to safeguarding the child.

n.0: Relevant safeguarding information should not be withheld pending verification.
n.1: Irrelevant historical material is not required and may cause harm.
n.3: Removing the child's name would stop the recipient acting to safeguard him.

12.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
12.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

12.q: Finn, 8 months, is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms orally. The stock is digoxin elixir 50 micrograms per mL. What volume should be given?
o: 0.8 mL
12.w: Volume = 62.5 micrograms / 50 micrograms per mL = 1.25 mL. Keep dose and stock in the same unit (micrograms) to avoid ten-fold and thousand-fold errors.

n.0: 0.125 mL is a ten-fold under-dose.
n.2: 0.8 mL comes from inverting the calculation (50 / 62.5).
n.3: 12.5 mL is a ten-fold overdose from a decimal slip.

12.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, has capacity and wants to return home after a fall. In a meeting her son says firmly that she must go to a care home and answers every question put to her. What is the most appropriate next step for the nurse?
o: Refer for a best interests meeting to settle the disagreement
Ask the son to put his concerns in writing for the discharge team
Speak with Mrs Lewis privately to explore her own views and wishes
Arrange a care home placement as her son holds strong views
12.w: NMC proficiency P1.9 requires decisions based on people's needs and preferences, recognising and addressing factors that may unduly influence them. Speaking with her alone lets her express her wishes freely (Code 2.3, 2.4, 4.1).

n.0: Best interests decisions apply when a person lacks capacity (MCA s4); Mrs Lewis has capacity, so the decision is hers.
n.1: This may record his concerns but leaves the undue influence unaddressed and does not establish what Mrs Lewis wants.
n.3: The son's views do not replace the decision of a person with capacity; Code 1.3 and P1.9 require decisions based on her needs and preferences.

12.q: Ronald, 80, is prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch, changed every 72 hours. The new patch is due today. His previous patch is on his upper left chest. What is the correct way to apply the new patch?
o: Apply the new patch to the same area once the old one has been removed
Remove the old patch and apply the new one to a different area of skin
Apply the new patch, then remove the old one at the next 72-hour change
Apply the new patch over the old one to maintain a steady dose
12.w: For transdermal patches the old patch is removed before the new one is applied, sites are rotated to reduce skin irritation, and the patch goes on clean, dry, hairless skin (AnnexB.11.8). Leaving an old fentanyl patch in place causes opioid toxicity.

n.0: Reusing the same site raises the risk of skin irritation and altered absorption.
n.2: Leaving the old patch for another 72 hours doubles the dose for that period.
n.3: Two patches at once would double the fentanyl dose and risk respiratory depression.

12.q: Ama, 68, has dark brown skin and is cared for in bed after a stroke. Over her heel you find an area that feels warmer and firmer than the surrounding skin, with a slightly purplish tone. It does not blanch with diascopy. What should you do?
o: Apply a dressing and recheck the area at the weekly skin review
Massage the area to stimulate blood flow and recheck it at the next shift
Record it as normal skin pigmentation and continue the current care plan
Start prevention and recheck her skin at least every 2 hours
12.w: NICE CG179: in darker skin tones non-blanching erythema may appear as colour change or discolouration, and warmth and firmness are additional signs. If non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention (including heel offloading) and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until it resolves.

n.0: Weekly review is far too infrequent; CG179 sets at least 2-hourly checks until resolved.
n.1: Massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179.
n.2: Dismissing changes as pigmentation misses early pressure damage in darker skin.

12.q: A nurse researcher wants to understand what living with a new stoma is like for young adults, in their own words. Which research approach is most suitable?
o: A qualitative design using in-depth interviews
A randomised controlled trial of stoma care products
A retrospective audit of stoma complication rates
A cross-sectional survey using closed questions
12.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022) recognises qualitative research approaches; interviews explore meaning and experience. Proficiency P1.7: understand research methods to critically analyse findings.

n.1: An RCT compares interventions; it does not explore lived experience.
n.2: An audit measures practice against a standard, not personal experience.
n.3: Closed questions limit responses and do not capture experience in people's own words.

12.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
12.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

12.q: Mr Booth, 58, has type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide. Before lunch he is sweaty and shaky but alert and able to swallow. His capillary blood glucose is 3.3 mmol/L. What should the nurse do first?
o: Withhold his gliclazide and recheck at the next meal
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give his lunch now and recheck the glucose in 1 hour
Give 15-20 g of glucose tablets by mouth and recheck
12.w: RCUK First aid guidelines 2025: treat hypoglycaemia when capillary glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L; if awake and able to swallow give 15-20 g glucose or dextrose tablets by mouth, repeat the measurement after treatment (repeat treatment if no improvement after 15 minutes), then give a snack once recovered.

n.0: Medication review may follow, but the low glucose needs treating now.
n.1: He is alert and can swallow; 999 and the recovery position are for an unresponsive person.
n.2: A meal acts too slowly; quick-acting glucose is needed first, then a longer-acting snack.

12.q: Beryl, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score to decide whether she needs falls prevention. What does NICE NG249 (2025) recommend?
o: Offer an assessment if she falls again on the ward
Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and plan
Complete the prediction tool and act on a high score
Use the prediction tool weekly to monitor her risk
12.w: NICE NG249 (2025): do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Offer all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over (or 50-64 at higher risk) a comprehensive, multifactorial falls assessment and management plan.

n.0: She already qualifies for assessment as an inpatient aged 65 or over.
n.2: NG249 advises against using prediction tools to identify risk.
n.3: Repeating a prediction tool does not make it a valid basis for care.

12.q: A unit of red cells for Hannah, 55, was removed from the blood fridge at 10:00. The transfusion was delayed while her cannula was resited and started at 10:40. By what time must the unit be completed?
o: By 14:00, 4 hours after leaving storage
By 13:00, 3 hours after leaving storage
By 14:40, 4 hours after the start
By 12:00, 2 hours after leaving storage
12.w: BSH (2017): red cells should be transfused within 4 hours of leaving temperature-controlled storage, to limit bacterial growth. The clock starts when the unit leaves the fridge, not when the infusion starts.

n.1: 3 hours is not the BSH limit; the standard is 4 hours from leaving storage.
n.2: Timing runs from removal from storage, so 14:40 is 40 minutes too late.
n.3: 2 hours is shorter than the BSH limit for red cells.
